title: Bronx: 156th Street (East) - Beck Street
text:
(1) East 156th Street, south side, between Beck and Fox Streets, showing the White Mansion and part of the estate. It was formerly located (1868 map) between Southern Boulevard and Leggett Lane slightly north of their junction. Randall Comfort states that the spot in the foreground marks the site of an old Revolutionary cave in which the remains of Americansoldiers were found. The G.W. Bromley map of 1923 as revised to September 1932, shows the site to be occupied by a 2-story brick building known as the Martinque Club. The aforementioned location refers to the exact site of the mansion. 1900. Gift of Randall Comfort.

(2) The same, as viewed from a different angle, showing the side and rear of the mansion. Comfort states that the summer house (right foreground) stands on a boulder said to mark the grave of an old Indian chief. 1898. Gift of Randall Comfort.

(3) A front view of the mansion at a later date. It was the home of the Unity Club of the Bronx at the date of this photograph. 1915.

It runs parallel to West 230th Street, the distance of one block from the foot of Corlear Ave. to the foot of Tibbet Ave. (where automobile house is located). WAVE HILL 675 West 252nd Street, Riverdale, Bronx. Built in late Federal style for William Lewis Morris about 1830, this three-story country house of local fieldstone has a decidedly English atmosphere. Among Wave Hill's famous residents were Theodore Roosevelt, Mark Twain and Arturo Toscanini. Guests in the house have included Thackeray, Herbert Spencer, Thomas Huxley and Queen Mother Elizabeth.

FONTHILL CASTLE  Mount St. Vincent-on-Hudson, Riverdale, Bronx. Built for Edwin Forrest, the tragedian, by Thomas L. Smith in 1849, this house has both Norman and Gothic elements. Inspired by Fonthill Abbey in England, loopholes and buttresses give the structure the appearance of a fortified castle. The highest of its grey granite octagonal towers rises to 70 feet. It now serves as the library of the College of Mount St. Vincent.

title: Bronx: Boston Road - 166th Street
text: 13 - PUDDING ROCK, formerly on Boston Road and 166th Street. A truly immense glacial bowlder, rising 25 feet in the air, and being 30 feet in diameter. On one side was a natural fire-place, where the Indians used to enjoy their corn feasts and oyster banquets. Under its cool shade, the Huguenots rested on their long Sabbath Day journeys from New Rochelle down to the old French Protestant Church in lower New York. After serving as a natural landmark to early settlers and to travelers in stage coaches enroute from New York to Boston, it has finally been blasted into countless fragments so as no longer to "obstruct the march of civilization."

title: Bronx: Bronx Park - Indian Well.

title: Bronx: Bronx Park - Rocking Stone.
text:
9 -ROCKING STONE, Bronx Park. Another "Glacial Waif," left stranded by the masses of ice during the Glacial Epoch. Not wishing to have this great boulder in the way of his farm yard, an early owner tried to have it dragged away, but twelve yoke of sturdy Westchester County oxen failed to move it an inch. Yet it is so nicely balanced on a rocky drift that the pressure of a strong finger will easily set it swaying
back and forth.

title: Bronx: Bronx Park - Delancey Pine.
text:
2 - DE LANCEY PINE, Bronx Park, Bronx Borough. Rises 150 feet from the ground, and is near the site of the old De Lancey Mansion of Revolutionary Fame, the rendezvous of the British officers. In the branches of this great tree the Americah sharpshooters used to climb, and from this well concealed place of vantage would pick off the Red Coats stationed at the De Lancey Block House just across the Bronx River.

"Memorial of the fallen great,
The rich and honored Pine;
Stands high in solitary state,
De Lancey's Ancient Pine."

This tree measures 11 feet, 5 inches in circumference, 3 feet from base.

title: Bronx: Bronxdale Avenue - Van Nest Avenue
text:
Bronxdale Ave. (running from right to left in front of park), south from Van Nest Ave. (right) to Sackett Ave., showing a general view, in a westerly direction, of the surrounding area as seen from the lower end of the Morris Park Race Track. In the center are the repair shops and extensive freight yards of the New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad, extending west to the Unionport Road bridge over the tracks. Directly east of the bridge is visible the railroad's Van Nest station. The old Morris Park station was located on the empty lot directly in front of the repair shops and to the right of the store house seen under construction. The New Morris Park depot is situated on Sackett Ave., at Paulding Ave.

About 1910.

title: Bronx: Bryant Avenue - Westchester Avenue
text:
Bryant Ave., West side, from Westchester Ave. to East 167th Street, showing the Hunt Inn which was erected in 1660. It stood in rear of the Foxhurst Mansion on the grounds bounded by the triangle of Westchester Ave., West Farms Road and East 167th Street. It was a prominent rendezvous of British officers during the American War for Independence. The inn was razed between 1900 and 1923 (according to d.W. Bromley maps) and its site is now (1937) occupied by a 6-story apartment house. 1890.
Gift of Randall Comfort.

title: Bronx: City Island Avenue - Belden Street
text:
City Island Ave. (City Island), north from Belden Street, showing the Horton Homestead, bearing No. 26, at the N.E. corner of Belden Street. The house was turned around in about 1908 when the avenue was widened so that the front of the house faces on the avenue and is on a level with it; the stairs having been eliminated. It is about one hundred and fifty years old and is the oldest on the island. At this writing (1937) there are two 1-story frame wings added to it, and together comprise the Duryea Restaurant, named after its present owner.

Gift of Randall Comfort.

title: Bronx: Dupont Street - Leggett Avenue
text:
Dupont Street, south (about 100 yards) of the S.W. corner of Leggett Ave., showing the Casanova Mansion (also known as the Whitlock Mansion). It was built in 1859 and was, in its day, one of the most magnificent private residences in the United States. The mansion bears its name from Innocencio Casanova, a Cuban who bought the house after the death of  Benjamin Whitlock. The ediface was razed between 1900 and 1911 (G.W. Bromley maps) and its site is still unoccupied (1932) even though the surrounding area has become a factory district. For Additional data see The Story of the Bronx by Jenkins, page 388.

Gift of Randall Comfort.

title: Bronx: Findlay Avenue - 167th Street (East)
text:
(1)
Findlay Ave., east side, between East 167th and East 168th Streets, showing the William E. Morris Mansion and a small stone building, said to have been a school house. The Mansion was built in 1816. A frequent visitor, here, was Jefferson Davis, President of the Confederacy. The Mansion and school have been demolished and on their site now (1938)
stands the Home of the Daughters of Jacob.
Gift of Samuel Landsman  1916.
(2)
Another front view of the mansion, facing south.
Gift of Samuel Landsman  1916.
(3)
A full view of the school house and the rear of the house (right).
The school house is east of the house.
Gift of Samuel Landsman  1916.
(4)
An exclusive view of the school house. In the left background is visible part of the rear of Public School No. 53 facing on East
168th Street.
Gift of Samuel Landsman    1916.
Additonal Note:
Mr. Landsman states that the house is near the site of an older house built in 1795 by Jas. Morris. He also states that in the rear of the house, on the easterly end of the lintel over the first-story
window, were inscribed the initi1s J.M.- 1816.

title: Bronx: Grand Concourse and Tremont Ave.
text:
Grand Concourse, The Bronx
Typical rows of apartment houses in Bronx Borough.
In older Manhattan multi-family units were known generally as tenements or flats; but when the Bronx began to decelope-with the opening of the first subway transit system 20 years ago- there appeared the modern apartment house. Before the subway came, the Bronx had 250,000 population; now 20 years later it has nearly 900,000.
1924  Kadel & Herbert

Grand Concourse, south from East 161st Street, showing (right) Franz Sigel Park extending to East 153rd Street. On the left appears Sheridan Ave. and the Melrose yard of the New York Central Railroad which is spanned by the East 153rd Street bridge. Note, under construction, on the block bounded by East 159th and 158th Streets, the large 6-story Thomas Garden Apartments, and south of it, the rectangular Fleischmann Company laboratory. Also shown is a panoramic view southward with the Hell Gate Bridge across the East River visible in the distant left background, and Manhattan discernible in the right background. title: Bronx: Grand Concourse - 168th Street
text:
A Palace Home for Millionaire Bankrupts.

Suppose you had once been rich. Suppose you had lived in luxury and mingled in exclusive social circles. And suppose you lost every dollar you had. If you had lived in New York or other big city, if you had been banker, judge, or even idle social panderer, you would still be able to live as you had formerly. For Andrew Freedman, multi-millionaire, died and left $4,000,000 for the building and furnishing of a palace on the Grand Concourse, New York City, where those once rich could enjoy the luxuries of life even though broke. The conditions are that you must be 60 or more, be cultured, and be absolutely "broke." Applicants are put through the most rigorous questionnaire and their stories carefully checked. Out of thousands of applications but thirty have taken in. The mansion covers an entire city block. Furnishings were collected and placed by most expert interior decorators. Every convenience of a millionaire's home is there. And it constitutes one of the most astounding heritages ever left.

United Newspictures, Inc., 461 Eighth Ave., N.Y.C.

title: Bronx: Hollywood Avenue - Schurz Avenue
text:
Hollywood Avenue, east side, between Schurz Avenue and the East River, directly within the grounds of the Silver Beach private real estate development, showing the Robert House. It was built by the founder of Robert College, Constantinople. It is now (1937) known as the Cooper House, after James Fenimore Cooper, the renowned author, who lived and worked here on some of his books. The house is still inhabited and is said, by its present owner, to be about 170 years old.
1906
Gift of Randall Comfort

title: Bronx: Morris Park Race Track.
text:
Morris Park Race Track (Bronx): North across the western edge of the famous race track, showing it after it was ordered closed by the State Banking Commission and dismantled. On the extreme left is Bronxville Avenue and in the center, running from right to left, is Morris Park Avenue under construction.

Bronxdale Ave.

title: Bronx: Morris Park Race Track.
text:
Morris Park Race Track(Bronx): A view northeastward across the race track after its dismantlement. The famous fashionable race track was abandoned as a result of faulty financial manipulations by its owners and was ordered to be publicly sold by the State Banking Commission. Joseph P.Day and J. Clarence Davies were the sales promoters who auctioned off the land in 1913. In the left foreground is part of the concrete base which supported the grand stand. In the center, with telephone poles thereon, is Morris Park Avenue.

1913

title: Bronx: Morris Park Race Track.
text: Morris Park Race Track (Bronx): Viewing east across the south end of the famous race track from the grand stand near Bronxdale Avenue. When the track was ordered closed by the State Banking Commission, streets were laid out and the property auctioned off in 1913. The bend of the race course is clearly visible as well as the outlines of new north-south avenues.

title: Bronx: Pelham Bay Park - Glover's Rock.
text:
7 - GLOVER'S ROCK, Pelham Bay Park. The tablet on this immense boulder tells the story:
"In Memory of the 550 Patriots, who, led by Colonel John Glover, held General Howe's army in check at the Battle of Pell's Point, October 18, 1776, thus aiding General Washington in his retreat to White Plains." After passing Glover's Rock with his army, Howe lunched under the branches of the Lord Howe Chestnut, already described, No.4.

title: Bronx: Poe Park.
text:
EDGAR ALLAN POE.
(Died Oct. 7, 1849.)
Hear the tolling of the bells—
Death bells!
What a strain of tragedy! Eider harsh instance knelling!
"He is dead!" rings seem to say,
"And Poe rests endless clay in
Is forgotten.

Is forgotten; in forgotten ere it's cold.
He is dead, dead, dead!
And there's none will shed a tear.

Never fear!
There are none with a tear.

Oh, the bells, bells, bells!
How each one seems awash with predication.
Every echo and vibration,
With a broken culmination,
Seems to hover in the air.
Seems to hover everywhere,
Seems in derision.

"He is dead, dead, dead!" sing the
bells.
Foolish bells, lying bells:
Hear the pealing of the bells—
Joyous bells!

What a tale of ecstasy their haunting
tells:
"He is gone!" So they seem to say,
"House seem to sing.

'Tis man we celebrate today.
"He is long years dead, ye cry? Cause your clatter, fine people.
Sing a the only thing steeple.
It is only fools that die!

Every echo seems to call him.
The man we celebrate today

And the grave deepens ever deeper. Hear the peal ever deeper, as it penetrates the tomb.

As it filters through the gloom And his spirit wraps the spirit of his
bride.

"I am his bride!
Young she died!
And his broken heart was buried at her
side.

So, together in the silence of the tomb, They lie, side by side, in that narrow, narrow
room.

Hear the bells, the bells, the bells, To the jibes, mocking laughter of the
bells.

VILDA SAUVAGE OWENS.

title: Bronx: Sacket Avenue - Colden Avenue
text:
Socket Ave. (left, on which railway depot is located), north from Colden Ave., showing the Morris Park station of the New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad. According to Bromley's map of 1900, an old Morris Park station was situated at what is now (1937) a plot adjoining the S.W. corner of Bronxdale and Van Nest Aves., near the railroad's present workshops. It was a frame depot at the very gate of the famous Morris Park Race Track. It was dismantled between 1900 and 1913 (Bromley maps) during which period many streets were laid out on the former track grounds and surrounding properties. The station here shown, was opened to passenger traffic in 1913 even though it had been completed for some time prior to that date.

1913.

title: Bronx: Soundview Avenue - Lafayette Avenue
text:
Soundview Avenue, west side, south of Lafayette Avenue, showing the Clason Point Military Academy. The view is northward with the school and chapel appearing on the right. In the center is the old Dominick Lynch Mansion, a stone structure. In this house was celebrated the first mass in Westchester County and the committee to design the American flag met here before proceeding to Philadelphia. The land in this area was owned by Lynch in 1793, part of which was sold, in the same year, to Issac Classon, whence the name is derived. In 1870 the mansion was bought by the Christian Brothers of the Catholic Faith, who changed it into the Sacred Heart Academy in 1883. It later became part of the Clason Point Military Academy.

June, 1926

Brown Brothers

text:
Active Atheism

These huge caricatures of the Church & Czarism, made by New York Communists, are like those constantly used in Russian antireligious propaganda.

These grotesque figures may have meant a great deal to real grown- up r e d s at meeting in Starlight Park, th Bronx, in New York City, March 16th, 1930, but they were just amusing toys to the youngsters gathered about them. The figure at left represents the Church - (Rasputin, the Black Monk) and at right is Imperialism in figure of Nicholas - Czar of all the Russians.

text:
Van Cortlandt Park: A view of the cairn of stones on Indian Field. The cairn is situated on the west side of Van Cortlandt Park East, at the head of West 237th Street and is dedicated to the Stockbridge Indians. The inscription of the tablet reads:

August 31, 1778.
Upon this field
Chief Nimham
And seventeen Stockbridge Indians
As Allies of the Patriots,
Gave their lives for Liberty.

Erected by Bronx Chapter,
Daughters of the American Revolution
Mount Vernon, N.Y.

title: Bronx: Van Cortlandt Park - Van Cortlandt Mansion.
text:
VAN CORTLANDT MANSION  Van Cortlandt Park, Bronx. Built in 1784 by Frederick Van Cortlandt, this Georgian mansion was visited by General Washington during the Revolutionary War. The ample stone house has an unpretentious exterior that contrasts strongly with the rich Georgian interior. The estate was held continuously by the Van Cortlandt family until 1889, when it was purchased by the city for a park.

title: Bronx: Kingsbridge Road (We - Heath Avenue
text:
W. Kingsbridge Road, south from Heath Avenue, up "Breakneck Hill" toward Sedgwick Avenue. Mr. Randall Comfort, historian of the Bronx, states that it is an old lane at Kingsbridge, which was part of a colonial highway that led up from Spuyten Duyvil Creek across the steep "Breakneck Hill" to Fordham and West Farms. It follows the course of the old King's Bridge Road which led from Manhattan over King's Bridge (now 230th Street at Kingsbridge Avenue), and another branch of which led over Farmer's Bridge (now W. Kingsbridge Road, directly west of Exterior Street) across the entire breadth of the Bronx, through Fordham and West Farms, then across the Bronx River at E. 180th Street, into Westchester County. King's Bridge Road, in older times, was the Boston Post Road, and it is possible that this is part of the road along which Mrs. Knight, mentioned in Wells's history of the Bronx (p. 315), traveled.

1906.

Gift of Randall Comfort.

title: Bronx: Westchester Avenue - Ward Avenue

title: Bronx: Westchester Avenue - Boynton Avenue
text:
Westchester Avenue (foreground), north side, from Boynton Avenue (right) to Wheeler Avenue, showing the second part of a panoramic view of the extensive Watson estate. In the center of the view, among the trees, appears the Watson Mansion, a sumptuous stone edifice. The view shows the land being leveled out for the laying out of thoroughfares and for future real estate development. Several apartment houses and store buildings were later erected on this section of the avenue. The road on the extreme left of the view is the former Watson's Lane, which led past the mansion and up toward West Farms Road. It is now (1939) Wheeler Avenue.

About 1910

title: Bronx: Westchester Avenue - Boynton Avenue
text:
Westchester Avenue (foreground), north side, from Boynton Avenue (right) to Wheeler Avenue, showing part 2 of a panoramic view of the Watson estate. On the right, in front of which Boynton Avenue was later laid out, is the sumptuous Watson Mansion. The estate is being leveled out for the laying of public thoroughfares and future residential development. The dirt road on the left is the former Watsons Lane, which led up past the mansion toward West Farms Road. It later became Wheeler Avenue. This is mount 2B and shows the same section of the estate seen on mount 2A, taken several months later.

About 1910

title: Bronx: Westchester Avenue - Wheeler Avenue
text:

Viewing from right to left can be seen the beds of Evergreen and Colgate Avenues. Shown, too, are the tracks of the New Haven Railroad and the sloping area lying on the right bank of the Bronx River. Many two-story brick dwellings were later constructed in this area.

About 1910

title: Bronx: Westchester Avenue - Wheeler Avenue

title: Bronx: Westchester Avenue - Hobart Avenue
text:
Westchester Ave., west side, between Hobart and Morris Park Aves., showing the "Spy Oak". It is said to be the largest of its kind east of the Rocky Mountains and the last remaining vestige of the vast primeval forest that once covered this entire area. History tells us that during the American Revolution, a British spy, captured in this neighborhood, was summarily hanged from one of its branches, hence its name.

June 1926.

title: Brooklyn: 18th Avenue - 83rd Street
text:
(1) Eighteenth Ave., east side, at the N.E. corner of 83rd Street; showing the New Utrecht Dutch Reformed Church, built in 1828, on site of the old New Utrecht schoolhouse, dedicated in 1829. The church was organized in 1677 in the schoolhouse. The services were held in private dwellings. A Church was erected in the Dutch burying ground, in 1700, at what is now the N.E. corner of Sixteenth Ave., and 84th Street. A local minister was installed in 1809.

title: Brooklyn: 18th Avenue - 84th Street
text:
Eighteenth Ave., west side, between 85th and 84th Streets. At the left, is seen the West End line of the B.M.T., on New Utrecht Ave. At the right, is the Gunther Railway line and private right of way. It was built in 1863, by C. Godfrey Gunther Fur merchant and Mayor of the City of New York. It ran from 25th Street and Fifth Ave., (Brooklyn), to Coney Island. It was also known as the Brooklyn Bath and Coney Island R.R. It is now operated by a trolley Company. At the left, in the triangle, once stood the foundry of Michael Feigel, builder of street and railroad Cars.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: 21st Street (East) - Caton Avenue
text:
112 East 21st Street, adjoining the S. W. corner of Caton Ave., showing the Clarkson Mansion, built in 1836. Early in its history the house was purchased by a group of prominent Flatbush men who formed the Midwood Club and so named the mansion. Later the Midwood Club was purchased by leaders of the Brooklyn Union League Club who made it their headquarters for a time. From 1927 to 1940 the house was the headquarters of the Flatbush branch of the Y. M. C. A. and was known as the Sperry Memorial Building. On January 21, 1940, a fire wrecked the structure and toward the end of the year, or early 1941, was torn down to make way for an apartment house. For additional data see "The New York Times," October 6, 1940.

1927
Views 1,2,3

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Brooklyn: 36th Street - 6th Avenue
text:
36th Street (foreground not seen) at Sixth Ave., showing the Brooklyn Rapid Transit terminal yards. At the extreme left on the top of the hill is No. 456-466 39th Street, at the N.W. corner of Seventh Ave. The "Old Road to Flatbush", and Gowanus Road extending north and south met in the foreground just north of 36th Street near Sixth Ave. The Gunther line to Coney Island extended east and southeast skirting the east side of Greenwood Cemetery, parallel to the freight line, upon which are seen the freight cars. This land was once known as Popes Park.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: 41st Street - 3rd Avenue
text:
41st Street (right) west of Third Ave., Also shown is Second Ave. (center of view) between 42nd Street (left) and 41st Street (right). In the foreground will be erected a two story building for the Shipley Construction and Supply Company. At the foot of 41st Street is Pier No. 7; and at the center right, sectionally shown, are several Bush Terminal Buildings. In the background, steepled, is the National Meter Co. Building formerly the National Metal Co. This is a set of two views.

1919.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: 55th Street (East) - Beverly Road
text:
(1)
East 55th Street, east side, between Beverly and Clarendon Roads, showing District School No. 2, also known as Flatlands Neck School. This structure was built in 1835 or 1837, to replace a smaller school house built in 1786. The older building had originally been standing a little further back, and was moved to the new site given by a member of the Lott Family, who needed the old site for building purposes. The building was razed in 1926, because the site was required for the widening of Kings Highway which cuts diagonally across East 55th Street at this point.
March 1923.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Brooklyn: 63rd Street (East) - Avenue U
text:
(1)
East 63rd Street, east side, between Ave. U, and Strickland Ave., showing the Schenck-Crooke house, which was also known as the Jan Martense Schenck house. The land was at one time known as Mill Island; probably named because of a mill that was built by Elbert Elbertsen Stoothoff about 1664. He sold in 1675 (not 1657) a half interest in the mill and island to Jan Martense Schenck. Bergen states: "The Schenck family built the house", and he gave the purchase year as 1657; hence, it is believed that the house was built about that year. If the Schencks built the house, it would date after 1675. Jan Martense evidently acquired title to the entire island, and mill as he devised both to his son Martin Janse Schenck by his will of 1688 9. This property was sold in 1785 by the heirs of John Schenck to Mrs. Susan Caton, a daughter of Joris Martense. Margaret, a daughter of Mrs. Susan Caton married general Philip Crooke. This mill became known as Crooke's mill and was demolished prior to 1881. The house still stands in 1929.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2)
A view of the front of the house.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3)
The same, showing the rear, viewed westward.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(4)
The same, viewed northwestward.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Atlantic Avenue - Clinton Street
text:
Atlantic Ave., at the N.E. corner of Clinton Street showing the Brooklyn Athenaeum designed by William Field and erected at a cost of $60,000. The first floor was for commercial enterprises; the second for reading and for private rooms, the third floor had a concert hall capable of seating 2000 people. It gave the first Italian Opera in 1858. The Philharmonic Society held its first concert here. The Reading Room was opened to the public on May 7, 1858. The Mercantile Library was here but later moved to Montague Street. John Homsey purchased it in 1922.  In 1929 it housed the Court of Special Sessions.
1922.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Bay Avenue - Kings Highway
text:
(1)
Bay Ave., north of King's Highway. The street in the foreground is Ryder Ave., a continuation of Bay Ave. Both of these streets are non existent in 1929. The house in the background is 1515 Mansfield (East 24th Street), in 1929. The house in the foreground if standing in 1929, would be at the N.W. corner of Bedford Ave. and King's Highway. This house was the property of one Wyckoff in 1857? and later of the C. Bennett Estate?. It definately [sic] belonged in 1873 to W. Convel and at a later date, to B.G. Hitchings, being known then, as "The Club House." From fore to background, those two houses occupied lots 142 and 144 in the Town of South Greenfield, according to Map No. 444 issued in 1854.
1922.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2)
The same, which was also known as the "Senate House" in 1860.
April 1923.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3)
The same, a view southward.
April 1923.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(4)
The same, showing the steel structure of a building that will shortly be a 6-story apartment building known as "Congress Arms."
August 1924.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Bradford Street - Fulton Street
text:
109 Bradford Street, east side, between Fulton Street and Atlantic Ave., showing the New Lots Town Hall. In 1937 it is the Bradford Street Hospital. The plot (100 x 50 feet), was purchased from Horace A. Miller for $1400 and the Town Hall was opened on December 11, 1873. The police station occupied the ground floor; the basement was used as a prison. After 1886 it served solely as a station house. On November 13, 1899 the present hospital was opened as the 26th Ward Homeopathic Hospital and Dispensary.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

It was formally opened on July 4, 1864. The small house next to the Hall was a school in 1873, but was subsequently converted into a court house.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Brighton Beach Avenue - 4th Street (East)
text:
(1) Brighton Beach Ave., south side, East 4th Street and Coney Island Ave showing the Brighton Beach Hotel, which was built by the Brighton Beach Co., in 1878, and opened for business the same year. The work was started on March 20, 1878. When this hotel was first erected it was 600 feet from high water, but in 1888 the Atlantic had undermined the foundations necessitating the placing of the hotel upon piles. However, on April 3, 1888 it was moved inland 500 feet by B.C. Miller and sons who contracted the work. The hotel was razed in 1924. The owners or lessees of this hotel were Breslin and Sweet 1879, Leland 1883, Cunningham and Hatfield 1888, and E. Clark King 1902-1909.

December 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2) The same, viewed eastward.

December 1923.

title: Brooklyn: Brighton Beach Avenue - Mayo Street
text:
(1) Brighton Beach Ave., north side, east of Mayo Street, showing a former Long Island R.R. station at Manhattan Beach, which ceased to be used as such, prior to 1929. This railroad was built by Austin Corbin in 1876-1877 and operated from the foot of West End Ave., Manhattan Beach, to Baldwin's Hotel in East New York. It was later extended to the foot of Quay Street, Greenpoint, and connected with New York at the 10th and 23rd Street ferries. Trains ran there first on April 9, 1878, but were diverted to Hunter's Point, a branch line built from Prospect Park in 1878. In 1880, the trains ran directly from Atlantic Ave. Station.

December 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster.

(2) The same, showing the platform fallen in decay. Note also an abandoned freight car between the two buildings. At the left is seen the Manhattan Beach Hotel at Nos. 156-158 West End Ave., and also Nos. 5961-5963 Brighton Beach Ave.

December 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3) The same, looking southward.

December 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(4) The same, looking north.

December 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

This railroad was built by Austin Corbin in 1876-1877 and operated from the foot of West End Ave., Manhattan Beach, to Baldwin's Hotel in East New York. It was later extended to the foot of Quay Street, Greenpoint, and connected with New York at the 10th and 23rd Street ferries. Trains ran there first on April 9, 1878, but were diverted to Hunter's Point, a branch line built from Prospect Park in 1878. In 1880, the trains ran directly from Atlantic Ave. Station.

December 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster.

(2) The same, showing the platform fallen in decay. Note also an abandoned freight car between the two buildings. At the left is seen the Manhattan Beach Hotel at Nos. 156-158 West End Ave., and also Nos. 5961-5963 Brighton Beach Ave.

December 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3) The same, looking southward.

December 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(4) The same, looking north.

December 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Broadway - Halsey Street
text:
Broadway, east side, south from Halsey Street. (In 1871 Paul W. Ledoux, a Canadian who resided in New York City, bought a lot of land bounded by Broadway, Bushwick ave., and Eldert and Halsey Streets, on which 13 stores and several dwellings were erected. In 1891, he refused $100,000 for a 200 feet frontage on Broadway. In 1905 he sold 180' X 100' on Broadway for $225,000. He, among others, was instrumental in having the Halsey Street trolley line extended). Overhead is a portion of the Broadway line of the Brooklyn Elevated system.

July 1924.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Bushwick Avenue - Powers Street
text:
(1)
85 Bushwick Ave., east side, between Powers and Grand Streets, showing the home of Martin Kalbfleisch, who was born on February 8, 1804 at Flushing, Holland.  He entered the United States in 1826 and built this house in 1864.  It was sold in 1916 by the Fleet family to the St. Catherine's R.C. Hospital, and used as a nurse's home.  Martin Kelbfleisch was Mayor of Brooklyn from 1861-1863 and 1868-1871.  The house was demolished in September 1930.
1922.

title: Brooklyn: Clarendon Road - 59th Street (East)
text:
(1)  Clarendon Road, south side, (formerly known as Canarsie Lane, at this point), between East 59th Street and Ralph Ave., showing the S.W. view of the Pieter Claesen Wyckoff Farmhouse, built in 1664.  The south side of the house is covered with the original shingles. In 1890 the original roof was replaced by a tin roof.  This house was originally occupied by Pieter Claesen Wyckoff and subsequently by his son Claes, followed by Claes' son Peter in 1719.  In 1860 it was occupied by John A. Wyckoff; in 1873 by John W. Wyckoff and in 1901, the heirs of John A. Wyckoff sold it to Francis Gross.

March 1924.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2) The same, in 1923.

1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

The house was occupied by John Lott in 1794, by Albert Terhune Lott, between 1860 and 1873, and sold and vacated by the Lott family about 1903. In an upper room were found the Terhune family papers. text: 340 Clarkson Ave., at the S.W. corner of East 34th Street, showing the J. B. O'Connor House, which was originally the Old Tavern and station of the Manhattan Beach Narrow Guage (steam) railroad, which ran from City Line, at the S.E. corner of Flatbush Ave., and Malbone Street, easterly through Malbone Street and Lefferts ave., to the "poorhouse road", which lay between the County Buildings. This line was promoted by Dr. Daly of the old City Hospital about 1877, and about 50 years ago, it was bought by the Brighton Line and discontinued. (Malbone Street, is now called Empire Blvd). 1922. title: Brooklyn: Clarkson Avenue - Brooklyn Avenue
text:
451 Clarkson Ave., north side, near Brooklyn Ave., showing the residence of the General Medical Superintendent of the Dept., of Public Welfare. Until 1824, each town in Kings County had cared for its own poor, but on November 27, 1824, the Board of Supervisors were empowered by an act of the legislature, to purchase land for a county farm for the poor. The poorhouse at Brooklyn, was leased, until a building was erected. In 1832, the inmates were removed from Brooklyn to Flatbush.

text:
(1) Clinton Street, east side, at and south of Pierrepont Street. Also shown is Pierrepont Street, south side, east of Clinton Street. title: Brooklyn: Clinton Street - Montague Street
text:
(1) Clinton Street, at the N. W. corner of Montague Street, showing the Holy Trinity Protestant Episcopal Church. The foundation for this edifice, of which Edgar John Bart was the builder, was begun in August 1844. The chapel opened for services on June 7, 1846, and the church on April 25, 1847. The steeple, which was erected in 1860, was removed in 1906. Two buildings (not in this view) at Nos. 122-124 Pierrepont Street were given to the parish by George Foster Peabody in 1905 and 1912, to be used as a guildhouse and parish house. The rectory was purchased in 1897, and is at No. 126 Pierrepont Street. The church proper cost $175,000; the spire 275 feet in height, cost an additional $65,000. Minard Lefevre was the architect. About 1906 Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2) The Montague Street side of the church, viewing eastward. The 3 ½ story building on the extreme left is the Trinity Club. March 1, 1929 P. L. Sperr

(3) Another view of the church, viewing northwestward across the roof of the Brooklyn Trust Company building (right foreground). March 1, 1929 P. L. Sperr

title: Brooklyn: Cortelyou Road - Canarsie Avenue
text:
Cortelyou Road, (Canarsie Lane), at the N.E. corner of Canarsie Ave. (Old Clove Road), showing Guard house of the Holy Cross Cemetery. This cemetery, named Galilee, was also referred to as the "Cemetery of the Catholic's". Bishop John H. Hughes acquired in June 1849, 17 acres of land from James Duffy. This land was once a section of the Van Brunt farm. In 1857, another 19 acres were purchased from the heirs of Adrian Vanderveer. In 1869, another 22 acres were purchased from Lefferts Cornell. The first body interred, July 14, 1849, was that of Thomas Moran, the first victim of the cholera in Flatbush.

May 12, 1922.

title: Brooklyn: Court Street - Montague Street
text:
A general view west from the Temple Bar Building located at the S.W. corner of Court and Montague Streets, showing the Brooklyn Heights section of Brooklyn between Remsen Street (extreme left) and Fulton Street (extreme rights). In the foreground is the Episcopal Church of the Holy Trinity at the N.W. corner of Montague and Clinton Streets. At the left background is the Hotel Bossert at the S.E. corner of Montague and Hicks Streets. Also shown is the Manhattan skyline and at the right a part of the Brooklyn Bridge. Note the junction of the East and North Rivers with Upper New York Bay. The New Jersey skyline vaguely appears in the left background.

1926.
Brown Brothers.

title: Brooklyn: Court Street - Montague Street
text:
Court Street, west side, from Montague (right) to Remsen Streets. On the extreme right is the Mechanics Bank Building at the northwest corner of Court and Montague Streets. To the left of it, at the S.W. corner of the two streets, is the Continental Insurance Building (narrow building) and the Phoenix Insurance Building. These two were torn down in 1926 and the 35-story Montague-Court Building erected on the site. The clear-ance to the left of the Phoenix Building, which is the northwest corner of Court and Remsen Streets, is the former site of the Garfield Building, where the 29-story Court-Remsen Building was later put up. The view is across Borough Hall Park from Fulton Street. The statue (center left) is that of Henry Ward Beecher, distinguished preacher of the Plymouth Church and abolitionist.

title: Brooklyn: Cranberry Street - Henry Street
text:
Cranberry Street, south side, between Henry and Hicks Streets, viewing west from near Henry Street and showing the Plymouth Church, from which the famous Brooklyn preacher Henry Ward Beecher delivered his sermons. The church was built in 1849 and extends through to Orange Street. The three-story house with the brownstone stoop, to the left of the church, is Henry Ward Beecher's old home and President Abraham Lincoln and General Ulysses S. Grant are said to have visited here. The house is No. 66 Cranberry Street and was remodelled, in 1940, into an apartment house for five families. For additional data see "The New York Times," October 5, 1940.

title: Brooklyn: Devoe Street - Lorimer Street
text:
36-42 Devoe Street, south side, just west of Lorimer Street, showing the J. A. Rhodes' saw factory. It was built on 1850. This is the rear of the factory. Although Mr. Armbruster states that the factory was located on Ainslie Street near Tenth Street, the present (1941) Keap Street, the writer of these lines was unable to locate any saw factory at that location from 1874 to the present. The only saw factory, or file factory (the two are used interchangeably in the old Brooklyn business directories), in this area appears in Bromley's 1880 map on the south side of Devoe Street (which is one block north of Ainslie Street), just west of Lorimer Street. It is very likely that this is the saw factory Mr. Armbruster has in mind.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Brooklyn: Eastern Parkway - Franklin Avenue
text:
Eastern Parkway north of Franklin Ave.

A general view west and northwest of Franklin Ave., showing in the background, in Institute Park, the Brooklyn Institute of Arts and Sciences. To the right is Eastern Parkway. Franklin Ave., is visible in the foreground. Washington Ave., is east and south in front of the Arts building; also is Classon Ave., and the Manhattan Beach and Coney Island branch of the Long Island R.R. Union and President Streets, now run east and west to the left of Eastern Parkway to Institute Park. In the foreground west of Franklin Ave., now stands the Girls Commercial High School, east of Franklin Ave., on property of M. & S. Smith, large apartment houses have been built. All buildings east of the Arts building and east of Eastern Parkway, have been demolished. The corner-stone for the Institute was laid in 1896 by Mayor Charles A. Schieren. The two sections of this building were completed in 1897 and 1904. The apprentices Library Association and the Old Brooklyn Institute founded in 1823 and 1843 respectively, were incorporated, in 1890, into this organization. The former building of the old institute was practically destroyed by fire on September 12, 1890.

About 1910.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Flatbush Avenue - Maple Street
text:
(1)
563 Flatbush Ave., east side, between Maple and Midwood Streets. This house clearly marked on the map of 1908 of Brooklyn. The view is the Lefferts Farmhouse, removed in 1918, to Prospect Park. It stood at 563 Flatbush Ave., upon which site is now the North Cliff Hall Apartments. It was built by Pieter Lefferts (1753-1791), on site of an earlier house (built 1666), destroyed in the Battle of Flatbush, during the Revolution.
1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2)
This is a post out of the Lefferts barn 112 years old, stood on the Canarsie Lane near Midwood Street. It was razed in 1904. It was built in 1792. 373-375 Midwood Street, occupy the site.
1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Bronx: Pelham Bay Park - Joshua Pell Mansion.
text:
Pelham Bay Park (Bronx): A view of the Joshua Pell Mansion, one of the Pell houses, also known as the Collins House, dating back to pre-Revolutionary days. It is situated on the east side of Prospect Avenue (also known as the Split Rock Road), midway between the New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad tracks and the city line of Pelham, Westchester County. Another Pell Mansion, said to be the most imposing of all, is located on the west side of Wolf's Lane, at Iden Avenue, on the Isaac Rodman property (1910 map), in Pelham, Westchester County.

1891

Gift of Urbrock Collection

title: Brooklyn: Flatbush Avenue - Toot Hill Road
text:
Flatbush Avenue: An early view of the avenue, showing the Hess House on the left. The exact part of the avenue is not known to the writer of these lines, but it is most likely the area below Beverley Road. The 1890 atlas of Kings County shows the Flatbush Avenue trolley line to have terminated just north of Beverley Road, Then Avenue B. No trolley line ran south of that point.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection
about 1890

Armbruster's identification of this photograph is incorrect.

This view shows Flatbush Avenue, east side, south from about where present-day Tilden Ave. is located. The John Hess house (left) was the second house north of the corner of Vernon Avenue (now Duryea Place). The building on the south-east corner of Flatbush and Vernon Avenues (just to the right of the Hess house in this photo, with porch) was the Willink House, a hotel run by two sisters, Mrs. Willink and Miss Ludlow.

The Hess house belonged in 1711 to Johannes Johnson, who sold it that year to the Reformed Dutch Church for use as a parsonage. In 1881 it was described as "rapidly going to decay," so this photo must be quite a bit earlier, perhaps 1870.

Ref.: Strong, History of Flatbush (1842), p. 87. Vanderbilt, Social History of Flatbush (1909 edition), p. 191, 194.

Joseph Halpern
Nov. 15, 1972

title: Brooklyn: Flushing Avenue - Cypress Avenue
text:
(1) 1325 Flushing Ave., north side, east of Cypress Ave., showing in the foreground, the Nicholas Wyckoff farmhouse, acquired in 1765; from a Schenck. Another Nicholas Wyckoff was owner from 1852-1860. For more data see the N.Y. Sun. February 18, 1939. 1922.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2) The same, looking south, showing a rear view of the out-buildings of the farmhouse.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection. September 1928.

(3) The same, showing another angle. Note that one of the barns is partially demolished by fire.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection. September 1928.

(4) The same, showing another close up of the barn. It was erected in 1650 or 1656 (marked on rafter) and partially demolished by fire in 1700. The original joists remained and the barn was rebuilt around them. It was again partially destroyed by fire in March 1922.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection. 1922.

title: Brooklyn: Flushing Avenue - Cypress Avenue
text:
1325 Flushing Ave., north side, between Cypress Ave., and Seneca Avenue, showing in a set of four views the Nicholas Wyckoff home, also known as the Peter Wyckoff home. Views 1 and 2 are the same. No. 3 is a rear view, looking southwest towards Flushing Ave. No. 4 is a partial view of No. 2. Peter Wyckoff occupied this house during the Revolutionary War. Prior to this, in 1765, it was the Schenck farmhouse. In that year Nicholas Wyckoff acquired possession. Eugene L. Armbruster states that a broad hall runs through the center of the house, on the left side of the hall is a parlor and sitting room. On the other side of the hall is a dining room, kitchen, and three bedrooms. In the sitting room is a colonial mantle piece, having pictures of the old Rapelye, Johnson, and Wyckoff houses. The upper floors contain eight rooms and a garret. In a corner of the hall is an ancient grandfather clock still keeping time. See other views for more data. For more data see the N.Y. Sun, February 18, 1939.

September 1928.
Views 1 & 4.
Views 2 & 3: 1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

The church was organized in this community in the farmhouse of a Denyse, at the N.E. corner of Fort Hamilton Parkway and 101st Street, on September 29, 1834. The Denyse heirs reserved a lot (100' x 125') the present site, on which a frame building was erected. It was consecrated on July 16, 1835. title: Brooklyn: Fulton Street - Water Street
text:
(1)
Fulton Street, north side, at and east of Water Street. At the corner is a view of the Franklin House, also known as the Brooklyn Hotel. It was established in 1840, by Ezekiel Baldwin, who was born in Hampshire, and whose trade was that of a blacksmith. He operated the place 41 years. It is said that William Caren, was the first proprietor in 1836, and held the place for several years. Captain King's Tavern, occupied the corner in earlier days. It was also later known as the Mariner's Tavern; later still, the Steamboat House, occupied a part of this site. The building of 1840, still stands. At the left, overhead is the Brooklyn Bridge.

title: Brooklyn: Fulton Street - Front Street
text:
(1) Fulton Street, at the N.E. corner of Front Street. The corner site, No. 1 Fulton Street, now 25 Fulton Street, was owned by John Rapelyea who had his home here in 1766. It was purchased in 1784 by Col. J. Sandis who then sold it to Abraham Remsen, who had it demolished. In 1807 Abraham Remsen erected a new building. This property subsequently was owned by the Brooklyn Bank, which in 1868, erected a new building. The Bank occupied this place from 1876 to 1889. This location also has the distinction of housing the first dry-goods store in Brooklyn, conducted by Abraham Remsen. The building adjoining, known as the Law Building, in 1840, had as tenants, Lott, Murphy and J. Vanderbilt; J. Greenwood and Duryea; Morse and Rolfe; William Day and D. Trembly. On the site prior to 1840, Wecks and Backs conducted a hardware store. In 1828 subsequent to the hardware business the building was occupied by Van Nostrand and Tolford's Leather store.

1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Fulton Street - Bridge Street
text:
Fastened to the wall of a building located on Fulton St. near Bridge St., Brooklyn, is this plaque tells a story that had its beginning more than three centuries ago.

In those early colonial times were open spaces, dotted with scattered structures. Among these stood an octagon Reformed Church in which, about July 4th, 1661, Carel DeBevoise, who had arrived a scant two years before as an emigrant from Holland, conducted the first school in Brooklyn.

From the record we find "Carel DeBevoise, a highly educated French Protestant, with his wife - nee Sophia Van Lodensteyn- and three children had sailed from Amsterdam, Netherlands, on the ship Otter, in February, 1659 and arrived on these shores shortly thereafter.

Carel DeBevoise was more than schoolmaster:

as the rescript testifies, to act as court messenger, to serve summons, conduct the services of the church, to lead the choir on Sundays, ring the bell for public worship, take charge of the school, and perform other occasional services. We can appreciate his embarrassment, and sympathize with his apprehensions in the performance of so many and such conflicting duties as are specially named; but when the monstrous addition is affixed 'and such other occasional services as the very worthy and ponderous shout and the dignified and exacting schepens should enact for his worriment,' human emotion is too feeble to be commensurate with the demand."

Yet insignificant as was the beginning the light has never been quenched. The tablet stresses this thought in the words:

The Spark Here kindled Has Become a Great Flame Illuminating the Path of Youth Unto Wisdom and Worth.

title: Brooklyn: Grace Court - Furman Street
text:
Grace Court from east of Furman to Hicks Streets, showing at the S.W. corner Grace Church. It was once the Emanuel Protestant Episcopal Church which organized in 1841 and built its edifice at the N.E. corner of Sidney Place and Livingston Street, which was consecrated on March 3, 1842. In 1850 the structure was sold to catholics and became St. Charles Borromeo R.C. Church. The present structure of St. Charles Borromeo was dedicated May 24, 1869, as the former structure was destroyed by fire on March 8, 1868. The present Grace Church (Protestant Episcopal) built its present edifice in 1848.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Bergen Street - 20th Street
text:
Grant Square, looking north from Bergen Street, showing the General Grant Monument. To the right of the monument is the Union League Club on the corner of Dean Street. The Avenue is Rogers Avenue. One block north of Dean Street, at the S.E. corner of Pacific St., is the Imperial House. On the left is the 23rd Regiment Armory, la- ter the 106th Infantry Armory. Rogers Avenue north from Dean Street is Bedford Avenue.

Urbrock Collection

About 1905

title: Brooklyn: racetracks - Gravesend Race Track.
text:
Gravesend Race Track (Brooklyn): Shown is a view of the remaining sheds of the Brooklyn Jockey Club's race track, which lay on the east side of McDonald Avenue, extending east to Ocean Parkway and north and south from slightly below Avenue U to Kings Highway. This photograph was taken from McDonald Avenue, just above Avenue U, and is in a north-easterly direction. The track in the foreground is of the B. M. T. system.

April, 1923

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Brooklyn: Hanson Place - Ashland Place
text:
Hanson Place, at the N.E. corner of Ashland Place, showing the towered structure of the Williamsburg Bank. The small buildings to the left of same (east side of Ashland Place) are the Salvation Army Quarters. Continuing to the left (north of the latter) is the Academy of Music Building. The vacant lot shown at the N.W. corner of Hanson Place and St. Felix Street was the site of the former Hanson Place M.E. Church. On the extreme lower right appears the low structure of the Long Island Railroad Station, one side of which is on Flatbush Ave., which has the Ave. Elevated Line thereon. In the background, intersecting Lafayette Ave., is Fulton Street and its Elevated Line. About 1929.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Brooklyn: Hubbard Place - Kings Highway
text:
4048 Hubbard Place, south side, west of King's Highway, once known as No. 13 Hubbard Place, showing The Hubbard Homestead, believed to have been built in 1705 by the Ditmas Family. The Reverend served as pastor for the Dutch Reformed Church from 1742 to 1796, when he died. This house was occupied by the Misses E. and J. title: Brooklyn: Irving Avenue - Putman Avenue
text:
Union Cemetery, Brooklyn:
Northwestward across the Methodist Cemetery on whose site was erected, years later, the Bushwick High School. The fence runs along the west side of Irving Avenue, from Putnam Avenue to Palmetto Street. The entire cemetery grounds, with the exception of the extreme right corner, later became the Bushwick High
School and play grounds.

Eugene L. Armbruster collection  About 1897

title: Brooklyn: Kings Highway - Flatbush Avenue
text:
Kings Highway, at the N.W. corner of Flatbush Ave. It is said that the land on which this house stands, was sold by Elbert Elbertsen in 1676 to Peter Wyckoff. In 1797 Simon Voorhies came into possession of it, and used it as a tavern. John B. Durges owned it until 1820, used it as a tavern for about 20 years. Abraham Terhune became the next owner and his estate sold it in 1843 to John Bergen who built a 2-story extension on the west side, the first floor becoming a ballroom and the second floor sleeping quarters. In 1855 John Logue became the owner. William R. Mc Neil became the owner in 1860 and in 1874 John Van Wyck bought the property and lived in it until 1882. Between 1882 and 1895 the place became an ice cream parlor and saloon, and from 1895 to 1902 the Amersfort Hotel was kept here. In 1902 the property reverted to the heirs of John Van Wyck and was demolished in 1923.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

text:

title: Brooklyn: Lincoln Avenue - Pitkin Avenue

(3) The same, showing the house facing Belmont Ave., after it has been remodeled. 1922. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Linden Boulevard - Grant Avenue
text:
Linden Boulevard, on the west side of the Grant Ave. street line. This house was demolished as it was in the line of the extended Linden Boulevard. It was originally located on the S.E. corner of the Road to the Neck and the Road to the Landing. There were three Forbell homes in 1873. The first to appear on any atlas is that in the above location, the second was on the N.E. corner of Grant and Dumont Aves., and may be still standing in 1929. The store was on the N.W. corner of Dumont Ave. and Old Mill Road in the line of Grant Ave.; the third on the N.E. corner of Linden Boulevard and Lincoln Ave. The owners in 1873 were: 1st house, H. Forbell; 2nd house, J.Y. Forbell; store, A. Forbell; 3rd house, W. Forbell. Eugene L. Armbruster, the Collector, states: Isaac Forbell farmhouse at Forbell's Landing. Isaac, the builder of the houses, was the father of Ambrose, who was the father of Isaac.

About 1908.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Lott Place - Flatbush Avenue
text:
Lott Place, at the S.B. corner of Flatbush Ave., and Kings Highway, showing the Rem Hegeman Farmhouse, which was later named the Van Wyck House. This house was reputed to date from 1780; others, however claim it was built much earlier in the century. It was demolished in 1910. The property was owned by C. Stevens, but in 1722 Jan Lucasse and Johanus Voorhees sold it to one Hogelands; Rem Hegeman bought it of a Van Dyke in 1795 and another Van Dyke bought it of H. Hogelands in 1825. This property was in the Van Wyck family and heirs until 1916.

1908.

title: Brooklyn: Meeker Avenue - Gardner Avenue
text:
(1)
Meeker Ave., south side, between Gard
er Ave., and Newtown Creek, alleged to have been built by Humphrey Clay in 1667, it stood until 1921 when it was demolished about 50 or 60 ft. from Newtown Creek. The owners of this property are as follows: patented in 1646 by Adam Mott who sold to William Goulding; who sold to Clandine Barbine and Anthony Jerve of Newgate Kills; who sold to Jacob Steendam in 1653. It was again patented by Humphrey Clay in 1667. He operated a ferry here as late as 1670. His son Clay sold to Alexander Baird of Hempstead, who left it to his wife Magdaleun. The first recorded sale is in 1749, from Josiah Paterson to Joost Dorre, who by will in 1793 left his real estate of Bushwick and Newtown to his sons, George and Peter. The former conveyed to Peter in 1795, the latters will convey in 1828 part to Anthony Hulst and the rest including the house to John Reis. From 1880 to 1924 William Blesser, and his heirs were owners.

1920.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2)
The same, another view.
About 1920.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Monroe Place - Clark Street
text:
Monroe Place, at the S.E. corner of Clark Street, showing The Church Of The New Jerusalem purchased in 1868, by the Brooklyn Society of The New Church (Swedenborgian), which was organized on June 15, 1859, from the congregation of The Church Of Our Father, a Universalist Society, founded in October 1842, who held their first services in a hall at the corner of Fulton and Cranberry Streets. The society later erected a new building at the corner of Pineapple and Fulton Streets. In 1848, the latter building was destroyed by fire, and the structure in this view was erected; and named "The Church Of Our Father". The congregation of this church with that of "The Church Of The Redeemer" - a group(dissenters) - again combined in 1868 and moved to the corner of Grand Ave., and Leffert's Place in 1883.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Myrtle Avenue - Palmetto Street
text:
(1)
At the intersection of Myrtle Ave., with Palmetto Street and Wyckoff Ave., showing (center) at the N.E. corner of Myrtle Ave., and Palmetto Street. The 4-story building owned by the Bushwick R.R. Co., had its offices and stables, on land owned by Peter Meserole in 1855. This building was partly destroyed by fire on September 15, 1923. The cafe at the right, is at the S.E. corner of Wyckoff and Myrtle Aves. To the left is a portion of the Myrtle Ave. Elevated line of the B.M.T. (The elevated makes a sharp turn from Myrtle Ave., into Palmetto Street at this point).
1922.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2) The same, showing a closer view of the R.R. Co's building.
1922.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3)
The same, showing the opposite corner occupied by the Parthenon Theatre. The theatre's site was originally part of the Ganta Farm, which was sold for $4,000 per acre, to the Bushwick R.R. Co., which erected its Ridgewood Depot and stables here in 1872. This corner while in Brooklyn in 1916, is now (1929) in Queens County.
1922.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(4)
The same, showing the R.R. Co's building after the fire.
1924.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Neck Road - Kenmore Place
text:
(1) Neck Road, north side, between Kenmore (East 21st Street) and Elmore Places (East 22nd Street), showing a house erected by Stephen J. Voorhies prior to the Revolutionary War. His son John S. occupied it later and finally George Stillwell who married Jane E. Voorhies became the owner. The oldest part of this house is said to date back to 1710. This house was demolished in May 1929. 1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2) The same, viewed from Kenmore Place. 1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3) The same, a front view. Ave. V now (1929) extends eastwood to Gerritsen Creek necessitating the demolishing of the house. April 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(4) The same, viewed from Ocean Ave. April 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

New Dock Street, west side, north of Water Street. The view shows the east side--viewing southward--of the store-house and storage yard being built by the W. P. A. for the New York City Department of Purchase, under the Brooklyn Bridge.

January 27, 1937

Works Progress Administration
Project 65-97-68

title: Brooklyn: New Dock Street - Water Street
text:

November 2, 1936

Project 65-97-68

title: Brooklyn: New Lots Avenue - Sheffield Avenue
text:
349 New Lots Ave., at the N.E. corner of Sheffield Ave., showing the remains of a building erected in 1750, by Daniel Rapelye. Ethan Allen was billeted in this house. To the west of this house, on the N.W. corner of Pennsylvania Ave., was the home erected by William Rapelye in 1875 (?). Both of these houses were demolished in May 1922.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2)

The same, showing the dutch baking ovens of the Rapelye house. In 1929, the whole frontage including these sites, was occupied by 3-story brick buildings.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster collection.

title: Brooklyn: New Lots Avenue - Van Siclen Avenue
text:
(1)
569 New Lots Ave., north side, east of Van Siclen Ave., showing the home of the Van Siclen's from about 1730 to 1887. This house was said to have been erected in 1730. It is now, 1929, used as a gasoline station. John Van Siclen during the War of 1812, was employed by the government as a mail carrier. The parsonage of the Dutch reformed church is visible on the left.
About 1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2)
The same, another view.
About 1929.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

text:

(2) The same, showing the barn being demolished. It was located at the N.E. corner of Church Ave., and Rockaway Parkway. January 26, 1927. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3) The same, showing the barn, partially demolished, and the house razed. Also seen is the side of the William F. Ryerson house. January 26, 1927. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(4) The same, another view. E.L. Armbruster, the photographer, states that one Van Brunt, who took down this house, intends to move it to a place believed to be Westchester County. January 26, 1927. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: New Utrecht Avenue - 84th Street
text:
(1) New Utrecht Ave., west side, just south of 84th Street, seen between the two brick buildings at right. The 2-story brick building is No. 8402 New Utrecht Ave. The building in process of demolishment, was the Van Brunt home, parts of which were approximately 200 years old. It faced 84th Street, at about No. 1752 at one time. Overhead is the West End Elevated Lines. October 12, 1928. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2) Same, showing only the Van Brunt house. October 12, 1928. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3) Same, showing the Van Brunt house, facing 84th Street, prior to the change of the 84th Street line, which made possible the 2-story brick building, seen in View No. 1. August 1924. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Oriental Boulevard - Ocean Avenue
text:
(1) Oriental Boulevard, south side, west of Ocean Ave., showing the Manhattan Beach Hotel built by Elbert Snediker in 1877 and owned by Austin Corbin, who opened it on July 18, 1877. The 4-story west wing was added in 1878, and it was again enlarged in 1879. Overall, the hotel was 660 feet long and accommodated 500 people. Its owners or lessees were H.J. Breslin, 1883; Simeon Leland, 1891; T.F. Silleck, 1899-1901; Alfred F. Amer, 1909-1910; and Joseph P. Greaves, 1911, when it was demolished in the same year. In 1937 the Manhattan Beach Baths used the site as a parking place for automobiles.

September 20, 1911.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Oriental Boulevard - Ocean Avenue
text:
(1) Oriental Boulevard, south side, west of Ocean Ave., showing the Manhattan Beach Hotel built by Elbert Snediker in 1877 and owned by Austin Corbin, who opened it on July 18, 1877. The 4-story west wing was added in 1878, and it was again enlarged in 1879. Overall, the hotel was 660 feet long and accommodated 500 people. Its owners or lessees were H.J. Breslin, 1883; Simeon Leland, 1891; T.F. Silleck, 1899-1901; Alfred F. Amer, 1909-1910; and Joseph P. Greaves, 1911, when it was demolished in the same year. title: Brooklyn: Pierrepont Street - Monroe Place
text:
Pierrepont Street, at the N.E. corner of Monroe Place, showing the First Unitarian Church of the Saviour. The first services conducted by this church were held in Classical Hall on Washington Street, August 17, 1833. The first pastor was Rev. David H. Barlow, who served until 1838. In 1835 it purchased and moved into the building formerly occupied by the Second Presbyterian Church on Adams Street, (afterwards known as Gothic Hall). The congregation incorporated and became known as the First Unitarian Church of Brooklyn, after the dedication of the present building on April 24, 1844, the present name was adopted. At the left is 50 Monroe Place, and to the right is 121-123 Pierrepont Street.

title: Brooklyn: Prospect Park - Leffert's Homestead.
text:
LEFFERTS HOMESTEAD   Prospect Park, Brooklyn.  This late Dutch Colonial house was rebuilt in 1777 by Lieutenant Peter Lefferts after partial destruction by fire during the Battle of Long Island.  Although the low gambrel roof of the building is typical of the style, the beautiful detail of the main entrance is unusual.  In 1913 the house was presented to the city by descendants of the original owner.

Bank of New York Calendar 1967-68

title: Brooklyn: Prospect Park - Fair Ground Inc.
text:
(1)
Prospect Park Fair Grounds Inc., bounded on the north by King's Highway, on the west by Mc Donald Ave., on the south by Neck Road, on the east by Coney Island Ave., was composed of 60 acres purchased by Geo. Powers and J. Payton, who established a one mile trotting course. These grounds were sold to a group of prominent Brooklyn residents, who formed the Brooklyn Jockey Club, which enlarged this tract to 460 acres at a cost of $400,000. It was opened in 1887. This view shows a straightaway and "Grand Stand" - To-day (1929) Stryker Street runs through the front of and along the site of the stand. The new tract was bounded on the north by Ave. Q, on the east by Ocean Parkway, on the west by Mc Donald Ave., and East 2nd Street, and on the south by Ave. V and Johnson Lane. The Dwyer brothers and the prominent Brooklynites incorporated under the name of the Brooklyn Jockey Club Track of Gravesend, Inc. The last meet was held in 1910. In 1922, the grounds were sold for $750,000 to William E. Harriman, and this section became known as the King's Club district.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2)
The same, after the demolition of track buildings.

title: Brooklyn: Avenue R - 35th Street (East)
text:
(1)
Ave. R, at about East 35th Street, showing a view of the beams of the razed Johannes Lott barn. This property, upon which stood the house and barns, was purchased from Coert Voorhies in 1719 for $(?)11,000. A section of the house was completed in 1775. This house was subsequently moved to about 1940 East 36th Street, by Hendrick I. Lott, in the middle of the 19th century. He added the extensions to the house. title: Brooklyn: Remsen Street - Clinton Street
text:
Remsen Street, west from Clinton Street. In the left foreground is the Hamilton Club, organized on November 2, 1830 as the Young Men's Literary Association; changing its name in October 1831 to the Hamilton Literary Association of Brooklyn. Henry C. Murphy became its first president. Ninety of these members founded the present club which was incorporated in May 1882. The first quarters of the organization were in the Hamilton Building, at the N.W. corner of Court and Joralemon Streets, now the Temple Bar Building. In 1884 its present site was purchased at a cost of $49,000. The Clubhouse cost another $51,000, The statue of Alexander Hamilton was erected in 1892. Also partially seen are the Church of the Pilgrims and
the Hotel Bossert.
1922.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Rockaway Avenue - Blake Avenue
text:
(1) Rockaway Ave., east side, north of Blake Ave., showing the First Congregational Church of New Lots, which was dedicated on May 31, 1869. The first services were held in June 1866, and a Sunday School was organized on July 28, 1868. Two lots 50' X 120' were donated by G.S. Thatford. The church is 30' X 45' and was erected at a cost of $3,500.

May 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2) The same, another view.

May 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Schenck Avenue - 92nd Street (East)
text:
9217 Schenck Avenue, north side, between East 92nd and East 93rd Streets, viewing toward the latter and showing Bill's Old Homestead Beer Garden. Here Billy Ray for more than thirty years operated a bar known as the "madhouse," because of electrical gadgets that shocked customers when they picked up their change or sat on certain chairs. The house, which was formerly three stories high, was practically razed by fire in 1933. It was later demolished to make way for the construction of the Belt Parkway.

title: Brooklyn: Voorhies Lane - Ocean Avenue
text:
Coney Island Jockey Club Inc., of New York City, was bounded on the south by Voorhees Lane, on the west by Ocean ave., on the north by Ave. V and on the east by Brown Street. This club, founded in 1879, held its first races on the Prospect Park Fair Grounds. In 1880 the construction of the Sheepshead Bay Race Track was completed, and it was opened on June 19, 1880. William K. Vanderbilt was president in 1904. This track was one mile in circumference, but it was extended in 1884 to 1 1/8 miles, and in 1886, a mile track was constructed inside the old. The oval track was between East 23rd Street and Nostrand Ave., and Aves. W and Z. Mrs. Harriman a daughter of one Gertisgen owned this track which comprised about 125 acres, that was purchased by Max Natanson, Joseph P. Day, and Charles F. Noyes for $2,400,000 on April 1, 1915. They in turn, cut it into lots and sold them at auction in August and September 1923. Parts of the track in (1937) in- cluding some of the stables may yet be seen. The grounds are still referred to as the Harkness Estate. This view shows the stands and straight-away. The foundations of the stands are still visible north of Jerome Ave. (1937)
19----?

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Sheepshead Bay Road - 6th Street (West)
text:
(1)
Sheepshead Bay Road, north side, between West 6th and 8th Streets, showing a rear view. Also seen is the rear of the Oceanic Hotel which was the original Coney Island House. It was built in 1829 and stood on Neptune Ave., opposite Shell Road, south of Coney Island Creek. This property was sold by a road Company to John and Albert Terhune, later owned by Peter Lott. One Tooker was the first keeper of the house Others who either owned or operated the house were James W. Cropsey in 1834; Cropsey and Woglom from 1835-1843; A. Petter, S.W. Petter, and John I. Snediker in the 1870s and 1880s. In the Brooklyn Atlas, it is now located at No. 2866 West 6th Street, west side, between Neptune Ave., and Sheepshead Bay Road.

title: Brooklyn: Shore Road - 77th Street
text:
(1) Shore Road, at the N.E. corner of 77th Street, showing the house of Teunis G. Bergen, from 1857-1873. In 1827 Elizabeth, daughter of Rulef Van Brunt, lived here with her father. She married Teunis G. Bergen in 1827. In 1828 this home was purchased by the father of Rulef Van Brunt. Henry Oldworth resided here from 1829 until his death in 1881. The land upon which this house is situated, was formerly a part of the Thomas Stillwell farm. This Stillwell kept the ferry running to Staten Island. 1922. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2) The same, showing a view from 77th Street. 1922. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3) The same, showing rear of house. 1922. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(4) The same, showing another rear view of the house, barn and house adjoining. 1922. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Shore Road - 83rd Street
text:
Shore Road, west side, opposite 83rd Street, showing the Crescent Athletic Club's boat-house, which was destroyed by fire in April 1933. This organization has its origin in a football club, organized in 1884 by William H. Ford, and was on leased grounds located at the corner of 9th Ave and 9th Street, Brooklyn. The club which was incorporated in Feb. 1888, took over in the spring of 1889 the land and boat-house of the Nereid Boat Club. In the same year they purchased from the Van Brunt and Bergen estates of Bay Ridge a tract of land extending from 83rd to 85th Streets, and from Shore Road to Colonial Road. On Decoration Day 1892, the club house which cost $80,000 was opened to the members.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Elliott Place S.) - Hanson Place
text:
South Elliott Place (left foreground), south of Hanson Place to Atlantic Ave. This view is also general and shows the southern section of Brooklyn. It was taken from atop the Y.M.C.A. Building located at 55 Hanson Place, which is between Fort Greene and South Elliott Places. To the right of South Elliott Place is Fort Greene Place. At the left, beyond the Long Island freight yards on the S.E. and S.W. corners of Sixth Ave. respectively are the Sheffield Farms Co. and the A.G. Spalding Co. Manufacturing buildings. Fifth Ave. is a continuation of Fort Greene Place. The trolley car on Fifth Ave. is crossing Pacific Street to enter Flatbush Ave. At the right beyond the triangle is the Fifth Ave. Elevated Line on Flatbush Ave., which swings sharply and continues southward on Fifth Ave. June 1926.

Brown Brothers.

title: Brooklyn: Surf Ave. - 12th St. W.
text:
(1) Suff Ave., north side, east of West 12th Street, showing Luna Park, wh ich extends to East 10th Street. This park was established, May 16, 1903, by Thompson and Dundy on 22 acres of ground, which increased to 38 acres in 1904. Frederick Thompson conducted same, alone, at a later date. In 1924, Barron Collier was the owner. September 1926.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2) Another view in the opposite direction.
January 1924.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3) A view of the entrance.
January 1924.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(4) An interior view of the park, undoubtedly quite early.
About 1905.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Throop Ave. - Willoughby Ave.
text:
Throop Avenue, at the S. W. corner of Willoughby Avenue, showing the Throop Avenue Presbyterian Church. It had its origin in a mission established in 1852 on the corner of Throop Avenue and Bartlett Street. The Throop Avenue Presbyterian Church was organized in 1862 and occupied the Throop Avenue Mission Building between Hopkins and Ellery Streets, which was later turned into a synagogue. In 1867 it removed to the S. W. corner of Throop and Willoughby Avenues, occupying a frame structure. The cornerstone for the brick edifice, seen in this view, was laid on November 2, 1889. In 1890 the church was destroyed by fire and a new site was acquired for a new edifice at the N. W. corner of Throop Avenue and Macon Street, where the church is located to this day (1940). The building beyond the church, seen in this view, is between Willoughby and Vernon Avenues. Mr. Eugene L. Armbruster is authority for above references.

1911

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Brooklyn: Throop Ave. - Hart St.
text:
(1)
Throop Ave., west side, north from, but not including Hart to Willoughby Streets, showing the Throop Ave. Presbyterian Church, which had its origin in a mission established in 1852, on the corner of Throop Ave., and Bartlett Street. The church as such was organized on June 8, 1862, at Throop Ave., near Hopkins Street. In 1867 it moved to a small frame building at the S.W. corner of Throop and Willoughby Aves. The cornerstone of this building, was laid on November 2, 1889. A part of the wall fell during a storm on January 9, 1890. The edifice was opened for service on November 2, 1890; shortly thereafter it was destroyed by fire. A new site was later acquired at the corner of Throop Ave., and Macon Street.
October 12, 1911.

title: Brooklyn: Tillary St. - Fulton St.
text:
13-15 Tillary Street, north side, between Fulton and Washington Streets, showing a set of four views of the home of Dr. James Tillary.

W. T. Cutting was the owner in 1919. The home partially seen at the left of the aforementioned house was the property of Kate Duoyea in 1919. Edward Salit appear as the owner from 1925 to 1933.

In this period of time the house which was partially brick and wood appears on the Brooklyn Atlas of 1929 as all brick. E. H. Kenmore was the owner of both of the aforementioned homes in 1933.

In 1936 the homes were condemned by the City of New York and demolished inorder to make a wider approach to the Brooklyn Bridge.

View No. 4 shows a rear view. This house adjoins the Fulton St. B.M.T. elevated structure.

Views 1 to 4

title: Brooklyn: Ave. U - Van Sicklen St.
text:
(1) Ave. U., south side, west of Gerritsen Creek. This property dating from a grant of 1645 to Hugh Gerritsen, has been transferred by wills to the following owners: Rem Gerritsen, Garret Gerritsen, and from Samuel Gerritsen, to Johannes Gerritsen, who in 1765 left it to his son Samuel. He, in 1822, left it to his son John S. and his daughters, Jane and Elizabeth. In 1864, John Samuel Gerritsen left this farm to Samuel J., who in turn left it in 1876 to Mary C., born 1822, and Helen Van Brunt born 1824. In 1864, Samuel J., sold what he did not bequeath to his two daughters, to one Pothemus. All this property in 1879, was purchased by Helen Van Brunt (Mrs. Stephen Harriman). Her heirs conveyed it to William C. Whitney in 1899; and he restored the mill to its original condition in 1900, and vastly improved the house. The first mill was erected in 1656, this one was erected in 1831. Harry Payne Whitney was the last owner. This house and most of the out buildings are on condemned property, which is to be used for Marine Park. 1922. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2) The same, the mill and house are to be demolished. The creek will be filled and will be a part of Marine Park. May 12, 1922. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3) The same, another view. 1922. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(4) The same, showing the outbuildings. 1922. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Brooklyn: Utica Ave. - Kings Hwy.
text:
Utica Ave., west side, south of King's Highway, showing the Garret Kouwenhoven farm house, occupied by him from 1860 to 1873. This house, which was destroyed by fire in 1925, stood on part of lands thought to have comprised the Kouwenhoven private estate on the Great Flat which was devised by Willem Willemsen in 1769 to his son Garrett. At the left, is seen the Mrs. James Ditmars farm-house, west of Utica Ave., and east of King's Highway, occupied by Mrs.. James Ditmars from 1860 to 1873.

March 1923,

title: Brooklyn: Ave. V - 73rd St. E.
text:
(1)
Ave. V, at the S.W. corner of East 73rd Street, showing the Stoofhoff-Bergen house. The Bergen house stands on what was Bergen Island, which was granted in 1646 by Governor Kieft to Captain John Underhill, the famous New Englander whom was employed by Governor Kieft to fight the Pequot Indians. The island was then called by the Dutch "Meller's Island," and by the Indians "Wmbascoe," and was sold by Underhill to Thomas Spicer, who bought from the Indians what rights they then held. Spicer is said to have built the old house in 1656, soon after the erection of the Schenck-Crooke house. The house was bought of Spicer's heirs in 1665 for 125 guilders in wampum by Elbert Elbertsen, who came from North Brabant and owned six hundred acres in Flatlands. And later, through inheritance and purchase, the house came into the hands of John Bergen, whose heirs finally sold it to the speculators who laid out Bergen Beach in 1893. Johannes Bergen (1764-1824) added the east wing and in 1819 enlarged the main building; his son, Cornelius (1798-1865) added the west wing.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection. 1922.

(2)
The same, a view of the front with the east wing on the right.
1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3)
The same, showing the west wing in the foreground.
1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.
