The same, as No. 3.

title: Brooklyn: Van Sicklen St. - Village Rd. N.
text:
(1) Van Sicklen Street, at the S.E. corner of Village Road North, showing the home of the Van Sicklen's, which was erected in 1776, by John who deeded the property to his son Court. Subsequent members to hold it were, J.C. 1860, C.I. 1873, and J.L. Van Sicklen in 1890. Mrs. Margaret Van Sicklen Goodchild who was residing in California, sold it in September 1925 to a builder. It was razed in 1929.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2) The same, at a later date.

April 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3) The same, a closer view.

April 1923.

title: Brooklyn: Van Sicklen St. - Neck Rd.
text:
(1) Van Sicklen Street, opposite Neck Road which is in the foreground. The home at the right, belonged to T. Lake in 1860 and Mrs. A. Lake in 1873. The house at the left, was known as that of Jacobus Lake in 1857-1873. In 1873 it was that of C. Lake. Later was that of Wm. B. Lake. It was also known as Cupola House. February 1923. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2) The same, showing from fore to background, Nos. 354-346 Van Sicklen Street. The Cupola House bears no number. February 1923. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3) The same, showing a closer view of No. 1. 1923. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(4) The same, showing the Cupola House at the N.W. corner of Lake Place and Van Sicklen Street. April 1923. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

In 1809 he together with his brother Rodman, purchased the New Ferry called the Catherine Street Ferry. In 1814, the Bowne brothers were the first to abandon the use of sail and oar as motive power and introduced, in 1822 the first horse boat, and in 1824, they introduced the first two steamboats, single-hulled, the first of this class to be used on the East River. They were named the "Independence" and the "George Washington". The brothers operated together until 1836. Samuel Bowne on March 24, 1852, disposed of the Ferry to Smith and Sulkley, who eventually merged their interests with those of the Union Ferry Co. Samuel Bowne died in this house, which was demolished in 1922 or 1923.

title: Brooklyn: Washington St. - Johnson St.
text:
Washington Street, at the S.E. corner of Johnson Street, showing Haverly's Theatre. This building replaced the former Brooklyn Theatre, which was destroyed by fire on December 5, 1876, and in which 300 people lost their lives, because of an inadvertent act on the part of the firemen in closing the doors before the building was emptied. Because of the furore resulting, when this building was erected it was considered the best in the United States from both a theatrical and safety standpoint. It was demolished in 1891, to make way for the new "Brooklyn Eagle" Building. In 1868, St. Johns Episcopal Church occupied the site.

1882.

title: Brooklyn: Ave. Y - 14th St. E.
text:
(1)
Ave. Y., north side, between East 14th and 15th Streets, showing the Emmans farmhouse known as "Old Homestead". Eugene L. Armbruster states that from 1857-1860, it was occupied by one Emmons, and in 1872 by A.J. Emmons. However the Beer atlas of Long Island (1873) states the house be that of J. Emmer. In 1890 it was owned by an M. Teets. Since 1912 a Bessie Mill has occupied it. It is not in the atlas of 1929, evidently having been demolished.

March 1923.

title: Manhattan: 1st Ave. - Houston St. E.
text:
First Avenue, east side, north from East Houston (extreme right and not seen), to E. 1st Street (buildings thereupon). At the latter point is the station of the Second Avenue Elevated Line running on 1st Avenue. Note the individuals retailing food stuffs and merchandise. These form a part of the overflow of the Orchard Street market. Behind the fence is equipment used for the Eighth Avenue Subway construction that passed beneath this spot and which necessitated demolition of the tenements that formerly stood here. Subsequently same will be cleared and a children's playground constructed. The buildings shown are on
the north side of E. 1st Street, east of the Avenue.

February 23, 1932.

P.L. Sperr

Incidentally this area was the scene of one of the bloody frays attending the Draft Riots of the Civil War. Details of this are to be found in Dennis Lynch's "Boss Tweed."

July 19, 1939

title: Manhattan: 1st Ave. - 70th St. E.
text:
1311 First Avenue West Side, and on the north west corner of West 70th Street, showing P.S. 82.

Board of Education, N.Y.C.        1920.

This image is of "Public School 82 Manhattan", at The Northwest corner of First Avenue and 70th Street. Abraham Cohen, PHD was the Principal from 1923 to 1940 followed by Miss Novy as Principal from 1940 until the building was demolished in the 1960s to make way for a Public Housing building. Just North of PS 82 was the "Lenox Hill Settlement House". "Lenox Hill" had two Gymnasiums large and small, an Olympic swimming pool, woodworking shop, meeting rooms and contained a large auditorium with a stage. That space became "The Neighborhood Playhouse" from which many actors were trained. I was a student at P.S. 82 Manhattan from 1946 to 1952.

title: Manhattan: 1st Ave. - 106th St.
text:
First Avenue, west side, from 106th to 108th Streets, inclusive.
For other views of this neighborhood see the Feast of St. Anthony of Padua (held during Labor Day week-end by the Buscianese colony who live here).
Notice the little one-story frame shack at 2045 First Avenue, ad-joining the double building on the S.W. corner of 106th Street.
May 23, 1934.

P. L. Sperr.

The New York Times of October 18, 1938 states that the buildings at the S.W. corner of 106th Street and the Avenue, consisting of No's. 2047-0 First Avenue and No. 348 E. 106th Street are to be demolished and replace by a gasoline station. They appear in the left center with a canopy extending over the sidewalk. The interesting feature in this real estate deal was the straightening out of the mortgage tangle and the mounting tax arrears which apparently necessitated a complete liquidation of the equity of the mortgage certificate holders.

text:
W.S., south from 12th St.

Second Avenue at S.W. corner of 12th Street showing site on which will be erected the Jewish Art Theatre. This property was formerly a part of the old Stuyvesant farm. June 1925.

On left, at 11th St., is the old Stuyvesant Mansion (with balconies). note the steeple of St. Mark's Church.

title: Manhattan: 2nd Ave. - 11th St.
text:
Second Avenue, west side, from 11th to 14th Streets, inclusive, showing the old Rutherfurd house on the corner of 11th Street, now part of St. Mark's Hospital, and the Yiddish Art Theatre. Lewis M. Rutherfurd was noted as an astronomer, although he had begun as a lawyer (he was admitted to the bar in 1837). The mansard roof was added to the house since its occupation by the Rutherfurd family. It has changed little outwardly since 1905 or earlier.

April 2, 1934.

P. L. Sperr.

[handwritten: The old mansion was also known as the Stuyvesant House. Built by Peter Gerard Stuyvesant in 1845.
Note: See the "New York Times," June 16, 1935]

title: Manhattan: 2nd Ave. - 16th St. E.
text:
Second Avenue, west side, north from E. 16th Street, showing prominently the former Lying In Hospital occupying the frontage between 17th and 18th Streets. This structure, erected about 1900, stands on a site that included the Hamilton Fish residence.
In September of 1932, this organization will lose its identity on entering the new medical center of the N. Y. Hospital and Cornell Medical College on York Ave. In 1935 the Manhattan General Hospital will take over this building.
Views 2 and 3 are limited to the hospital building. Note the surface car and tracks. This line will be discontinued in 1933 and replaced by bus service.

P. L. Sperr

View 2 - Neg.# 793
View 3 - Neg.# 794

title: Manhattan: 2nd Ave. - 16th St. E.

title: Manhattan: 2nd Ave. - 34th St. E.
text:

To the right is St. Gabriel's Park, the white building housing the New York Public Library branch of that name, the Hall structure, and the Church proper on 37th Street. All of these will be gone in early 1940 as this entire block will be cleared for the plaza approach to the Queens-Midtown Tunnel. Note in the background the group of apartment buildings forming Tudor City. Close observation will distinguish the fact of almost completion of same. Subsequently other units will be erected and the skyline changed, thereby obliterating a view of the long roofed Hospital for Ruptured and Crippled Children. This appears in the due center of this photo.

title: Manhattan: 2nd Avenue - 97th Street (East)
text:
Second Avenue, east side, north from E. 97th Street, showing tenements interspersed with clearances which are the result of the enforcement of the multiple dwelling law and thereby eliminating squalor, vice and disease. These Harlem rookeries, built en masse over swampy areas have been a perpetual eyesore, being uniformly of the dumb-bell plan which originated from the competition of 1879, after the repeal in 1872 of the 1st tenement house law of 1867. Under Mayor LaGuardia and his Tenement House Commissioner, Langdon Post these are gradually coming down.
Overhead is the Second Avenue "El" indicating by its height the low elevation of this former swamp; thru which flowed the riverlets that formed Harlem Mere.

September 14, 1938.

P.L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: 3rd Avenue - 6th Street (East)
text:
Third Avenue, east side, from East 6th to 7th Streets, the site of Tompkins Market and Armory. This view shows the Hall Place and East 7th Street side of same. The building was erected in 1860 for the Seventh Regiment. A new Armory was erected in 1877-1880 at Park and Lexington Avenues, between 66th and 67th Streets for this organization. Meanwhile the 69th Regiment, organized in 1852, has been meeting here. In the basement are the drill-rooms. On the first floor are markets; on the second floor, ten company rooms and offices; and on the third floor, a drill room. The Abram S. Hewitt Memorial (Cooper Union Annex) building was later erected here; the market being discontinued and the 69th moving to their new Armory on Lexington Avenue between East 25th and 26th Streets.

About 1895

Gift of Urbrock Collection

title: Manhattan: 3rd Avenue - 7th Street
text:
Third Ave., east side, north from East 7th Street to St. Marks Place (8th Street), showing at the N.E. corner of the first point, the former Metropolitan Savings Bank Building. This structure, bearing Nos. 1-3 Third Ave. and 59-61 Cooper Square, housed this institution from 1867 to 1935. It was constructed for them two years after it took that name; being formerly known as the Mariners Savings Institution which was organized in 1852. According to the New York Times of December 8, 1937, this, one of the oldest fireproof business buildings in the City, has been sold to the First Ukrainian Evangelical Pentecostal Church Inc., and will be used by them for religious purposes.

February 5, 1938.

George D. Chinn.

title: Manhattan: 4th Avenue - 9th Street (East)
text:
Fourth Avenue, east side, north from East 9th Street, showing a second hand book center that sprawls over both sides of the Avenue and into various side streets.  These stores do a brisk trade among alien and native stocks alike, all seeking the content and not the cover.  Several of the enterprises conduct auctions and issue mimeographed catalogues which are widely circulated.  These in performing their function are responsible for the wide variety of attending buyers; bibliophile and student alike being represented.  The outside counters in serving a different public, are utilzed by those passing by or employed in the vicinity.  June 12, 1933

P.L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: 4th Avenue - 19th Street (East)

Fourth Ave., east side, north from East 19th to 23rd Streets, showing two churches and a hotel, prominent of which is the All Souls Unitarian Church at the S.E. corner of East 20th Street. Occupying the S.E. and N.E. corners of East 21st Street respectively are the New Amsterdam Hotel and Calvary P.E. Church. The Unitarian Church that which George F. Baker, Joseph Choate, William Cullen Bryant and Peter Cooper were worshipers, was demolished in 1929 and the property sold for a Club hotel which never materialized and the site vacant since. The congregation meanwhile moved into a newly constructed edifice at Lexington Ave. and East 80th Street. According to the New York Times of March 26, 1938 a new 6-story apartment house will shortly rise here at a cost of $600,000.

title: Manhattan: 4th Avenue - 20th Street (East)
text:
Fourth Avenue, at the S. E. corner of East 20th Street, showing the All Souls Unitarian Church, erected 1855. The Society was incorporated in 1919 as the "First Congregational Church of New York", from the outcome of a few services held by William Ellery Channing. Edward Everett preached at the dedication of the church, in Chambers Street, in 1820. The Rev. Henry Ware, Jr. was the first pastor, and his successor was Dr. Henry W. Bellows, the President of the Sanitary Commission during the Civil War. He was succeeded by the Rev. Theodore C. Williams. William Cullen Bryant and Peter Cooper were parishioners here. It will shortly be demolished and the site remain vacant until 1939, when a 6 story apartment house will rise here.

title: Manhattan: 4th Avenue - 32nd Street
text:
Fourth Avenue, west side, from 32nd to 34th Streets, showing the old Park Avenue Hotel and the new Vanderbilt Hotel nearing completion. The view is from the roof of the old Fourth Avenue Railway (Metropolitan Railway) carbarns. At the N.W. corner of 34th Street, the first building on that side of Park Avenue, stands the Unitarian Church of the Messiah, later known as the Community Church, erected in 1867. To the right, on the east side of the Avenue opposite the Vanderbilt Hotel, stands the 71st Regiment Armory (1893).

1911.

title: Manhattan: 4th Avenue - 32nd Street
text:
Fourth Avenue, north on west side from 32nd to 34th Streets. The Park Avenue Hotel, originally built in the 1870's by A.T. Stewart is a semi-charitable organization, on the site of the old N.Y. & Harlem Railway round-house (engine-house). It will stand here till 1925, (see Park Avenue). Compare this with the same view in 1906 (by Brown Bros.), which will show little change beyond better pavement, electrified street-cars, and subway entrances at 33rd Street. The old frame hotel and bar on the S.W. corner of 32nd Street will not be demolished till after 1910. About 1895.

Ewing Galloway, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 13th Street
text:
61-59 & 57 fifth Ave., at, adjoining: and south of the south east corner of East 13th St., showing at the corner (No. 61) a 4 story structure under demolition. This property, held by the Hoffman family for more than 40 years, has been leased to the Frank G. Shattuck Co. for use as a Schraffts Restaurant in a modern Colonial style.

The history of this property goes back to the early Dutch days, same being a part of the estate of Hendrick Brevoort. The east branch of Minetta Brook ran just above it, turning south east across what is not Fifth Ave, and was in 1824, the northern extremity of the Ave.

About 1850, the home of James Lennox stood here and a picture of same is in the possession of the Museum of the City of New York. In 1895 the present owners took possession, but never resided here. For a further account of this, see the New York Times of March 18, 1938, page 38.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 22nd Street
text:
Fifth Avenue at 22nd Street and north, showing at right the old Hotel St. Germain.

On the S.E. corner of 22nd Street a small house has just been demolished. The brick house below it, in right foreground, is new. The hotel, built in 1853-54, is also new. The remainder of this triangular block, today (1935) the site of the Flatiron Building, will by 1859 be filled with four small houses facing on Fifth Avenue.

The houses on the S.W. corner of 22nd Street are new. On the N.W. corner of 23rd Street stands the short-lived Franconi's New York Hippodrome, about to be torn down for the erection of the Fifth Avenue Hotel (at first called the Mount Vernon Hotel), 1859-1908.

In the background may be seen the spire of the Marble Collegiate Church (Dutch Reformed), at N.W. corner of 29th Street. Some of the houses which may be seen on E. 26th Street across Madison Square were standing as late as 1912.

Compare this early photograph with the same view in 1903 and 1925.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 24th Street
text:
Fifth Avenue and Broadway, north from W. 24th Street. These two thoroughfares cross each other at 23rd Street and all buildings fronting on this open area acquire Fifth Avenue numbers, though technically they are on Broadway. North of 25th Street (above the Worth Monument) Broadway resumes its identity. Buildings on the right, face on to the normal building line of Fifth Avenue and extend from 25th to 26th Street. At the left is the Albemarle Hotel, adjoining the 2 larger units of the famous Hoffman House.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 26th Street
text: Fifth Avenue, east side, north from and including 26th Street, showing the N.W. corner of Madison Square and the Hotel Brunswick on the N.E. corner of 26th Street. According to King's Handbook of New York (1892), parades of the Coaching Club always started in front of the Brunswick, and he mentions it as much favored by English tourists. This photograph was taken by one of such Englishman, and was annotated in his own writing "Where I stayed with Lucas C. E. en route from Venezuela to England". About 1906 this building will be replaced by the 12-story Brunswick Building, as Madison Square changes into a strictly business district. 1888.

This structure surplanted the original edifice on the corner of Beekman and Nassau Streets; the latter being erected in 1767. Fifth Avenue, west side, south from 42nd Street, showing the old reservoir occupying the avenue frontage. Upon this site was erected the present New York Public Library Building.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 40th Street
text:
130-2 W. 42nd Street (Bush Terminal Building), between 6th Avenue and Broadway showing a general view eastward from atop this 29 storied office building. 42nd Street is to the left and 40th Street on the right, skirting the N. Y. P. L. on Fifth Avenue. In the background, from right to left, are the outstanding, No. 10 E. 40th Street, Chanin, and Lefcourt-National Buildings. This will overshadow its neighbor, the Salmon Tower.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 42nd Street
text:
Fifth Avenue, north from a point slightly to the south of 42nd Street, showing a procession of electric cabs and their earlier prototypes, the horse drawn hansom, silhouetted against buildings on the east side of this thoroughfare.

The photographers vantage point is in front of the old reservoir, now the site of the New York Public Library.

To the left of center is the twin towered synagogue, Emanu-El. The uncompleted office structure at the S.E. corner of 45th Street was finished in 1899 and thereby dates this photo. Beyond are the spires of St. Patrick, St. Thomas, and St. Nicholas Churches.

1898-9

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 42nd Street
text:
Fifth Avenue, north from 42nd Street, showing traffic conditions on this main arterial thoroughfare at an early date. In the foreground, at the N.E. corner of the Avenue and East 43rd Street is the original Temple Beth-El which subsequently moved uptown. Outlined in the distance are the spires of St. Patricks Cathedral opposite that atop the Collegiate Church of St. Nicholas. On the left is the old Bennett Bldg. which stood for years at the N.W. corner of Fifth Avenue and W. 42nd Street. The row of 5 story brownstones bearing advertising material will provide a site for the subsequent Postal Life Insurance Co. Bldg. The interesting point in reference to this, is that the corner building was the home of "Boss" Tweed. This photostat is one of a set depicting traffic conditions and filed under Police Activities and various Fifth Avenue locations and are evidently part of a group published in the March 11, 1909 issue - page 229.

Leslies Weekly
Copyright-Judge Co.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 45th Street
text:
Fifth Avenue, east side, north from East 45th Street (right, not included). At the right is the Church of the Heavenly Rest (No. 551) that was built through the efforts of Dr. Robt. S. Howland then the Rector of the Church of the Holy Apostles. The parish originated in services held in the Hall of Rutgers Female College (q.v.) in 1865. Cast across the front, is the shadow of the Church of the Divine Paternity (Universalist) that stood at the S.W. corner of 45th Street. In the center is Windsor Hotel, prior to its destructive fire in 1899. The construction shown beyond is for the new St. Patricks Cathedral that was protected by Archbishop Hughs in 1850 from plans by James Renwick. The cornerstone was laid in 1858 and opened in 1879. 1892 saw it nearly completed with the exclusion of the Lady Chapel. The steeples were added in 1888.

Possibly 1888

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 46th Street
text:
Fifth Avenue, east side, north from and including 46th Street, showing the Windsor Hotel from 46th to 47th Streets. The 7-Story building on the S.E. corner of 50th Street is the Buckingham Hotel (opened 1876); and beyond it may be seen the trees on the grounds of the Catholic Orphan Asylum, from 51st to 52nd Streets, the block above the Cathedral.

Compare this picture with Fifth Avenue, north from 46th Street, about 1890, which will show the ground floor of the house on the S.E. corner of 46th Street remodeled for business, and the new 8-story Belgravia on the N.E. corner of 49th Street where this picture shows a vacant lot. The spires of St. Patrick's Cathedral, begun in the fall of 1885 and finished three years later, will also rise from behind the Buckingham; in this picture only the preliminary construction work is visible.

The same scene in 1906 will show the Windsor Arcade, which was built after the hotel was destroyed by fire on March 17, 1899.

Late 1885.

Brown Brothers.

Later pictures of this block show the three-story Windsor Arcade for stores and offices, shortly to be erected, which filled the entire Fifth Avenue side of the block. A part of this will still be standing in 1920 alongside of the eight-story W. &. J. Sloane Building, built between 1910 and 1916, on the S.E. corner of 47th Street. title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 46th Street
text:
Fifth Avenue (across the center of view, from right to left margins) from 46th (right) to 54th (left) Streets and environs, as viewed from the air, prominently showing the cleared area on the west side of the Avenue where Rockefeller Center (Radio City) will rise. Sixth Avenue is along the lower edge and forms the westerly border of this major building enterprise. The photographer is viewing eastward to show in the center, St. Patrick's Cathedral, Saks Fifth Avenue Department Store, No. 444 Madison Avenue, the new (under construction) Waldorf-Astoria Hotel, and the General Electric (at this date known as the R.C.A) Building. To the right appears the Grand Central Building. The Rockefeller Center demolition has progressed to a point where the only obstacle is the building in the center foreground, east of Sixth Avenue. It is reported to be occupied by an alleged speak-easy and the owner refuses to vacate. Court assistance will aid this situation and excavation will then be started.

August 1, 1931.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 49th Street
text:
A Set of Seven Canvases of Old New York

These paintings come from a country house called 'Glencairn' near Dublin in Ireland, where they adorned the walls of the billiard room. The house was built by Richard 'Boss' Croker (1841-1922), an Irishman who for many years was associated with Tammany Hall in New York, holding political positions under William M. 'Boss' Tweed, and later, after the latter's ousting, under 'Honest John' Kelly. Following the Lexow Committee investigations (1889-90), he left for England where he took up residence in Wantage, Berks, returning to America periodically, attempting to regain his lost position in the Democratic Party. After his final defeat in 1900, he crossed the Atlantic once again, built 'Glencairn' and started a racing stable. Despite his past reputation (he paid, in all, $550,000 for his Irish estates), he lived up to the high standards demanded by British racing circles, and when his horse Orby won the Derby in 1907, did not even back him.

These pictures were painted to remind him of New York, and it is assumed that they were executed here around the turn of the century. All are painted in tones of sepia and green.

The British Government has recently acquired this mansion for the use of the British Ambassador to Ireland.

PARKE-BERET Sale 2234, Nov. 29-30, 1963

text:
Fifth Avenue, west side, north from West 54th Street, showing prominently Dr. Hall's Fifth Avenue Presbyterian Church at the N. W. corner of 55th Street. Organized in 1808, their first church was erected on Cedar Street. The Rev. John Brodhead Romeyn became the first pastor, retaining his connection with the parish until his death in 1825. In common with all the earlier churches, the Cedar Street parish made several removals farther uptown; in 1834 to Duane Street; in 1852 to its first Fifth Avenue church, at the corner of 19th Street, when the corporate name was changed, and again, in 1875 to the present location. To the left is St. Lukes Hospital, occupying the Avenue frontage from 54th to 55th Street's.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 54th Street (West)
text:
Fifth Avenue, west side, at W. 54th Street, showing St. Lukes Hospital at the N. W. corner of same. This structure was erected in 1858, thru the efforts of the Rev. Dr. William A. Muhlenberg, the rector of the Church of the Holy Communion. He began this work in 1846 and in 1850 raised a subscription of $100,000. A corporation was formed and in 1854 opened an infirmary in a Sixth Avenue house to be conducted by the Sisters of the Holy Communion. In 1888 a Training School for Nurses was established. In 1892, the Trustees purchased a tract on W. 113th Street, near the (then) proposed Cathedral of St. John and erected a new hospital. This site in 1939 is occupied by the 9 story University Club.

This view shows, a vacant lot at the S. W. corner of this point, at the left of which stood for years the Rockefeller residence. See views on 54th Street for same.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 54th Street (West)
text:
Fifth Avenue, at the N.W. corner of West 54th Street, showing St. Luke's Hospital, erected in 1858. Beginning in 1846 under the guidance of the Rev. Dr. Wm. A. Muhlenberg, rector of the Church of the Holy Communion, a public appeal for funds in 1850 resulted in the formation of a corporation and in subscriptions amounting to S100,000. An infirmary was opened on Sixth Avenue in 1854. This work was transferred to the newly erected hospital in
1858.
Increased demands necessitated the abandonment of this structure and the erection of a new building on 113th Street, near the Cathedral of St. John. The corner stone there was laid, May 6, 1893. For further details of this humanitarian work see pages 471-3 of
Kings Handbook of New York, 1893.
1894

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 57th Street
text:
Fifth Avenue, north from 57th Street, seen from the Heckscher Building on the S.W. corner of 57th Street. 1 East 57th Street, on the corner, and the small house adjoining it, have been demolished in November and are to be replaced by a 15-story building. On the S.E. corner of 58th Street the 32-story Squibb Building, 745 Fifth Avenue, is shown in the later stages of construction. The new Savoy Plaza Hotel occupies the block from 58th to 59th Streets, and the Sherry-Netherland the N.W. corner of 59th Street, on the sites respectively of the old Hotels Savoy and Netherland. Beyond, on the S.E. corner of 61st Street, the George A. Fuller Company is erecting a tall apartment house on the site of the old Elbridge T. Gerry mansion.

Ewing Galloway, Photographer.
Early 1930.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 57th Street
text:
Fifth Avenue at N.E. corner of 57th Street, the last remaining house of "Marble Row", built early in 1871 by Mrs. Mary Mason Jones, who inherited the block from her father, John Mason. The group of houses, known as Marble Row, were notable as representing practically the first break with the brownstone tradition in New York. This house, the first of the group, was occupied by Mrs. Jones herself. Its last resident was Mrs. Hermann Oelrichs; and in 1918 the New York Trust Company bought and remodelled it. In November 1929 it will be demolished to make room for the new 15-story New York Trust Company Building.

June, 1925.

The first church spire on the west side is the Fifth Avenue Presbyterian; beyond it are those of St. Thomas's (Protestant-Episcopal), Collegiate Church of St. Nicholas (Dutch Reformed), and, dimly in the background, the Brick Presbyterian and the Marble Collegiate (Dutch Reformed). These churches are still standing (1935); but St. Thomas's has been rebuilt after it was partially destroyed by fire.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 58th Street
text:
A Set of Seven Canvases of Old New York.

These paintings come from a country house called 'Glencairn' near Dublin in Ireland, where they adorned the walls of the billiard room. The house was built by Richard 'Boss' Croker (1841-1922), an Irishman who for many years was associated with Tammany Hall in New York, holding political positions under William M. 'Boss' Tweed, and later, after the latter's ousting, under 'Honest John' Kelly. Following the Lexow Committee investigations (1889-90), he left for England where he took up residence in Wantage, Berks., returning to America periodically, attempting to regain his lost position in the Democratic Party. After his final defeat in 1900, he crossed the Atlantic once again, built 'Glencairn' and started a racing stable. Despite his past reputation (he paid, in all, $550,000 for his Irish estates), he lived up to the high standards demanded by British racing circles, and when his horse Orby won the Derby in 1907, did not even back him.

These pictures were painted to remind him of New York, and it is assumed that they were executed here around the turn of the century. All are painted in tones of sepia and green.

The British Government has recently acquired this mansion for the use of the British Ambassador to Ireland.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - [Between 61st and 64th Streets]
text:
Town houses of Fifth Avenue in the East Seventies.
[Unidentified as to exact location]

A Set of Seven Canvases of Old New York

These paintings come from a country house called 'Glencairn' near Dublin in Ireland, where they adorned the walls of the billiard room. The house was built by Richard 'Boss' Croker (1841-1922), an Irishman who for many years was associated with Tammany Hall in New York, holding political positions under William M. 'Boss' Tweed, and later, after the latter's ousting, under 'Honest John' Kelly. Following the Lexow Committee investigations (1889-90), he left for England where he took up residence in Wantage, Berks., returning to America periodically, attempting to regain his lost position in the Democratic Party. After his final defeat in 1900, he crossed the Atlantic once again, built 'Glencairn' and started a racing stable. Despite his past reputation (he paid, in all, $550,000 for his Irish estates), he lived up to the high standards demanded by British racing circles, and when his horse Orby won the Derby in 1907, did not even back him.
These pictures were painted to remind him of New York, and it is assumed that they were executed here around the turn of the century. All are painted in tones of sepia and green.
The British Government has recently acquired this mansion for the use of the British Ambassador to Ireland.

This organization was formerly located at the N.E. corner of Fifth Avenue and East 43rd Street in a synagogue erected in 1868. Their earlier meetings were held in the Grand Street Court-room (1845 to 1850). Subsequently they purchased a former church on Chrystie Street and remodelled same for their purpose (1850 to 1856). Built in 1875 from funds donated by James Lenox, whose collection of books, manuscripts, missels (?),incunabula, etc., was made in this way available to the public, it stood until around 1912; when the library was consolidated with the Astor Library to form the New York Public Library.
The building was then demolished, and the mansion of Henry Clay Frick erected on the site.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 70th Street
text:
The Lenox Library, Fifth Avenue, east side, from 70th to 71st Streets. This library was founded by a wealthy and eccentric bibliophile and collector who, after arousing considerable public feeling by refusing to let the historian Prescott consult certain documents in his collection suddenly opened his library to the public and created a trust fund to assure its continuation after his death. The Lenox Library has combined with the Astor and Tilden foundations to form the New York Public Library, and will move into the new building, which is now under construction on the site of the Fifth Avenue reservoir, around 1910.

Henry Clay Frick will build his mansion on this site, and in 1935 this mansion will be converted into a public art gallery.

1905.

August Loeffler, from P. L. Sperr Collection.

This facade is a replacement,stone by stone, of the front of the old United States Assay Building on Wall Street, recently torn down, and originally built in 1824

The south facade of the American Wing. Formerly the facade of the U.S. Branch Bank, and later of the U.S. Assay Office, at 15 Wall Street. It was built about 1822-24 by a well-known New York architect, W.S. Thompson. Torn down in 1914, the stones numbered and stored, and re-erected at the museum.

title: Manhattan : 6th Avenue - Bleecker Street.
text:
Sixth Avenue-Extension, south from Bleecker Street, showing the slice-through that eliminated Hancock Street from Manhattan maps. Under construction is the Municipal subway. The center foreground was the former site of the R. C. Church of Our Lady of Pompeii (St. Carlos Missionary Fathers). On the left are several six story apartment houses, that formerly bore No's. 1-3, 5-7 and 9-13 Hancock Street. These will remain, acquiring 6th Avenue identities. On the extreme right is the rear of the Downing Street site, upon which in 1941 will rise a modern apartment structure, No. 10 Downing Street. The new west line of the Avenue will run there, forming the easterly side of this building plot. The partially demolished 6-story structures shown there front on West Houston Street. They will remain. Through the center is Congress Street, a short thoroughfare extending south of West Houston to King Street. This is to be included in the new thoroughfare.

P. L. Sperr

May 12, 1927

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - Waverly Place
text:
Sixth Avenue, east side, north of Waverly Place, showing two 3-story structures that were formerly No. 80 and 82. The first is reputed to have been at one time "The Allens" a notorious gambling place. The store's last tenent was the wholesale hotel chinaware firm of R. Seccos and Sons. View 2 shows the cleared site of this and adjoining buildings. The rear tenements are at the back of NO's 58-60 W. 8th St. The "Allen" location would be on the extreme right margin, abutting the side wall of the Van Voorst, the 9-story apartment house at No. 123-5 Waverly Place. Overhead appears the distinctive elevation of the apartment dwelling identified as No. 1 Fifth Avenue.

P. L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - 9th Street
text:
(1)
Sixth Avenue, east side, at 9th Street, showing the new West Side Savings Bank building (erected 1928) on the N.E. corner of 9th Street. It contains the entrance to the Hudson and Manhattan railroad to New Jersey.
In the foreground is shown part of the old Jefferson Market Court House building and the excavation caused by demolition of the old Jefferson Market and construction of the municipal subway. On this site the new House of Detention for Women is to be built. To the right is the 8th Street Station of the Sixth Avenue Elevated Line.
On the skyline in the left of the picture are 55 Fifth Avenue, the Consolidated Gas building on 14th Street east of Irving Place, and the tower of the new 40 Fifth Avenue apartment building on the S.W. corner of 11th Street. In the right background may be seen the new One Fifth Avenue apartment hotel at 8th Street, and the skeleton of the new apartment building under construction at 1 University Place, opposite the N.E. corner of Washington Square.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)
The same, a closer view.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - Christopher Street
text:
Sixth Avenue, west side, at the convergence of Christopher Street and Greenwich Avenue, showing, a diner at the southerly apex, both the new Detention House for Women at the northerly apex, opposite the W. 8th Street "El" Station. The clock tower seen is atop the Jefferson Market Court.

View No. 2 is northwestward from a vantage point on the east side of the Avenue, near Waverly Place. In this instance the "El" has been partially razed. Note the iron grille near the curbing. This is a ventilator shaft for the new subway which at this date is under construction.

January 7, 1939.
View 2: February 19, 1939.

(3)

A view similar to No. 2 several months later. The Times of April 4, 1939 reports the renaming of this open area as "Village Square" under local legislation introduced by Councilman Howard H. Spellman. This was arrived at in a contest among villagers conducted by the Sixth Avenue Association.

It was formerly known as "Jefferson Market Square" and is at the intersection of Eighth Street, Christopher Street, Greenwich Avenue and Sixth Avenue.

May 19, 1939

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - 18th Street (West)
text:
Sixth Avenue, south from West 18th Street, showing this newly recovered Manhattan thoroughfare. The old "El" structure that formerly occupied this zone has been demolished and a municipal subway constructed underground. Prior to the first World War (1917-18) this was the shopping center of the City. Extending from 14th to 23rd Street it later removed to 34th Street. The former Macy Department Store building is clearly apparent in the center of View 1. This is the large building at 14th Street that has two water tanks atop its roof.

View 2 is limited to several of the buildings on the left of the preceding photo. They lie between 17th and 18th Streets. No. 600 (old No. 278) now occupied by the Liberty Shoe Company was formerly the McCrorey Building. The Price and Company Building is self-obvious.

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - 18th Street (West)
text:
Sixth Avenue, north from and across West 18th Street, showing mainly the west side of this Avenue.  The corner building with the A. Shulte store was formerly part of Altman's Department Store. This bears No. 615-9 Sixth Avenue and is at the N.W. corner of W. 18th Street.  The store covered the entire block front from 18th to 19th Streets.  The New York Times of March 7, 1939 reports the 1st transfer of this holding since 1817 when it was acquired as farmlands by John Tonnele. He left it in trust for John L. Tonnele who died at the age of 86 years and the tract passed in 1918 to the present sellers.
In making the title search, numerous difficulties arouse because of the inaccurate definitions of boundaries when streets were originally put through, encroachments due to faulty surveys, etc. necessitating a large amount of negotiation finally to clear up the fee.
The Astor interests own the balance of the block front and the combined holdings were divided into two units, of which the southerly portion has now been sold.
March 29, 1939

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - 24th Street (West)
text:
725-727 Sixth Ave., west side, south of, and adjoining the S.W. corner of West 24th Street, showing (No. 725) the Sixth Ave. "Playground". It is provided with a rifle range, many slot-machine games, and cheap recorded music, as a diversion for people with not too fine an appreciation of good entertainment. It is similar to many such places found in Coney Ialsnd.

December 24, 1936.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - 24th Street (West)
text:
Sixth Avenue, south from W. 24th Street, showing the "El" structure and its 23rd Street station undergoing demolition. The 19 story office structure at the left (No. 71 W. 23rd Street) is owned and partially occupied by the Masons. On the opposite corner (S.E.) is a 6 story loft building standing on the former site of Booths Theatre. The low units on the west side of this thoroughfare, between 23rd and 24th streets are nondescript, though the corner building at 24th Street identifies itself as being formerly Koster & Bials. This sign is out into the cornice roofing and does not appear here. An additional sign does, bearing "The Corner". The Koster & Bials Concert Hall of the 1890's was located around the corner at 15 W. 23rd Street and this may have been an annex. Two doors to the south is a structure containing a penny arcade, "Playland". This, the writer believes is one of the last, if not the last, of many similar and popular venture.

February 19, 1939

F.L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - 29th Street (West)
text:

Construction of the 6t Avenue subway system imposed an engineering problem under this point. New platforms were constructed and the underground tubes entwined.
The old 6th Avenue "E1" system will be discontinued and the structure demolished in 1939.
Note the hotel McAlpin at the right center.

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - 31st Street (West)
text:
Sixth Avenue, north from a point between W. 31st and 32nd Streets, and across the latter to Greeley Square, showing Manhattan's famous shopping center. At the left margin are Gimbels and Saks department stores.

The modern white center structure is the Herald Square Building and was erected several years ago. This site formerly was occupied by the Herald and which in turn had succeeded the old 71st Reg. Armory. To the right is the Hotel McAlpin.

View No. 2 is photographed from the S.W. corner of 32nd Street and shows Greeley Square cluttered with subway building materials. The "El" structure and its 33rd Street station will be demolished in the latter part of March and Easter will see the entire Sixth Avenue "El" completely relegated to the past.

February 18, 1939

P. L. Sperr

The same after removal of "El".

P. L. Sperr

September 7, 1940

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - 32nd Street (West)
text:
Sixth Avenue, west side, north from West 32nd Street. At this date the old "El" line has been demolished though the south-bound station remains. This is at 33rd Street and provides an entrance to the two department stores here, Gimbels and Saks, through an enclosed bridgeway. After the amicable adjustment by these stores, the Hudson Tube officials, the City and the "El" line authorities, the station will be removed. Beyond same appears the dominant Herald Square Building.

View 1: March 29, 1939
View 2: April 5, 1939

P. L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - Broadway
text:
Sixth Avenue and Broadway, north from W. 33rd Street, showing the "El" tracks upon the numerical Avenue. To the right is the diagonal Broadway. 34th Street is where the Broadway Tabernacle appears. The distinctive Herald Building is north of 35th Street, separating Broadway (left) from 6th Avenue. At the left is the southbound platform obstructing the sign that identifies Jim Corbett's Saloon. The latter was a world's heavyweight boxing champion.

1899

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - 34th Street (West)
text:
(1)
6th Avenue, south from W. 34th Street, showing the "El" structure and its 33rd Street Station. This was mainly patronized by shoppers to Gimbels, Sak's and Macys. The first two of these enterprises appear here occupying the 34th - 33rd and 33rd-32nd Street frontages. Note the interstore bridge connecting these.
Views 2 and 3 show the absence of the "El" and the station remaining. This will remain for about a month and then join the balance of this structure. Underground, at this date, the 6th Avenue Subway is under construction. At the left is Broadway, which intersects with 6th Avenue and leaves two triangular parks; the southerly of which (Greeley Square) appears partially here.
Views 1,2 and 3:April 5, 1939.
P.L.Sperr

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - Broadway
text:
Sixth Avenue and Broadway, north from West 34th Street, showing the subway construction shaft occupying the former park site that was identified as Herald Square. This received its name from the newspaper plant above. One-half of this site still contains the low original building, the remainder being improved with the towering Herald Square Building.

Broadway is on the left and 6th Avenue on the right. The former thoroughfare is the vantage point for the photographer in view 2 and from which he is viewing north-eastward towards the office building at the N. E. corner of 6th Avenue and W. 35th Street.

View 1: March 29, 1939
View 2: February 18, 1939

P. L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - 43rd Street (West)
text:
Sixth Avenue, east side, from West 43rd
to 44th Street's, showing prominently the old Hippodrome. This structure erected about 1912, housed many famous productions, from pageants to talking pictures. Famous artists including Paderewski have played here. In 1922, Richard Strauss conducted a series of concerts with the Philadelphia Orchestra. Prior to its demolition in the Fall of 1939, it was a motion picture house. Various sport affairs wore held here.
View 1: March 9, 1929
2: May 27, 1930
3: May 1, 1933

text:
1220 to 1236 Sixth Avenue, east side, north from W. 48th to 49th Streets, showing a row of structures, several slightly improved and the Center Theatre. title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - 48th Street
text:
1220 to 1230 Sixth Avenue, at adjoining and north of the N.E. corner of W. 48th Street. All of these structures appear in View 1 while No.2 shows only three, No's. 1220 to 1224.

At the rear of these buildings the R.K.O. Center Theatre is being erected. The Sixth Avenue "El" line in April 1939 will have disappeared and the brownstone buildings at this site ready for demolition.

The New York Times of April 3, 1939 reports the immediate erection of a 20 story Rockefeller Center structure on this site, same consummating this vast midtown commercial and amusement center which started in 1931.

Occupancy is scheduled for March 1, 1940. An interesting feature will be the overlapping of the new building at the 8th floor on the steel work of the Center Theatre. The theatre was constructed with this provision in mind.

March 18, 1932
Views: 1-2

P. L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - 48th Street (West)
text:
Sixth Avenue, east side, north from W. 48th Street, showing prominently the excavation for the new Rodkefëler Center Building. This is at the N. E. corner and is to be titled "the U.S. Rubber Co. Building." The enclosure is provided for the public who, as quite obvious, enjoy watching the foundation construction. The publicity agent capitalized on this quirk and had the fence lettered "Sidewalk Superintendents Club". The insignia is titled, "De.beste stuurlin staan an wal", which translated is "The best pilots stand on the shore". This originated with the Netherlands Building, an adjoining Rockefeller Center unit.

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - 53nd Street (West)
text:
Sixth Avenue, west side, at W. 53rd Street as viewed north-westward from 52nd Street. Formerly this corner was darkened by the old 6th Avenue "El" which made a 90° bend to run west on 53rd Street. The vacant lot at the left has recently been cleared by the demolition of a 4-story frame building with a brick front. The adjoining 5-story tenement is being removed in Views 2 and 3. This bears No. 1309 (old No. 927) Sixth Avenue. At the left margin, in the later view, is the 6-story dwelling that is to be razed and its site improved by a modern apartment structure. This is to be the first major development on the avenue. For details and the architects' drawing--see New York Times of January 7, 1940 and the Herald Tribune of January 21, 1940 and the New York Sun of March 19, 1939.

title: Manhattan: 7th Avenue South - Grove Street
text:
Seventh Avenue South, east side, and 76-70 Grove Street, at and south of the Sheridan Square subway station at West 4th Street. The subway entrance is in a little island which used to be the N.W. corner of Grove (formerly Burrows Street, originally Columbia Street) and West 4th (formerly Asylum Street) Streets. Sheridan Square (q.v.) is properly the triangular open space shown here in the left background, but it is loosely applied to both sides of Seventh Avenue South, from Christopher to Grove Streets, inclusive.
About 1928.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: 7th Avenue - 24th Street
text:
An Unfortunate Incident in a Great Engineering Task

(The scene is Seventh Ave., N.Y.C., at Twenty-fourth St., just after an explosion has caused the street to collapse for an entire block. It is particularly interesting as showing graphically how the metropolis is being honeycombed for its underground transportation system. In order not to interfere with the ordinary use of the streets during the three years necessary to complete the work, the tunneling method is used rather than open excavation work. For a long period after the earth has been dug up and before the steel & concrete work is completed, the surface of the street is merely boards propped up by wooden beams. An extra-heavy blast, with perhaps other contributing factors, caused the supports to collapse, and the whole street - with its occupants, including a crowded street car - dropped to the bottom. Seven persons were killed & scores seriously injured. There are forty-five miles of subway under construction in New York, one line being under the most important & congested thoroughfare, Broadway. Three days after the accident shown in this illustration, a second one - somewhat less serious - occurred on Broadway)

North of 42nd Street this thoroughfare loses it's identity, becoming a portion of Times Square: the buildings on all sides bearing Broadway addresses. This structure adjoins the low building at the S.W. corner of 42nd Street. On the opposite corner (N.W.) is the Rialto Theatre. title: Manhattan: 7th Avenue - 58th Street
text:
Seventh Avenue (right to left), east side, north from W. 58th (right) to Central Park South (actually W. 59th Street), showing the westerly side of that group of buildings that were known as the "Spanish Flats". They were erected at a cost of $4,000,000 by de Navarro, the father-in-law of Mary Anderson the actress, and were considered unsurpassable, consisting of 8 units: The Madrid, Granada, Lisbon, Cordova, Barcelona, Valencia, Salamanca and Tolosa.
These structures were demolished in 1928 and the site built upon by the present New York Athletic Club.
Central Park is on the left side and does not appear as the photographer is viewing north eastward from the S.W. corner of Seventh Avenue and W. 58th Street.

April 1925.

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - 48th - 51st Street
text:
Sixth Avenue (across the center, from left to right margin and with Elevated Line thereon), from West 48th to 51st Streets, as viewed northwestward from a point at W.48th Street near Fifth Avenue. Shown is the Rockefeller (Radio) Center excavation extending between the aforementioned thoroughfares. At the far corner is the R.K.O. Bldg, under construction. The 70 storied R.C.A. Bldg. will rise in the westerly portion of the center clearance between the two corner tenements. To the south of the latter will be built the Center Theatre. The dwellings in the left foreground were subsequently demolished leaving a vacant space which until 1933 was used as a Parking lot. In October of that year plans were filed for the Netherland Bldg. Across the skyline appears structures forming the Times Square-Broadway-Central Park -Columbus Circle area and composed mainly of hotels; prominent of which are the: Bristol, Maryland, Plymouth, Taft, Park-Central and Essex House. These extend across the view, from left to right and are easily identified, having signs bearing their names.

Wurts Bros.

December 16, 1931.

title: Manhattan: 7th Avenue - 150th Street
text:
Seventh Ave., north from about West 150th Street, to the Central Bridge West 155th Street. A panoramic view of the new U.S. Government slum clearance and housing project in Harlem; a local subdivision of Manhattan and bordering onto the Harlem River. This scene consists of 3 views; each a continuation of the other, and showing mainly the development on the east side of Seventh Ave. View No. 1 being mainly the area comprising 152nd to 155th Streets; view No. 2, 151st to 152nd Street; and view No. 3, 151st to 150th Street. West 150th Street is the northern boundry of the Interborough Rapid Transit Car Yard. Across the Harlem River is shown the Borough of Bronx, with the Yankee Stadium south of the bridge.

September 19, 1936.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: 8th Avenue - Horatio Street
text:
Eighth Avenue, south from Horatio Street, showing mainly the easterly side of same. The photographer is viewing towards Abingdon Square where the dominant 16-story apartment house appears. This bears No. 20 Abingdon Square and is at the S. E. corner of W. 12th Street.

Returning to the foreground one observes the diagonal sweep of W. 4th Street across the Avenue, this is on right and running to the left center. This leaves a triangular block in the center, the apex of which touches upon Jane Street. The latter, though not seen, runs in a horizontal plane across the midground and is obstructed from view by the buildings at the right and left.

P. L. Sperr

April 9, 1940

text:

Across same is a row of buildings on the north side of W. 12th Street. These will be removed for the new apartment house site identified as No. 299 W. 12th Street. Buildings on the right and beyond the street car, extend from this street to Jane Street. These are to remain.

title: Manhattan: 8th Avenue - Hudson Street
text:
Eighth Avenue, north from Hudson Street, showing in the foreground the Abingdon Square area. The Park identifying same is at the left. In the background, at 14th Street, appears the County Trust Company Building.

View 2 is the same area several years later and showing the new apartment houses that have sprung up around the Square. At the left is the 20 story building, No. 299 W. 12th Street. On the right is the 16-story structure, No. 20 Abingdon Square. On the margin one observes the 6-story residential building that replaced the former Abingdon Hotel (demolished 1931) and adjacent homes.

The last is the latest of all three, having recently been completed. The other two were finished in 1931.

title: Manhattan: 8th Avenue - Hudson Street
text:
Eighth Avenue, north from Hudson Street (left and foreground) showing the Abingdon Square locale and its towering apartment houses. title: Manhattan: 8th Avenue - 155th Street (West)
text:
Eighth Avenue, at West 155th Street, showing various aspects of this locale. View No. 1 is northward along the line of the Avenue showing the "El" trains thereupon. At the left is the baseball park, the Polo Grounds. View No. 2 is eastward showing the viaduct carrying 155th Street over this point. In the background is the Bronx shore of the Harlem River. Beyond the 155th Street Bridge appears the super structures of the Yankee Stadium and the new Borough Hall Building. No. 3 is limited to the viaduct entrances to the "El" at the left and the Street at the right. The view is northward. Note High Bridge is the distance.

title: Manhattan: 9th Avenue - Gansevoort Street
text:
Ninth Avenue, at Gansevoort Street, showing the curve in the first "El" line at this point. Emerging out of Greenwich Street, it continues northward to 29th Street. The view in this instance is southwestward silhouetting the steel framework against the limited west frontage lying between Gansevoort and Little West 12th Street. The last thoroughfare is on the right. Note the flag poles at the corners of same. For additional views of this early phase of the Charles C. Harvey line, see Ninth Avenue at 29th Street, and Greenwich Street at Dey Street.

1867-8

Gift of Major Quinn

title: Manhattan: 9th Avenue - Gansevoort Street
text:
Ninth Avenue, at Gansevoort Street, showing the "El" curve at this point after its emergence out of Greenwich Street. The photographer is viewing southward from a point slightly above Little West 12th Street. The latter appears at the right. Note the drum like apparatus required to continue the wire cable. This method of locomotion was replaced with small steam locomotives.

1867-8

Gift of Major Quinn

title: Manhattan: 9th Avenue - 18th Street
text:
Nos. 122 to 112 Ninth Ave., at, adjoining and south of the S.E. corner of West 18th Street, showing a row of frame structures that nearly occupy the entire block front from 18th to 17th Streets and which will be demolished according to the New York Times of May 9, 1938 as a portion of planned site of a modern 6-story apartment house. This will rise on a plot 100 x 130 feet and will include two 4-story brick houses Nos. 366 and 364 West 18th Street; the side wall of one of these appearing on the extreme left of view No. 1. Views 2 and 3 show portions of this wooden row, some of which have brick fronts. This property has been sold by the Emigrant Industrial Savings Bank to the 364 West 18th Street Corporation for $100,000 through Eugene J. Busher Company, who arranged a building loan of $175,000 for ten years to finance the improvement.

Views 1 & 3:- March 12, 1933.
View 2:- March 7, 1929.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: 9th Avenue - 18th Street
text:
Ninth Avenue, east side, at 18th Street. The houses in this picture from No. 112 in the right foreground to No. 128 on the N. E. corner of 18th Street are frame structures which will stand in 1934. McParland's Malt and Hops Store, in the centre, is an interesting product of the rapidly dying prohibition era. Stores such as this, selling ingredients and equipment for home brewing, were legion; but the advent of legal beer on April 7, 1933, was a blow which most of them failed to survive.

1932.

J. Clarence Davies Collection, Museum of the City of New York.

title: Manhattan: 9th Avenue - 18th Street (West)
text:
Ninth Avenue, east side, north from W. 18th Street (right, not seen), showing a general view of this west side area with one of its arterial transportation lines. Several new apartment buildings are contemplated which will cause radical changes in its contour; one such seen is at the N.E. corner of W. 20th Street. To the right in No. 1 appears a portion of the huge Textile High School. This property, north of 19th Street, and extending to Eighth Avenue, was formerly the easterly part of the Clement C. title: Manhattan: 9th Avenue - 31st Street (West)
text:
Ninth Avenue, east side, north from West 31st to 33rd St's., showing the Pennsylvania Railroad yards to the rear of the General Post Office. The latter faces on Eighth Avenue. West 33rd Street is on the far side, containing the rears of the Y. M. C. A.'s. Sloan House and the J. C. Penney Bldg. Adjoining the last is the Glad Tidings Assembly. The old Manhattan Opera House and the Hotel New Yorker, both on 34th Street near Eighth Avenue, project above the roof of the latter. In the center background is the dominant McGraw-Hill Bldg. on West 42nd Street. The photographers vantage point is given as the Sears Roebuck Bldg. at the S.E. corner of Ninth Avenue and West 31st Street.

About 1933

Bernice Abbott

title: Manhattan: 10th Avenue - 14th Street (West)
text:
Tenth Avenue, north from West 14th Street, showing the thoroughfare that is popularly known as "Railroad or Death Avenue." Train tracks in the foreground determined that appellation. At the left, are the National Biscuit Co. Building and the Merchants Refrigerating Co. plant. The former also occupy the structure on the right. The one story garage between 14th and 15th Sts. has only recently been completed.

July 24, 1924

Standard Photographic Service
Gift of Borough President of Manhattan

Seen a cross the same are the structures of the Merchants Refrigerating Company and the National Biscuit Company between 17th and 15th Streets. These are emphasized in No. 3. Note the diesel drawn train using the street bed. This feature has now been eliminated and such trains run on the raised tracks seen in No. 1.
View No. 2 is similar to the preceding from a point slightly southward and shows demolition debris on the 19th to 18th Streets block front. Note also the Railroad yard between 18th and 17th Streets.

title: Manhattan: 11th Avenue - West Street
text:
11th Avenue, north from its beginning at West and Gansevoort Streets. In the foreground is the Gansevoort Market Stand. To the left are the distinctive buildings that constitute West Washington Market. Beyond are the Hudson (North) River municipal piers that line the west side of 11th Avenue. The 11-story utilitarian structure on the right is the National Biscuit Company plant. This extends between 10th and 11th Avenues. Incidentally the latter thoroughfare begins here; converging with 11th at Delamater Square (foot of W. 13th Street).

P. L. Sperr

View #2 - Neg # 2632

title: Manhattan: 11th Avenue - 21st Street (West)
text:

text:
Eleventh Avenue, north from W. 32nd Street and showing a New York Central Railroad freight car turning into the milk shed yard on the eastern side of the Avenue. Note the cobblestone condition of this thoroughfare which, popularly was called "railroad" or "death" Avenue; the latter because of the dangers involved in the juxtaposition of railroad, horse and foot traffic. In 1938 this feature was eliminated as then the railroad cut was opened to direct this freightage from the open street. Photographs of same will be found under individual locations and the West Side Improvement Project.

text: 11th Avenue, north from W 34th street showing this thoroughfare prior to the removal of railroad equipment and its general rehabilitation. title: Manhattan: 11th Avenue - 34th Street
text:
11th Avenue, north from W. 34th Street, showing prominently the westerly side of this thoroughfare. At the left, occupying the 34th to 35th Street frontage is the former Manhattan Market of 1871. This has been reduced to a one story building in View 1 and partially removed in View 2. The street sides will come down in 1938 and thereby clear the entire block.
In the midground are buildings at 36th Street. The largest is the Williams Printing House. This occupies the 36th to 37th Street frontage and will remain; those to its rear being removed in May 1938.
Note the towering R. H. Macy and Company warehouse on the right. The lower stories are being reconstructed to permit an underground railway to pass through its basement on its way under 11th Avenue.

title: Manhattan: 11th Avenue - 34th Street (West)
text:
Eleventh Ave. (foreground), from West 34th (right), to 36th (left) Streets, showing work in progress for the New York Central Railroad's track removal project as a part of the West Side Improvement, viewed in a southeastward direction from the latter point and westward of the Avenue. At the left foreground is a part of the old Eleventh Ave. grade, over which the railroad operated for Eighty-eight years. Note that the present Avenue is elevated about ten feet and about one-third of this extension being shown in this view; the new yard tracks passing underneath same and connecting the southern two and one-half mile stretch with the rook cut bed. Undergoing remodeling is the old R.H. Macy warehouse at the N.E. corner of the Avenue and West 25th Street.

Gift of New York Central System, Publicity Bureau.

title: Manhattan: 11th Avenue - 35th Street (West)
text:
Eleventh Ave., south from West 35th Street, showing work progressing on the track removal project of the New York Central Railroad at this point. Note the steel bridgelike structure on the easterly side of the thoroughfare that will raise this Avenue ten feet above its former level and permit the railroad tracks to pass underneath, connecting the trackage in the rock cut with the yard layout on the westerly side of the Avenue. Appearing on the left, at the N.E. corner of the Avenue and West 35th Street is the old R.H. Macy Warehouse undergoing structural renovation to further this work and permit freight handling facilities to its future tenants under Railroad ownership. 1937.

Gift of New York Central System
Publicity Bureau.

title: Manhattan: 11th Avenue - 34th Street (West)
text:
Eleventh Ave. (center, fore to background), south from West 35th Street, showing constructional aspects of the track removal program of the New York Central Railroad as their portion of the West Side Improvement Project. The photographer's vantage point is the former R.H. Macy warehouse at 35th Street and he shows about one-third of the Eleventh Ave. stretch and one-half of the 34th Street stretch elevated to their new levels. This will be continued southward on the Avenue for an additional 5 blocks and the yard tracks that now cross it at grade will be rebuilt several feet below their present grade and on a radically different pattern. title: Manhattan: 11th Avenue - 56th Street
text:
Eleventh Ave. (right, foreground), east side, south from West 57th (left, foreground) to 56th Streets, showing the foundation of the New Sheffield Farms plant under construction. The New York Central Railroad tracks shown will be enclosed and two private sidings built for the sole service of this company. The buildings shown to the left and at the rear of this clearance will shortly be demolished and their sites added to permit this ultra modern milk plant to extend to its full length of 550 feet. The photographer is viewing in a southeastward direction to show silhouetted against the sky the 42nd Street and Times Square building outline.

Gift of New York Central System Publicity Bureau.

1937.

title: Manhattan: 11th Avenue - 56th Street

Beneath same runs the new road bed of the New York Central Railroad which appears on the right emerging at a tangent to cross the Avenue to the 60th Street yards. The old plant to the rear of this new building will be razed and the new structure extended shortly. Two private railroad sidings service this enterprise.

July 24, 1937.

Gift of New York Central System
Publicity Bureau.

title: Manhattan: 12th Avenue - 43rd Street
text: Twelfth Avenue, west side, at West 43rd Street, showing street activity outside of the pier that formerly housed the Hamburg - American Steamship Line. The photographer states the line consists of relief recipients awaiting their dole for the work performed by them at Bear Mountain Palisade Park. This was a phase of the local experiment under the C.W.A. It was replaced with the direct government directed projects under the W.P.A. August 29, 1933. P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: 12th Avenue - 55th Street
text:
Twelfth Avenue, at the N.E. corner of W. 55th Street, showing the 6 story Rishel Building at that location. Behind same appears the smoke stack of the Dept. of Sanitation. This civic unit in 1937 will have a modern incinerator plant here occupying the entire avenue frontage from 57th to 55th Streets. The photographer is viewing north eastward across Twelfth Avenue from the river side of same.

title: Manhattan: 1st Street - Avenue A
text:
(1)
1st Street, north side, between Avenue A and First Avenue, seen from the clearing at the S.E. corner of Houston and Ludlow Streets. The small structure is a new Synagogue and the spire in the background belongs to St. Nicholas Roman Catholic Church, on 2nd Street.
The building in the right foreground is 222 East Houston Street. That and four more houses not shown in the picture are all that remains of a long triangular block between Houston and 1st Streets. The rest of the buildings have been demolished in constructing the new subway, as have the houses that stood on the clearing in the foreground.
Neg: 2911 March 13, 1932
P.L. Sperr.

(2)
A closer and more restricted view of the same scene, seen from the S.W. corner of Ludlow and Houston Streets. The clearing is for a Brooklyn line of the city-owned Eighth Avenue subway. In No. 2 the tower with the cross is part of the Roman Catholic Church of the Holy Redeemer at 161 East 3rd Street.
February 23, 1932
P.L. Sperr.

text:
East 2nd Street, east from the Bowery and showing a gasoline station under construction at the S.E. corner. title: Manhattan: 3rd Street (East) - New Dorp Lane
text:
J. M. BERLINGER, R.A.
ARCHITECT
17 EAST 49TH STREET
NEW YORK CITY
PLAZA 3-5256-7

November 17, 1941

The first Garden Apartment alteration on the lower East Side in a section where such an innovation would be considered as unwise is proving, as anticipated by Mr. Samuel Fassler, the owner, to be a fast renting proposition. The buildings are located at 302-304 East 3rd Street and go through to the next block on East 2nd Street with very attractive gardens in between.

Contrary to the general opinion of real estate experts who claim that it is practically impossible to procure increased rents from this type of tenant for garden facilities, leases are being signed for these suites consisting of three and four rooms in the development at rentals at least ten percent higher than for comparable recently modernized apartments without gardens in the same neighborhood.

Mr. Robert Moses, Park Commissioner accompanied by Commissioner Wilson of the Department of Housing and Buildings, made a recent inspection of this rehabilitation as he is very much interested in reclamation of our City's slums and advocates gardens with as many modernization operations as possible.

J. M. Berlinger of 17 East 49th Street, New York City, was the architect and the contractor, Ernest Callipari, has just completed the work which cost $100,000.00 for the entire job.

J. M. Berlinger

title: Manhattan: 4th Street - Christopher Street
text:
4th Street (to the left) north from Christopher Street, at Seventh Avenue South. This part of 4th Street is an old Village street, shown on an 1803 map as Chester Street and on the 1811 city survey (when the numbered streets and avenues were first planned) as William Street. Before long, however, the true 4th Street on the East Side was extended to this point, and that number was applied to this street all the way to its terminus at 13th and
Gansevoort Streets, west of Eighth Avenue.
The block on the east side of 4th Street, from Christopher to 10th (formerly Amos) Streets, was broken up when Seventh Avenue South was cut through around 1914. All that was left west of Seventh Avenue South were Nos. 229-31 West 4th Street, shown in this picture with the Sinclair Motor 0il advertisement on the side of 229. The building shown in part on the left is the new one built in 1931 on the site of the Greenwich Village Theatre, which itself was built on the old N.W. corner of 4th and Christopher Streets after Seventh
Avenue South was cut through.
233 West 4th Street, on the N.E. corner of 10th Street, is a fairly
new apartment house.
March 25, 1933.
P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: 4th Street - Washington Place
text:
4th Street (right), and Washington Place (left), east from Grove Street, showing also Sheridan Square in the foreground. Sheridan Square is a triangle with its apex pointing west and located at the western end of Washington Place (originally West 5th Street); the northern side is the northern side of Washington Place, and the southern side follows the line of West 4th Street (formerly Asylum Street). Sheridan Square house numbers begin on the short eastern side, which was originally the eastern end of Reason Street (now the eastern section of Barrow Street, q.v.), and follow in order clockwise around Sheridan Square.

P. L. Sperr.

June 24, 1933.

title: Manhattan: 4th Street - 10th Street
text:
4th Street, north from 10th Street (a little to the west of Seventh Avenue South). The car track in the foreground is the west-bound track of the 8th Street crosstown line. This intersection at right angles of two theoretically parallel streets (it also occurs at 4th and 11th and 4th and 12th Streets) is something Greenwich Villagers sometimes take great glee in calling attention to. This part of 4th Street is one of the old Village streets; it was once called William Street, but has been known as Fourth Street since the first quarter of the 19th Century, forming as it does a continuation of the true 4th Street on the East Side. After the Civil War, three of the cross streets, which happened to coincide at Greenwich Avenue with 10th, 11th, and 12th Streets, lost their old names and took these numbers instead. The 5-story apartment house at the N.E. corner of 10th Street (formerly Amos Street) is only a few years old. April 3, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: 8th Street - 5th Avenue
text:
15-13-11-9 East 8th Street (formerly 53-59 Clinton Place), north side, east of Fifth Avenue.
13 East 8th Street (formerly 55 Clinton Place), the house with the large vine, has been for some years the home of Richard Watson Glider, author and Editor-in-Chief (since 1881) of The Century Magazine, who will continue to reside here till his death, in 1909. Eighth Street, west of Broadway, used to be called Clinton Place, the houses being numbered west from Broadway. The name and numbering was changed in 1899. As may be seen in this picture, the street has already lost its residential character. Nearly thirty years later this scene will not have changed greatly. Mr. Glider's house will have been remodelled like No. 9; the parlor store will be occupied by Fred Leighton's Indian Trading Post, and the basement by a gown shop and an interior decorator.

April 11, 1906.

Brown Brothers.

title: Manhattan: 8th Street - University Place
text:

The building on the S.E. corner of University Place used to be the Merck Building, erected about 1895, replacing three old residences facing 8th Street (then known as Clinton Place). West from University Place, on the south side, are old houses remodelled into apartments, owned by Sailors Snug Harbor; Beyond them towers One Fifth Avenue, on the S.E. corner, built around 1926. In the background may be seen the Sixth Avenue Elevated station, at the western end of 8th Street. In the right foreground may be seen shops of various kinds, on the north side of the street.

The Germania was originally St. Ann's Roman Catholic Church; it was converted into a theatre in 1879. It was known as Amberg's in 1885 and as the Eighth Street Theatre, a Hebrew playhouse, around

title: Manhattan: 8th Street (East) - 4th Avenue
text:
East 8th Street, at, adjoining and west of the N. W. corner of 4th Avenue, as seen from Astor Place (foreground) at Lafayette Street. The corner building mentioned (extreme right) bears No. 38 4th Avenue in the Perris, New York Insurance Map of 1854. Adjoining same is St. Ann's R. C. Church, with No's. 145, 143 and 141, progressing westward to Broadway. Across the background appears the new A. T. Stewart Building, which today (1937) is the north unit of Wanamaker's. The south unit being raised on the area occupied as shown in this view, exclusive of No. 38 4th Avenue and adjacent. In 1879, a Jacob Aberle converted the church building into a variety theatre, known as the 8th Street Theatre. About 1890, performances were given in Hebrew by native actors. It was called the Germania and German Theatre in 1897 and 1902 respectively. About 1905 it formed a portion of the present site of the aforementioned department store.

Prior to 1879.

The Library was founded on November 9, 1820, by clerks of merchants. In 1821 it was located in one room at #49 Fulton Street, with 150 members and 700 volumes. From this time it grew rapidly and in 1830 a Clinton Hall Association was formed for the purpose of erecting. In 1854 the Association purchased the Astor Place Opera House, remodeled it for a Library as shown in picture, later this was replaced, in 1891 by the present building,with capacity for 475,000 volumes.

Ref: King's Handbook of New York. P. 328.

About 1860

Urbrock Collection

text:

8th Street (formerly also known as Clinton Place), south side, west from 24 West 8th Street to Sixth Avenue. This is one of the principal shop and restaurant sections of Greenwich Village. title: Manhattan: 8th Street (West) - MacDougal Street
text:
52-4 and 56 West 8th Street, south side, between Macdougal Street and Sixth Avenue.

52-4 is a rather modernistic structure built about 1927, replacing the two old 3-story houses in the rear of which was Clinton Court. (This part of 8th Street was formerly also known as Clinton Place). The 8th Street Playhouse started out as the Film Guild Cinema, but has changed hands since 1930 and settled down as just a good movie theatre. On the floors above, the Knickerbocker Democrats of the 10th Assembly District will have their headquarters during the municipal election of 1933.

56, a 4-story building standing where the lunch wagon is now shown, was taken down after 1930. In the summer of 1935 a 1-story store will be built on this site.
