title: Manhattan: 10th Street (West) - 6th Avenue
text:
55-43 West 10th Street, north side, just east of Sixth Avenue. No. 51 (old No. 15, 10th Street), with the Bell Telephone sign on the stoop, is the Tenth Street Studios, Incorporated, the first building to be devoted entirely and primarily to artists' studios. St Gaudens and John LaFarge, among other notable artists, have maintained studios in it. Built in 1857 at old 13-21 10th Street (10th Street was then numbered east from Sixth Avenue), it will still be standing in 1935. About 1923.

Gift of E. M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: 10th Street (West) - Patchin Place
text:
111-01 West 10th Street (formerly 11-1 Amos Street), north side, from Patchin Place to Sixth Avenue. These are old wooden houses which have been faced with brick. The corner lunch room was a drug store prior to 1929. There are quite a number of law offices and bail bond firms in this block of 10th Street, the Jefferson Market Magistrates' Court being on the south side at the corner of Sixth Avenue. The clearing where the camera man is standing is the site on which the new House of Detention for Women is being constructed.

The name Amos Street was dropped about the time of the Civil War, inasmuch as the eastern end of Amos Street met the western end of 10th Street at this point.

June 15, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: 10th Street (West) - 6th Avenue
text:
101-11 West 10th Street (formerly 1-11 Amos Street), at and adjoining N.W. corner of Sixth Avenue. There are old frame houses which were later refaced with brick. The drug store on the corner will be succeeded about 1929 by a lunch room, and the building will be remodelled downstairs so as to put the stairs on the western end, making more room for the restaurant. The shoe repair shop will go out of business at that time or earlier. Notice the law and bail bond offices; Jefferson Market Court is situated on the south-west corner, right across the street.
This street, which is parallel with Christopher, Charles, and Perry Streets, happens to coincide at the point with the western end of Amos Street was dropped, and the street later renumbered as an extension of West 10th Street, 100 being added to the Amos Street numbers.

February, 1922.
Gift of K. M. Jenks.

text:
(1)
Jefferson Market Courthouse and clock tower, with the excavation on the site of the old jail and the law and bail bond offices on the north side of 10th Street (formerly Amos Street), from

The courthouse, on the S.W. corner of Sixth Avenue and 10th Street, was erected in 1875. The neighborhood is low-grade residential in character. The car track on 10th Street is the westbound track of the 8th Street crosstown line. title: Manhattan: 11th Street (West) - 6th Avenue
text:
11th Street, west from 109 West 11th Street, west of Sixth Avenue, to Seventh and Greenwich Avenues (Mulry Square). 111 West 11th Street is the brownstone house with the front portico, on the north side of the street. The Rhinelander Gardens, 112-124, on the south side, are set back from the street so that only the front of the yards, with their ailanthus trees, is visible here. The Unadilla apartment house beyond them (126-128) was erected around 1900 on the site of two old three-story houses. 125 West 11th Street, on the north side, used to be the residence of Daniel Chester French, the sculptor. 133 West 11th Street, the six-story apartment building on the north side, is known as the Elmendorf, but was originally called the Moffatt; it is contemporary with the Unadilla, and was erected on the site previously occupied by the Third Universalist Church. No. 137-139 and some of the other houses beyond them are occupied by male student nurses. St. Vincent's Hospital, the part of it rebuilt in 1898 and 1905, occupies the rest of the north side to Seventh Avenue. In the background is 201 West 11th Street, a fairly new apartment building on the N.W. corner of Greenwich Avenue. Here 11th Street ends and that portion which was once Hammond Street, and which runs southwest instead of west to the Hudson River, begins. Up to about 1880, 11th Street was numbered west from Broadway. In the block from Sixth to Seventh avenues, 36 should be added to the present house numbers to convert them to the old numbers.

March 6, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

This little block of houses was built about 1857, on a lot that had previously contained a florist's gardens. Notice the iron balconies, and the deep front yards, with three or four fair-sized ailanthus trees.
11th Street used to be numbered East from Fourth Avenue and West from Broadway; the numbering was not straightened out, to conform with the modern system, until around 1880.

North Baptist Church, 232-6 West 11th Street, and adjoining houses, south side, between Waverly Place and 4th Street. This view shows the doorway of 240 West 11th Street and part of St. John's Church, which is on the corner at Waverly Place. title: Manhattan: 11th Street (West) - 4th Street
text:
11th Street, south side, east from North Baptist Church at 232 West 11th Street (formerly about 32 Hammond Street), between 4th Street and Waverly Place. The classical building on the S.W. corner of Waverly Place is St. John the Evangelist (Protestant Episcopal). On the S.W. corner of 11th Street and Greenwich Avenue the old Continental Brewery was demolished around 1914 when Seventh Avenue South was opened. St. Vincent's Hospital, 153 West 11th Street at Seventh Avenue, is seen in the background. This part of 11th Street, parallel to Charles, Perry, and Bank Streets, lost its own name around 1870, and was renumbered as a continuation of the true 11th Street, which is all east of Seventh Avenue. May 20, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: 11th Street - Waverly Place
text:
11th Street (formerly Hammond Street), south side, from Waverly Place to Seventh and Greenwich Avenues (Mulry Square): Hammond Street met the western end of the true 11th Street at that point, which was the southern end of Seventh Avenue; around 1870 it lost its own name and was renumbered as part of 11th Street. 214-08, the four brownstone-front houses shown here, are all that was left of the block on 11th Street from Waverly Place to Greenwich Avenue after Seventh Avenue South was cut through (about 1915), at the time of the construction of the Interborough West Side subway line. The old Continental Brewery, which stood on the S.W. corner of Greenwich Avenue and 11th Street, directly in the way of the subway, was demolished, and later the little one-story building, for shops, was erected to fill in the space along the new Seventh Avenue South. This picture was taken the year Prohibition was repealed; the following year the 11th Street shops shown here were taken over by a liquor store. May 20, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

The North Baptist Church, built in 1882 to replace the original edifice on Christopher Street, is shown at 236-232 West 11th Street. (2)

title: Manhattan: 11th Street - Washington Street
text:
11th Street (formerly Hammond Street) at Washington Street, the S.E. corner and adjoining houses seen from the clearing on the N.W. corner where the railroad viaduct is to be built. Notice the Spanish sign on the drug store. There is a small Spanish colony, mostly waterfront people, scattered through this neighborhood; it extends north to 14th Street and east on 14th Street to Seventh Avenue. The dominant element is still Irish, however. There are practically no Italians; this is much too far north and west for stragglers from the Italian colony south of Washington Square.
July 9, 1932.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: 11th Street (West) - 7th Avenue
text:
St. Vincent's Hospital, 153 West 11th Street, at and adjoining N.E. corner of Seventh Avenue, at Mulry Square, seen from 11th Street (formerly Hammond Street) west of Greenwich Avenue. This hospital was founded in 1849 under the patronage of Archbishop Hughes and in charge of his sister, Mother Angela. At that time there were only two other hospitals in New York City (Manhattan and the Bronx). The hospital moved to this site in 1856 or '57, taking over the building of the Catholic Half-Orphan Asylum which stood at 153 West 11th Street. In 1898, after demolition of that building, half of this building was erected on the site. The western half, on the corner of Seventh Avenue, was added in 1905, replacing the old houses 163-5 West 11th Street and 1-5 Seventh Avenue. See Seventh Avenue, also 12th Street, for the other buildings of the hospital.

The hospital is in charge of the Sisters of Charity of St. Vincent de Paul. Mulry Square, where Seventh Avenue begins, at the intersection of 11th Street and Greenwich Avenue, was named after the late Thomas M. Mulry, President of the United States Society of St. Vincent de Paul and President of the Emigrant Savings Bank; he lived nearby, at 10 Perry Street.

March 12, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: 13th Street (West) - 7th Avenue - [Rhinelander Row.]
text:
(1)
West 13th Street, south side, west from Seventh to Eighth Aves., showing at the S.W. corner of Seventh Ave., an empty lot; the site of the former "Rhinelander Flats". Between this lot and P.S. No. 16 are two small houses (Nos. 204 and 206) which have similar small buildings at their rears. These structures are owned by the Hoguet estate and undoubtedly were erected shortly after the Rhinelander row. For further data see the New York Times, May 10, 1937 (illustrated) and the New York Sun of May 1, 1937.

July 19, 1937.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)
A view from inside the cleared lot showing the rears and sides of the aforementioned Hoguet houses. Shown on the right is the Metropolitan Temple an edifice at the N.W. corner of Seventh Ave. and 13th Street.

July 19, 1937.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: 14th Street - University Place
text:
14th Street (across foreground), at the S.E. corner of University Place, showing the former Springler Hotel under demolition.  It will be replaced by a 2 story commercial structure.  It is on a part of the old Brevoort farm of 22 acres that Elias Brevoort sold about 1758 to John Smith and whose heirs four years later sold to Henry Springler.  The demolished building was originally a private dwelling and became a hotel after the Springler House of No. 5 Union Square burned down in the 1870's.  It was a favorite rendezvous for actors playing at the old Academy of Music, Tony Pastors, the Union Square and other theaters of the vicinity.  Tradition has it that well known Thespians lived here and that the "Lambs" had their inception here, tho that organization has no record of having formally used these rooms.  A fuller account may be found in the New York Times of June 2, 1938.  Note through the center the extensive view southward on the east side of University Place.

June 15, 1938
F.L. Sperr

text:
Old Cruger or Douglas Mansion, 128 West 14th Street, south side, between Sixth and Seventh Avenues.  Originally built as a reproduction of Boscobel House, the Douglas family nest in Scotland, it has had a long and varied history.  Louis Kossuth, the Hungarian patriot, stayed here in 1851.  Theodore Roosevelt the Elder played here as a boy.  From 1873 to 1879 it was occupied by the Metropolitan Museum of Art.  Then it became a saloon, and finally ended its days as the Salvation Army training college, like a tired old man turning to religion at the end of a colorful life.

This building was opened in 1866 as the Theatre Francaise [sic], and during the first year Jacob Grau presented Ristori there in her American premiere. The house was rebuilt in 1871 and renamed the Lyceum. As time passed, the type of productions changed , tho at one time it was a center of the social and dramatic life.

It became the 14th Street Theatre later and since 1926, the Civic Repertory Theatre. The New York Times of April 1, 1938 carried an article to the above effect.

title: Manhattan: 14th Street (West) - 6th Avenue
text:
West 14th Street, west from Sixth Avenue.  At the right is the 14th Street Theatre.  Adjoining same is the 9th Regiment Armory. The photographer's vantage point is|the Sixth Avenue "El".  View 2, taken at a later date includes the Salvation Army Memorial Bldg. at the left, and the Lawyers Trust Bldg. in the background.

The theatre was opened in 1866 as the Theatre Francaise [sic].  It was rebuilt in 1871 as the Lyceum. Subsequently it was the 14th Street and the Civic Repertory (1926).  It was demolished in 1939.

The Ninth Regiment can be traced back to 1812.  In 1848 it was re-organized, as an Irish regiment, and disbanded a few years later.  In 1859 it was again reformed.  In 1861, the entire command went to Washington, independently, and was sworn into the United States service for three years.  They formed the 83rd New York Volunteers, seeing service in the Wilderness, at Antietam, Fredericksburg, the second Bull Run, and Gettysburg.  Between 1870 and 1872 James Fisk was the colonel of the Ninth.  The armory was built by the City in 1893 at a cost of $300,000, plus land at $422,000.

St. Bernard's Roman Catholic Church, the first New York church to be dedicated by an American cardinal, was built in the face of the economic depression of the 1870's by the new parish laid out in 1868 by Cardianl McCloskey. The cornerstone was laid in May, 1873, and the church dedicated May 31, 1875.  A contemporty drawing of it shows a conical spire surmounting each tower, either these were never completed, or they were later taken off.

title: Manhattan: 15th Street - 5th Avenue
text:
New York Hospital, 15th Street adjoining N.W. corner of Fifth Avenue, seen across clearing from 14th Street. This institution is the oldest hospital in New York. It was chartered in 1771 and the cornerstone of the first building laid in 1775. When it was nearly completed, it was destroyed by fire. Work of rebuilding was at once begun, but was interrupted by the outbreak of the Revolution, and the institution did not receive patients until January 1791. In 1869, the original buildings were demolished and work on this building, which was completed in 1877, began. It will be demolished in 1934.

February 12, 1928.

P.L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: 19th Street (East) - Irving Place
text:
136-124 East 19th Street, from the center of the block west to the S.E. corner of Irving Place. 132 East 19th Street is a new 7-story basement house with a north light studio; it was built since 1910. The 7-story building on the corner of Irving Place was erected around 1900.
In the 1930's this block will have changed little except by remodelling. 138-6 and 134 will lose their stoops, and the former front doors will become windows. The same thing will happen to 130; and the garage at 128 will be made over into a dwelling. The white balls will have been taken off the gateposts of the new house, No. 132; and No. 126, adjoining the little one-story studio, will have lost its portico.

About 1912.

title: Manhattan: 21st Street - 6th Avenue
text:
Old Jewish Cemetery for Spanish and Portuguese Jews, 21st Street, south side, just west of Sixth Avenue. This cemetery was first established in 1729 on the New Bowery at Chatham Square, the gift of Louis Gomez, a wealthy Portuguese Jew. Later, as the growing city began to encroach on the property, a new cemetery was built on open green spaces of the present location, where it was believed that the Partola Building, on the N.W. corner of Sixth Avenue and 21st Street, and is no longer used for burials.

title: Manhattan: 23rd Street (East) - 4th Avenue
text:
East 23rd Street (left), at the N.W. corner of Fourth Avenue (right), showing the National Academy of Design. This institution is the equivalent of the Royal Academy and of the Salon and was formed in 1826 by the New York Drawing Association. The building, designed by P.B. Wight, is of white and dark marble, in the Venetian Gothic architecture, and was paid for by public subscriptions. Adjoining on the right is the Lyceum Theatre. The Metropolitan Life Insurance Co. building included these sites at a later date.

title: Manhattan: 23rd Street (West) - 6th Avenue
text:
West 23rd Street (left), st, adjoining and east of the S.E. corner of Sixth Avenue, showing prominently Booth's Theatre. It was opened February 3, 1869, with Edwin Booth as manager, and with such artists as Mary McVicker, Edwin Adams, Fanny Morant, Mark Smith, Kate Bateman, W.E. Sheridan and Agnes Booth as members of the company. Among the significant performances given here were those of, 'A Winter's Tale, April 25, 1871; Men O'Airlee, it's first in America on June 5th; 'Julius Caesar', with Edwin Booth, Lawrence Barrett, F.C. Beings, D.W. Weller and Belle Petemen, in the cast, December 5th; Adelaide Neilson's first appearance in America as 'Juliet', November 18, 1872; George Ringold's production of 'Henry V," February 8, 1875; and Sarah Bernhardt's American debut in 'Adrienne', November 8, 1880. J.B. Booth succeeded his brother as manager in 1873; Jarret & Palmer followed in 1874; James C. Duff, in 1878; and then after several quick changes, Henry E. Abbey became the manager, April 12, 1879. John Stetson succeeded him, August 31, 1881 and he held the house until it was permanently closed, April 30, 1883. The site is now occupied by a large business block.

For a similar pen drawing of this view, see The Manual of the City of New York, 1869, facing page 88.
1869

title: Manhattan: 23rd Street - 9th Avenue
text:
23rd Street, north side, west from Ninth Avenue. At right is the original London Terrace, a row of cottages and apartment houses built in 1845 by Bishop Clement C. Moore, author of "The Night before Christmas". These houses were modeled on similar structures popular in London at the time, and for many years constituted a very fashionable address. They were demolished in 1929 and 1930, and replaced by a series of large, modern apartment houses which retain the name London Terrace.

About 1927.

Price Studios, Inc.

title: Manhattan: 23rd Street - 10th Avenue
text:
23rd Street, north side, east from Tenth Avenue.  On the left, from Tenth to Ninth Avenues, is the original London Terrace, a row of cottages and apartment houses built in 1845 by Bishop Clement C. Moore, author of "The Night before Christmas". These houses were modelled on similar structures popular in London at the time, and for many years constituted a very fashionable address. They were demolished in 1929 and 1930, and replaced by a series of large, modern apartment houses which retain the name London Terrace.

In the right background may be seen the tower of the Metropolitan Life Building.
June, 1925.

title: Manhattan: 23rd Street (West) - 11th Avenue
text:
W. 23rd Street, north side, east from Thirteenth (left), to Eleventh (right) Avenues, as viewed northeastward from a point at W. 22nd Street near the North (Hudson) River. In the right foreground is a small park with cabs at the westerly side of same, awaiting passengers from the Erie Railroad ferry that docks at this point. The 11 story Zinn Building seen, is at the S.E. corner of Eleventh Avenue and W. 25th Street. To the left margin is a 2 story frame structure that bears a sign identifying it as Godwins Hotel. This is at the N.E. corner of Thirteenth Avenue and W. 23rd Street and was replaced by the 4 story garage shown in the other views. No. 2 is from a similar angle and shows this feature prominently. No. 3 is northwestward from Eleventh Avenue and 22nd Street and has the ferry house at its left margin. Subsequently the West side Express Highway will loop across the park to continue northward on Thirteenth Avenue and thereby follow
the westerly edge of Manhattan.
September 1911
View 2: April 22, 1931
View 3: April 2, 1929.
1. Geo. L. Balgue.
2&3.P.L. Sperr

24th Street, south side, between Ninth and Tenth Avenues, showing a closeup view of part of the original London Terrace, a row of cottages and apartment houses built in 1845 by Bishop Clement C. About 1927

title: Manhattan: 25th Street (West) - 8th Avenue
text:
West 25th Street -- East from No 267

No. 2 of this set shows the West Side Lumber Company at No. 223-243. Adjacent to same is a clearance where a row of 3 story structures stood which bore No's 219-231.

March 21, 1938.

P.L. Sperr.

According to the New York Sun of September 22, 1938, a six-story apartment house is to be erected on the site shown in the picture (219-229 West 25th Street). This building will be erected at a cost of $175,000. It will have a base 126x38.7 and will contain a total of 171 rooms, with eleven apartments on a floor.

title: Manhattan: 26th Street - 5th Avenue
text:
26th Street east from Fifth Avenue, taken from roof of the Cafe Martin. This picture gives a good view of Madison Square Garden (1889-1925), and the lovely Diana of St. Gaudens, poised atop its tower. The Garden was acquired by the New York Life Insurance Company in 1915 at a foreclosure sale, and in 1920 was saved from demolition by Tex Rickard, who signed a ten year lease on it. In 1924 the New York Life bought back this lease and in 1925 tore down the Garden, to build their present edifice on its site. Diana, however, is still to be seen in Fairmont Park, Philadelphia. In the centre, with the Uneeda Biscuit sign on its roof, is the Hotel Brunswick, and at the extreme left is the Hotel Victoria, made famous by the patronage of President Cleveland. To the right of the Garden is the former Jerome residence, later the University Club and now (1935) the Manhattan Club. About 1898.

Browning Studios.

title: Manhattan: 31st Street (West) - 9th Avenue
text:
West 31st Street (right), east from but not including Ninth Ave., showing in the foreground the yards of the Pennsylvania Railroad and the rear of the General Post Office. The latter faces on Eighth Ave., and extends north to West 33rd Street (left). On the opposite of Eighth Ave. is the Pennsylvania Railroad Station extending to Seventh Ave., and across it, the Equitable Life Assurance Society Building, on the east side of Seventh Ave., from West 31st to West 32nd Streets. On the left (West 33rd Street) appears the Collegiate Baptist Church and the Printing Crafts Building; the latter being on the west side of Eighth Ave. and extending from West 33rd to West 34th Streets. Shown under construction are the Nelson Tower, on the west side of Seventh Ave., between  West 34th and West 35th Streets, and the 19-story building of R.H. Macy and Company, on the east side of Seventh Ave., between West 34th and West 35th Streets.

1929

Ewing Galloway

title: Manhattan: 34th Street (East) - Flatbush Avenue
text:
East 34th Street, at the East River station of the 34th Street spur line that connected the ferries at this point with the Second and Third Avenue "El" lines. This spur line originated as the result of legislation requiring all public transportation systems to provide a terminal at a ferry or railroad depot and was incorporated in their franchises. A similar structure was until recently on E. 42nd Street between the Third Avenue "El" and the Grand Central Station. The photographer is viewing northwesterly and shows same prior to demolition. This was accomplished in two steps. First to be razed, about this date, was the section shown. This included all tracks between the East River and Second Avenue. The section between the latter point and Third Avenue was torn down in the Summer of 1938. In the right background appears the Chanin Building at 42nd Street and Lexington Avenue.

March 21, 1929.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: 34th Street - East River Drive
text:
E. 34th Street, at the East River, showing the locale of the old Borden Avenue (Greenpoint) Ferry. This service, discontinued for several years, was in its last stages restricted to vehicular traffic. The photographer is viewing generally northward from the dock at 33rd Street and shows the New York Steam Co. plant and the Department of Sanitation dock (35th Street), for a background; the tenements are on the north side of 34th Street and extend to First Avenue.

About 1938

title: Manhattan: 34th Street (East) - 2nd Avenue
text:
E. 34th Street, south side, west from Second to Third Avenues, showing a row of structures that will remain and face the entrance to the 38th Street tunnel under the East River. On the two Avenues mentioned appear their respective "E1" lines and 34th Street stations. Previous to the Summer of 1938 these were joined by a spur line, a remnant of a link with the Ferry to Borden Avenue. Early legislation necessitated same, stating that all transportation facilities join up with either railroad terminals or water facilities. The writer believes the drug store appearing on the left to be place of business from which Col. O'Brien emanated and was fatally attacked during the Draft Riots of 1863. For accounts of same, see "Gangs of New York" by H. Asbury and "Boss Tweed" by Dennis Lynch etc.

title: Manhattan: 35th Street (East) - 2nd Avenue
text:
E. 35th Street, east from Second Avenue to the East River, showing buildings on the south side of this thoroughfare facing St. Gabriel's Park. Slightly east of the Avenue is the four story building housing The Institute of Public Administration of Columbia University (No. 302-306). This formerly housed the College of Dental and Oral Surgery and which now occupies a new structure on 34th Street.

To the left margin appears the shadowy outline of the New York Steam Co. plant that is between First Avenue and the river. Across the latter is the triple chimneyed American Sugar Refining Co. plant in Greenpoint, Brooklyn.

January 7, 1939

Somach Photo Service
New York City Tunnel Authority

title: Manhattan: 35th Street (East) - 2nd Avenue
text:
E. 35th Street, east of Second Avenue, showing mainly the southerly side of St. Gabriel's Park. This occupy an entire square block between 35th and 36th Streets, and First and Second Avenues. Diagonally thru the upper portion (foreground) of the area will run the underground approach to the 38th Street tunnel, necessitating the entire demolition of buildings show n at the left center. These occupy the frontage on the north side of 36th Street, between the aforementioned Avenues. To the right, is the New York Steam Co. plant at the East River's edge.

January 7, 1939

title: Manhattan: 36th Street (East) - 1st Avenue
text:
East 36th Street, west of First Avenue, as photographed across the avenue and St. Gabriel's Park. This entire block is to be cleared for the Midtown-Queens Tunnel approach. Note on the right a part of this activity already under way. St. Gabriel's Church and Parochial School were included. Forming a backdrop are the skyscrapers oonstituting the Grand Central-42nd Street outline. From left to right respectively, these are, the Chanin, R. C. A., Chrysler, News, Waldorf-Astoria and General Electric Buildings. The Tudor City Hotel Woodstock is on the right.
1939
Alexander Alland
This photo is one of a series that appeared in the published volume "Portrait of N.Y." by Felix Reisenberg and Alex. Alland, IRGV.

Standing intact in all views is the St. Gabriel's branch of the New York Public Library. This is the last of the buildings remaining on the "plaza" and it too will be razed in early 1940.

Adjoining same and partially destroyed in the early views are St. Gabriel's Hall and Parochial School.

To the extreme right appear buildings on the east side of First Avenue, between 36th and 37th Streets.

P. L. Sperr

View 3 June 28, 1939

title: Manhattan: 42nd Street (East) - Lexington Avenue
text:
For the first time in the history of photography, the principle so successfully used in serial camera work of compositing into a single illustration a series of pictures covering one subject, has been applied to a vertical object over 1,000 feet in height. Mal Walton, widely known New York Photographer, has produced this unusual illustration of the 1040 foot Chrysler building at Lexington Avenue and 42nd Street in New York. Many weeks of tireless experimental work were necessary. Perspectives had to be scaled and rescaled and control points accurately established before the actual work of taking pictures could begin.

Inability to get far enough away from the Chrysler Building to obtain a single picture of the entire building front from sidewalk to spire made the question of correct perspective in the production of this work a very disconcerting factor. Structures of various heights surrounding the building stood in the way of securing one photograph that would show the elevation of the building which is on Lexington Avenue.

To make a series of pictures which when composited would bring out the natural perspective of a single picture taken from one point distant enough to include the entire building, it was necessary to establish two fixed controls or focal points, one at a ground point and the other at a point in the spire.

Definitely to locate the spire point of control, the Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company placed its blimp, the Mayflower, at the disposal of Mr. Walton and his associates. After a series of reconnoitering flights around the building the control point was established and the necessary photographs made from the blimp while poised in mid-air at various levels below the top of the spire of the building. The ground point of control was determined with much less difficulty and the numerous photos made from neighboring buildings at carefully calculated angles extended from the sidewalk to the lowest level of the blimp-made pictures.

Beyond the point of being a photographic problem, as Mr. Walton points out, this illustration of the Chrysler Building involved intricate engineering problems. To Mr. Walton is due full credit for conceiving and executing the airflight and ground pictures into a perfect mosaic-composite, which bids fair to be an epoch in the history of photography.

After such a perfect first effort at pioneering a brand new style of photography doubtless there will be many occasions to use it as a sense of obtaining heretofore impossible actual illustrations of many of the new skyscrapers which are too completely hidden by other buildings to be photographed by a single exposure.

title: Manhattan: 42nd Street - Vanderbilt Avenue
text:
East 42nd Street at the N.E. corner of Vanderbilt Ave. Old Grand Central Terminal, at the northern end of Park Ave., from 42nd to 45th Streets. The view at the left is north on Vanderbilt Ave. At the right may be seen the station of the 42nd Street elevated spur from Third Ave. Immediately adjoining it on the north side of 42nd Street is the archway through which trains, bound for Madison Square via the Murray Hill-Park Ave. tunnel, used to emerge from the Grand Central. When this station was built in 1871 the railroad began by leaving the engine here and having the cars pulled down to Madison Square by horse; some years before the date of this picture even that had ceased, and this station became a terminal for all trains. At the N.E. corner of Vanderbilt Ave. and 42nd Street, notice the florist's shop and the barber's, also the two ladies carrying parasols.

About 1892.

East 42nd Street at the N.E. corner of Vanderbilt Ave.
Grand Central Station, Park Avenue at 42nd Street, showing the new automobile viaduct, which in this view seems only recently completed. If that is true, then the new Interborough Subway lines have just been opened (notice passengers from the new Grand Central express station coming up to the street in the foreground), the name Pershing Square for this block has just been suggested by John M. Bowman, and not yet officially adopted, General Pershing is still distinguishing himself in the War, and this is
Summer, 1918.

title: Manhattan: 42nd Street - Vanderbilt Avenue
text:
East 42nd Street at the N.E. corner of Vanderbilt Ave.
Grand Central Station and Park Avenue, north from and including 42nd Street, seen from the roof of the newly completed Pershing Square Building on the east side of Park Avenue where the Grand Union Hotel stood prior to 1914. On the right may be seen the old spur from the Third Avenue "L", to be taken down in 1924, and a glimpse of the little alley, between Grand Central Station and the Hotel Commodore, which used to be DePew Place, balancing Vanderbilt Avenue.
Traffic is quite light over the viaduct, even if it is only 11:15 A. M. Both north and south bound traffic travels around the west shoulder of the station, between 42nd and 45th Streets; the viaduct to the east is yet a dead-end leg, for the convenience of the Commodore Hotel. As yet no statue of Commodore Vanderbilt stands in front of the great central window, facing north bound automobile traffic.
Late 1922.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: 42nd Street - Vanderbilt Avenue
text:
On front of photo is the caption:
"Photo by Harcourt Strange, 1966"

On back of photo is a map of the area in Mount Vernon, N.Y. where the eagle depicted on the front of the photo was located.

The following 2 blocks of text appears directly on the map:
"Villa St. is only 4 blocks S. of The Westchester Cross County Parkway."

"The present aerie of two of the old Grand Central Eagles on Villa St. Mount Vernon, N.Y.  Like the Mercury on the present Grand Central they're all poised for flight but never fly."

A return address label is attached to the map with the following on it:
HARCOURT STRANGE
145 Fourth Avenue
Mount Vernon, N. Y. 10550

On a separate slip of paper attached to the back of the photo appears the following:
"According to a feature article appearing in The N.Y. News Coloroto  [sic] Magazine Jan. 2, 1966 the above cast iron eagle was one of 16 which once adorned the top of the old Grand Central Station on 42 St. N.Y.C.  Those birds were added to the remodelled station in 1898.  But only remained on their perch for 5 years. Then were removed when the station was rebuilt in 1903. The News illustrated 9 of the 16 in their present locations. The one above and another are now on Villa St. Mount Vernon, N.Y. (over for map.)"

title: Manhattan: 42nd Street - Vanderbilt Avenue
text:
60 to 72 East 42nd Street, south side, west of Pershing Square (Park Avenue), showing the Lincoln Building site under preparation. Here, formerly stood the old seven story structure housing the Lincoln National Bank and Safe Deposit Co. and the five story Hotel Athens. Both of these extended through the block to 41st Street and their demolition has opened a view of buildings on the south side of that street. The dark structure to the left is the old Murray Hill Hotel. Adjoining same are two low buildings numbered 58 & 56 E. 41st Street. The Chemists Club is No. 50-54, the ten story dominant. A four story affair, No. 46-48 separates this from the twelve story office building, No. 40-44. The latter adjoins the S. E. corner structure at Madison Avenue.

View 1: August 22, 1928

P. L. Sperr

Views 2-6: Summer 1928

P. L. Sperr

The Grand Central Depot shown is the first to be erected on this site and stood from 1871 to 1900.

About 1890

title: Manhattan: 42nd Street (West) - 5th Avenue.
text:
42nd Street, at Fifth Ave., as seen from the Republican Club (54-56 West 40th Street) and across Bryant Park. Shown from left to right are, Stern Bros, Aeolian Hall Building (under renovations), Salmon Tower (newly completed), No's 9 to 3 West 42nd Street inclusive (5-story brownstones), and the Bristol Building (N.W. corner of Fifth Ave.); the last two items have been replaced by the building called No. 500 Fifth Ave. The rear of the New York Public Library is shown at the eastern side of Bryant Park; the front of which is on the west side of Fifth Ave. This building extends from 40th to 42nd Streets. title: Manhattan: 42nd Street (West) - 6th Avenue.
text:
West 42nd Street, east from Sixth Ave., and showing prominently Bryant Park, which is on the south side of the afore mentioned street. The New York Public Library is at the eastern end of this park and it faces onto the west side of Fifth Ave., between 40th and 42nd Streets. Shown under construction is the skyscraper, No. 500 Fifth Ave., at the N.W. corner of 42nd Street. Adjoining same is the Salmon Tower, with the Morris Building (formerly Aeolian Hall) and Stern's Dept. Store westward. Across the Library Building is silhouetted the mid-town 42nd Street skyscraper district; with its Chrysler, Lincoln, Chanin, Lefcourt and Colonial and 10 East 40th Street Buildings. This picture donated to the New York Public Library, by Mr. Hoffman on March 27th 1937.

June 1930.

Copyrighted by William Frange.

West 42nd Street, at the N.W. corner of Fifth Ave., showing the site cleared for the skyscraper, No. 500 Fifth Ave. The 4-story building, adjoining the clearance, and whose side wall is exposed, is No. 508. North of same, at the S.W. corner of West 43rd Street is the 8-story Ziegler Building, No. 510-14. Appearing on the right are three buildings, Nos. 513-11, 509 and 507; the 10-story Postal Life being the first and located at the S.W. corner of East 43rd Street.
January 16, 1930.
Irving Underhill.

West 42nd Street, north side, between Fifth and Sixth Avenue's, showing the West Presbyterian Church. It was organized in 1829 with 18 members and it's first house of worship was erected on Carmine Street in 1832. The structure shown was erected in 1862. About 1905

title: Manhattan: 42nd Street (West) - Broadway
text:
West 42nd Street, south side, west from (No. 138; the Cameo Theatre) a point slightly east of Broadway and across same. The 15-story structure on the left is the former Knickerbocker Hotel that has been converted to business purposes. It bears Nos. 1462-1470 Broadway and stands at the S.E. corner of West 42nd Street. West of same appears a low structure occupying the apex of a triangular plot between Broadway and Seventh Ave. Progressing in the same direction one sees the 24-story Candler Building and the modern Graybar Building; the latter being between Eighth and Ninth Aves. This set consists of a negative and a positive view.

September 1935.

W.P.A. Photo.

title: Manhattan: 48th Street (West) - 5th Avenue
text:
Rockefeller Center, New York
February 12, 1975

For more than four decades, the elegant Rainbow Room and Rainbow Grill located 65 floors above midtown. Manhattan in Rockefeller Center have been New York City's most talked about restaurant and nighclub [sic] with outstanding entertainment and top cuisine plus an unexcelled view of the Manhattan skyline.

Opened to the public as a formal skyscraper supper club in 1934, the Rainbow Room, above two stories in height, occupies the entire eastern end of the RCA Building's 65th floor. Its 24 floor-to-ceiling windows line the north and south sides of the spacious dining room permitting breathtaking views of Manhattan island and surrounding areas for 50 miles. Panels between the windows are covered with plum colored silk tafetta, complimented by gold draperies and emerald green carpeting. The tables are set on three levels beneath a magnificent crystal chandelier of classic design.

Cocktails and dining ar [sic] offered nightly, seven days a week. Brunch is served from 11:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. Saturday and Sunday.

#2726

title: Manhattan: 49th Street - 5th Avenue
text:
(1)
49th Street, west from Fifth Avenue, showing the houses along "Speakeasy Row." During prohibition, most of these houses were illegal saloons. One resident in this neighborhood was compelled to place over his doorbell a card reading "Private House," to avoid being awakened at any hour by thirsty revelers. All of these houses are now gone, and the site occupied by Rockefeller Centre.
August 18, 1929.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)
The same, a year earlier, and not including Fifth Avenue.
May 6, 1928.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: 54th Street (West) - 5th Avenue
text:
18 to 4 West 54th Street, south side, east from but not including Sixth, to but not including Fifth Aves., showing the 9-story (No. 10) and contiguous to it eastward, the 4-story (No. 4), Rockefeller residences. These two houses are to be demolished and the land will be used by the Museum of Modern Art as a garden for the display of sculpture. It was presented to the Museum by Mr. and Mrs. John D. Rockefeller Jr. as a gift, shortly after the demise of the elder Rockefeller. No. 4, the 4-story residence which stands within an enclosed garden, was the residence of John D. Rockefeller Sr. It was built in 1865 and was bought by Mr. Rockefeller in 1895. The 9-story house, No. 10, is the residence of John D. Rockefeller Jr. and is one of the largest private homes in the city. It was built in 1912 at a cost of 200,000 dollars. (For further information see the New York Times of June 18, 1937, page 1).

December 28, 1936.

P. L. Sperr.

Deems in 1870 by the Universalist Church of Our Saviour, was sold to the present occupants about 1899 and will shortly be demolished. View No. 2 shows the Church mainly, as observed northward across a excavation on the south side of the Street. Moses King's hand book of New York (1892), on page 351, states that Church of the Strangers at No. 299 Mercer Street was purchased by Commodore Vanderbilt in 1870 and presented to Dr. Deems, a former M.E. clergyman from North Carolina. His preaching attracted great attention and he organized this church in 1868 with out organic connections with any other denomination. July 11, 1927. Views 1 and 2

title: Manhattan: 59th Street (East) - Park Avenue
text:
East 59th Street, south side, west from Park Ave., showing at the S.W. corner of same (left), No. 500 Park Ave., the administrative offices of the Board of Education. In November 1936, the City of New York acquired a 12-story structure (the former Elks clubhouse) at 102-14 Livingston Street, Brooklyn and will house these offices there after extensive alterations (800,000). The edifice with the sloping roof is the Savoy Plaza Hotel and is on the east side of Fifth Ave. between 58th and 59th Streets.

August 4, 1937.

P. L. Sperr.

West 59th Street, south side, between Columbus Circle and Ninth Avenue, showing a clearance there extending to 58th Street. The direction of the view is eastward from a point near Ninth Avenue. At the far end of the parking space are several buildings; that with the white stripe is the Park Theatre. This is entered from the Circle where a corner abuts. The balance of the building is on 58th Street. In the background is the General Motors Bldg. and its neighbors, all on Broadway.

title: Manhattan: 59th Street (West) - Columbus Avenue
text:
W. 59th Street, north side, from Columbus Circle (right of No. 3) to Columbus Avenue (left of No. 1) as viewed from a clearance on the south side, showing a panoramic set of 3 views. No. 1 shows a row of tenements (No's 333 to 349) and a glimpse of the Roman Catholic Church of St. Paul the Apostle; the latter being at the S.W. corner of Columbus Avenue and W. 60th Street and is an outstanding feature of New York containing numerous works of art. No. 2 shows buildings near the Circle. These bear No's. 311 and 313-315. They are repeated in No. 3, being at the foot of the 23 story Gotham National Bank Building (No. 307). Note that the latter is not on the Circle as a thin veneer of structures line same.

September 4, 1938.
Views 1, 2 and 3.

P.L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: 59th Street (West) - 10th Avenue
text:
West 59th Street, south side, east from Tenth Avenue, showing details of the Roosevelt Hospital that occupies the entire block to Ninth Avenue. The Nurses Home is at Tenth Avenue; in the center is the Administration Bldg.; at the corner of Ninth Avenue is the famous Syms Operating Theatre. Across the glass enclosed roof of the latter, appears portions of the massive American Women's Association Club and Bldg. at 57th Street. To the left, above the Ninth Avenue "El" station (demolished in January 1941) are the towering apartment buildings on Central Park South.

April 15, 1939
No's. 1-2-3

P. L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: 61st Street (East) - Avenue A
text:
421 East 61st Street, north side, between York and First Aves., showing the Col. Smith House (also known as the Adams Mansion). This house was built in 1799 by Colonel Smith, a son-in-law of President Adams. One version states that it was built in 1777 by Peter Pra Van Sairt for a stable to his residence and he sold (1795) the mansion, stables and other buildings to Col. Wm. S. Smith. The latter failed in business and his stable became a tavern and was used as such until 1830 when Jeremiah Fowle purchased it, whose daughter occupied it until 1906. The Consolidated Gas Company sold this building in December 1924 to the Colonial Dames. This set consists of 4 views taken at the same time.

February 1924.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

Second attached page: Press release
----------------------------------NEW HOME OF GIRLS CLUBS OF AMERICA, Inc.

Five-story brick and limestone town house at 133 East 62nd Street, Manhattan, which has been acquired by the Girls Clubs of America, Inc., federation of girls' clubs in the United States and Canada, for its national headquarters.

Built in 1885, the house was given an ornate limestone trim in 1900 by Robert McAllister Lloyd, pioneer electrical engineer, then owner.

Girls Clubs of America, Inc., founded in 1945 in Springfield, Mass., and located in New York City for seven years, has until now occupied rented quarters.

Mrs. John V. Lindsay, wife of the Mayor of the City of New York, accompanied members of GCA's national board on their first visit, as owners, to their first permanent home.

Girls Clubs of America, Inc.,

title: Manhattan: 68th Street (East) - Park Avenue
text:
East 68th Street, Aest from Lexington, to Park (left) Avenues, showing the southerly side of Thomas Hunter Hall (right) and the old Normal College for Women (now Hunter College). The latter, in 1938, is demolished, having been severely damaged by a fire in
1936.
The New York Times of Aug. 2, 1938, in an article on Page 21 announces the ceremonies to be held here on the construction of a new building that will cost $6,414,000. of which the City's share $3,527,700 and the P.W.A's $2,886,300. Charles H. Tuttle will preside and speeches will be made by the Mayor, Howard A. Gray, Colonel k. E. Gilmore and Mrs. Walter S. Mack. This new structure will be 16 stories high and accommodate 5,0O0 students in 100 class rooms. Included also will be a library, auditorium,
gymnasium, swimming pool, theatre and laboratories.
For further views of this structure see, Park and Lexington
Avenues, and East 69th Street.

June 12, 1937
P.L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: 70th Street - York Avenue
text:
70th Street at and east of York Avenue, seen across the clearing from 69th Street east of York Avenue. The photographer is standing near the site of the Lenox Hill Settlement House and Neighborhood Club, 511-515 East 69th Street. The south side of 70th Street is marked by the wooden fence. On the north side of 70th Street the buildings are being demolished.

This block, from 69th to 70th Streets, used to be Washington Park, prior to about 1895, and then was built up, mostly with tenement houses. It will now be part of the site of the New York Hospital and Cornell Medical College, (see York Avenue).

P. L. Sperr.

Would you like a print for the NY scrapbooks or picture files?

built-in garage.

Adjacent to the brownstone enumerated is a clearance that forms an "El" to provide a frontage on the Avenue, between 78th and 78th Streets. The apartment house to rise here is the Kensington. The former home of Mrs. Jacob H. Schiff stood here from about 1901. Occupying the corner locations are the 16 story No. 960 Fifth Avenue and the darker 15.story No. 969. The twelve story structure seen at the aforementioned corner became the Hotel Colonial and bore No. 443-449 Columbus Avenue. (Also, No. 51 West 81st Street later). Empty lots and private residences intervene between this and No. 17-15 West 81st Street (right margin) which in 1905 housed the American Geographical Society. This view remained the same in 1922 with one exception: the two four-story residences on either side of the vacant 25 ft. lot were razed and upon this site were erected a twelve-story apartment house, No. 39-35 West 81st Street.

title: Manhattan: 110th Street (West) - 8th Avenue

West 110th Street, at Eighth Avenue (right), and westward, showing thereupon the curved "El" trestle of the Sixth and Ninth Avenue's Elevated Line. At the left, this structure veers southward to continue on Columbus Avenue. The hilly ground beyond is the Morningside Heights section, that will later contain the Cathedral of St. John and Morningside Park. The photographers vantage point is upon the thoroughfare that became Central Park West after development.

title: Manhattan: 120th Street (West) - Amsterdam Avenue
text:
West 120th Street, north side, between Amsterdam Ave. and Broadway, showing the tower atop Russell Hall as viewed northward from University Hall. This structure, a unit of Teachers College (one of the affiliates of Columbia University) was erected at a cost of over $2,000,000 in 1923 as a memorial to James Earl Russell, the dean here for 25 years. Inside of the tower are book stacks of the Library; the reading rooms occupying the upper floors. The lower stories house the administrative offices.

THE NEW YORK TIMES MARCH 1940
A negro group, the Twelfth Church of Christ, Scientist, a branch of the First Church of Christ, Scientist, of Boston, is making extensive changes to this building, purchased from the former occupants, St. Paul's Evangelical Lutheran Church. The latter are now affiliated with Grace Lutheran Church at 123 West Seventy-first Street. They started here in a little frame building about seventy-five years ago, and have occupied the structure shown about forty-one years. The Reverend F. H. Bosch has been the pastor for thirty-five years.

title: Manhattan: 125th Street (West) - 7th Avenue
text:
Manhattanville: Dr. John E. Ferdinand home at No. 230 West 125th Street, south side, west of Seventh Ave. Today (1937) this site is included in the lot upon which stands L.M. Blumstein's Department Store, No. 230-244 West 125th Street. Dr. Ferdinand resided here between 1880 and 1887 having lived (according to Phillip's Elite Directory) in the years 1874-1875 at No's. 29, 31, 35 West 127th Street.

Unknown date.

title: Manhattan: 125th Street (West) - Amsterdam Avenue
text:
Manhattanville: The home of Isaac A. Hooper, City Councilman from Carmansville in 1856-57. The late John J. Hooper, Register of the County of New York, lived here in his early boyhood, when this structure bore No. 75 Manhattan Street. It later became No. 513 West 125th Street, north side, west of Amsterdam (former Tenth) Ave. Today (1937), an apartment house stands on this site, and has from prior to 1922.

Unknown date.

This set back frame structure bore No. 77 Manhattan Street which now is No. 515 West 125th Street, north side, west of Amsterdam (formerly 10th) Ave.

title: Manhattan: 129th Street (West) - Amsterdam Avenue
text:
(1) Manhattanville: The Manhattanville Free School (left) and P.S. 43 (right) as viewed in a northward direction on Tenth Ave. (now Amsterdam) (right). These buildings were at the N.W. corner of West 129th Street. The first stood from 1827 to 1850, while the latter was finished in 1854. These structures have been demolished and today a similarly numbered school stands at this site.

Unknown date.

(2) A view of the eastern side of Ward School No. 43. This entrance was on Tenth Ave., which today is known as Amsterdam Ave.

Unknown date.

(3) Mr. Seiberg, who was principal of No. 43.

Unknown date.

(4) A group photo of the teachers, consisting of Mr. Seiberg, Principal; Mr. Sullivan, Drawing; Mr. Daley, Music; Miss Hosford; Mrs. Lee; and Miss Mary Moore.

Unknown date.

title: Manhattan: Amsterdam Avenue - Cathedral Parkway - 113th Street
text:
THE CATHEDRAL OF SAINT JOHN THE DIVINE AS IT WILL APPEAR WHEN COMPLETED

The apse at left and the central portion under the proposed tower are already in place (???), and the foundation has been laid for the nave occupying the right half of our picture. The whole structure will be 600 feet long, and the spire 500 feet high. It will be larger in every way than St.. Paul's or Westminster Abbey, in London, or the great Cathedrals at Winchester and York. It will be exceeded in size only by St. Peter's in Rome and the Cathedral of Seville in Spain. title: Manhattan: Amsterdam Avenue - Cathedral Parkway - 113th St.
text:
CATHEDRAL NAVE TO RISE ON THESE FOUNDATIONS.

Bishop Manning announced on Sunday, Oct. 19, 1924 that contractors have been asked to bid on the Nave of the Cathedral of Saint John the Divine, 119th Street and Amsterdam Ave. New York. The foundations, shown in the photographs, are already complete. The Nave will be 225 feet long, and the cost is estimated at between $5,000,000 and $6,000,000. The temporary wall at the eastern end of the Nave foundation will be torn out when the Nave is built, so that Nave and crossing will join.

The portion of the Cathedral here shown-the crossing with the choir in black- was completed in 1921. The Nave's width will be 132 feet and the height of the interior is to be 130 feet. Transcripts to be erected at each side of the crossing will make the total width of the Cathedral 315 feet.

from the Review of Reviews

title: Manhattan: Amsterdam Avenue - Cathedral Parkway - 113th St.
text:
Construction on New York's great cathedral to be resumed soon.

New photo of the Protestant Episcopal Cathedral of Saint John the Divine, on which construction is to be resumed soon. This photo shows the apse, or East end, with seven radiating chapels; and the crossing, with its temporary dome.

The nave, or staff of the cross, which this completed church will form, is the next part to be built. It is also planned to erect a great tower, 500 feet high, above the present, temporary dome.

March 10, 1924  Underwood and Underwood

Even in its unfinished condition the Cathedral represents an expenditure of more than $5,000,000 and when completed will have cost four times as much. There will be seats for 7,000 persons. Some of the seven chapels are as commodious as many churches. It is expected that the Cathedral will be completed within ten years.

Review of Reviews

OLD WORLD GRANDEUR IN NEW WORLD CATHEDRALS. CATHEDRAL OF SAINT JOHN THE DIVINE.

New York--- the ambulatory of the Cathedral. This is a passage about twenty feet wide which runs completely around the choir and gives access to the seven chapels of tongues. At the left the photo shows the tomb of the founder of the Cathedral, Bishop Horatio Potter; sixth Bishop of New York. Its Position, immediately behind the altar is that traditionally reserved for the founder of a cathedral. It was designed by in the English Gothic style of the Fifteenth Century after studies of the tomb of Edward the Confessor, in Westminster Abbey. The photo was taken from the doorway of the Chapel of St. Martin of Tours. In the distance is the wrought iron screen before the chapel of Saint Columba and beyond that the screen before the chapel of St. Boniface is invisible.
Dec. 2, 1924

International Newsreel
from the Review of Reviews

title: Manhattan: Amsterdam Avenue - Cathedral Parkway - 113th Street
text:
'CATHEDRAL OF SAINT JOHN THE DIVINE. ONE OF THE SEVEN CHAPELS WHICH EXTEND IN A SEMI-CIRCLE AROUND THE CHOIR.

The Cathedral scheme embraces the holding of religious services in many different languages. Our picture shows the Holland Chapel, named for St. Boniface and representing the German rite. It was completed in 1916. All the chapels are Memorials. This chapel is seen through screen from sanctuary.
Feb. 1925
from the Review of Reviews

title: Manhattan: Amsterdam Avenue - Cathedral Parkway - 113th Street
text:
INTERIOR OF THE CATHEDRAL OF SAINT JOHN THE DIVINE AS NOW IN USE.

This shows the choir and altar, and a portion of the crossing. The eight massive pillars around the altar are of Maine granite 54 feet high, each composed of only two pieces. Present plans call for replacing the semi-dome with a much higher structural roof. There would thus be another series of windows, 120 feet from the floor.

Interior of the Cathedral of Saint John the Divine, looking east toward the High Altar. The photograph shows the great pillars which stand about the Sanctuary.

Feb. 1925

The Review of Reviews.

title: Manhattan: Astor Place - Lafayette Street
text:
Astor Place, north side, west from Lafayette Street to Broadway, showing prominently the Mercantile Library's Clinton Hall. This structure was the former Astor Place Opera House, remodelled in 1854 for the Association on their removal from Nassau and Beekman Street's. A new building will be erected here in 1891 for their purpose. The library was founded November 9, 1820, by clerks of merchants. In 1821, in one room at 49 Fulton Street, it had 150 members and 700 volumes. In 1826, in the building of Harper & Bros. in Cliff Street, it had 6000 books. In 1828 the merchants made enthusiastic by the achievements of the clerks, organized the Clinton Hall Association for the purpose of giving a building to the library. This association, in 1830, erected the first Clinton Hall on the corner of Nassau and Beekman Streets. The building herewith shown is the second Clinton Hall. On the right is East 8th Street; Broadway is at the left.

Prior to 1891

Gift of Urbrook Collection

title: Manhattan: Barrow Street - Commerce Street
text:
Barrow Street, east from Commerce Street. The house at the right is 41 Commerce Street. The point of view is the old boundary line between the Trinity Church Farm on the west and the Herring Farm on the east.
This part of Barrow Street is the older part, laid out around 1800 under the name of Reason Street, a name characteristic of the age of Romanticism and of the French Revolution. Other streets in this part of town were named Commerce Street, Art Street, and Science Street, of which only the first named survives as such. The Villager credits the name Reason Street to Thomas Paine's "Age of Reason" (see Grove Street).
May 20, 1933

title: Manhattan: Barrow Street - Greenwich Street
text:

Chapel, on Hudson Street, west side, at the N.E. corner of Hudson and Grove Streets. At the right is a large 6 story apartment (erected 1926) at the N.E. corner of Barrow and Hudson Streets that replaced a dozen or so of 2 1/2 story frame dwellings. Just beyond same is the point where Commerce Street branches off, to run parallel to the eastern section of Barrow Street that was formerly Beason Street. The larger view is limited to No's. 90 to 96 Barrow Street inclusive. At the left appears a portion of the U.S. Appraisers Stores building on the far side of Greenwich Street.

title: Manhattan: Battery Park - Aquarium.
text:
Battery Park: A set of 4 views of the Aquarium, located in the southwestern corner of the Park at the waters edge.  This structure was completed in 1805 as Fort Clinton, subsequently known as Castle Garden during which period (1822-1855) numerous celebrities performed here.  In 1855 it became the State Immigrant Depot and nearly ten millions of immigrants passed through its walls.  In 1893, these duties being assured by the federal government, it was ?? for the new Depot on Ellis Island and became the present Aquarium in 1896 under the direction of the New York Zoological Society.
Aug 11, 1923

View 4-May 1929
Eugene L Armbruster Collection.

title: Manhattan: Battery Park - [Aquarium].
text:
Battery Park: The present Aquarium at the time when it was the Emigrant Landing Office "Castle Garden". It was erected in 1807 and known as "Castle Clinton".  Ceded to the City in 1822, it was leased as a place of amusement.  Various celebrities appeared here, including the world wide renowned Jenny Lind.  It was placed in the depicted service in 1855, continuing until the fire of May 23, 1870.  Rebuilt internally, it was used for concerts for several years.  The Park Commissioner had it altered to its present form.
Between 1855-70.

Gift of Urbrook Collection

title: Manhattan: Battery Park.
text:
Battery Park: A view limited to the present Aquarium and which at the time of the photograph was the Emigrant Landing office "Castle Garden". Erected in 1807 as Castle Clinton it was ceded to the city in 1822 and leased as a place of amusement.  In May 1855 it was placed in the depicted use, continuing the same until the fire of May 23, 1870.  Rebuilt internally it was used for concerts for a short time.  The Park Commissioner then altered it for its present purpose.
Between 1855 & 70
Gift of Urbrook Collection

title: Manhattan: Battery Park.
text:
Battery Park: The monument erected by the city in 1818 to mark the S.W. bastion of Fort George. It disappeared in some mysterious manner, probably during the filling in of the Battery in 1851. It was unearthed during the excavations for the subway, and was replaced near the sidewalk in the grounds of the park in 1907. It is now in the N.Y.H. Society, Aug. 1942, S.V.

title: Manhattan: Battery Park.
text:
Battery Park: The Bulletin Board that was presented to the City by John D. Reilly, the head of the Todd Ship Yards. This is a constant source of interest to business men, employees, visitors and others, emphasizing the importance of New York as a great sea port. In the background are the various structures forming the well known skyline. Prominent among these are the Irving Trust, the Standard Oil, and the Bank of Manhattan buildings.
The New York Herald-Tribune of November 12, 1939, Section VII (gravure) carried a similar view.

P. L. Sperr

July 28, 1939

title: Manhattan: Battery Place - West Street
text:
Battery Place, east from West to State Streets and showing buildings on the north side of same which at this date contained numerous rookeries, the result of their proximity to Castle Garden; the immigrant landing depot. The latter is in Battery Park; which appears partially on the right. Prominent edifices are (from left to right) the Standard Oil Building; the Welles Building; the Washington Building; The United States Custom House (flag atop) and the Battery Park Building. Note at Greenwich Street the elevated station of the first elevated line in New York; this today (1937) is used as a portion of the Sixth and Ninth Ave. lines.

About 1889.

Brown Brothers.

title: Manhattan: Bedford Street - Houston Street
text:
(1)
Bedford Street, northwest from Houston Street at Congress (Sixth Avenue Extension). Bedford Street runs northwest, parallel to the third section (originally Herring's Street) of Bleecker Street, to Christopher Street, and, like the corresponding section of Bleecker, lies almost entirely within the old Herring farm. The farm line crosses Bedford Street at Nos. 10 and 17 (about where two cars are parked together on the east side of the street a hundred feet north of the plaza).
The little plaza in the foreground is formed by the junction of the original Houston Street (from the Bowery to this point), the former Hammersley Street (at the left), which in 1858 was made part of Houston Street, and Bedford Street, which on the angle of Bleecker Street, might have been absorbed by Houston had it not been for Hammersley Street. At the right, Hancock Extension, comes into the plaza at right angles to Houston Street. At the left of View No. 2, may be seen the billboards at the right angle junction of Congress (originally Smith) Street and Houston Street.
October 11, 1928.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)
Another view, with the cameras more to the west.
October 11, 1928.

P. L. Sperr.

(3)
The same, from the ground, from and including Sixth Avenue, three and a half years later.
February 20, 1932.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Beekman Street - South Street
text:
Beekman Street, west from the East River, showing at South Street (foreground) the Fulton Fish Market. title: Manhattan: Bleecker Street - Hancock Street
text:
Bleecker Street, north from Hancock Street (in the line of the future Sixth Avenue Extension) and Minetta Street (right). At this point, which is on the old line between the West Bayard Farm on the east and the Herring Farm on the west, there is a bend of about 30 degrees in Bleecker Street, where two separate streets once met. The section of Bleecker Street from here north to Christopher Street was originally Herring Street. It gave up its own name in 1829.
At the left, on the south corner of Downing Street, is the Church of our Lady of Pompeii, organized in 1901, and occupying the building which used to be the Church of St. Benedict the Moor, the negro Roman Catholic Church. In the mid-nineteenth century this part of Bleecker Street was in the middle of the Greenwich Village negro colony, which at that time was numerically quite strong.
All the buildings in the immediate foreground are slated for demolition, being directly in the path of the Sixth Avenue Extension and municipal subway. The new Church of Our Lady of Pompeii is under construction at the N.W. corner of Carmine Street; the skeleton of its tower may be seen behind the lamp-post.
Autumn 1926.

title: Manhattan: Bleecker Street - Barrow Street
text:
309 (old no. 293) Bleeker Street, northeast side, between Barrow and Grove Street, This was once Mrs. Ryder's house on Herring Street, between Reason and Columbia Streets, to use the contemporary names. Here Thomas Paine, author of "The Age of Reason," spent most of the last year of his life, although he died in another house on Grove (then Columbia) Street, to which he was moved in April 1809. The house shown here will be taken down in 1932.

In 1829 Herring Street became part of Bleeker Street, and was renumbered accordingly; the house numbers were again changed around the time of the Civil War. At that time this house, then 293 Bleeker Street, became 309 Bleeker Street.

title: Manhattan: Bleecker Street - Grove Street

309, 307-305 (old Nos. 293, 291) Bleecker Street (originally Herring Street), north side, between Grove (originally Columbia) and Barrow (originally Reason) Streets, just north of Seventh Avenue South. Both are frame houses, but No. 307-305 is faced with brick. No. 309 is the old Ryder house on Herring Street, in which Thomas Paine lived (see Wurts Brothers' 1914 view of it). Herring Street is the third morphologically distinct section of Bleecker Street, from Hancock (later Sixth Avenue Extension) to Christopher Streets. It lost its own name in 1829. No. 307 will be replaced by a new building prior to 1932, and No. 309 not long after.

title: Manhattan: Bleecker Street - Christopher Street
text:
329 to 343 (old Nos. 313-327) Bleecker Street, east side, at, adjoining, and north from Christopher Street. 329-331, 339, and 343 are frame houses with brick facings. The frame house on the corner is No. 93 Christopher Street or 329 (old No. 313) Bleecker Street, the house where the New York Commissioners met from 1807 to 1811 to plan the checkerboard layout of New York's numbered streets and was reached by crossing open fields.

From here north they named this particular street George Street. From Christopher Street southeast to Minetta and Hancock Streets (the latter was absorbed in 1928 by Sixth Avenue Extension), a street called Herring or Herring's Street was already laid out, in the territory which had been the Herring Farm. Thomas Paine was living, in 1808-1809, about two blocks down the same side of Herring Street. At the Hancock-Minetta end, Herring Street met an east-west street called David Street, Bleecker Street, on the map of 1811, was a short street west from, and parallel to, the Bowery, extending to Broadway. But in a few years Bleecker and David Streets had been more gracefully joined, and Bleecker swallowed up the other three streets, absorbing Herring Street in 1829 and David Street even earlier. Later, around the time of the Civil War, 16 was added to the house numbers in this part of Bleecker Street.

June, 1925.

BROWN BROS.

(3)
The same as No. 2, but at an earlier date. The Thalia Theatre, as shown here, was erected in 1826 as the Bowery Theatre; the Mayor laying the corner stone in May and it being opened in October of that year. It was destroyed by fire four times. First on May 26, 1828, when it was rebuilt and reopened in 90 days. It was destroyed again September 22, 1836; for the third time, February 8, 1838; and last on April 25, 1845. It retained the name Bowery until 1879, when it was re-christened the Thalia. Its final and last fire occurred on June 15, 1929 and the remains disfigured the area for several years. Today (1937) this old landmark is completely gone, a low business structure occupying the site. The Bull's Head, a tavern used for the sale of cattle stood on this site from prior to 1763 to 1826, when it was taken down.
February 1924.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Manhattan: Bowery - Grand Street
text:
133-139 Bowery, north of the N.E. corner of Grand Street. No. 135 Bowery, north of the N.E. corner of Grand Street, is a frame building with a brick front.

1932.

J. Clarence Davies Collection, Museum of the City of New York.

The structure at the right (No.133) was formerly occupied by the restaurant and saloon of Pat Farley, politician and one of the "Boodle Aldermen" who figured in the old Broadway trolley franchise scandal. Title to this holding was recently (about 1939) transferred thru Hiram Rinaldo, broker. See, The New York Times of May 26, 1939 for a reference to this, on the reported sale of blds. across the street (No's. 138-140, Callahan the Hatter) thru the same individual.

title: Manhattan: Bowery - Broome Street
text:
138-142 Bowery, south of the S.W. corner of Broome Street. No. 140 Bowery, south of the S.W. corner of Broome Street, is a 2-story frame building.

1932.

J. Clarence Davies Collection, Museum of the City of New York. Negative No. 584.

The New York Times of May 26, 1939 reports the sale of this and it's adjoining structure (No's. 138-140). John "Callahan the Hatter" occupied No. 138 and attracted the patronage of many of the beaux and dandies of the "Gay Nineties". At his death, the business was continued by his clerks. Recently the store was divided and occupied by crockery and novelty dealers. No. 138 is a leased branch of the National Cash Register Company.

text:
The Bowery (Third Avenue "El" thereon), at Delancey Street (foreground, and which becomes Kenmare Street after crossing the Bowery) as viewed southwestward from the subsequently razed Libbys Hotel. Note the Woolworth Bldg. outline at the left and the New York Telephone Bldg. at the right. Beneath the latter appears the dome of the Central office of the New York Police Department. This area, a portion of the old Bayard Farm, is to the north of Chinatown and is a densely ghetto district, being populated mainly by individuals of Italian extraction.

title: Manhattan: Bowery - Houston Street (East)
text:
The Bowery, east side, north from East Houston Street to Cooper Union (extreme left) and showing an early view of this important thoroughfare prior to the construction of the Elevated Line. The Savings Bank appearing on the right and adjoining the N.E. corner of Houston Street is the Mechanics and Traders, No. 283 Bowery, according to Gouldings Business Directory of 1875. Rands New York City Business Directory of 1877 list: same as a National Bank with a location given as Ho. 153. The building bearing the flags is the Germania Assembly Rooms. North of the latter and occupying the S.E. and N.E. corners of East 1st Street are two low buildings; one with a hip roof. These remain today (1938) though the rest of the outline has disappeared. Note the 4 sets of rails in the road bed, several of which appear with horse drawn cars thereon.
1870.

title: Manhattan: Bowery - Houston Street (East)

About 1890.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - Battery Place
text:
1-- Bowling Green, a northward view up Broadway from "Steamboat Row", showing a view of New York's first park. Note the iron railing around same and the lanterns thereupon. In the center is a pool and fountain.

Early views (circa 1850 and 61) show this latter feature and which in subsequent views (1884) is absent, tho the pool remained. The last date given is that of Produce Exchange Building construction, replacing the buildings on the right.

To the left on Broadway, appear ovate shaped sewer pipes and a partial excavation for same. These were introduced in 1860 and were 4x2.8 feet in diameter. In 1864 vitrified pipe was first laid. Across the foreground are suspended electric wires and at the extreme right is an old street illuminating gas lamp.

For dedication ceremony (April 6, 1938) see New York City newspapers for February and March. Views similar to this are in these files and in a volume of newspaper clippings titled "New York City Views" American History Division - Room 300 New York Public Library, several of which are credited to the Consolidated Edison Company.

Rockwood Photo

2-- Broadway north from Bowling Green

Thadéus Wilderson
522 W. 145th Street
New York City

title: Manhattan: Broad Street - Wall Street
text:
Broad Street, south from Wall Street, showing mainly the westerly side of this thoroughfare. To the left, center, and right respectively are, the old Mills Building (replaced in 1926 by the 38-story Equitable Trust Co. Building), the Produce Exchange (distinctive tower atop) and the New York Stock Exchange Building. Adjoining the latter is the renovated 6-story building adjoining the corner structure. These were subsequently demolished and their site improved by a larger building and which in time was replaced by the north wing of the Stock Exchange.

See King's Handbook of New York (1893), page 155 for a slightly later view.

Between 1889-1893

Gift Thru New York Historical Society

At the extreme right is the Wilks Building separated from the New York Stock Exchange Building by a renovated (between 1889-1893) five-story structure. Towering above same is the graceful Mackey Building. The Johnston Building is to the south, while beyond appears the dim outline of the Produce Exchange. Note between these the Edison Building.

At the left margin is the Drexel Building and its adjoining Mills structure.

About 1893

title: Manhattan: Broad Street - Exchange Place
text:
Broad Street from and including Exchange Place to and including Wall Street, also showing the west side of Nassau Street from Wall to Cedar Streets. In the centre, the 38-story Equitable Trust Company Building is being erected on the site of the old Mills Building, built in the 1880's. Above it, on Wall Street, is the Sub-Treasury Building, built in 1842 on the site of the old Federal Hall, where the Federal Government of the United States was inaugurated and George Washington inducted as the nation's first president. In the left background may be seen the New York Stock Exchange, on the S.W. corner of Broad and Wall Streets. Across from it between the Equitable Trust excavation and the Sub-Treasury, is the building of J.P. Morgan & Company.

1926.

title: Manhattan: Broad Street - Stone Street
text:
Broad Street (right), north from Stone Street (foreground, street level not seen), as viewed northward from the New York Telephone Building at No. 104. Broad Street. Shown in the background are buildings at Wall Street, consisting of, the Irving Trust (under construction), the Bankers Trust (pyramidal roof), the Equitable, and the Equitable Trust Co. Buildings. To the right foreground is the new 35 storied International Telephone Building, and to the left, the low Produce Exchange.

View No. 2 is the same at an earlier date and photographed in the same direction from atop the roof of the last mentioned feature. To the right in this instance is the 18 story structure (No. 26-28 Beaver Street) shown in the center of the preceding view. Note the absence of the Irving Trust Building and the prominence of the Equitable Trust Co. Broad Street is obscured from view by the buildings on the westerly side of same.

P. L. Sperr.

August 6, 1930.
No. 2 August 28, 1929.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - Stone Street

Broadway, east side, from Stone to Beaver Street's, showing the distinctive building of the New York Produce Exchange, as photographed across Manhattan's first park, Bowling Green. At the right is the row of residences that became "Steamship Row" and was later replaced with the U. S. Custom House. Above their roofs appears the 8 story Kemble Bldg. on Whitehall Street (continuation of Broadway) from Stone to Bridge Street's. To the left is an eastward perspective on Beaver Street, to include the incomplete New York Cotton Exchange Bldg. (erected 1883-5). Beyond this is the vague buttress of the Manhattan side of the Brooklyn Bridge. The photographers vantage point is the Washington Bldg. at No. 1 Broadway. title: Manhattan: Broadway - Liberty Street
text:
Broadway, at, adjoining and north of the N. W. corner of Liberty Street (left, not shown), showing the site of the later date Singer Building.

No. 161 Broadway, the five story building contains, the Knickerbocker Life Insurance Co., the Columbia Fire Insurance Co. and the Yonkers-New York Fire Insurance Co. The latter might be the re-organized firm consisting of the separate companies that failed in the Boston fire of 1871. This structure was the home of the Greenwich Insurance Co. in the 1890's. An illustration showing this occupancy appears on page 643 of Moses Kings Handbook of New York, 1893.

The Williamsburg City Fire Insurance Co. occupies the store of No. 165. This firm was organized in 1853. They later moved to their newly completed (about 1885) home across the street (N. E. corner of Liberty St.)

For purposes of information, the various remaining insurance companies after the fire of 1835 were required to organize individually and were prohibited from accumulating functions. They were required to be chartered for specific purposes, such as fire, life, fidelity, casualty, etc. On the repeal of the Act of 1829, many foreign firms (mainly English) entered this field. After the second conflagration in the business center of New York (1845), an association of city underwriters was formed that developed into the National Board in 1866.

About 1870's

title: Manhattan: Broadway - Vesey Street
text:
Broadway, west side, north from Vesey Street, showing prominently the old Astor House, built 1832, occupying the entire block frontage to Barclay Street. Early records inform us that this site was an encampment for negro slaves in 1780. Numbers of these died of smallpox and were buried where the Sun (formerly A. T. Stewart) Building stands at the N. E. corner of Broadway and Chambers Street. The Woolworth Building was erected in 1912 and the Transportation Building in 1926. The latter at the far corner, while the former in the block above.
