title: Manhattan: Broadway - Vesey Street
text:
(1)
Broadway, west side, north from Vesey (left) to Barclay (right) Streets, showing the Astor House, built in 1832 and opened in 1836 by Boyden, a hotel keeper from Boston. It was reopened September 1, 1875 by F.J. Allan and A.J. Dunn. The portion at the N.W. corner of Vesey Street was demolished and is today (1937) the site of the Astor Building; No. 217 Broadway. On this site in 1780 there was an encampment of Negro slaves, enticed by Lord Dunmore from Virginia. Large numbers died from small pox and were buried in the ground later occupied by Stewarts (Department Store) at Chambers Street and Broadway.

Date----?

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2)
The same, at a later date and showing a more extensive view to and including Park Place. Note the portion of the Astor House still standing. This was taken down in March 1926 and there upon was erected the 44-story Transportation Building, No. 225 Broadway, at the S.W. corner of Barclay Street. The Woolworth Building occupies the block between Barclay Street and Park Place.

May 1924.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3)
A similar view, slightly more inclusive northward.
About 1890.

A Set of Seven Canvases of Old New York

These paintings come from a country house called 'Glencairn' near Dublin in Ireland, where they adorned the walls of the billiard room. The house was built by Richard 'Boss' Croker (1841-1922), an Irishman who for many years was associated with Tammany Hall in New York, holding political positions under William M. 'Boss' Tweed, and later, after the latter's ousting, under 'Honest John' Kelly. Following the Lexow Committee investigations (1889-90), he left for England where he took up residence in Wantage, Berks, returning to America periodically, attempting to regain his lost position in the Democratic Party. After his final defeat in 1900, he crossed the Atlantic once again, built 'Glencairn' and started a racing stable. Despite his past reputation (he paid, in all, $550,000 for his Irish estates), he lived up to the high standards demanded by British racing circles, and when his horse Orby won the Derby in 1907, did not even own him.

These pictures were painted to remind him of New York, and it is assumed that they were executed here around the turn of the century. All are painted in tones of sepia and green.

The British Government has recently acquired this mansion for the use of the British Ambassador to Ireland.

PARKE-BERNET Sale 2234, Nov. 29-30, 1963

title: Manhattan: Broadway - Barclay Street
text:
229-237 Broadway, west side, from Barclay Street to Park place, showing at this location, the 55 story Woolworth Bldg. The general direction is northward from a vantage point at No. 165 Broadway (City Investing Bldg.) in views 1, 2, and 3. View 4 is photographed from No. 30 Church Street. Broadway is the thoroughfare clearly shown at the right. Note the spire of St. Pauls Chapel, the quadrangular Astor House, the ornate Post Office, City Hall Park and the white marble Sun (formerly A. T. Stewarts) Building. The St. Paul Bldg. appears at the right margin of views 1 and 3. Today, (1939) this view is more or less the same. The most radical change is the replacement of the old Astor House by the 44 storied Transportation Bldg. and the present demolition of the Post Office.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - Thomas Street
text:
Broadway, west side, at Thomas Street (unopened), showing the old New York Hospital buildings that stood here from the American Revolution to 1869, when their function was removed to the new hospital on West 15th Street. The structure shown is the second, as the first (cornerstone laid in 1775) was destroyed by fire prior to completion. It was immediately rebuilt and nearly complete when the Revolution began. The unfinished building was occupied by the British and Hessian soldiers as a barrack and hospital, and it was not until January, 1791, that it was in a proper condition to receive patients.

Prior to 1869

Gift of Urbrock Collection

title: Manhattan: Broadway - Houston Street
text:
Broadway, north from a point slightly south of Houston Street, showing vehicular and pedestrian traffic on this main artery of Manhattan during a spectacular period in the Citys history. Note the paved condition of the street bed and the lack of mechanical transportation; gas street lamps appearing midst overhead wire communications. The Grand Central Hotel which became the present Broadway Central Hotel is in the mid-distance with Grace P.E. Church farther northward, at the bend. The structures in the foreground, (both right and left sides) have disappeared today, vacant lots being thereon, caused by demolition work during construction of the Independent Subway. This photograph, made from one of the early dry plates, comes from a book entitled "How to make photographs" by T.C. Roche.

1883.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - Houston
text:
Broadway, east side, between Houston and Bleecker Street's, showing the Olympic Theatre at No. 624. This structure was opened on November 18, 1856 and soon afterward re-christened Laura Keene's New Theatre. This name was attached to half a dozen theatres during the period from 1850 to 1870. She retired in 1863, and John Duff, who then became the manager, re-opened the house as Mrs. John Woods Olympic Theatre. After Mrs. Woods retirement in 1866 it had a checkered career and was demolished in 1880. Joseph Jefferson appeared here in the play "Our American Cousin" on its first performance on October 18, 1858.

Betw. 1863-66

text:
Broadway, west side, south from Waverly to Washington Places, showing the old New York Hotel occupying the entire frontage involved. This structure bore No. 721 and was a favorite resort of the Southerners before and after the Civil War. Many stories were told of how blockade running plots originated here. it was erected in 1847. Randolph Guggenheimer had it removed in 1896 for his 12 story New York Commercial Building. Note the absence of street car tracks.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 9th Street (East)
text:
Broadway, east side, north from East 9th (Wanamaker Place) to and including 10th Streets, showing the north building of John Wanamaker's Department Store and Grace Protestant Episcopal Church. Note the NRA banner on Wanamaker's flagstaff. At the date of this picture the National Industrial Recovery Act was only five months old and the National Recovery Administration (NRA) had recently been established, headed by General Hugh S. Johnson. The NRA was greeted with enthusiasm which closely resembled war-time hysteria. An NRA parade took place in September of this year (see Parades for photographs) which was the largest in New York's history, surpassing even the war parades. Later, however, the popularity of NRA waned and early in 1935 it was declared unconstitutional by the United States Supreme Court in the Schechter case, popularly called the "sick chicken" case.

October 19, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 13th Street (East)
text:
842 Broadway, at the N. E. corner of East 13th Street, showing the Star Theatre. This structure was erected as Wallacks Theatre and opened on September 25, 1861. It was here that the name Wallack gained its brightest laurels. Charles Fisher, John Sefton, Mark Smith, John Gilbert, James Williamson, E. L. Davenport, J. H. Stoddard, Henry Montgue, Dion Boucicault, Charles Coghlan, Fanny Morant, Rose Eytinge, Katherine Rogers and Rose Coghlan appeared here. The plays presented were the standard old comedies and the best of the works of contemporaneous English dramatists. The house and company were famous for the general excellence of the productions, rather than for the brilliance of particular events. It became the Germania in 1881, and the rechristened Star in 1883. Theodore Moss was the manager for many years and remodelled the interior in 1883 and in 1889. Note the sign in the store window announcing the proposed demolition. On the right is an eastward view on the north side of East 13th Street, across Fourth Avenue. Huber's 14th Street Palace and Museum appears there.

H. N. Tiemann, photo
Gift of Urbrock Collection

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 21st Street
text:
Broadway, east side, north from 21st Street. The entire two blocks in the foreground, from 21st to 23rd Streets, will be unchanged some twenty-seven years later, in 1936, except for a 12-story loft building, which will occupy the clearing shown here in the block between 21st and 22nd Streets. This clearing is the result of the demolition of three four-story houses. In 1936 the Bancroft House will be the Hotel Courte; and the Hotel Bartholdi, on the S.E. corner of 23rd Street, will be the Bartholdi Building, remodelled into an office building. But during this period of twenty-seven years there will be no demolitions and, with the exception noted, no construction work -- a long period in New York. April, 1909.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 25th Street
text: Hoffman House, 1111 Broadway, at Fifth Ave., at and adjoining the S.W. corner of 25th Street. The oldest part of the hotel, in the centre of the block, was opened in 1864. The hotel was enlarged by annexing and remodelling on 24th and 25th Streets, and in 1885 the eight-story fireproof building, adjoining the 25th Street corner, was completed and opened. This was one of the most famous hotels of its time, and noted especially for its bar-room, on the 24th Street side, which was a veritable art gallery. In 1904 the old part of the hotel, facing on Broadway, will be demolished and rebuilt. The hotel will fina1ly close its doors in 1914, and the following year loft buildings will replace the Hoffman House and the Albemarle, in this block.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 28th Street (West).
text:
Broadway, at the N.W. corner of West 28th Street, showing that side of the former Fifth Avenue Theatre, facing on the latter thoroughfare. This structure was the fourth playhouse to bear this name. It replaced its name sake, burned January 2, 1891. The present (and last) house opened May 28, 1892 with the production "The Robber of the Rhine." Its predecessor was built by the Gilsey estate in 1873 on the site of a building which opened October 16, 1868 as Apollo Hall and was variously known as Newcomb's Hall and the St. James Theatre. Mary Anderson made her New York debut here, November 12, 1877, Modjeska on December 22, 1877, and Mrs. James Brown Potter on October 31, 1887. The first authorized performance in America the Gilbert and Sullivan opera "The Mikado" was given September 24, 1885.

Demolition occurred in 1939 and a 1 story taxpayer erected on the Broadway frontage.

November 2, 1938

Berenice Abbott, photo

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 29th Street
text:
The old Gilsey House, now serving as an office building, Broad-way at the N.E. corner of 29th Street. The Gilsey House, although not a large hotel, was famous for its comfort and the excellence of its cuisine. Its dining room was said to be one of the half a dozen which could be mentioned in the same breath with Delmonico's. It was built in the early 1870's, and was converted into an office building between 1910 and 1916. It will still stand in 1936.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 30th Street (West)
text:
Broadway, west side, south from West 30th Street, show- prominently Daly's Theatre. This was opened as Banvards Museum in 1867, and during the succeeding twelve years, it was known as Wood's Museum and Metropolitan Theatre, Wood's Museum and Menagerie, and the Broadway Theatre. In it's early days it was both a museum and a playhouse, and in the early '70's it was the home of burlesque. Augustin Daly took possession, remodelled it, and gave it its present name in 1879. It was again remodelled in 1891. The wing to 29th Street was added in 1892. Demolished in 1920, it was replaced with an 8 story office building.

About 1905

April 22, 1929.

According to the New York Times of July 1, 1939, the abovementioned structure has been leased by the Metropolitan Insurance Company until December 31, 1949 to a syndicate headed by Frank W. Kridel, operator of several other large hotels.

The 600-room hostelry has been improved and modernized; public rooms and some other parts of the building have been air-conditioned. Many of the original features for which this hotel is famous have been retained in a more modern setting. The elaborate Roman-style ceiling is admired by many. It was laid by Italian workmen brought to this country for this purpose. The inlaid tiles in the lobby and corridors and the ancient Wynwood Martinique clock are retained to delight lovers of antiques and clock experts. The clock is perhaps the most interesting decorative piece in the building. It was fashioned by hand by H.T. Crawford, clockmaker to royalty, in 1691, under a special commission from Sir Ralph Wynwood. It furnished the English craftsman carved the figure of St. Matthew, standing and kneeling, attended by cherubs around the day of the month. At Sir Ralph Wynwood's death the fifteen-foot

It was later bought for $8,500 by Mrs. Elizabeth C. Cole of New York. William H. Martin purchased it in 1911 from the estate to add to this collection. Later owners were Cornelius Vanderbilt and Oliver H. Belmont, but Mr. Martin again thought to install in the Broadway hotel which has been in operation for forty years.

1287-1289 Broadway, west side, between 32nd and 33rd Streets. This block morphologically belongs to Sixth Avenue, but is given Broadway house numbering, and hence must be considered the west side of Broadway.

The Eagle Theatre, in the centre has just recently opened. In 1878 its name will be changed to the Standard Theatre, and it will finally be replaced by the Manhattan Theatre. This block will be occupied about 1915 by Gimbel Brothers' department store.
Within a few weeks foundation work will begin on the Sixth Avenue Elevated Railroad.

Early spring, 1876.

In the center background is the Hotel Normandie, and in slightly left-center background is the Metropolitan Opera House. Dominating the skyline is the new building of the New York Times.

Broadway, west side, from West 35th to 36th Street's, showing prominently the Herald Square Theatre. This is at the N.W. corner of 35th Street. It was first opened in 1883 as the New Park. Later Harrigan took a lease and produced "Old Lavender" "Pete" and other successes. The name was changed to that shown in 1895. The following year Belasco's play "The Heart of Maryland" was produced here. Lew Fields was the final lessee. The house was torn down in 1912. At the left and right margins respectively appear Macys Department Store and the Hotel Marlborough. Slightly to the right of the former is the Arsenal tower at Seventh Ave.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 39th Street
text:
The Metropolitan Opera House, Broadway, west side, from 39th to 40th Streets, showing also 39th Street, north side, from Broadway to Seventh Avenue.  The Metropolitan was built in 1883, and its interior was rebuilt in 1892, after it was destroyed by fire. For some years there was bitter rivalry between the Metropolitan and the Academy of Music, but the Academy could not compete with its younger rival, and at last gave the production of opera,  It is today (1936) the only permanent opera company in New York, although occasional and sometimes successful attempts are made to produce opera at popular price, especially at the Hippodrome.

About 1928.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 39th Street
text:
From the CHANIN ORGANIZATION
EXECUTIVE OFFICES: CHANIN BUILDING, 122 EAST 42ND STREET, NEW YORK

TELEPHONE OXFORD 7-2200
Elbert Severance, Press Representative
HOME TELEPHONE: BOULEVARD 3-1189

4/21/67

NEW YORK'S OLD METROPOLITAN OPERA HOUSE MAKES WAY FOR OFFICE TOWER

Abandoned by the Metropolitan Opera Company, which gave its 1966-67 season in its new home in the Lincoln Center of Performing Arts, New York's old Metropolitan Opera House now is being demolished to make room for a 40-story office tower.

The new building was designed by the Offices of Irwin S. Chanin, Architect, which over the years has given the city, and the Middle Atlantic Coast from New England to Virginia, great office buildings, urban apartment houses, hotels, legitimate and motion picture theatres, suburban residential communities, a great shopping center and commercial and industrial buildings.

Erected in 1883, the old Metropolitan was the last survivor in a theatrical, opera and concert district, mostly located south of 42nd Street, which over the years has moved northward by a mile or more with its spine, in general, still Broadway, upon which the old Metropolitan faced.

The new building, to contain about 1-million square feet of office and commercial space, will stand on land that still belongs to the Metropolitan Opera Association. It has been leased for a long term of years to the sponsors of the office building, who will pay a ground rent of about $500,000 a year. The ground rent will help meet the operating deficit of the opera company.

Like all other opera companies and symphony orchestras, the opera company's boxoffice receipts, even at capacity, cannot meet operating costs.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 43rd Street (West)
text:
Broadway (Times Square), at the N. E. corner of West 43rd Street, showing the Hotel Cadillac prior to demolition in 1940. At the left is the adjoining Hotel Claridge at 44th Street. In the foreground are the Police Information Booth and a subway kiosk.

The Hotel Cadillac was erected in two units. The first to rise was the eight story corner structure. This was built as the Barrett House in 1883. The adjoining unit rose several years later.and was the first to bear the name Cadillac. In 1900 they were combined. For a brief period between 1910 and 1915 they were known as the Hotel Wallick. The land upon which they stand has been owned by the Goelet interests, passing from Ogden Goelet to his daughter May, the wife of the Duke of Roxburghe, and to her son the present Duke.

For a more complete account see the New York Times of March 19, 1940.

July, 1935

George L. Balgue

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 47th Street (West)
text:
1570-1564 Broadway, at and adjoining the S.E. corner of West 47th Street. The 2-story building comprises a double lot, Nos. 1570-1568, with the 11-story office building, No. 1564 adjoining. The Palace Theatre, a former vaudeville house now (1937), shows only motion pictures. Considering all the former aspirations of variety players to perform at this house, motion pictures are a tragedy. The theatre actually is in the 5-story building at the rear of both of these lots; with an entrance and lobby through the office building. These buildings, geographically on Seventh Ave., form a part of Times Square and bear Broadway numbers. October 1, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 72nd Street
text:
Broadway (then known as Boulevard), west side, from 72nd to 74th Streets, showing the Hotel St. Andrew in the foreground, and the Rutgers Memorial Church. The Hotel St. Andrew will stand in 1936, but the church will give way between 1920 and 1925 to a five-story building.

About 1895.

Brown Brothers.

According to the New York Times of October 3, 1937, the Hotel built in 1893, will be replaced by a 4 or 5-story business structure. This site was the result (to himself and at a total cost of only $6,500) of a shrewd land speculation deal, by Robert Robertson in January 1886. It became the property of Morris Schinasi, the cigarette manufacturer at a later date whose heirs are involved in the present transfer.

This organization in 1890 sold its property at Park Ave. and 39th Street, preparatory to the erection of the edifice shown; services being held meanwhile in a brick chapel in West 81st Street. title: Manhattan: Broadway - 84th Street (West)
text:
Broadway, east side, at West 84th Street, showing the house in which Edgar Allan Poe wrote "The Raven". In the "Life of Poe" by William F. Gill (published 1877) on page 147-8 appears a drawing of this building. It is stated to have been a "few hundred feet from the corner of 84th St. and St. Nicholas Blvd. (formerly Bloomingdale Road)." A Mrs. Brennan lived here for 47 years and rented same to Poe in the Spring of 1844. He finished "The Raven" in the Winter of that year. In the following Spring he moved to the City proper. It is inferred that General Washington and his officers used it as a shelter. G. E. Woodberry in his "Life of E. A. Poe" (V. 2 page 113) reports the location as being "near what is now the eastern corner of 84th Street and Broadway. The sign hanging from the house reads "John Negel, Mason Builder, Ovens Built & Burners Set, 'Kalsomining'." The inscription on the rock reads "R. Hamilton, Upholsterer, 11th Avenue.

Date ?

(1) Broadway, west side, north from West 116th to 122nd Streets, showing in the foreground, Barnard College and grounds, with the Riverside Baptist Church, overpowering same. The Gothic structure on the extreme right, is a portion of the Administration Building and Library of the Union Theological Seminary. Preceding same, is a unit of Barnard College, containing Fiske, Milbank and Brinkerhoff Halls. 1936. Walter L. Bogert.

(2) A limited view to West 120th Street, from a slight altitude, showing the Students Building of Barnard College completely. 1936. Walter L. Bogert.

(3) A detail of the same, to a point slightly southward, from a different angle. Right to left appear; the southern portion of the Students' Building of Barnard College, the Barnard College Dormitory, and Brooks Hall Dormitory. 1936. Walter L. Bogert.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 116th Street
text:
Broadway, north from, but not including, 116th Street, favoring the east side. The first street seen, on the left, is 119th Street; 117th and 118th Streets do not intersect Broadway because of the grounds of Columbia University, whose buildings flank Broadway to 119th Street. The U-shaped building on the north side of 119th Street is Barnard College. Behind the college is the Union Theological Seminary. At the extreme left is Grant's Tomb. North of 122nd Street the subway may be seen emerging from its tunnel. From 122nd to 125th Streets, the subway trains run on an elevated trestle, with an elevated station at 125th Street.

May, 1926.

Brown Brothers.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 119th Street
text:
Broadway, west side, north from and including 119th Street, giving a close view of Barnard College in the foreground. The Union Theological Seminary, which will occupy the grounds from 120th to 122nd Streets, has not yet been built. Broadway is being torn up for the excavation work on the city's first subway. September 25, 1900.

William B. Parsons Collection.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 120th Street (West)
text:
Broadway, at West 120th Street, showing in the foreground (S.W. corner), the Athletic Field of Barnard College. Across West 120th Street and partially hidden by trees, are three units, Fiske, Millbank and Brinkerhoff Halls, of the College. The latter is at the N.W. corner of the afore mentioned streets. Across its roof, appears the tower of the Administration and Library Buildings of the Union Theological Seminary. The large tower shown on the left, is that of the Riverside Baptist Church, which is located on Riverside Drive, at the S.E. corner of West 122nd Street.

1936.

Walter L. Bogert.

text:
(1)
Broadway, south from West 160th Street and showing a declivity in this Washington Heights area. Note the central plaza being utilized as a taxi stand.

About 1914. Slide 259

(2)
A view in the opposite direction from West 158th Street and showing mainly the west side of this thoroughfare.

About 1914.

The Rio Theatre, shown in the left center of No. 2 and occupying that irregular block bounded by Fort Washington Ave., Broadway and West 160th Street has been completely acquired by Cardinal Hayes, who formerly had only a half interest in this and others, from the relatives of the late John Whalen according to the New York Times of April 17, 1938. The other real estate involved is the easterly block front of Amsterdam Ave. between 154th and 155th Streets.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 166th Street (West)
text:
Broadway, west side, north from and including West 166th (foreground), to and including West 168th (extreme right) Streets, showing Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center. The prominent building (center) is the Babies Hospital; on its right, Vanderbilt Clinic; and on its left, Presbyterian Hospital (Sloane Hospital). On the extreme left appears the Presbyterian School for Nursing, between Fort Washington Ave., and Riverside Drive.

1936.

W.P.A. Photo.
Federal Writers Project.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - Nagle Avenue
text:
Broadway (midground, between the bluff and the apartment structures which obscure the street level) from Nagle Avenue. (foreground and partially hidden by the shrubbery) photographed in a northwestward direction from Fort George towards the Dyckman Street gap. This thoroughfare separates Fort Washington (now 1938, Fort Tryon Park) and Inwood Hill (now a City park also). In the northern extremity of the former and where the small cleared area appears, stands the recently constructed Cloisters of the Metropolitan Museum of Art. At the extreme right is the vague outline of Marble Hill on the far side of the Harlem River.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - Nagle Avenue
text:
Broadway (across midground of panoramic views) from Nagle Avenue (left foreground and across view to the right) observed in a northwestward direction from a vantage given by the photographer as near Fairview Avenue. The view is towards the Dyckman Street gap, from the Fort George area. To the left stood the Revolutionary Fort Washington, overlooking the North (Hudson) River. This site is shown occupied by the castle-like mansion of Dr. Chas. V. Paterno, the Geo. Barnard Grey studio and the C.K.G. Billings manor. Today (1938) the 1st is being demolished for a new apartment site; the 2nd has been replaced by similar buildings and the 3rd was razed and the area included in Fort Tryon Park. To the right on the north side of the gap rises Inwood Hill. This today is also a City park. At the far side of the latter the Harlem River flows into the Hudson.

October 26, 1927.
Views 1 and 2

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 204th Street (West)
text:
Dyckman House. Broadway and East 204th Street, Manhattan. This is the only remaining farmhouse of the eighteenth century in Manhattan. Built in Dutch Colonial style William Dyckman in 1783, it replaced his earlier house on the same site which was destroyed during the Revolutionary War. In 1915, following restoration of the house and grounds, it was given to the City of New York by Dyckman's descendants.
Bank of New York Calendar 1967-68

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 204th Street (West)
text:
The Dyckman House, Broadway at the N.W. corner of 204th Street. This house was built early in the eighteenth century, and at the time of this photograph is not quite two hundred years old. The two wings are not a part of the original house, but were added during the 1860's. The house is falling into disrepair through long neglect, but it will soon be restored and converted into a museum, with the surrounding land a city park. The north wing will be demolished, but the south wing will stand as late as 1936, at which time it will be in use as a caretaker's residence.

1895.

Gift of John H. Judd.

title: Manhattan: Broome Street - Crosby Street
text:
430 Broome Street (right), at the N.E. corner of Crosby Street (left), showing a 5-story structure that was formerly a Masonic Temple; Continental Lodge No. 287, F. & A.M., New York City, meeting here from 1855 to 1857 or 1858. It was the center of Masonic activities and more Lodges met there between 1850 and 1858 than at another point. The Municipal Building Department states this to be the structure standing at that early date. The donor is Past Master and Historian of the aforementioned Lodge and is also the present (1938) Secretary of the Masonic Board of Relief of New York City.

1938.

Gift of Francis J. Arkins.

title: Manhattan: Broome Street - Hudson Street
text:
Holland Tunnel Entrance (580) and 578 to 570 Broome Street, north side, between Hudson and Varick Streets. The tunnel has not quite yet been opened to the public. No 570 is the Roman Catholic Church of our Lady of Vilna. No 574 is the Duane Methodist Episcopal Church, which settled down at this address late in 1929. The old church (about 1862), at 292 Hudson Street, on the east side, south of Spring Street was demolished in 1923 (see Hudson Street). Originally the church was on Duane Street, where it was established in 1797 and stood till destroyed by fire in 1861.
September 27, 1927

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - 42nd Street
text:
The Crystal Palace, Sixth Avenue, east side, from 42nd to 40th Streets. The idea of an industrial exposition housed in a building of glass and iron originated in London 1851, in Hyde Park. The New York building, however, was smaller than its London predecessor, and entirely different in appearance. It was originally planned to build the Crystal Palace in Madison Square Park, but the protests of residents in that fashionable neighborhood compelled the abandonment of the scheme. The land in back of the Croton Reservoir, now Bryant Park, but then known as Reservoir Square, was leased from the City for a nominal rental of one dollar a year. Construction work began in 1852, and the building, housing the first World's Fair to be held in the United States, was formally opened on July 14, 1853, by President Franklin Pierce. The building, however, was not a financial success, as its London predecessor had been. The city took possession in May of 1858, and on October 5 of that year, while the City Fathers were debating the question of the removal of the building, and while the annual exposition of the American Institute was in progress, fire broke out, and the building was completely destroyed. The land was then converted by the city into the present Bryant Park. This is a photograph made for the sake of preservation from the original, a rare and badly faded photograph, whose plate has long ago been lost. The original is on deposit in the Library.

About 1853.

J. Loeffler, from P. L. Sperr Collection.

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - 41st Street
text:
Bryant Park, looking east from Sixth Avenue at 41st Street, with the New York Public Library and the skyscrapers of the Grand Central area in the background, and showing the Park as remodelled under Park Commissioner Robert Moses. The flower beds are mostly planted with ivy. The fountain has been moved west from its old position in front of the seated statue of William Cullen Bryant, by Herbert Adams, 1911. For a number of years the only statue in Bryant Park was a bust of Washington Irving, which seems to have disappeared in this latest rearrangement.

Spring 1935.

Photo by Nathan Schwartz
N.Y.P. Library.

title: Manhattan: 42nd Street (West) - 5th Avenue
text:
Bryant Park, north section, eastward along West 42nd Street. Buildings shown are on the north side of West 42nd Street, east from Sixth to Fifth Aves. Note the structural work at the N.W. corner of Fifth Ave. This will be the skyscraper, No. 500 Fifth Ave. when completed. Views 2 and 3 show a portion of the rear of the New York Public Library which faces on the Ave. Also note in these, the uncompleted spire of the Chrysler Building.

May 10, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - 42nd Street
text:
Bryant Park, center and south side, seen from Sixth Avenue and 42nd Street, the roof of the Elks' Club.
May 27, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

The same; the Federal Hall replica seen through a gap in the trees planted along Sixth Avenue. This photograph was made the month following the Washington Bicentennial Pageant. "Federal Hall" was kept open all year as a public exhibit.
May 15, 1932.

P. L. Sperr.

The same, a closer and unobstructed view, showing the Federal Hall replica. This is a copy of the old New York City Hall which stood on Wall Street at Nassau, and which became the property of the Federal government when New York became the temporary capital of the country, in 1789. President Washington was inaugurated on its balcony; and that scene was reenacted here in 1932.

May 15, 1932.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Burling Slip - Front Street
text:
Burling Slip, south side, west across Front, to Water Street's. In the right background is the distinctive Singer Building. At the left is the Kuhn, Loeb & Company building (52-4 William Street). The Equitable Building (under construction) is obscured by the New York Mutual Life Insurance Company building and the triangular Great American Insurance Company structure. The New York Steam Company plant replaced the low warehouses on Water Street, at the right.

October, 1914

George L. Balgue

title: Manhattan: Burling Slip - South Street
text:

title: Manhattan: Burling Slip - Pearl Street
text:
Burling Slip, north side, east from and including Pearl Street to the East River. Demolition work seen in the foreground is at the N.W. corner of Pearl Street where the 26-story No. 111 John Street Building was later erected. Also shown is a portion of the South Ferry division of the Second and Third Aves. Elevated Lines on Pearl Street, and in the background, pier 16, East River, with the Brooklyn shore faintly discernible. Also shown are Nos. 240 to 246 Pearl Street, at, adjoining and north of the N.E. corner of Burling Slip. Burling Slip is actually a continuation of John Street when east of Pearl Street.

June 3, 1928.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Cabrini Boulevard - 181st Street (West)
text:
Cabrini Boulevard, west side, north of W. 181st Street, showing the Dr. Chas. V. Paterno estate being cleared. Under demolition are the greenhouses and the castle-like home of this real-estate operator. The latter, constructed in 1908 at a cost of $500,000 is of Roman and English architecture. A modern apartment house similar to Doctor Paterno's adjacent Hudson View Garden Apartments will be erected here at a reported cost of $6,000,000. Note the close proximity of the George Washington Bridge which is slightly to the S.W. of this location.

August 23, 1938.
Views 1, 2 and 3.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Canal Street - Ludlow Street
text:
(1) Canal Street (running from foreground to rear) east from and in- cluding Ludlow Street (left fore, where truck is visible), to and including East Broadway (where it terminates), and showing the latter thoroughfare forming approximately a 160 degree angle and proceeding, essentially, in the same (eastward) direction. Also shown (center of view) is Seward Park extending from Essex, east to Jefferson Streets. Across same, appears the Seward Park branch of the New York Public Library, on the east side of Jefferson Street, from East Broadway to Division Street. In the right foreground are shown Nos. 135 to 143 Division Street, south side, where it meets Canal Street. It suspends its course there and resumes again at the eastern edge of the park, at the library. This picture was taken from the 12-story building No. 54-58 Canal Street, at the S.W. corner of Orchard Street and includes a panoramic view of the surrounding area with the Williamsburg Bridge in the distance.

May 9, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

(2) The same, showing a more inclusive view. Note (on the right) the 10-story Jewish Daily Forward Building, 173-175 East Broadway, and slightly eastward, at the S.E. corner of Jefferson Street, the 5-story Educational Alliance Building.

May 9, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

(3) The same, from a different angle and viewed in a southeasterly direction, showing the East River and the Brooklyn shore. At the right appears the steeple of St. Teresa's R.C. Church, at the N.W. corner of Rutgers and Henry Streets.

May 9, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

Canal Street, north side, west from and including Broadway. Canal Street was laid out along a canal dug to empty the Fresh Water Pond, or Collect (which lay to the northwest of City Hall, roughly between the future Lafayette and Baxter, Pearl and White Streets) into the North River. title: Manhattan: Canal Street - Thompson Street
text:
(1) Canal Street, north side, from Thompson Street to West Broadway (formerly South Fifth Avenue), seen from the eastern end of Laight Street. September 24, 1927. P. L. Sperr.

(2) The same, a year later, seen from York Street at West Broadway, across the site of the buildings between York and Canal Streets. Canal Street is being supported on stilts which the construction of the subway goes on underneath; the view at the left is practically north along the future east side of Sixth Avenue. title: Manhattan: Canal Street - Greenwich Street
text:
Canal Street, south side, east from Greenwich (9th Avenue "El" thereon), to Watts (left) Streets, showing a triangular block bounded by these thoroughfares. A former 4 story structure (No. 500 Canal and 477 Greenwich Streets) has been replaced by a gasoline station and opened to view the side of a frame house No. 475 Greenwich Street. Adjacent to same is a similar 2 1/2 story frame building with brick front, bearing No. 473. Across these buildings appears lofts on the south side of Watts Street; the narrower of which is to be rebuilt and have a modern translucent glass front. For an account of same see the New York Times of October 20, 1937, page 42 L.

View No. 2 shows details of the structures occupying the middle of this block front. The narrow 2 story affair at the left is a rear entrance to an addition to the aforementioned No 473 Greenwich Street. The adjoining property (No's. 496 and 498 Canal Street) is composed of 2 units; one, two stories in height and the other, one story. Note the doorway leading into the back yard of the first 2 1/2 story frame dwelling. In this instance the photographer is viewing towards Greenwich Street and upon which appear lofts on the west side of same.

View No. 3 is similar to No. 1. Note at the left the absence of the 4 story brick structure and the gas station replacing same, thereby giving this front an additional vacancy. The 12 story factory at that margin replaced the 3 story pitched roof residences that appear to the left in View No. 1.

P.L. Sperr

J. Clarence Davies Collection
Museum of the City of New York

October 25, 1927.
View 2: June 30, 1931
View 3: 1932.

title: Manhattan: Carl Schurz Park.
text:
Carl Schurz Park: This park consists of 13 acres, east of East End Ave., (left) to the East River and extending northward from Gracie Square (East 84th Street) to East 89th Street. The northern portion of this park was known as "Horn's Hook" and figured very prominently in the wars of the Revolution and 1812. This northern tip contains a spacious house, known as Gracie Mansion; built in 1813 by Archibald Gracie and now occupied by the Museum of the City of New York. Playground, walks, skating rink, landscape gardening, building improvements etc; all are the work of the W.P.A. Notice on the right the new Triboro Bridge (a P.W.A. project) silhouetted against the curved span of the Hellgate Bridge.

1936.

W.P.A. Photo
Federal Writers Project.

title: Manhattan: East End Avenue - 88th Street (East)
text:
GRACIE MANSION  East End Avenue and East 88th Street, Manhattan. Built in the Federal style about 1799 on the site of a revolutionary fort, it was the country home of Archibald Gracie, shipping merchant and a director of The Bank of New York. The house was completely restored in 1927, and until 1932 it housed the Museum of the City of New York. It became the official mayor's residence in 1942 during Fiorello LaGuardia's third term.

Bank of New York Calendar 1967-68

title: Manhattan: Carl Schurz Park - Gracie Mansion.
text:
Carl Schurz Park. A view of the Gracie Mansion, built in 1813 by Archibald Gracie and now (1937) occupied by the Museum of the City of New York. Samuel Provost, the first Bishop of New York and later president of Columbia, owned a farm of 90 acres here, the woodlands of which extended between 66th and 75th Streets and was called Jones Woods. Archibald Gracie bought this property from the heirs of Jacob Walton. His wife was Esther, a grand-daughter of Thomas Fitch of Connecticut. Two other grand-daughters of Governor Fitch married President Timothy Dwight of Yale and Moses Rogers, Merchant, who built the house at No. 7 State Street. (present R.C. Mission of Our Lady of the Rosary) respectively. This set of four views show the front of the house that faces the East River. In the background appears a row of houses that are on the west side of East End Ave., at East 89th Street.

May 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

On January 8, 1942 the Board of Estimate officially designated the mansion as to future residence of New York City’s mayor.

See "The New York Times," January 9, 1942.

title: Manhattan: Central Park - Aerial view from Radio City.
text:
Central Park: Aerial View from Radio City (Sixth Avenue and 51st Street), showing the Park and the Fifth Avenue side. In the center foreground may be seen the Pond, north of it the Mall, then the Lake, of which the eastern bay is at the northern end of the Mall and the main body on the west side of the Park, about 70th to 80th Streets. The bare spot further north is the site of the old reservoir; above it may be seen the north reservoir, still in use. The buildings of the Metropolitan Museum of Art may be seen on the Fifth Avenue side at 81st Street.

August 9, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

The same, another view. In the southwestern quarter of the Park may be seen a ball ground, and north of it the Meadow or Green. The 72nd Street cross drive separates the Green and the Lake.

August 9, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

The same, also showing the West Side of town and the Hudson River. The Riverside Church, at 122nd Street, and the George Washington Bridge, at 181st Street, stand out very clearly.

August 9, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Central Park.
text:
Central Park: Aerial View from Hotel Sherry-Netherland at the southeastern corner of the Park, showing the old Arsenal and the Zoo, which is to be rebuilt in 1934, in the right foreground. To the left may be seen the Green, or south meadow, and behind it Central Park West at 72nd Street. The Mall is in the center of the picture, just south of the Lake. On the east side, at Fifth Avenue and 80th Street, are the buildings of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and to the left of them the old Lower Reservoir, rectangular in shape, which at the time of this picture is shortly to go into disuse, with the view of later making it into a garden. The North Reservoir is the large body of water above it.
Central Park West, from 72nd to 96th Streets, is shown at the left.
Summer, 1930.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: Central Park - [View of the Arsenal Building.]
text:
Central Park: A set of 5 views of the Arsenal under reconstruction as viewed westward (north and southward) from Fifth Ave. (foreground) at East 64th Street. This structure was erected in 1848 at a cost of $30,000 (as given in 1853). The City of New York purchased same in 1856 from the State for a sum of $275,000. The first floor was used for Administrative offices while the 2nd and 3rd were occupied by the Museum, which later became the American Museum of Natural History. The Meteorological Observatory for years occupied a large upper room.

January 1924.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Manhattan: Central Park - The Drive.
text:
Central Park: The Drive, connecting link between Sixth and Seventh Avenues, showing 59th Street, west from and including Seventh Avenue. The Manufacturers' Trust Building in the background is at 307 West 59th Street, adjoining Columbus Circle; it used to be the Gotham National Bank Building. The branch to the left leads to the Sixth Avenue entrance; and the branch in the lower right hand side of the picture leads north to the Mall, where it joins the driveway from the Fifth Avenue entrance and forms the East Drive. Since the date of this picture that branch has been reserved for one-way traffic, going north; and the connecting link shown here is used by eastbound cars exclusively, whether bound for Sixth Avenue or for the East Drive. May 25, 1928.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Central Park entrance at Columbus Circle.
text:
Central Park: Southwestern entrance (originally called Merchant's Gate), at Columbus Circle, with the ball ground and Green in the center background. The monument at the entrance of the Park was erected to commemorate the sailors who were lost when the battleship Maine was blown up -- the incident which led to the Spanish-American War. The Columbus statue, by Russo, stands on the tall pedestal in the middle of the Circle, in the left foreground. Along the horizon may be seen the buildings on Fifth Avenue and the East Side.

About 1922.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: Central Park - The Lake.
text:
Central Park: The Lake, view nearly due south, showing five ducks swimming in the foreground, and the midtown skyscrapers on the horizon. The Hotel Plaza, with the Chrysler Building behind it, is a little to the left of center.
May 17, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

The same, another view. Notice how the Empire State Building at Fifth Avenue is hidden by the building between Essex House and the R. C. A. Building at Radio City. A little to the left of these, just in the center, a dirigible balloon is seen against the sky, probably the Goodyear blimp.
May 17, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

The same, two years later. Another contrast is provided by the fact that this third picture is an afternoon view, possibly as late as four, which explains the blackness of the shadows along the shore to the right.
June 24, 1935.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Central Park.
text:
TEN THOUSAND NEW YORK SCHOOLBOYS DRILLING IN CENTRAL PARK.
This is a great army of schoolboys from all boroughs of the big city, attired in white shirtwaists & dark knickerbockers, gave an exhibition drill in the physical exercises in the city's largest park last month before a distinguished company of invited guests, relatives & friends.  The purpose of this impressive demonstration, which was held under the auspices of the Public Schools Athletic League, was to show the results of physical and hygienic training in the schools.  Colonel Roosevelt, who was one of the spectators, spoke of the work of the League as a great force for good not only in the city but in the nation.

Dated:  June 10, 1913.  American Press Ass'n

The Obelisk known as Cleopatra's Needle which was given to the United States by the Khedive of Egypt in 1877 and set on its base on this site on January 22, 1881; the cornerstone being laid, October 9, 1880. It originally stood in Cairo in front of the Temple of the Sun, having been erected about 1500 B.C. by Thothmes III. In 12 B.C. it was removed to Alexandria by Augustus Caesar. Wm. H. title: Manhattan: Central Park - Reservoirs - Lower reservoir.
text:
(1)
Central Park: Lower Reservoir, western side, view northwest. This old reservoir, built around 1840 when the Croton water system was first constructed, and some time before Central Park was conceived of, went out of use a year or two prior to this date. The work of filling it, and demolishing the retaining walls, has now begun.

January 8, 1931.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)
The same, another view, more to the north; the southwestern corner of the reservoir is shown at the extreme left of the picture.

January 8, 1931.

P. L. Sperr.

(3)
A similar view as No. 2, showing the Reservoir in use. Buildings appearing on the left, line the western boundary of the Park; Central Park West. Note the original appearance of the San Remo, which appears in the latter views with twin towers.

1927.

title: Manhattan: 59th Street (West) - 6th Avenue
text:
Central Park South (West 59th Street ), south side, west from a point (No. 126-30, the new 15 story apartment house at left margin that replaced the former 8 story Hawthorne) between Sixth and Seventh Avenues, and to the latter (right). Under construction there is the new N.Y. Athletic Club occupying the former sites of 2 of the old "Spanish Flats", the Madrid and the Lisbon. The Cordova and the Granada (45 story, Essex House erected here prior to 1934)are still standing while to the left is a cleared space where the Valencia stood (present site of the 36 story Hampshire House). Across the latter feature appears a corner of the rear of the Salamanca which faces on W. 58th Street. In 1930 this site was completely vacant. The photographer is viewing southwestward from the "Cliffs"
of Central Park.
May 25, 1928.
P.L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: Central Park West - Broadway
text:
Central Park West and Broadway north from 59th Street. The building in the immediate foreground, with the "Prince Albert" sign, is the American Circle Building. The next building north of it from 61st to 62nd Streets is the Mayflower Hotel, and beyond the Mayflower is the Century Theatre, demolished in 1930 for the erection of the Century Apartments. The picture gives a good view of construction work on the Eighth Avenue subway.

1927.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: Central Park West - Broadway
text:
1 & 2

Central Park West (right) and Broadway (left), north from Columbus Circle (W. 59th St.), showing buildings to the west of Central Park. The latter is at the right and the entrance to same partially shown. Note the Maine Monument there. The triangular two-story structure in the center is the American Circle Building. This divides the thoroughfares and stands on the former site of the old Baltimore & Ohio Railroad Station. To the rear of same is W. 60th Street. North of this and facing the Park is the Mayflower Hotel (erected 1921). The twin-towered Century Apartments shown in view 2, replaced the old Century Theatre, a portion of which appears in the earlier photo. Geographically, Central Park West, is Eighth Avenue, an identity it resumes, south of this point, and north of 110th Street.

P. L. Sperr

March 11, 1929
March 19, 1938

title: Manhattan: Central Park West - 70th Street
text:
Central Park West, west side, from 70th to 74th Streets. From 71st to 72nd Streets stands the new Hotel Majestic. Above it is the Dakota, and beyond the Dakota is the San Remo. Of these three, only the oldest, the Dakota (built between 1879 and 1885) stands today. The Majestic and San Remo have been replaced by apartment houses bearing the same names. The wooden building nearer the Majestic is a saloon, with a beer wagon in front of it drawn by the brewer's big horses. 1895.

August Loeffler, from Ewing Galloway Collection.

title: Manhattan: Central Park West - 71st Street
text:

Immediately beyond it, from 72nd to 73rd Streets, is the Dakota, one of the oldest apartment houses in the city. The two apartment houses beyond the Dakota are the Langham and the San Remo.

January 8, 1931.

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Central Park West - 70th Street
text:

Following this are seen the Langham, the Dakota, and the Hotel Majestic. The first two still stand; the Majestic has been replaced by an apartment house bearing the same name. The white marble building at the right is the New York Historical Society.

Central Park West, west side, from West 88th (left of No. 1) to 91st Streets. The large ornate apartment house is the St. Urban. To the south is the Walden School. Occupying the 89th - 90th Street frontage are various older structures. From left to right these are, the Melbourne, the C. P. W. Hospital, the New Windsor and the Cayuga. The last two are to be removed (N. Y. Sun, July 22, 1940) to provide a site for a modern 18-story apartment dwelling: At the right of View 2 appears a portion of the twin towered El Dorado. This structure occupies the 90th-91st Street frontage. The photographers vantage point is in Central Park and from which he is viewing westward.

title: Manhattan: Centre Street - Leonard Street
text:
Centre Street, west side, from Leonard, across Franklin to White Streets, showing at that location the Tombs and the Criminal Courts Bldg., joined by the "Bridge of Sighs". These are to be replaced by modern structures which will be erected in the near future on the cleared lands seen in the foreground. An article on same appears in the New York Times of August 1, 1938 on page 21. The photographers vantage point is on Baxter Street, viewing westward from Leonard St (in No. 1), between Leonard and Franklin Streets. The new Criminal Courts Bldg. and city prison will cost $18,500,000. of which the P.W.A. will supply $10,175,000. It will have four wings; the northerly unit, containing the 16 story prison building will be separated from the courts by an open courtyard. A 17 story structure, providing for Magistrate, Special and General sessions and Supreme Courts with their staffs, will also house 28 court rooms, two grand jury rooms and four floors of offices for the District Attorney and have its main entrance on Center Street.

P. L. Sperr

June 12, 1938.

title: Manhattan: Charlton Street - MacDougal Street
text:
Charlton Street, west from, but not including, MacDougal Street. The slightly taller house at the extreme right is No. 1 1/2 Charlton Street. Between Nos. 9 and 11, on the north side, is a little gap, which exactly marks the old boundary line between the West Bayard Farm, on the east, and Trinity Church Farm, on the west.

In the middle of Charlton Street, between this point and Varick Street (where a new building is nearing completion), once stood the famous Richmond Hill House, built by Major Abraham Mortier in 1760, used in 1776 as a headquarters by General Washington, occupied in 1789 by Vice-President and Mrs John Adams, and then leased by Aaron Burr. Charlton Street was originally laid out as Hetty Street or Burr Street, and took its present name in 1807. The old mansion ended as a roadhouse, and was demolished in 1849.

This picture was taken the year before the digging of the Eighth Avenue (municipal) Subway and the extension of Sixth Avenue south from Minetta Lane to Walker and Church Streets. In the process, Nos. 2 to 10 Charlton Street, on the south side, and 1 to 7 on the north side, will be demolished, leaving No. 9, the building with the round-arched doorway, as the house at the N.W. corner of Sixth Avenue.

1926.

title: Manhattan: Charlton Street - Varick Street
text:
Charlton Street, north side, east from No. 65, west of Varick Street, to the eastern end of Charlton Street at MacDougal and Prince Streets. The old houses 65 to 57, adjoining and at the N.W. corner, were demolished in January 1926. The Greybar-Varick Building, across the way on the east side of Varick Street, shown nearing completion, took out Nos. 53-45 Charlton Street, inclusive.
In the middle of the street, in front of about No. 35, is the site of the Richmond Hill house, where Presidents Washington and Adams both lived, and which was the house of Aaron Burr at the time he shot Alexander Hamilton. Charlton Street was originally called Betty Street or Burr Street, but received its present name in 1807.
April 23, 1930.
P. L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: 27th Street (West) - 9th Avenue
text:
Chelsea Park: A set of 3 views, northeastward from various points on West 27th Street between Ninth and Tenth Avenues, showing the rear of Public School No. 33 and a Public Health Station, both located in the easterly half of this park. Across same appears the town of the Empire State Bldg. and the spire of the P.E. Church of the Holy Apostles; the latter is located at the S.E. corner of Ninth Avenue and W. 28th street and has a very interesting history, being representative of a single individuals tenacity of purpose and the reward thereof.
In 1937 the Board of Education proposed to erect a new school here to replace that shown, but decided not to. Note the 1 story free milk station seen in the foreground.

P. L. Sperr.

August 4, 1938.
Views 1, 2 and 3.

Chelsea Park: A set of 3 views, northeastward from various points on West 27th Street between Ninth and Tenth Avenues, showing the rear of Public School No. 33 and a Public Health Station, both located in the easterly half of this park. Across same appears the town of the Empire State Bldg. and the spire of the P.E. Church of the Holy Apostles; the latter is located at the S.E. corner of Ninth Avenue and W. 28th street and has a very interesting history, being representative of a single individuals tenacity of purpose and the reward thereof.
In 1937 the Board of Education proposed to erect a new school here to replace that shown, but decided not to. Note the 1 story free milk station seen in the foreground.

P. L. Sperr.

August 4, 1938.
Views 1, 2 and 3.

title: Manhattan: 27th Street (West) - 9th Avenue
text:
Chelsea Park: A partial view of the southerly side of same as photographed on West 27th Street. This open area occupies the block of 27th -28th Streets between 9th & 10th Avenues and has P. S. No. 33 therein. The extra-curricular activities are under the auspices of the Hudson Guild. A free milk station operated by them is shown to the rear of the school structure.

The spire of the P. E. Church of the Holy Apostles appears across the trees at the east end and though seeming to be amid same is not. This is on the opposite side of 9th Avenue (El. line there upon), at the S. E. corner of 28th Street. Beyond is the towering Empire State Building.

P. L. Sperr

July 21, 1934

title: Manhattan: Cherry Street - Roosevelt Street
text:
Cherry Street, east from (No. 24, left margin), a point between Franklin Square and Roosevelt Street, and to the latter, showing a slum area, long known as Cherry Hill and in which numerous sociological studies have been conducted. Irrespective of same, it still has a similar appearance in 1938, although several of the buildings on the right have been demolished as part of a slum clearance project under the joint auspices of the City and the Works Progress Administration. Included in same was the demolition of No. 29 1/2 which is reputed to be possible the oldest structure in Manhattan, containing from the writers personal observation old Dutch brick, same being half the present size and composed of yellow clay.
Note the narrow walks and the cobblestoned street bed, the latter sloping downhill with horse drawn vehicles there upon. forming the contour which has given this area its name. Several gas lamps appear in conjunction with numerous saloons and former residences converted into tenements.
Urchins in the foreground are the progeny of the inhabitants of the squalid buildings lining this street. These differ radically from the former residents who in their day formed the select of the City; No. 1 being the first Presidential residence. A tablet to this effect is now attached to the base of the Brooklyn Bridge at this point. "Boss' Tweed is humorously reported by Dennis Lynch, in his book bearing that title, to have offered to donate the funds to erect a church there, stating it to have been his birth place. True or false, it is a fact that he was born on this street, as was his father.

title: Manhattan: Cherry Street - Roosevelt Street
text:
(1) 33-23 Cherry Street, south side, between Roosevelt and Dovers Streets. Buildings shown standing are Nos. 31, 29 1/2 and 27. No. 29 1/2 being two 12 1/2 feet fronts, utilized as a single unit; there being a common stairway with a box arrangement of the rooms (4 to a floor). These buildings were being demolished as a slum clearance project, by the W.P.A., when it was discovered that No. 29 1/2 contained old Dutch brick. It has been stated by the Historic Building Survey, (conducted by the National Park Service), that this may be a Dutch town house of the 18th Century, and at least 50 years older than any other known dwelling in Manhattan. Possibly antedating the famous Jumel Mansion (1765) and the old Fraunces Tavern. For further information see- The New York Times- November 15, 1936.

November 19, 1936.

P. L. Sperr.

(2) A view solely of No. 29 1/2. Note absence of upper floor.

November 19, 1936.

P. L. Sperr.

(3) A rear view as seen from Water Street. No. 29 1/2 Cherry Street, being directly under the tower of the New Federal Courts Building (Foley Square).

November 19, 1936.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Cherry Street - Rutgers Street
text:
Cherry Street, east from a point (No. 264, tenement at left in No. 2) slightly above Rutgers Street.
View 1 favors the southerly side with stables thereupon. A clearance appears at Jefferson Street.
View 2 is of the tenements on the opposing side. The W.P.A. slum clearance demolition seen is a portion of a wide program designed to enforce rehabilitation. This site was formerly occupied by tenements that bore No's. 266 and 268. A notice of same appeared in the N. Y. Sun of February 23, 1939.
Beyond is a 6 story stable that adjoins the Beth Israel Hospital. The latter is at the S. W. corner of Jefferson Street. The lower portions of these features are depicted in View No. 3.

title: Manhattan: Cherry Street - Corlears Street
text:
Cherry Street, west from, a point between Corlears and Jackson Streets, and across the latter, showing this slum area in various stages of clearance. To the left is Corlears Hook Park and to the right are tenements that are not to come down (according to signs).

View No. 2 is at Jackson Street and westward. Note at the right margin the W. P. A. work and time shack. This stands at the N. E. corner and appears in several other views. This agency is responsible for the preparatory razing necessary for Vladeck Houses.

title: Manhattan: Christopher Street - Grove Street
text:
Christopher Street, Greenwich Park, and Grove Street, east from West 4th Street, at and east of Seventh Avenue South. At the eastern end of Christopher Street (left) may be seen the Sixth Avenue Elevated and the white bank building at the N.E. corner of Sixth Avenue and 9th Street. At Waverly Place, which forks here, is the Northern Dispensary, one of Greenwich Village's older landmarks, built in 1801. It is a building bounded on two sides by one street (or at any rate, what is nowadays one street in name), and on the third side by two streets, Christopher and Grove; its northern side follows the line of Grove Street. The triangular park, on the south side of Christopher Street and the north side of Grove Street, was officially named Greenwich Park in 1856; but the name is hardly ever used. 10 Sheridan Square (q.v.), the new apartment building under construction at the right is the Shenandoah apartment house, which replaces the old houses at 80 and 82 Grove Street, at and adjoining the corner of Grove Street and the western end of Washington Place (originally West 5th Street). About 1928.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: Christopher Street - Washington Street
text:
163 Christopher Street, at the N. W. corner of Washington Street, showing "McAvoy's Drug Store" which was operated by a local character lovingly known as "Mother McAvoy." To sailors and truckmen of the neighborhood she was more than a druggist. She was a friendly counselor, and a "bank" and "post office" for sailors on their brief stays ashore. From her old-fashioned desk in the store and through her self-acquired knowledge of various foreign languages, and acting as a Notary Public she helped many sailors turn to land lubbering. Proximity to the Federal Building increased her field of operations. She was born in Rome, N. Y. and was graduated from N. Y. C. P. in 1902. After clerking in several drug-stores she bought this little store for $3500. At this time her clientele consisted of many New Jersey people who commuted on the Christopher Street Ferry. She died at the age of 64. For further details, see "The New York Times" as of November 12, 1940.
Alexander Alland

This photo is one of a series published in the volume "Portrait of New York" by Felix Reisenberg and Alex. Alland, IRGV.

title: Manhattan: City Hall Park - [View of upper downtown skyline.]
text:
New York City: A remarkable view of upper downtown skyline from the Northeast showing how completely the Woolworth Building, 60 stories, 792 feet high, dominates its surroundings. At the extreme left is the tower of the Singer Building; alongside the Woolworth is the far less attractive Transportation Building. Far to the right is the New York Telephone Building. The old three cornered building is the old main post office and Federal Building, and the building in the foreground is the City Hall.
Sept. 1929
Ewing Galloway

title: Manhattan: City Hall Park - [Fountain - statue of "Civic Virtue"].
text:
City Hall Park as photographed northeastward from the 24th floor of the New York Telephone & Telegraph Bldg. Shown is the newly added portion at the apex of this triangular civic zone. This was until recently the site of the old Post Office and Federal Bldg. The fountain-statue "Civic Virtue" by MacMonnies still stands in front of the City Hall. This is to be removed to Queens and placed near the new Borough Hall. Note the old "Tweed" County Court House, the new Hall of Records, and the base of the Municipal Bldg. in the background. Broadway is on the left while on the right is Park Row.

July 2, 1940

221 E. 31st St., N.Y.C.

title: Manhattan: City Hall Park - [Municipal Building.]
text:
New York's most beautiful City Hall and its unique Municipal Building. A New photo showing two of the most famous buildings in New York - two buildings which visiting artists and architects invariably go to see. They go to see the exquisite old City Hall because it is a fine example of Colonial Architecture - and curiosity draws them to look at the unique Municipal Building, towering in the background one of the oddest bits of architecture in the history of America's many odd buildings. Behind the City Hall is the rear of the State Court.

10/22/1922
Underwood and Underwood

title: Manhattan: City Hall Park.
text:
City Hall Park: A view of the New York City Hall, when the Tweed Ring was building the County Court House. The wooden structure shown atop the latter was placed there, so that the public could not observe the slow progress being made. It cost the city $8,000,000 more than it should have; Tweed and his Ring taking the money.

title: Manhattan: City Hall Park
text:
The facade of City Hall with the buildings of lower Broadway behind it; people stroll beneath the trees of the park at left.

A Set of Seven Canvases of Old New Yor

These paintings come from a country house called 'Glencairn' near Dublin in Ireland, where they adorned the walls of the billiard room. The house was built by Richard 'Boss' Croker (1841-1922), an Irishman who for many years was associated with Tammany Hall in New York, holding political positions under William M. 'Boss' Tweed, and later, after the latter's ousting, under 'Honest John' Kelly. Following the Lexow Committee investigations (1889-90), he left for England where he took up residence in Wantage, Berks, returning to America periodically, attempting to regain his lost position in the Democratic Party. After his final defeat in 1900, he crossed the Atlantic once again, built 'Glencairn' and started a racing stable. Despite his past reputation (he paid, in all, $550,000 for his Irish estates), he lived up to the high standards demanded by British racing circles, and when his horse Orby won the Derby in 1907, did not even back him.

These pictures were painted to remind him of New York, and it is assumed that they were executed there around the turn of the century. All are painted in tones of sepia and green.

The British Government has recently acquired this mansion for the use of the British Ambassador to Ireland.

PARKE-BERNET

King's Handbook of New York of 1893, page 184 states that this statue by MscMonnies is to be erected here by the Sons of the Revolution.

MacMonnies exhibited this in the Paris Salon of 1891 and was awarded a second gold medal, this being the first time an American sculptor had attained this honor.

title: Manhattan: Coenties Slip - Pearl Street
text:
Coenties Slip, east from but not including Pearl, to and including South Streets, showing the South Ferry division of the Second and Third Aves. Elevated Line winding its course from Pearl (left foreground) down Front Street (right center) to the Battery. Also seen is Jeanette Park, a quadrilaterally shaped area which divides Coenties Slip in two parts. Coenties Slip is shaped in the form of an isosceles triangle, with Pearl Street as its vertex and South Street as its base. In the background appears the East River and the Brooklyn shore, across it. Pier 7 is visible on the left.

About 1885.

title: Manhattan: Columbus Avenue - 60th Street
text:
Columbus Avenue, west side, at 60th Street, showing the Church of St. Paul the Apostle on the S.W. corner of 60th Street; the view is southwest.
This is the second church of the Paulist Fathers, succeeding an earlier edifice which was built around 1860. The cornerstone of this church was laid in 1873, and the church dedicated in 1885. At the time, it was supposed to be the second largest church edifice in the country.

November 1, 1928.

P. L. Sperr.

According to the New York Times (May 15, 1938) "the group of six five-story tenement buildings comprising the northwest corner of Columbus Avenue and Sixtieth Street known as 20 to 26 Columbus Avenue and 101-105 West Sixtieth Street, will be offered at auction May 26 in the Vesey Street salesrooms." These buildings were erected in 1886 at an estimated cost of $130,000.

The New York Sun of September 12, 1938, reports the demolition of Nos. 20 to 26 Columbus Ave. and No's 103 and 105 West 60th Street; forming a corner plot 100 x 100.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - [59th Street]
text:
Columbus Circle: The Christopher Columbus Monument viewed northeastward towards and up Broadway. One inscription attributes its erection: "By the initiative of Il Progresso Italo-Americano, the 1st Italian daily newspaper in the U. S." Another reads: "To Christopher Columbus, the Italians resident in America-----on the 12th of October, 1892, the 4th centenary of the discovery of America, in imperishable remembrance."

To the right is the old Baltimore & Ohio Railroad station occupying the triangular site between Broadway and Central Park West (Eighth Avenue). To the left and not shown is West 59th.

title: Manhattan: Columbus Circle - [Broadway - 8th Avenue - 59th Street.]
text:
COLUMBUS CIRCLE, WHERE BROADWAY CROSSES EIGHTH AVE. AT FIFTY-NINTH
ST.
The upper part of Manhattan was laid out more than a hundred years ago upon the gridiron plan. Avenues run north and south and streets run east and west with mathematical and geometrical precision. Practically the only variation from that scheme - north of the "downtown" section - is Broadway, the old post road to Albany, whose slant the city planners found it impossible to change. Broadway intersects at a sharp angle most of the other thoroughfares, thus affording the only vistas in the entire borough and creating what are known as Union Square, Madison Square, Greeley or Herald Square, and Times Square. The picture above shows Broadway at the left and Central Park west, with the Maine
Memorial at the entrance to the park.
1924
Kadel and Herbert

title: Manhattan: Columbus Circle - Celebrations - Tribute to Columbus.
text:
Celebrations: Pay Tribute to Columbus. About 1,000 gathered around Columbus Circle October 12, to pay tribute to the Great Navigator on the 441st Anniversary of his discovery of America. Wreaths were placed at the base of the statue, and addressed in tribute to Columbus were made. Mayor O'Brien was one of those to speak. Here is a general view looking into Central Park in Background.

Associated Press Photo

October 12, 1933.

title: Manhattan: Convent Avenue - 141st Street
text:
(1)
Hamilton Grange, the residence of Alexander Hamilton from 1802 to 1804, 287 Convent Avenue, adjoining St. Luke's (Protestant Episcopal) Church on the N.E. corner of 141st Street. The original site of the house was on the west side of Convent Avenue between 142nd and 143rd Streets. It was chosen by Hamilton in order to be near Morrisiana, the home of Gouverneur Morris, and was about eight miles from town. 1913.

(2)
A close-up of Hamilton Grange. 1913.

(3)
Hamilton Grange nineteen years later. In the intervening period, the wooden railways have been removed from the roofs. 1932.
J. Clarence Davies Collection, Museum of the City of New York. Negative No. 523.

(4)
An early view of same. 1891.
Gift of Randall Comfort.

title: Manhattan: Convent Avenue - 143rd Street (West)
text:
Convent Ave. at West 143rd Street, showing a row of 4-story structures on the Avenue and Alexander Hamilton's famous thirteen trees at what would be today (1937) the S.W. corner of the aforementioned intersection. The last of these symbols of the thirteen original states was cut down in 1908 and a portion of the trunk retained by Hamilton Grange; the former residence of this heroic individual, which originally stood to the rear of the same. Photographer is viewing eastward from a point east of Amsterdam Ave. and north of West 142nd Street. For further information see: New York, Old and New by Rufus Rockwell Wilson, Illustration facing page 326.

1891.

title: Manhattan: Cooper Square (North) - 6th Street (East) - Astor Place
text:
Cooper Square, east side, north from, but not including East 6th Street to Astor Place, showing Cooper Park; a triangular area between East 6th and 7th Streets. Directly north of same, is the Cooper Union Institute, and facing (side with clock) on East 7th Street. Fourth Ave., which starts at this point, forms the western side. At the extreme north end of the park is a statue of Peter Cooper; the founder.

January 13, 1936.

P. L. Sperr.

The Institute according to the New York Times of July 7, 1938 is undergoing general renovations, consisting mainly of repainting the exterior and reconstruction of the original elevator cage and shaft. This structure, often credited with being Manhattan's first "sky-scraper," was started in 1856 by the founder, and is said to be the first building in which iron was used as part of the interior framework. Since no iron girders were being manufactured at that time, Cooper utilized ordinary railroad rails from his iron mills in New Jersey and Pennsylvania for the floor beams and arches. Since it was completed in 1859, the finish has been a dark reddish brown to match the brownstone which comprises most of the exterior. A warm sandstone color is now being applied to bring out the architectural details; the old reddish brown paint being used only on the exterior of the fourth and fifth floors, which were constructed of Caen stone because labor difficulties halted the shipments of brownstone in 1858. The elevator was installed around 1863 and was incorporated in a cylindrical shaft. The major change here is the reconstruction of the cage.

title: Manhattan: Cooper Square (North) - [Astor Place]
text:
52 to 34 Cooper Square, west side, south of Astor Place (center). Shown on the right is Cooper Institute a 7-story structure occupying the entire block west from Third Ave. (elevated line thereon) to Fourth Ave. and East 7th Street (north side of triangular park) north to Astor Place. In the background is the huge department store of John Wanamaker's (formerly Stewarts). Note the Cooper statue in the foreground on the approximate site where this great philanthropist sat daily and looked down the Bowery. It is the work of Augustus St. Gaudens, a graduate of the Institute and was unveiled May 29, 1897.

About 1925.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: Cooper Street - 204th Street
text:
Cooper Street, west side, north of 204th Street. This is a three-story frame house., Nos. 54-56. October 26, 1927.

P. L. Sperr.

This structure was erected by Julius Roekell, Architect, of No. 233 Grand Street, corner of Bowery, for Henry Patterson, owner, of No. 160 Mott Street. Erection began on the 20th day of September, 1872 and was completed on the 30th day of June, 1873, according to the report filed July 1, 1873 by Building Inspector, Timothy L. West. Construction consisted of a foundation of brick with a wooden superstructure. A mansard roof topped all, including an installed hot air furnace. The cost was $12,000.00

title: Manhattan: Division Street - Pike Street.
text:
113 Division Street, south side, east of Pike Street, showing the Scharlin snuff shop and its wooden identification. Sandy the "Scotch Indian" has had a series of adventures since this photo was taken. Confiscated by the Manhattan Department of Borough of Works for obstructing the sidewalk, he was hauled off to the city dump in April, heartless officials paying no heed to his antiquity or authentic folk-art beauty. Rescued when his owner paid a $1.00 fine, the snuff shop figure was sold to a collector. This photo was reproduced on page 68 of the published volume "Changing New York."

January 26, 1938

Berenice Abbott, photo
Federal Art Project

Another copy filed under "Occupations-Tobacco"

title: Manhattan: Division Street - Allen Street
text:
Division Street, east from Allen Street, showing nearly completed Second Avenue Elevated Railroad.

This was the last of the elevated lines to be built, service being inaugurated in 1880.  Elevated construction had begun in 1867 with a single trunk line, operated by cables and stationary engine, on Greenwich street from Battery Place to Cortlandt Street, and subsequently extended up to Ninth Avenue and 30th Street. By 1876 the financial structure of the elevated companies was in shape, and construction of the Sixth and Third Avenue lines begun.  By 1880 substantially the present lines on Manhattan were completed; but steam was used till 1903.

The southwestern corner of the old Herring Farm, within which lies all but the westernmost few feet of Downing Street, is just off the picture to the right, the observer is standing in the former Trinity Church Farm. Downing Street is the first of seven streets laid out in the Herring Farm at right angles to Bedford and Herring (now Bleecker) Streets.

text:
(1)
Doyers Street, west from the Bowery.
1932.

J. Clarence Davies Collection, Museum of the City of New York.

(2)
The same, at an earlier date. Note entrance to the Chinese Theatre, at Nos. 5-7 on the left of view. Buildings on the right (Nos. 6, 8, and 10), are 3-story frame houses.
About 1890.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

In the older view, note at No. 8, the Chatham Club; the cabaret where Irving Berlin, the famous songwriter first started. Facing same is the old Chinese Theatre, that has now become the Chinatown Mission. This, in conjunction with the Arcade (wooden structure at the head of the bend) played a major role in the intermeicine strife that habitually flares up in this locality and thereby caused this turn to be known as the Bloody Angle. No. 3 has been stated as the site of the home of Anthony H. Doyer in 1809, the individual whose name is perpetuated here. Around the bend on the right, Scotchy Lavelle maintained a dive at No. 14. Occupying the Bowery corners were similar enterprises, Barney Flynn's and Callahan's.
