(1)  Duane Street, north side, east from and including City Hall Place, to but not including Park Row, as seen from Chambers Street, in the foreground. The St. Andrew's Catholic Church is seen on the S.E. corner of City Hall Place and Duane Street.

February 24, 1929.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)  The same, three years later.

October 22, 1932.

P. L. Sperr.

(3)  The Church under demolition, prior to the construction upon this site, of a new edifice. Note the changed background in this view; Municipal and Federal structures surrounding same and forming a Civic Centre on Foley Square.

January 27, 1938.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Duane Street - City Hall Place
text:
(1) Duane Street, east from and including City Hall Place, to but not including Park Row. This view shows "St. Andrew's" Roman Catholic Church on the N.E. corner of Duane Street and City Hall Place. September 24, 1927.
, P. L. Sperr.

(2) The same, five years later, showing the clearance for the new Federal Courts Building. October 22, 1932.
P. L. Sperr.

(3) The same as No. 1 and showing a farther view to Park Row. Adjoining the church are No's. 25 and 29 Duane Street, the 6-story and corner building being No. 100 Park Row. St. Andrews R.C. Church was originally a Congregational organization (1808) which was succeeded by a Methodist group. It was used for some years as a wine house. The present group first occupied the premises in 1842. A falling wall of an adjacent building damaged the property in 1875. October 1928.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

for further information, see The New York Post : Wednesday Sept. 8, 1937.

title: Manhattan: Dyckman Street - Henshaw Street
text:
(1) Dyckman Street, north side, from but not including Henshaw Street, to but not including Staff Street. This is a two story frame house.

October 26, 1927.

P. L. Sperr.

(2) A more inclusive view eastward.

October 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3) A view similar to No. 2. These frame structures have disappeared today (1938), their sites being included in Inwood Hill Park with the newly constructed Henry Hudson Parkway traversing same. Old Bolton Road curved around at the rear of this view and several the homes shown fronted on same. About 1922 the City took title and permitted the inhabitants to remain until plans matured, which as before-mentioned came to a satisfactory conclusion recently. Several individuals of prominence resided here and the writer believes that Gen. U.S. Grant's son was one and not necessarily in those shown.

May 1920.

George L. Balgue.

title: Manhattan: East Broadway - Market Street
text:
68 East Broadway, adjoining the S.W. corner of Market Street, showing two views of Botanic Hall where Continental Lodge No. 287, F and A.M., New York City was constituted on April 22, 1853. They remained in this Masonic Temple for two years; the Lodge room being on the upper floor according to Dr. Frank Law of Flushing, Long Island, the last descendant of his line. At this time Doric Lodge No. 280 and Independent Lodge No. 185 met here also, this being a well known center of Masonic activities. Botanic Hall was on the second floor, the store being occupied by Law and Boyd, Botanical Pharmacists, who later bought the building. The original picture was taken from a yellowed billhead of this firm showing an old wood cut engraving of this structure as it appeared when Metropolitan Medical College was an occupant. Percy Boyd Plumb, the last descendant of the Boyds and who continued the business until 1916 supplied this, and is the authority for the statement that Abraham Lincoln spoke here on the occasion of his memorable visit to New York when he spoke at Cooper Union. Trows City Directory first lists the College at this address in the 1857 edition. Note the lantern hanging over the stairway door at the left, with the square and compasses which were lighted on Lodge nights. In the rear, above the fifth floor there is a two room apartment that is believed to still remain. Francis J. Arkins, Past Master and Historian of Continental Lodge No. 287 and Secretary of the Masonic Board of Relief of New York City unearthed this after a five year search, completing the collection of the total number of Masonic Temples in which Continental Lodge has met since 1853. An air brushed view removing the College signs accompanies this and shows this building as it originally appeared.

About 1860.

Gift of Francis J. Arkins.

title: Manhattan: East Broadway - Montgomery Street
text:
East Broadway, west from Montgomery Street, showing a perspective along the north side of this thoroughfare. In the background is the municipal center at City Hall Park distinguished by the tall structures there. Blending together are the Municipal Building, the Woolworth Tower and the slightly lower Transportation Building. These overshadow the latticed approach to the Manhattan Bridge. On the left is the building housing the Jewish Daily Forward.

1939

title: Manhattan: Houston Street (East) - Mulberry Street
text:
39 East Houston Street, south side, west from Mulberry (left), to Lafayette (right) Streets, showing the Puck Building, erected sometime between the 2nd and 3rd quarters of the 19th Century. This structure occupies the block bounded by East Houston to Jersey Streets, and Mulberry to Lafayette Streets. It is an edifice in the Italian Renaissance style and is occupied by the J. Ottman Lithographing Co., foremost establishment of its kind on the American continent and the publishers of the magazine "Puck," a periodical, satirizing political and social groups. The clearance, shown in the foreground was caused by demolitions on the north side of East Houston Street, during the construction of the Eighth Ave. Subway. Also shown, on the left, is an extensive view southward on Mulberry Street.

June 3, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Houston Street (East) - Mott Street
text:
East Houston Street, south side, west from (No. 47) but not including Mott, to Lafayette Streets, showing prominently the Puck Building (from Mulberry to Lafayette Streets). It is a handsome edifice in the Italian Renaissance style, and is occupied by the J. Ottman Lithographing Co., the foremost establishment of its kind on the American continent, and the magazine 'Puck', a publication satirizing the political and social life of our country. The building was erected sometime between the second and third quarters of the 19th century and is 9-stories tall.
June 3, 1933.
P. L. Sperr.

A detail of the Puck Building (the S.W. corner of East Houston and Mulberry Streets) at an earlier date, showing the pretty, emblematic figure of Puck, standing on a long, graceful column, with a crayon as a staff in one hand and a mirror in the other.

title: Manhattan: Houston Street (East) - Chrystie Street
text:
(1)

105-109 East Houston Street, south side, between the Bowery and Chrystie Street, showing St. Augustine's Chapel (Trinity Parish). It is one of the striking architectural features of the city and is a Chapel of Old Trinity, erected in 1876. It has two main parts, a mission house and the church proper. The five floors of the mission house contain a large hall, school, guild-rooms and a parish room. The work is almost entirely among the indigent classes of the neighborhood. Besides a Sunday-school, it has a day school for boys and a night school for both men and women; giving instruction in sewing and cooking.
March 13, 1932.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)

title: Manhattan: Houston Street (East) - Tompkins Street
text:
(1)

518 to 500 East Houston Street, north side, west from Tompkins Street (extreme right), as seen north on Mangin Street. The 6-story structure consists of two units and bear Nos. 518 and 516. This will eventually be the N.W. corner of the new East River Drive. The 2-story garage is on building lots between 500 and 516. A 1-story affair (barely discernible) just west of the garage is No. 500. The clearance shown at the S.E. corner of Mangin and East Houston Streets was a former scrap-iron yard and bore Nos. 130 to 136 on the latter and 511 on the former. title: Manhattan: East River Drive - 24th Street (East)
text:
East River Drive (under construction) south from E. 25th Street, photographed from atop the J. J. Little and Ives Co. plant at No. 425-35 E. 24th Street.
The shore line is being extended above 23rd Street, where the existing Exterior Street begins. The Drive will incorporate the latter to 17th Street. There it will veer to the waters edge (over new ground) to skirt Willard Parker Hospital and the N. Y. Edison Co. plant. The chimneys of the last mentioned are on the right and appear above the darkened utilitarian structure, the City's Motor Transport Building.
Note the playground area being constructed in the foreground of View 1. This lies between 24th Street and 25th Street. The former recreation pier at the foot of 24th Street has been removed. Incidentally, this title is a misnomer, as the use for same was discontinued during the 1st World War. The U. S. Government took control for transport service and never relinquished it.
A future seaplane landing platform has been constructed at the foot of 23rd Street. The Greenpoint Ferry slips were formerly there.

P. L. Sperr

October 13, 1939
Views 1,2,3

title: Manhattan: Edgecombe Avenue - Jumel Terrace
text:
MORRIS-JUMEL MANSION  West 160th Street and Jumel Terrace, Manhattan. This Georgian structure was built as a country estate in 1765 by Roger Morris, a wealthy merchant Loyalist who returned to England in 1775. It served successively as headquarters for General Washington and the British-Hessian forces. After the war it was sold for a tavern and used as a stop-off point by Boston-New York stage coaches. It was bought in 1810 by Stephen Jumel, a wine merchant, for his wife.

Bank of New York Calendar 1967-68

title: Manhattan: Edgecombe Avenue - 161st Street (West)
text:
(1) Edgecombe Ave., at the N.W. corner of West 161st Street. The view shows the Jumel Mansion in Roger Morris Park. It was built in 1758 by Capt. Roger Morris, and became the headquarters of General Washington (1776), Sir Henry Clinton (1777), General Knyphausen (1778). Subsequent to the war it was confiscated by the State and became an Inn; known as Calumet Hall (1790), when President Washington had dinner there. John Jacob Astor sold it in 1810, to Stephen Jumel, who died in 1832. His wife, Marie died in 1865. During this interval of time it was occupied for at least a half century by Nelson Chase, who had married a Mary Bonner; niece of Mme. Jumel. About 1882, the property was sold, and General Ferdinand P. Earle was the last owner (1900). At that time it was known as "Earlcliff". The City of New York acquired it in 1901. October 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2) The same, showing the side facing east from a point of view slightly northward. October 1923.

John Ericsson, the inventor and builder of the famous war-vessel "Monitor" resided at one time at what was No. 30 Beach Street and in his honor this portion which contained his house has been named Ericsson Place. The site would be in the center, directly in front of the chimney tower shown.

May 20, 1937.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Exterior Street - 19th Street (East)
text:
Exterior (Marginal) Street, east side, south from the foot of East 19th to 18th Street's, showing the waters edge of this thoroughfare. The new East River Drive is to include this and year around the buildings shown on made land. Temporary structures seen are to be razed. The utilitarian building on the right is the garage, storage, and workshop of the City's Motor Transport. This is on Avenue C, a thoroughfare that continues from this south from East 18th Street.

July 18, 1939

title: Manhattan: Exterior Street - 21st Street (East)
text:
Exterior (Marginal) Street, north from East 21st Street, showing the waterfront thoroughfare that skirts the East River, and which will be incorporated into the new East River Drive. Extending to 24th Street, it will be continued on filled ground to sweep pass the institutional Bellevue Hospital buildings. Busses seen in the center are at the foot of 23rd Street. The old Greenpoint Ferry that was there for years has been removed. Towering above the gas station that occupies the 22nd to 23rd Street frontage, is the J. J. Little & Ives bookbinding plant. At the left is the massive Empire State Building. In the background appear the skyscrapers that compose the Grand Central-42nd Street outline. The New York Steam Co. plant is on the right, this side of the Tudor City buildings.

P. L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: Exterior Street - 23rd Street (East)
text:

The fenced-in gravel pit at it's rear will be removed and a swimming pool constructed here. The J. J. Little & Ives Co. bookbinding plant is on 24th Street. To the right are the institutional Bellevue Hospital buildings. The General Construction Corp. yards between 24th and 25th Streets will be cleared during the constructional period of the East River Drive (1940-1).

title: Manhattan: Foley Square - Municipal building.
text:
Foley Square, northward, from the Municipal Building, showing this civic center prior to improvement. Thru the center runs Centre Street (cartracks). On the left and right respectively are Lafayette and Park Streets. The solitary one story clinical (narcotic addictions) faces on Worth Street. Columbus Park is in the right background. This open area, the Collect Pond site, has not as yet been improved because of shifting sands. Engineering advances will enable this danger to be avoided. Incidentally this was the scene of the first work relief program in New York; the Pond being filled in by men that were thrown out of work by the embargo declared by President Jefferson in 1812. He, fearing naval complications with Great Britain closed the port.

Gift of E. M. Jenks

title: Manhattan: Foley Square - Pearl Street
text:
Foley Square, easterly side, north from Duane, across Pearl, to Worth Streets, showing respectively, The Federal Courts Bldg., the New York County Court House and the New York State Bldg. all facing on what technically is Centre Street.

Views 2 and 3 emphasize the New York County Court House and are viewed eastward from Elm Street (the westerly boundary of the square) which in its self is really a continuation of Lafayette Street.

All of these structures are built upon and around what in early days was Collect Pond and where in 1796, John Fitch tried his new steamboat under the observation of Chancellor Livingston and other prominent New Yorkers. Where Centre and Leonard Streets intersect today it had a depth of 60 feet. During the English and French conflict, President Jefferson (1807) ordered an embargo on all shipping and New York suffered. To alleviate same, individuals were set to work to fill in this pond and morass and thereby set a precedent for public work relief. A drainage canal was cut thru in 1809 which later became Canal Street.

Propositions for the use of the area as a Park were introduced as early as 1789, though naught came of them and it remained a dreary vacant area awaiting modern scientific engineering. Their main difficulty was not water but quicksands and most of these buildings have what is called a floating foundation.

P. L. Sperr

June 12, 1938.
Views 1, 2 and 3

text:
Fort Washington Ave. (foreground) at the S.W. corner of Northern Ave. (right). At this point, Overlook Terrace, both of these thoroughfares lose their identity, the former continuing through Fort Tryon Park as Park Drive. title: Manhattan: Fort Washington Park - [Lighthouse.]
text:
Fort Washington Park: A view showing Manhattan's only lighthouse nestling beneath the George Washington Bridge. This sets on a promontory formerly known as Jeffery's Hook. A moon shaped battery, built here in 1775, overlooked the spot where ships were sunk to obstruct the British fleet during the American Revolution.

October 21, 1938

George D. Chinn

title: Manhattan: 178th Street (West) - Cedar Avenue
text:
Fort Washington Park: Southward from the pedestrian bridge crossing the New York Central Railroad tracks, at a point about on a line with West 178th Street, The area to the right forms what was formerly known as Jeffrey's Hook, a promontory upon which a light house sets. It boasted, at one time, a one gun "lumette" or moon shaped battery built in 1775, overlooking the spot where ships were sunk in an effort to obstruct the British fleet during the American Revolution.
View 2, of this set is similar though several years later.

1923.

title: Manhattan: Franklin Street - Baxter Street
text:
Franklin Street, west from Baxter Street (immediate foreground) showing beyond the future Criminal Courts Bldg. site, the famous "Bridge of Sighs" connecting the Tombs (left) and the old Court Bldg. The two structures will shortly be demolished and their sites possibly sold to private individuals. These, including the new sites rest upon filled land where prior to about 1812, Collect Pond was; This particular task being New York's first public work program. The photographer is in Columbus Park, near what was formerly the infamous "Five Points".
View 2 is eastward across Lafayette Street, to show the opposite side of the aforementioned covered passageway.

P. L. Sperr,

title: Manhattan: Fulton Street - William Street
text:
111-113 and 115-117 Fulton Street, north side, between William and Nassau Streets, showing the 4-story structure, No. 111-113, that occupies the former site of the North Dutch Church, (erected 1769). The Noon Day Prayer group utilize a portion of this structure today. May 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

The Herald-Tribune of March 22, 1939, page 21, carries an article stating that this structure and the adjoining buildings to the east, comprising the lower half of this block (all owned by the Collegiate Reformed Protestant Church since 1664) are to be demolished and their sites improved with a modern 7 story office building. This will be erected by the George A. Fuller Co. and completed in 1941 for the use of the Aetna Casualty and Surety Co. and its' affiliates. It will front 150 feet on Fulton St., 120 feet on William St., and about 150 feet on Ann St. An investment of $4,000,000 is involved; the church receiving $3,000,000 in rent during the life of a lease, which is for 21 years with two renewals, a total of 63 years.
The building shown here is the oldest of the group and was erected about 1855, directly after the congregation had moved to the Marble Collegiate Church (1851-4) at the N.W. corner of Fifth Avenue and W. 29th Street. The Fulton Street Prayer Meeting has met here since their organization in September 1857.

title: Manhattan: Gansevoort Street - Hudson Street
text:
Gansevoort Street, south side, east from and including Hudson Street. Gansevoort Street, originally the western end of Southampton Road, in Sir Peter Warren's farm, was later known as Great Kills Road. It was made part of Greenwich Lane (now Greenwich Avenue) early in the 19th Century. Later (in the 1830's) it was closed east of 13th Street at the upper end of Asylum Street (upper West 4th Street), and named Gansevoort Street. In the foreground appears Gramercy Park South; on the left, low buildings on Gramercy Park West, and in the right background, a view north of Lexington Ave. from its starting point at Gramercy Park North. Note also (left background) the tower of the Metropolitan Life Insurance Building. The name of Gramercy Park is said to be derived from Krom Moerasje (Crooked Little Swamp) formed by Cedar Creek, which formerly flowed from Madison Square to the East River. The present park once formed part of a large farm acquired in 1761 by James Duane, once Mayor of New York City and by him christened "Gramercy Seat". It is an exclusive park, not open to the public; in the center of which appears a statue of Edwin Booth in the role of Prince Hamlet. About 1932.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 58th Street
text:
Fifth Ave., at 58th Street, showing the Pulitzer Memorial Fountain, located on the west side of the Ave., between 59th and 58th Streets. This area is known as the Grand Army Plaza. It was erected in 1915 to the memory of Joseph Pulitzer, former owner of the New York World, and was sculptured by Karl Bitter. The fountain is surmounted by a bronze female figure symbolizing Abundance, bearing a basket laden with the fruits of the earth. It is often referred to as the Fountain of Abundance. At the extreme left appears a portion of the Savoy-Plaza Hotel, at the N.E. corner of East 58th Street, and (center) a portion of the Squibbs Building, at the S.E. corner of the latter street. 1936.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 58th Street (West)
text:
Fifth Ave., west side, between West 58th and West 59th Streets, showing prominently, the Pulitzer Memorial Fountain at the S.W. corner of West 59th Street. The fountain was erected from funds left by Joseph Pulitzer, and is constructed of limestone and consists of six basins rising in pyramidal form. In the center of the top basin, on a pedestal, is a bronze statue, eight feet high, of a nude female figure holding a basket of fruit. The fountain is often called the Fountain of Abundance. The sculptor is Carl Bittner, who lived from 1865 to 1915 and the architects are Carrère and Hastings. It was given to the city in 1916. August 15, 1929.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Grand Street - Ridge Street
text:
(1)

438 to 430 Grand Street, north side, west from Ridge, to but not including Attorney Streets, showing St. Mary's R.C. Church (No. 438 Grand Street) at the N.E. corner of Ridge Street. The cornerstone of this church was laid April 30, 1832, by Bishop Du Bois. Its original edifice (1826) was on Sheriff Street, between Broome and Delancey Street and destroyed by fire in 1831, which was commonly believed to have been caused by a burglar.

January 1924.

title: Manhattan: Greenwich Street - Battery Place
text:
Greenwich Street, north from Battery Place, as photographed from the downtown "El" platform. Shown are details of the 6th and 9th Avenue "El" station prior to demolition. This is the first station out of South Ferry and is the oldest of any in the city. Charles C. Harvey, the inventor, was permitted to erect an experimental line from this point to 29th Street. Commencing service in 1867 by wire rope locomotion, it failed in 1870 and was succeeded by the N. Y. Elevated Railroad Company. This in turn became the Manhattan Railway Company.

title: Manhattan: Greenwich Street - Trinity Place
text:
The convergence of Greenwich Street (left) and Trinity Place (right), at Morris Street. Shown at that point is the triangular structure that separates the first two mentioned thoroughfares. This building bears No. 28 Greenwich Street. Note the fact that the Sixth Avenue Elevated that formerly ran on Trinity Place has been removed. The Ninth Avenue Line that still remains on Greenwich Street is to be demolished sometime in 1940-1.
At the left margin is a portion of the 35 story No. 19 Rector Street Building. Thru the center is the Electric Bond & Share Building. On the right, and separated by Trinity Churchyard are the Trinity and the Empire Buildings.

April 28, 1940

title: Manhattan: Greenwich Street - Dey Street
text:
Greenwich Street, at Dey Street, showing the "El" station at the S.E. corner under construction. This view shows the Dey Street side, as the "El" tracks are on Greenwich Street. To the right center are buildings at the S.W.
corner of this intersection.
Kings "Handbook of New York" states that the inventor Charles C. Harvey was permitted to build an experimental track along Greenwich Street from the Battery to 29th St. If it succeeded he was to have permission to extend the line to the Harlem River, but if it failed he was to take it down. The system was commenced in 1867 and the means of locomotion was a wire rope drawn by a stationary engine. The method was unsuccessful and the matter lay in sbayence for several years. The company failed in 1870 and was succeeded by the New York Elevated Railroad Co. which began the use of small locomotives on the tracks.

title: Manhattan: Greenwich Street - Christopher Street
text:
June 27, 1973.
Pictures of the razing of 9th Ave "EP".
Taken from 663 Greenwich St.
This block of houses facing " were razed 1953 to build St. Luke's School. The old Federal style houses belonged to Trinity Church. Part of the block of houses around landmarks St. Luke's Chapel, have been restored on Hudson + Barrows Sts.) for clergy, staff and parish were 1,000,000 spent on the restorations.)
Mrs. Gilbert L. Soye.

Note:
We lived in this beautiful house 663 Greenwich St. for 18 years. The bulbs & plants from our garden were trucked to Trinity Churchyard, & many have thrived year by year. I planted the willow tree & 2 silk trees (Morus) which are now in Trinity Churchyard.

title: Manhattan: Grove Street - Bedford Street
text:
Grove Street, south side [in three views:]

[View 1], west from Bedford, to Hudson Street. This thoroughfare makes a decided turn midway between these points; the area to east of same (foreground) was the old Hering Farm, and that to the west, the Trinity Church Farm. Upon the latter, on the west side of Hudson Street, is St. Luke's Protestant Episcopal Chapel, erected 1821-4. The cornerstone for this edifice was laid June 4, 1821;

View 2 is photographed in an eastward direction from Hudson Street;

View 3 shows the gateway entrance to Grove Court, for photo of same see files under that classification.

1) About 1913
2) March 15, 1932
3) October 9, 1938.

title: Manhattan: Grove Street - Bleecker Street
text:
39-41 and 45 Grove Street, west of and adjoining the N.W. corner of Bleecker Street (right). The corner building shown is No. 316 Bleecker Street. Adjoining same to the west is No. 45 Grove Street. This is a double front (47 foot) structure and is refered to in Phillips "Elite Directory" of 1880-1 as the Whittemore House. Prior to this, (1874 to 1879) this authority gives no listing. That quaint volume, Doggett's "New York City Directory" of 1851 refers to this site by listing No's. 41 and 43 as being vacant, and 45 occupied by one, A. B. Haxturn.

P. L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: Hanover Square - Water Street
text:
Hanover Square, west from (where man is seen crossing the street, in the foreground) and including Water, to and including Beaver Streets, showing (left) the 7-story W.R. Grace & Co. Building, a portion of the South Ferry division of the Second and Third Aves. Elevated lines running on Pearl Street, and across it the 3-story India House and the 11-story Maritime Agency Building. On the right, across the elevated structure, is visible a portion of the New York Cotton Exchange Building. The foreground is Old Slip, which actually, is a continuation of Hanover Square eastward to the East River. The 7-story Arbuckle Building appears at the S.E. corner of Water Street. On the right is the south wall of Hook and Ladder No. 15 of the Fire Dept.

About 1920.

Hanover Street at Exchange Place makes a bend in an easterly direction, thereby hiding from view the east side of the street, and exposing the west side, from Exchange Place to Wall Streets, showing the National City Bank Building, occupying that block. A foot bridge can be seen connecting the latter building, with the 35-story Wall and Hanover Buildings.

June 13, 1929.

title: Manhattan: Hanover Street - Exchange Place
text:
Hanover Street, west side, between Exchange Place (right), and Beaver Street (left), showing the 8-story building of the Canadian Bank of Commerce. It was demolished in 1929, and on its site now stands the 59-story City Bank and Farmer's Trust Company Building. The clearance in the foreground, is at the N.E. corner of Beaver Street, and was created by the demolition of the Brown Bros. and Co. Building. On its site now (1937), stands the 35-story Wall and Hanover Building.
June 30, 1928.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Harlem River Drive - 194th Street (West)
text:
Harlem River Speedway, at about West 194th Street, and viewing northwestward towards the embankment atop which is Amsterdam Avenue. Upon the east side of that thoroughfare is the distinctive "Fort Wendel", a hotel cafe erected in 1891. The ferris wheel is in Paradise Park, an amusement area that adjoins the Fort George Amusement Park. The latter lying between Amsterdam and Fort George Avenue's, is on the Revolutionary War site that held Fort George. The amusement buildings there were erected in 1895. Incidentally, that year saw the ferris wheel moved slightly to the left, and revolving in a more northerly and southerly direction.

About 1895

Brown Brothers

title: Manhattan: Haven Avenue - 173rd Street
text:
Haven Avenue, east side, from 173rd to 176th Streets. The house in the foreground is the old farmhouse of A. F. Smith, who had a six and one-half acre farm here. The main body of the house probably does not antedate 1870, although it was preceded by an earlier structure on the same site. The little brick wing on the south was added between 1902 and 1910. The little house farther along on the avenue is the modernized house standing on the old Howland farm, which adjoined the Smith farm on the north. The apartment houses beyond, on the S.E. corner of 176th Street, were built around 1924. Around 1910, Haven Avenue used to be known as Buena Vista Avenue. May 27, 1927.

P. L. Sperr.

The same, more than seven years later. The two old houses have been demolished; and the land is being cleared and made over into a park to be called J. Hood Wright Park. October 30, 1934.

title: Manhattan: Henry Hudson Parkway - Dyckman Street
text:
Henry Hudson Parkway: An aerial view from a point, slightly south of Dyckman Street (shown in foreground with bridges crossing same) showing the Parkway, a feature of the West Side Improvement Project progressing northward through Inwood Hill Park and across the Henry Hudson Bridge over the Harlem River to the Spuyten Duyvil section of the Bronx. Note the New York Central Railroad tracks which more or less parallel this roadway in conjunction with the North (Hudson) River bank. The U shaped basin of the Harlem River, shown at the right top formed by the peninsula projecting southward will soon disappear, a ship canal is now under construction that will bisect the latter and the basin filled in. For an account of same, see the New York Times of April 27, 1927. This photograph appeared in a brochure published by the Department of Parks on October 12, 1937 and issued at the public ceremonies attending the opening.

1937.

Gift of Department of Parks.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 32nd Street
text:
Broadway, north from and including 32nd Street. In the centre is the old Seventy-First Regiment Armory Building, which later became the Herald Building, and now houses a clothing store. In 1928 this building will be cut in half. The southern half will stand, but the northern half will be demolished and on its site will be erected the Herald Square Building.
In the left foreground is Sak's 34th Street, and above it is R. H. Macy & Company, two large department stores. In the distance is the Metropolitan Opera House, the Times Building, and the Hotel Astor.

1923.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: Herald Square - Broadway - 34th Street (North).
text:
Broadway, north from 34th Street. R. H. Macy and Company, a large department store, is shown at the right. Above it, in the distance, is the Metropolitan Opera House, the New York Times Building, and the Hotel Astor.
In the centre, the former Seventy-First Regiment Armory and Herald Building has been cut in half; and the northern half demolished. On the site of the latter has risen the Herald Square Building, which the southern half is occupied by Rogers Peet & Company.
About 1930.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 6th Avenue
text: Broadway and the west side of Sixth Avenue, north from 34th Street. The centre building, fronting on Broadway and Sixth Avenue, was formerly the Seventy-First Regiment Armory, and is now the New York Herald Building. Later, in 1928, it will be cut in half; the narrower, southern half will remain, and in 1936 will house the Rogers Peet Company. The 35th Street half, however, will be demolished and replaced by the 24-story Herald Square Building. In the background is the recently built Times Building, which has caused the name of Longacre Square to be changed to Times Square. About 1905.

title: Manhattan: Hudson Street - Reade Street
text:
Hudson Street, north across Reade Street. At the right is West Broadway. The several low structures there are at the triangular apex formed by the convergence of these two thoroughfares. The writer believes that the photographer is standing on the "El" platform station at Chambers Street. The wooded area in the left center is the small Duane Park. Beyond appears the American Express Building at the S.W. corner of Jay Street. The opposite corner (with canopy) will become the site of the House of Relief of the New York Hospital and which later housed the present Marine Hospital.

About 1870's

text: Hudson Street, south from Spring Street, a view taken in connection with the digging of the Holland Vehicular Tunnel under Spring Street. The work began the previous October; and the tunnel will be opened in 1927, around Thanksgiving. Nos. 298, 296, 294-292 Hudson Street, at and adjoining the S.E. corner of Spring Street, under which the westbound tube of the tunnel curves, have been demolished. No 294-292 was the Duane Methodist Episcopal Church, established 1797, which moved up here after the burning of the original church in Duane Street, in 1861. Not long after 1925 this church will settle down in the old house at 574 Broome Street, on the Holland Tunnel Plaza, two doors away from Our Lady of Vilna. September, 1923.

title: Manhattan: Hudson Street - Bank Street
text:
Hudson Street, west side, from Bank (left of No. 1), to W. 12th (right of No. 2) Streets, showing buildings thereupon as viewed across a clearance on the east side of Abingdon Square between Bank Street and Eighth Avenue.

"The thoroughfare in the center separating these blocks is Bethune Street and thru which appears a glimpse of the Ninth Avenue "El" running on Greenwich Street. The G. E. Supply Corp. building occupies the Bank-Bethune Street frontage, while to the north are dwellings between Bethune and W. 12th Streets.

Eighth Avenue begins at this point and runs at the right over the exposed sub-basement and to the front of the exposed building rears.

The six story building with the white trim, located at the S. W. corner of Hudson and W. 12th Streets is the Laura Spellman Hall of the Young Women's Christian Association. The trees partially hiding same are in the triangular park named for the daughter of Sir Peter Warren. This separates Eighth Avenue from Hudson Street.

Upon the foreground site formerly stood No's. 1, 3, 5, and 7-9 Abingdon Square (q.v.); the last being the Abingdon Hotel. These were demolished in May 1931.

Gift of Committee on Housing Charity Organization Society

1935 Views: 1-3

title: Manhattan: Inwood Hill Park.
text:
Inwood Hill Park: A set of three views photographed the same day and showing different aspects of this wooded area. No. 1 is in a westward direction towards the Jersey highlands and shows the old foundations and the roof of the Jewish Memorial Hospital. Today (1938) these have disappeared; the Henry Hudson Parkway having incorporated same. To the left is Dyckman Street. No. 2 is northward along the Hudson River and across the Harlem River gap showing the New York Central Railroad bridge across the latter. On the Bronx shore appears the Casa Victoria, a modern apartment house. No. 3 shows a tulip tree below the House of Mercy. This is not to be confused with the big tulip tree near the Indian Museum.

January 14, 1932.

P. L. Sperr.

The Consolidated Gas Company building shown here was built before 1867. Before 1916 it will be superseded by a 20-story building on this site, about the same time 30-24 Irving Place, the house shown here at and adjoining the S.W. corner of 16th Street, will be replaced by a 13-story loft building. title: Manhattan: Irving Place - 14th Street (East)
text:
Irving Place, east side, from 14th to 15th streets, showing the Academy of Music, with the Consolidated Gas offices at 4 Irving Place, on the SE corner of 15th street.  2 Irving Place used to be (around 1880) the home of the Lotus Club.

The Academy of Music, originally intended as a permanent home for Italian Opera, was opened on this site in October 1854, with a production of "Norma"  One of the notable performances in the old building was a concert at which Jenny Lind sang.  On October 12th, 1860, a grand ball was given here for Edward (the future Edward VII) Prince of Wales, on the occasion of his visit to New York during his tour of North America.

The original Academy of Music, on this site, was burned May 22nd, 1866 and the building pictured here was opened the following February.  In 1887 the Academy Company decided not to compete further with the new and fashionable Metropolitan Opera House, and accordingly sold this building, after which it became a dramatic house.

As a legitimate theatre it was famous, among other things for the phenomenal run of "The Old Homestead" from August 30th 1888 to May 1891.  The elder Sothern and others also played for long runs.

On the afternoon of November 16th, 1919 the Prince of Wales, grandson of Edward VII, will pay the Academy a visit.  By that time it will have become a motion picture house.  Finally in 1926, it will be demolished and the ground under the building will become part of the site of the new Consolidated Gas Building.

March 1909

Brown Brothers.

title: Manhattan: Irving Place - 15th Street (East)
text:
Irving Place, at and adjoining the S.W. corner of East 15th Street (right), showing at the corner, the Irving Place Theatre. This structure was known as Amberg's Theatre in 1892, which opened here in 1888 and at which the Muenchener Company played on November 5, 1890. Upon this site formerly stood Irving Hall, opened December 20, 1860 for balls, lectures and concerts, and which was famous as a rendezvous for one faction of the Democratic party, to which it gave its name. Today (1938), this building is given over to Burlesque performances, a feature which aroused local interest when Judge Crain was District Attorney of Manhattan recently; this and adjoining property being in his family for years. A negative print accompanies this, forming a set of two.

title: Manhattan: Irving Place - 15th Street (East)
text:
Irving Place, west side, 15th to 16th Streets, inclusive, showing the clearing on the site of the old Westminster   Hotel on the N.W. corner of  16th Street, where the new Borgfeldt Building is about to be erected. The Hotel Du Nord, shown on the N.W. corner of 15th Street has only recently been known by that name, from around 1890 to after 1902.  This was the older Hotel America. (now at 102-06 East 16th St); In 1885 it was Hotel del Recreo, and in 1879 Belvedere House (probably its original name).

This building will finally be replaced around 1928 by a new 4-story structure called the Irving Plaza.  The houses above it, 21-33 Irving Place, will be demolished shortly after the time of this picture to make place for the 12-story structure later to be known as the Nemo Building.

March 1909

title: Manhattan: Lafayette Street - 4th Street (East)
text:
428-34 Lafayette Street, west side, between East 4th Street and Astor Place, showing the distinctive row of houses known as the "Colonnade". This was formerly called "La Grange Terrace", in honor of General Lafayette's home. They were erected in 1827 and for a time were the home of Washington Irving and John Jacob Astor. The Churchman, the leading paper of the Protestant Episcopal Church was published here at the time when this was the center of New York's intellectual supremacy, at what was then No. 47 Lafayette Place. For a number of years this building has been occupied by the Conte Restaurant.

1938-9

Works Progress Authority
Federal Writers Project

title: Manhattan: Lafayette Street - 4th Street (East)
text:
(1)

428-434 and 436-440 Lafayette Street, west side, between East 4th Street and Astor Place. No. 428-434 is known as the "Colonnade Buildings." It is a part of the row of houses which was known as Colonnade Row, where John Jacob Astor and other prominent merchants lived in the 1870's. The buildings shown in this view is the northern half of the Row and its northernmost section was for many years occupied by the Churchman, the leading paper of the Protestant Episcopal Church. It was then known as 47 Lafayette Place and was the centre of New York's intellectual supremacy. For a number of years the building has been occupied by the Conte Restaurant and is still there to date (1937).

September 26, 1929.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)

The same, showing an exclusive view of the Colonnade Buildings.

September 26, 1929.

P. L. Sperr.

No. 432 Lafayette Street was the home of Julia Gardner, bride of President Tyler.

title: Manhattan: Lafayette Street - Bleecker Street
text:
Lafayette Street (Elm Street), north from but not including Bleecker, to and including East 8th Streets (where it terminates), showing the street under construction. The building of the street necessitated the razing of many houses in a northerly direction from Elm Street, which terminated at a point slightly south of Jersey Street, to Lafayette Place, which commenced at Great Jones Street. The new thoroughfare was named Lafayette Street several years later, and under it was constructed the Interborough Rapid Transit Co. (I.R.T.) subway.

title: Manhattan: Leroy Street - Greenwich Street
text:

The bend in the street, in the background of the picture, coincides with the old boundary line between the Trinity Church Farm, on the west, and the Herring Farm, on the east. In the 1840's the northern half of the cemetery, which originally extended from Clarkson to Morton Streets, was given up by Trinity Church. Leroy Street, on being cut through, met the western end of Burton Street, and absorbed it, the whole being renumbered west from Bleecker (formerly Herring) Street. title: Manhattan: Lexington Avenue - 22nd Street (East)
text:
9 Lexington Avenue, at the S.E. corner of East 22nd Street, (left), showing the home of the former Mayor Abram S. Hewitt, who was the son-in-law of the beneficent Peter Cooper. His son, Erskine Hewitt, succeeded to same in turn. The photographer silhouettes same against a background of apartment dwellings that face on Gramercy Park. Note the lanterns extending from the balcony over the portico. These are reminiscent of the old New York custom indicating the residence of the chief executive. A similar feature is to be found around the corner at No. 4 Gramercy Park West, the home of the former Mayor Harper of the publishing firm of that name.
February 4, 1938.
P. L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: Lexington Avenue - 22nd Street (East)
text:
11 to 15 Lexington Avenue, at, adjoining and north of the S.E. corner of E. 22nd Street (right), showing the former houses of Lucy W. Hewitt, A.S. Hewitt and Amy H. Green respectively. From 1926 to 1932 inclusive, the following were the owners: The Manhattan Trade School for Girls, Amy H. Green and Erskine Hewitt. In 1933 the Trade School title was transferred to the Frank Work Memorial. From 1934 to the date of demolition (Fall of 1938) ownership was registered as: The New York Association for the Improvement of the Condition of the Poor, Christopher H. Wyatt and the American Society for Psychic Research. To the left of the latter is the new building of the College of the City of New York. The Childrens Court on E. 22nd Street will erect an annex to fill the site between same and the latter feature.

title: Manhattan: Lexington Avenue - 46th Street
text:
Lexington Avenue, west side, at 46th Street, looking southwest from 47th Street, showing the new Grand Central yards under construction. Practically everything from Lexington to Madison Avenues has been torn up in the process.

The Tiffany Studios, On the S.E. corner of Madison Avenue and 45th Street, occupy the old building of the Manhattan Athletic Club. In 1917 that building will be replaced by a branch of the Equitable Trust Company. To its left may be seen the Hotel Manhattan (about 1898) at Madison Avenue and 42nd Street, and farther to the left a tower and part of the old Grand Central Station along Vanderbilt Avenue. The Hotel Belmont (1906), at the S.W. corner of Park Avenue, stands out pretty conspicuously behind the new Post Office, on the west side of Lexington Avenue from 45th to 44th Streets. The latter, in the left foreground, is connected by a bridge to the new Grand Central Terminal, which is under construction on the east side. Of the old Terminal the offices along Vanderbilt Avenue remain.

July, 1909.

Ewing Galloway.

The lower block (46th - 47th Street) front in conjunction with adjoining buildings will be cleared (with the exception of a 20 foot parcel at No. 493) and the space improved with a 1 story commercial building to contain 11 stores, and an automobile parking lot. This will cost $150,000. A fuller account was carried in the New York Sun of December 19, 1938. View No. 3 shows only this limited area. Note in No. 1, the Grand Central Palace opposite same.

title: Manhattan: Lexington Avenue - 49th Street (East)
text:
Lexington Avenue (center, view), at East 49th Street (intersection seen across clearance) showing the new Hotel Waldorf Astoria site, as viewed south eastward from the Columbia Broadcasting Company Building at No. 485 Madison Avenue (S.E. corner of 52nd Street). This will occupy the entire block from Park to Lexington Avenues, between 50th and 49th Streets and to the south of St. Bartholomews P.E. Church. Surrounding same are numerous hotels which from left to right are, the 30 storied Beverly; the 15 storied Montclair; the 31 storied Shelton; the 14 storied Barclay; and (across the roof of the latter) the 25 storied Lexington. Beyond these, in the same order, are the various printing and publishing buildings; Tudor City and the Daily News Building. The East River and its Brooklyn shore form a background for these Grand Central zone edifices. Note the absence of the present General Electric (originally the R.C.A.) Building which would appear over the Church roof and obstruct a view of the Hotel Beverly.

text:
Alley between 4 and 8 Macdougal Street, east side, and the view north from it inside the block between Macdougal and Sullivan Streets, north of Spring Street, during the reconstruction of the southern end of Macdougal Street as part of Sixth Avenue Extension. In the center of the block is a 5-story inside tenement house at the rear of what used to be the 4-story house at 14 Macdougal Street. To the right may be seen the rear of 104 and 102 Sullivan Street, and, more to the right, part of the rear of the old 6-story stables at 96-100 Sullivan, with its little 2 story wing in the rear. The south side of this old stable exactly marks the old boundary line between the Trinity Church Farm and the West Bayard Farm.

title: Manhattan: MacDougal Street - Spring Street
text:
Macdougal Street, north from the eastern end of the westernmost section (originally Brannon Street) of Spring Street (q.v.). This is the real beginning of Macdougal Street, although during the southward extension of Sixth Avenue (1927-1930) the latter will absorb the first two blocks of it. The Butterick Building, built in the winter of 1902-1903 as 1 Macdougal Street or 223-221 Spring Street, will become the N.W. corner of Sixth Avenue and Spring Street. Nos. 20 to 34 Macdougal Street, on the east side from Van Dam Street to Prince Street, will become 186 to 204 Sixth Avenue, and Nos. 2 to 18 and 9 to 35 Macdougal Street will be demolished. At the right of this picture, you can see the frame side of 219 Spring Street, which, with its neighbors 217 and 215 Spring Street, two similar brick-faced houses, is directly in the path of Sixth Avenue Extension. No. 2 Macdougal Street is the first five-story tenement house at the right, adjoining 219 Spring Street. Between No. 4 and No. 8 (the two-story stable) there is a short alley at right angles to the street. Macdougal Street is the seventh of a set of streets laid out west of and parallel to Broadway. After the end of the American Revolution they were renamed in honor of various Generals in the successful war for independence.

1926.

title: Manhattan: MacDougal Street - Van Dam Street
text: MacDougal Street, north from No. 20 MacDougal, east side, opposite and including the eastern end of Van Dam Street. When the Independent (municipal) Subway has been dug and Sixth Avenue extended south to Walker and Church Streets; Nos. 20 to 34 MacDougal Street will become 186 to 204 Sixth Avenue. No 24-26, the police station, adjoining the third of the group of six-story tenement houses at the right, will become 194-196 Sixth Avenue. All the buildings on the west side, to and beyond Charlton Street, opposite the western end of Prince Street, will be demolished. This includes the five houses 17 to 25 MacDougal Street, adjoining and north of the garage at 1 Van Dam Street on the north corner; all but the second of these houses are frame, faced with brick. 1926.

title: Manhattan: MacDougal Street - King Street
text:

This building dates back to around 1890; prior to then the school occupied the old church edifice, next to the new one at 153 Sullivan Street (q.v.).

title: Manhattan: MacDougal Street - Prince Street
text:
Macdougal Street, south from and including the junction of Charlton Street, on the west side, and Prince Street, on the east. The drug store at the right is 2 Charlton Street, and will be demolished the year after this view, together with the rest of the west side of Macdougal Street from Charlton to Van Dam Streets. No. 34 Macdougal Street, at the S.E. corner of Prince Street, will become 204 Sixth Avenue, No. 32 is the Second Assembly District Republican Club, and No. 28 (future 198 Sixth Avenue), next to the five-story police station, which is flying the flag, is, or used to be, the Richmond Hill settlement house, named after the Richmond Hill mansion which stood in what is now the middle of Charlton Street (q.v.) between Macdougal and Varick Streets. Charlton Street received its present name in 1807, and has so far escaped being made an extension of Prince Street, the way Brannon Street was swallowed by Spring Street, and (later), Hammersley by Houston (q.v.).

title: Manhattan: MacDougal Street - Stone Avenue.
text:
Provincetown Playhouse
133 Macdougal Street, Manhattan

Federal Art Project
"Changing New York"
Berenice Abbott, photographer

[Note: negative at Museum of the City of New York]
Code III D-1
Dec. 29, 1936

p.104, Changing New York

... Organized at Provincetown in 1915, the Prov. Players found themselves a theater at 139 MacDougal St. in 1916. Moved to 133 in 1918 and remodelled same. Closed in 1922, the theatre reopened in 1923, changed management in 1925 and ran until the "crash." Dark from 1930-1936, it was reopened this time to house the Studio Theatre of the Community Drama Unit of the WPA Federal Theatre.

title: Manhattan: Madison Avenue - 23rd Street
text:
Madison Avenue, north from 23rd Street, showing the east side of Madison Square, and four buildings on 26th Street. The smallest of these, the third from the corner, is the last of the old brownstone houses which used to fill that block, and will be rebuilt before long. The four-story building on the corner (A.S.P.C.A.) was built shortly prior to 1900.
On the N.E. corner of 24th Street is the latest of the Metropolitan Life Insurance buildings (1920), which replaced the Madison Square Presbyterian Church (built 1906). On the N.E. corner of 25th Street may be seen the Corinthian columns of the New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, erected about 1898. Madison Square Garden (1890-1925) stands in the block from 26th to 27th Streets. About 1922.

International News Photos, Inc.

title: Manhattan: Madison Avenue - 24th Street (East)
text:
Madison Square Presbyterian Church, Madison Avenue at N. E. corner of 24th Street, built by Hokis, Head & White from designs by Stanford White, and dedicated on October 14, 1906. It succeeded a brownstone steepled Church which stood on the S.E. corner and was then being removed to make room for the Metropolitan Life Insurance Building Tower.
The new church was demolished in 1919 and gave place to the Metropolitan Annex (1920). The Corinthian columns across the front of the church were sent to Hartford, Conn; and from part of the facade of the new building of the Hartford Times. Two small buildings to left of church were erected about 1913.
1918-1919
Ewing Galloway, Photographer

title: Manhattan: Madison Avenue - 26th Street (East)
text:
Madison Avenue at 26th Street, seen from Madison Square. The house with the flagpole, on the right, was once the Lawrence Jerome residence, and is now the University Club. Later it will house the Manhattan Club.
Of principal interest, however, is the new Madison Square Garden at the left. For about twenty years before its erection, the first Madison Square Garden, which was once the New York Central station, occupied the site. Work was begun on the second Garden in 1889, and it opened on June 16, 1890. The figure of Diana is of special interest. This statue, by St. Gaudens, will be removed in September, 1892, and sent to Chicago for the World's Fair. A second statue will be made by St. Gaudens and placed on the tower in 1893, where it will remain until removed for the demolition of the building in 1925.
About 1890.

On the N.E. corner of 26th Street is the New York Life Insurance Company Building, erected on the site of Madison Square Garden. The small house on the S.E. corner is the clubhouse of the Manhattan Club. It has been the clubhouse for various clubs at different times in its history, among them the Union League Club and the University Club. Originally it was the residence of Lawrence Jerome, father of William Travers Jerome. The iron balconies on the front of the house were removed about 1925. title: Manhattan: Madison Avenue - 26th Street (East)
text:
STAGE GROUP PLANS
FOR 50TH BIRTHDAY

Two Women, only Survivors of
First Cast, to Attend Celebration Tomorrow.

The fiftieth anniversary of the founding of the Amateur Comedy Club, Inc., will be marked tomorrow night at the Heckscher Theatre when the club presents its annual production, "Aren't We All?" by Frederick Lonsdale.

Members of the club, one of the oldest amateur dramatic organizations in the country, gave their first performance on Feb. 13, 1885, in the University Club Theatre, Madison Avenue and Twenty-sixth Street, formerly the home of the late Leonard Jerome, whose heirs still own the property. The club presented on that occasion two plays "Which Is Which" and "One Too Many For Him."

Roles in the first production were portrayed by Miss Katherine Montague, now Mrs. E. Pinckney Collins, and Miss Alice Witherspoon, now Mrs. George Pratt Ingersoll. They, the only survivors of the first cast, will attend the performance tomorrow night.

[Newspaper article on back of this print is from the New York Times, February 12, 1935, page 18. It is pasted over a label that I cannot read.]

title: Manhattan: Madison Avenue - 26th Street (East)
text:
Madison Avenue, north across East 26th Street. Occupying the easterly frontage, from 26th to 27th Streets is the first Madison Square Garden. It was the abandoned passenger station of the N. Y. Central and Hudson River Railroad. Because of a series of band concerts under P. S. Gilmore, it popularly became Gilmore's Garden. Serving this purpose for twenty years it was removed for the second Madison Square Garden designed by Stanford White. On the right is the University Club, organized in 1865. The 5-story brownstone site at the left will (after about 1895) house the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals.

WHERE THE DEMOCRATIC CANDIDATE WILL BE PICKED#

New view of Madison Square Garden, taken from Madison Square Park, New York, today--herre the Democratic National Convention will be opened on June 24 next, the party platform made up, the candidate for President will be nominated, New York won the right to the convention in the auction at Washington yesterday, bidding $255,000.

title: Manhattan: Madison Avenue - 26th Street (East)
text:
Diana, goddess of the tower of Madison Square Garden, Madison Avenue, east side, and Fourth Avenue, west side, from 26th to 27th Streets, showing also a detail of the tower. Diana took possession of the tower in 1893, and for thirty-two years reigned as the undisputed queen of the New York skyline. Her predecessor was a larger Diana, placed on the tower in 1890. Both Dianas were gifts of the sculptor, whose expenses were paid by Stanford White personally. The first Diana proved to be much too large. She was not an ornament for the tower; rather, the tower became her pedestal. She was removed in 1892, and sent to Chicago for the World's Fair. There she remained until five years later, when she was partially destroyed by fire. It is believed that she is still in existence.

Meanwhile, St. Gaudens had made another Diana, again receiving nothing but his expenses, which Stanford White again paid. The two Dianas were the only nude figures ever created by St. Gaudens.

The new goddess was smaller and more graceful than the first. Like the first she turned with the wind, her flowing drapes acting as the sail of a weathervane. It is thus that we see her now, about twenty-three years since she first leveled her unsped arrow, with about nine years left of her reign. The picture clearly shows the beauty and grace of Diana; it does not catch the loveliness of her face, with its wistful expression.

During the war Diana's drapes were removed, and she turned no more. From then on her arrow menaced the north alone; but she was careful never to release it.

At last, in 1925, the New York Life Insurance Company, which had in 1915 acquired title to the Garden by foreclosure, decided to demolish the beautiful old building (old being used in its New York sense), and to replace it with their own structure. On May 6, 1925, Diana left her tower, and demolition work began. Many collectors offered to buy Diana from the New York Life; but that concern was unwilling to let her pass into private hands, and doubted its ethical right to sell a great masterpiece of art for which it had paid nothing.

She was given to New York University on condition that her tower be re-erected on the campus at University Heights. This condition the University was unable to meet. Finally in 1932, she was given to the Pennsylvania State Museum and placed in Fairmont Park, Philadelphia. New Yorkers may see their former goddess there; or they may admire her loveliness in a smaller reproduction in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

About 1916.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: Madison Avenue - 38th Street (East)
text:
Old South Church (Dutch Reformed), Madison Avenue at S.E. corner of 38th Street.
The edifice dates back to about the time of the Civil War, acquired by South Church in 1891 from Zion Protestant Episcopal Church at the time Zion and St. Timothy's parishes were merged. The building was remodelled by South Church; it was probably at that time that the pointed steeple, which used to surmount the tower, was taken off. The property is being offered for sale; a syndicate will think of an apartment house, but later throw the property back on the church's hands. In 1917 August Heckscher will buy the property, and finally in 1922 it will pass into the hands of William H. Silk, who will erect on the site the Fraternity Clubs Allerton House, 18-story apartment hotel.
About 1912.

title: Manhattan: Madison Avenue - 38th Street (East)
text:
Madison Ave., west side, from East 38th (left) to 39th (right) Streets, showing an entire block front that is owned by the Baker family. The photographer is viewing westward across a demolition on the east side of the Ave. and upon which an open-air car parking enterprise will continue in business until the present (1938). This set consists of three views.

The former residence of William Goadby Loew, at the S.W. corner of Madison Ave. and East 39th Street (shown on the right) has been purchased by the Henry Visiting Nurse Service. They will move their executive offices from No. 99 Park Ave., a structure that they have occupied since 1921 and which has been purchased by the City as a portion of the site for the new Appellate Division Court House. For a fuller account see the New York Times of March 25, 1938.

August 25, 1931.

P. L. Sperr.

The Baker Estate interests are endeavoring to re-zone the balance of this Madison Avenue frontage from residential use to commercial and are offering same for sale at this date April 11, 1938.

title: Manhattan: Madison Avenue - 36th Street (East)
text:
Madison Avenue, west side, from 39th to 36th Streets, showing the Heckscher Building newly erected on the S.W. corner of 38th Street, and houses between 38th and 39th Streets, which still stand in 1935.
The Heckscher Building was erected on the site of the old Theodore A. Havemeyer residence (built about 1870), which was bought by August Heckscher in 1915 and demolished in October of that year. Erection of this 16-story building was unsuccessfully contested in court by J. P. Morgan and other Murray Hill residents.
1916 or early 1917.

title: Manhattan: Madison Avenue - 39th Street (East)
text: Madison Avenue, east side, from 39th to 40th Streets. Only No. 265, the corner house at 39th Street, will remain in 1935. In the center of the block Nos. 269-71 will shortly be replaced by two story Thibault (wall papers) showroom, then in 1927 a tall office building will be erected. Between this and the 39th Street corner house, No. 267 ("Floor for rent" sign) will be replaced about 1929 by a small structure. Another tall building will be erected 1930-31 on site of 275-77, S.E. corner of 40th Street. Buildings on N.E. corner of 40th Street were demolished in 1925. About 1920.

About 1921.

text:

The houses on the N.W. corner of 41st Street will be demolished in 1919. The Manhattan Hotel is shown on the N.W. corner of 42nd Street; opposite it on the southwest corner the Central Trust or Union Carbide building will be erected about 1914. Part of old St. Bartholomew's Church, to be demolished in 1919, may be seen beyond on the S.W. corner of 44th Street. The buildings on the N.E. corner of 40th Street will stand till nearly
1925.
About 1912.

title: Manhattan: Madison Avenue - 41st Street
text:
Madison Avenue at S.E. corner of 41st Street, showing the old Thompson Mansion as remodelled for the use of the American Trust Company, after this property was acquired by the American Trust Company and the New York Title and Mortgage Company, in January 1924. In 1929 the Lefcourt Colonial Building will rise on this site. By contrast with the picture of this corner about 1922, this view shows less of Madison Avenue and all of the south side of 41st Street east to the farther side of Park Avenue. Note the Chemists' Club, 50-54 East 41st Street, also the old-fashioned iron balconies and fire escape on the Murray Hill Hotel at the S.W. corner of Park Avenue and 41st Street. Note also that Madison Avenue is temporarily a one-way street. 1924.

Edwin Levick, Photographer.
Gift of E. M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Madison Avenue - 41st Street
text:
297 Madison Avenue at S.E. corner of 41st Street: the old Thompson Mansion in the block belonging to the Estate of Mary Clark Thompson. Prior to its occupation by Frederick Fox and Company it was used for a while by the Aero Club.
This picture should be compared with a later view (1924) showing the building remodelled, and also showing 277 Madison Avenue, adjoining, with the stoop removed. In 1929 the two houses will be demolished, and the tower of the Lefcourt Colonial Building will rise from this corner. The remainder of the block down to the corner of 40th Street, will be demolished in 1925.
About 1922.

Morris Rosenfeld, Photographer.
Gift of E. M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Madison Avenue - 55th Street
text:
Madison Avenue, north from and including 55th Street, seen from 54th Street east of Madison Avenue. The streets have been graded, but building is only just getting under way.

On the N.E. corner of Madison Avenue and 57th Street the Madison Avenue Reformed Church, afterwards to become the Central Presbyterian Church, is nearing completion. This edifice will be demolished in 1928 (see New Fuller Building Progressive Series, 1928-29, Madison Avenue N.W. corner of 57th Street). On the N.E. corner of 57th Street stands the newly erected 1 East 57th Street, residence of Mrs. Mary Mason Jones, and the first of the block known as Marble Row. (See Fifth Avenue at N.W. corner of 57th Street, 1925, and other views). It will be demolished late in 1929. Two or three of the houses shown under construction on the north side of 57th Street, notably 17 West 57th Street (the western wing of the house with the mansard roof), will be standing in 1935.

In the background, on a line from the observer through the intersection of Madison Avenue and 56th Street, may be seen the old Arsenal in Central Park, used as a police station.

This photograph is reproduced in Valentine's Manual for 1923, on page 10, and credited to the collection of George S. Weston. We have taken the date as given by Valentine's Manual.

May 5, 1871.

International News Photos, Inc.

title: Manhattan: Madison Avenue - 70th Street
text:
This photograph shows the original rendition of the Presbyterian Hospital, Madison Avenue between 70th-71st Streets, as planned by Richard M. Hunt. Hunt's stamp, at the lower right, is dated Dec. 13, 1869.

James Lenox was the prime mover behind the Presbyterian Hospital, and he donated the site. This rendition by Hunt was owned by Lenox, and is marked as coming from the Lenox collection (below).

title: Manhattan: Madison Avenue - 100th Street
text:

The data on the reverse side of this print gives the location as Amsterdam Avenue and 100th Street on Sept. 21, 1894. It appeared in the N. Y. Sun on February 11, 1929 as No. 122 in the series titled "Old New York in Pictures" and identified as Amsterdam Avenue.
Mr. Hoffman of the New York Historical Society identifies this as the corrected location, basing his conclusions from a view taken from atop the Ruppert house at 5th Ave. and 93rd Street. Both of these views are in their collection.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 23rd Street
text:
Madison Square, looking northeast from the corner of Broadway and 23rd Street. Madison Square Garden is about three years old. The first Diana of St. Gaudens was removed from the tower the preceding September to be sent to Chicago for the World's Fair, where she was destined to remain until she was destroyed by fire, a few years later. Shortly after this photograph was made the second Diana (also by St. Gaudens), somewhat smaller than the first, was placed on the tower and remained there until May 26, 1925, when she was removed for the demolition of the building. The house on the N.E. corner of 25th Street and Madison Avenue will be demolished about 1898. By 1920 the houses on Madison Avenue between 24th and 25th Streets will all be replaced by office buildings. At the S.E. corner of Madison and 24th Street, where the Metropolitan clock tower will rise in 1907, we see the old Madison Avenue Presbyterian Church, built in 1854. In the right foreground is the Hotel Bartholdi. Note the brand new Metropolitan Life building at 23rd Street and Madison Avenue, the first of the buildings which will ultimately take up the whole block.

Brown Brothers, Photographers.

1893.

title: Manhattan: 23rd Street - Madison Avenue
text:
Madison Square, looking north across the park from the buildings on 23rd Street just east of Broadway. On Madison Avenue, S.E. corner of 25th Street, the Madison will be demolished between 1910 and 1916 to make room for a 20 story office building. On the N.E. corner of 25th Street is the brand new marble building housing the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court, on the S.E. corner of 26th Street the former Lawrence Jerome residence, housing the Manhattan Club. With a little remodelling the buildings in this block will be unchanged in 1935. On the N.W. corner the Madison Square Garden, about ten years old, will be demolished in 1925 to make room for the New York Life building. Most of the buildings along 26th Street on the north side of the Square will give way to office buildings between 1910 and 1916; the Hotel Brunswick on the N.E. corner of Fifth Avenue and 27th Street will go down before 1910. The small new white A.S.P.C.A. building on the N.W. corner of Madison and 26th Street will be standing in 1935. To the left, on Fifth Avenue, may be seen part of the Dewey triumphal arch. A mile to the north, seen across the flat roofs in the center background, is the new Manhattan Hotel on the N.W. corner of Madison Avenue and 42nd Street. Winter 1899-1900.

Brown Brothers, Photographers.

title: Manhattan: 26th Street - Madison Avenue
text:
A general view of the Madison Square area, photographed from the Fuller (Flatiron) Building. Fifth Avenue is on the left and Madison Avenue on the right. East 26th Street forms the northerly margin of the park. The distinctive Madison Square Garden is silhouetted against the nondescript district fringing Murray Hill. On the lower right is the recently erected Appellate Division of the Supreme Court Building.

Close observation thru the center discloses the cleared site of the fire-destroyed 71st Regiment Armory at 34th Street and Fourth Avenue. Upon 5th Avenue are observed, the Marble Collegiate Church, the Hotel Waldorf-Astoria, the Brick Presbyterian Church, the Collegiate Church of St. Nicholas and St. Thomas P. E. Church. The spires of St. Patricks Cathedral are outlined against the Hotel Sherry-Netherland. On the lower left is building debris at the S. W. corner of 5th Avenue and 26th Street. A structure there, that adjoined the corner (No. 202 Fifth Avenue) was removed in June of 1902.

About 1902

Ewing Galloway

title: Manhattan: Madison Avenue - 24th Street
text:
(1)
Madison Square, southwestern portion, looking northeast across the park at the tower of Madison Square Garden. In the foreground is the statue of William H. Seward, from a design by Randolph Rogers; and at the right is the brownstone steeple of the Madison Square Presbyterian Church (1854-1906), Madison Avenue at S. E. corner of 24th Street. Dr. Charles Parkhurst was pastor of this church, and from its pulpit launched his famous attack on Tammany Hall which drove Croker into exile, and swept a reform administration into power. To the right of the Church is the Metropolitan Life Building, whose expansion will destroy this church and its successor, built on the N. E.
corner.
About 1905.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2)
The same at a later date. Note the additional large buildings on the 24th to 25th Streets block. These in 1937 were demolished by the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company which at this date utilizes two
square blocks for their office structures.

1916.

Nicholas Savostayanoff.
Gift of George D. Chinn.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 24th Street

Fifth Avenue, west side, south from 24th Street. At the right is the Fifth Avenue Building, which replaced the famous Fifth Avenue Hotel, and which it resembles, except in height. In the centre is the Fuller, or Flatiron Building, whose fabulous height of 21 stories made it one of the sights of New York in other days. On the left is the statue of Admiral Farragut by the great American sculptor, Augustus St. Gaudens. About 1924.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: Madison Avenue - 26th Street
text:
Madison Square, looking southwest across the park from Madison Avenue and 26th Street, a singularly beautiful night view showing the Flatiron Building, and the new Fifth Avenue Building on the site of the Fifth Avenue Hotel. The low building to the right is the old Albenarie building, formerly the hotel of that name; it will shortly be replaced by a more modern structure.

In the foreground, the statue of President Chester A. Arthur is rather prominent.

1911.
New York Edison Company Collection.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - 23rd Street (East)
text:
Madison Square Park, bounded by Fifth Ave. (foreground) east to Madison Ave. and East 23rd (right) north to 26th Streets. Prior to 1806 this was a waste area, and in olden times a burial place for the poor. It was the site of a U.S. Arsenal, between 1806 to 1823. The first House of Refuge was founded here in 1825, which burned down in 1839. During the Mayoralty of James Harper (one of the famous publishers); between 1844 and 1847; this dreary region was cleared and beautified, and became the famous Madison Square. To-day this park is surrounded by large buildings, of which the Madison Ave. contingent predominates; possessing, as it does the Metropolitan Life Insurance Co. Buildings and Tower; the Madison Ave. Building; the Appellate division Supreme Court; the Manhattan Club and the New York Life Insurance Co. Building. The William H. Seward Statue shown in the foreground, (N.E. corner of Fifth Ave. and East 23rd Street), was unveiled in 1876, and is inscribed: Governor, U.S. Senator, Secretary of State U.S.

1936.

W.P.A. Photo.
Federal Writers Project.

title: Manhattan: Maiden Lane - Front Street
text:
Maiden Lane, west from and including Front Street (across the foreground), showing what appears to be a tobacco center at this location. This thoroughfare which derived its name from the Dutch, divides at a point above Gold Street to form in addition Liberty Street (left). The large structure forming the apex at that point is the Great American Insurance Company Building. To the left of same is the 24 storied Fire Companies Building. Note the Singer Building tower (with flag atop) in the background.

October 1914.

George L. Balgue.

title: Manhattan: Marble Hill Avenue - 227th Street
text:
Marble Hill Ave. (formerly Kingsbridge Ave., running from right fore, to center background), north from and including West 227th Street (formerly Wicker Place), showing King's Bridge, thrown across Spuyten Duyvil Creek (no longer in existence) and connecting Manhattan with the Bronx. The 3-story white frame house (right) bears No. 86; next to it, but slightly separated is No. 96, a 2½-story frame house, partially obstructing from view St. Stephen's (M.E.) Church, another frame structure, at the S.E. corner of Marble Hill Ave. and West 228th Street (formerly Terrace View Ave.). The 2½-story frame house, shown prominently, on the left, bears No. 91 Marble Hill Ave., at the N.W. corner of West 227th Street, and is seen facing the latter Street. Between Marble Hill Ave. and the Creek is visible a portion of West 228th Street, and across the Creek, in a northeasterly direction, is the Borough of The Bronx, as seen from the former site of Fort Prince Charles (hill, left foreground). The fort was built in 1776 during the Revolution and was named after Prince Charles William Ferdinand, brother-in-law of King George III. It was constructed for the purpose of controlling passage across King's Bridge, over Spuyten Duyvil Creek, which in turn was built in 1693 by a royal grant given to Frederick Philipse, by King William III, after whom it was named. In 1776 when the Hessian Army made decisive advances against the Colonials the fort was abandoned and in November, the Hessians who took possession of it, named it Fort Prince of Brunswick, a brother-in-law of King George III of England. This area is rich with the glorious traditions of the Colonials, who fought in these environs many a battle under George Washington's command. A flag pole now commemorates the site of the Fort. March 28, 1906.

Brown Brothers.

title: Manhattan: Marble Hill Avenue - 227th Street (West)

On the right slightly hidden by tree, is No. 96, a 2½ story frame house, obstructing from view (partially) St. Stephen's Church (M.E.), at the S.E. corner of 228th Street. Across the Creek are visible the hills in the Bronx, as seen from the former site of Fort Prince Charles (hill, left foreground, now 1937 occupied by a 6-story apartment house, the Fort Prince Charles Court). For further data see view 1.

March 28, 1906.

Brown Brothers.

title: Manhattan: Marble Hill Avenue - 228th Street (West)
text:
Marble Hill Avenue, adjoining the N.W. corner of West 228th Street. This house was razed between 1916 adn 1925 and stood directly in rear of the apartment house now (1939) bearing No. 157 West 255th Street.

The thoroughfare in the foreground is the old Kingsbridge Road which on the Manhattan side of the former Harlem River bed became Marble Hill Avenue. Note the declivity at the rear of the house indicating the creek. On the right are buildings on the Bronx shore; the larger of which is St. Johns Roman Catholic Church. This stands on Kingsbridge Avenue between 230th and 231st Streets.

Views 2 and 3 show various details; the privy vault in yard, and a rubber water supply from pump there to a second story.

title: Manhattan: Market Slip - Cherry Street
text:

This building, formerly occupied by the White Dental Co. has been converted into a Music School under the auspices of the Madonna House; a Roman Catholic organization occupying the adjoining structure on Cherry Street; No. 171. On the extreme right appears No. 433 Water St., a 5 story building at the S. E. corner Market Slip. The Manhattan Bridge traverses the entire background.

text:
15 to 27 Mercer Street, west side, south of and towards Grand Street. No. 15-17, at the left, which is not quite entirely included in the picture, is a six-story loft building, faced with iron, of a type which began to be built in the 1870's. No. 19 is a brick loft building, faced with stone, of the type built during and shortly after the Civil War, in the 1860's. Mercer Street is the first of a group of seven streets parallel to and west of Broadway.

title: Manhattan: 6th Avenue - Minetta Street
text:
Sixth Avenue, east side, between Minetta Street and Minetta Lane, showing in the open foreground area the site of the garden court, Minetta Place. Extension of the Avenue and related demolition caused this Greenwich Village feature of yore to disappear. Shortly two modern apartment houses will rise here. One to the right and one to the left of the dwellings, the rears of which are in the center. Incidently, these will remain, facing as they do, on Minetta Street. The tenement at the right is on the opposite side of this street.

About 1939
