title: Manhattan: Minetta Street - Minetta Lane
text:
Minetta Street, north from its bend to Minetta Lane. At the left are two 3-story buildings, No's. 12 and 14 that are to remain and separate two modern 6-story apartment houses. The preparatory stages of that one at the S. W. corner can be barely perceived. This was reported in the N. Y. Times of December 16, 1939. A report dated September 9, 1940 announces the second at
No's 2-10. This will be at the left margin.

The 3-story residence in the background is No. 16 Minetta Lane and adjoins the warehouse at No. 12.

April 13, 1940
P. L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: Minetta Street - Minetta Lane
text:
Minetta Street (left) at the S.W. corner of Minetta Lane (right) and southward, showing the preparatory stage for a new 6-story apartment house on this site. Thru the clearance appear buildings that are across 6th Avenue. Predominant is the new Roman Catholic Church of Our Lady of Pompeii. This is at the N.W. corner of the Carmine and Bleecker Streets.

Note the bend in Minetta Street and the isolated structures remaining on its west side. These are No's 12 and 14. Another apartment house is to be erected to abut on the far side of same as per the N.Y. Times of September 9, 1940. This site was formerly occupied by several frame buildings with brick fronts. At their rears was an inner court, Minetta Place. On the extension of 6th Avenue this and its rear buildings were exposed to view and subsequently obliterated.

April 13, 1940
Views 1, 2
P.L. Sperr

text:

The Federal Writers' Project of the W.P.A. states on page 426 of its New York Panorama that No. 65 Mott Street has been occupied since 1825 and gives as the authority for that statement, the "Plumber and Sanitary Engineer" of December 1879. This building appears in the center of this view, being the third structure from the left with fire escapes thereupon. Note that the roofing cornice has been removed. The tenements to this side of same are of the dumbbell type which originated in 1879 subsequent to the repeal in 1872 of the first tenement housing law of 1867.

title: Manhattan: Mott Street - Canal Street
text:
(1)& 2)

85 to 69 Mott Street, at, adjoining and south of the S. W. corner of Canal Street (right), showing prominently two old 3 story structures directly at the corner. These bear No's. 85 & 83, and have been the property of George Bull (owner of Saratoga race track) and Albert W. Maclay since 1836. The vacant lot seen to the rear of same is a portion of this platoge (76.6 x 50.6) and will shortly be improved with a one story addition, as per View No. 2.

The NEW York Times, of March 11, 1939, reports the lease of this site to the Low Cost Housing Corporation for a period of 51 years, same being negotiated by Joseph P. Day. The present buildings, said to have been erected about 150 years ago, will be razed and a two-story store and office building erected on the site.

No. 1 1922.
No. 2 June, 1929.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Manhattan: Nassau Street - Wall Street
text:
WHEN THE MARKET BROKE IN RECORD PANIC--CROWDS GATHER AT SUB TREASURY TO WATCH MOBS SURGE ABOUT STOCK EXCHANGE ACROSS THE STREET

NEW YORK.--PHOTO SHOWS: An exciting moment during the break of the market in the record panic when nearly 13,000,000 shares were traded. Here the crowds are gathered at the Sub Treasury, watching the excitement of still another crowd at the Stock Exchange, across the corner--at Broad and Wall Streets.

WALL STREET CROWD.

S/119x207

EVENING WRAP FOR THE NEW YORK HERALD.

title: Manhattan: New Street - Wall Street
text:
WATCH RELEASE DATE
Wide World Photo: Please Watch Credit
Main Caption for Pictures #829148, #829151 and #796402

NEW YORK CITY FIFTY YEARS AGO IN THE MIDDLE OF THE GREAT BLIZZARD

New York, N.Y. - Fifty years ago on March 13 New York was paralyzed by the worst storm in its history--the blizzard of '88. It had snowed steadily for twenty-four hours on March 12, and the snow continued to fall on the 13th, while the temperature dropped to four degrees below zero and the wind rose to a velocity of eighty-four miles an hour. It was estimated that the storm took a toll of 400 lives and $20,000,000 in property damage. The complex life of the city was at a complete standstill for two days. Thawing temperatures on March 14 aided in the slow task of digging out, which continued for several days. There were countless freak consequences of the storm, such as the sending of messages from Boston to New York by way of London, because all land telegraph service was disrupted, but the submarine cables were undisturbed. The average fall of snow was three feet four inches, but the high winds piled the drifts up to second-story window levels in many places. Three scenes from the blizzard are sent you.
H-3/9/38 (S)

(Special feature layout for release March 13)

Also shown is Hanover Square, south side, which begins at this point (Water Street), and continues westward to Stone Streets, being actually a continuation of Old Slip. The W.R. Grace & Co. title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 32nd Street
text: Park Avenue, east side, north from 32nd Street, showing the New York Central building over the roof of the Grand Central Station. The two blocks from 32nd to 34th Streets began to be called Park Avenue upon completion of the new buildings No. 1 and No. 2 Park Avenue, between 32nd and 33rd Street, in 1926-27. No. 2 is shown here in the left foreground, on the site of the old Park Avenue Hotel. The block from 33rd to 34th Street is occupied by the Vanderbilt Hotel (1911). At the N. W. corner of 34th Street is the Community Church (Unitarian), shortly to be demolished. On the S. W. corner of 37th Street the Union League Club's new house is nearing completion. To the left of the Grand Central Station stands the Hotel Belmont, on the west side, from 41st Street to 42nd Street. Built about 1904, it is shortly to be demolished. To the left of it rises the tall Lincoln Building, 60 East 42nd Street, and directly in front of it may be seen the old Murray Hill Hotel, between 40th and 41st Streets. Compare this with Brown Brothers' photograph of Park Avenue north from 32nd Street in 1906. 1930. Ewing Galloway, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 32nd Street
text:
Park Avenue, west side, north from and including 32nd Street. The new Park Avenue Building, on the west side from 32nd to 33rd Streets, was built in 1927, on the site of the old Park Avenue Hotel. The Vanderbilt Hotel, in the next block north, was built in 1911. Two street cars of the Madison and Fourth Avenue line are shown, a downtown car waiting for the light at 32nd Street, and an uptown car about to plunge into the old railway tunnel, which will be made over for automobile traffic in 1935, after this street car line has been discontinued and superseded by motor coaches.

The Community Church (Unitarian), on the N.W. corner of 34th Street, will be demolished in 1931; and its place will be taken by an apartment building. The new Union League clubhouse will be built in 1930 on the S.W. corner of 37th Street. Up at 41st to 42nd Streets the Hotel Belmont, rising from behind the old Murray Hill Hotel, will be demolished in 1931. At the time of this picture the old Lincoln Bank building, adjoining the Biltmore at 42nd Street, has not yet been demolished; and the tower of the New York Central Building, north of the Grand Central Station, is still under construction.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 32nd Street
text:
Park Avenue, north from 32nd Street and Fourth Avenue, a point just north of the old Sunfish Pond.
The Street car tunnel is the old tunnel under Murray Hill cut by the New York and Harlem Railway in its early days. An engine house with a turntable stood where the Armory is now located, and there was a roundhouse or engine house in the block where the Park Avenue Hotel is shown. The name Park Avenue was first applied to that portion of Fourth Avenue between 34th and 42nd Streets, and is so shown on maps, with the little green parks in the middle of the avenue in each block, as early as 1867. Above 42nd Street the name Park Avenue was not applied till nearly 1890. After the building of the first Grand Central Station in 1870, train service down to Madison Square was discontinued, and the tunnel taken over by the horse-cars. In 1898 this surface line was electrified. In 1935, when the Madison and Fourth Avenue street cars have been superseded by buses, the tunnel will be remodeled for automobile traffic.
On the east side from 32nd to 33rd Streets stand the barbarns of the Metropolitan Street Railway; they will be torn down in 1925. The 71st Regiment Armory, shown in the next block, was erected in 1893. On the west side of the avenue, the Park Avenue Hotel, built by A. T. Stewart in the 1870's, will give place in 1926 to the new No. 2 Park Avenue building. On either side of 33rd Street may be seen subway entrances; the subway has been open about two years. The 333rd to 34th Street block, west, will be demolished in 1910 to make room for the Vanderbilt Hotel.
On the horizon may be seen the new Hotel Belmont on the southwest corner of 42nd Street, and one dome of the old Grand Central Station. Compare this picture with Galloway's view of the west side of the avenue, looking north from this point, in 1930.

Brown Brothers, Photographers.

E. corner of 33rd Street stands the 71st Regiment Armory. On the west side between 32nd and 33rd Streets, the old Park Avenue Hotel is shortly to be demolished and replaced by another office building. Opposite the Armory stands the Vanderbilt Hotel (erected 1911).

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 32nd Street (East)
text:
Park Avenue, east side, from E. 32nd (right) to 33rd (left) Streets, showing the New York and Harlem Railroad carbarns. The photographer is viewing same in a south eastward direction from a vantage point at the N. W. corner of Park Avenue and E. 33rd Street
(Vanderbilt Hotel today).
At the time this photo was taken, this thoroughfare was Fourth Avenue; Park Avenue beginning at 34th Street. When the present multi-story building No. 1 Park Avenue was erected, this Avenue was extended southward to begin at 32nd Street. In the renumbering, this office building took the number formerly held by Mrs. Bacon at the N. E. corner of Park Avenue and E. 34th Street.

Behind the board fence in the foreground ran the trains to Harlem, thru the tunnel to Grand Central Station at 42nd Street. It was here that the famous Tunnel Gang originated and from which came Boss Crocker of Tammany, a worthy successor to Boss Tweed.

In earlier days this was the bed of Sunfish Pond. The ground slope clearly seen here indicates the size and depth of same.

Remaining today (1939) are only two of the buildings appearing here. They are the 4 story structure seen at the left margin and the St. Stephen's Roman Catholic Church at the right. No. 197 Lexington Avenue, the first mentioned, is now an automobile garage.

1860's

Notice the street sign reading "4th Avenue." The name Park Avenue will shortly be extended down to 32nd Street. The name One Park Avenue will be the subject of a litigation between the One Park Avenue Corporation and Mrs. Robert Bacon, owner of the house on the N.E. corner of 34th Street; the matter will not finally be settled in favor of this building till February 1928.

On the S.W. corner of 37th Street may be seen the new Union League clubhouse, and behind it the New York Trust Company's skyscraper is nearing completion on the S.E. corner of Madison Avenue and 40th Street. Close together and a little to the right of this are the Lefcourt Colonial Building at 41st Street and the Lincoln Building at 60 East 42nd Street (both 1929). On the west side of Park Avenue, from 41st to 42nd Streets the Hotel Belmont, shortly to be demolished, rises behind the much older Murray Hill Hotel. The New York Central Building (1928) rises behind the Grand Central Station, at the head of the Avenue. To the right of the former may be seen the towers of the new Waldorf-Astoria Hotel on the east side of Park Avenue, from 49th to 50th Streets; it is still under construction, and they are surrounded by scaffolding.

February 27, 1931.

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 35th Street
text:
Park Avenue, west side, from 35th Street, to a point between 36th and 37th Streets.

On the N. W. corner of 35th Street, where the old Church of the Covenant stood from 1865 to 1895, is shown the house occupied by the Women's City Club. Behind it towers the new building at 10 East 40th Street.

March 10, 1929

P. L. Sperr

(2)

A portion of the former view at a slightly later date. Note the vacant lot at No. 30. This site was utilized for a wing to the adjoining structure.

The dominant No. 10 East 40th Street Building (erected 1928) partly obscures the newer No. 500-Fifth Avenue Building. To the right appears the southerly side of the recently constructed Union League Club. This building is at the S. W. corner of Park Avenue and East 37th Street and was erected in 1930.

February 23, 1931

P. L. Sperr

(3)

Details of the demolition of the Women's Club and its isomorphic structure, No. 28 Park Avenue, the property of F. F. Guthrie. Upon this site will rise a tall apartment building. The five-story affair at the left will not be included. This bears No. 39 East 35th Street and is occupied by the United Lutheran Church of America.

October, 1938

George D. Chinn

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 36th Street
text:
Park Avenue, north on east side from 36th to 39th Streets, seen from the N.W. corner of 35th Street in front of the Women's City Club.

The 9-story apartment building on the S.W. corner of 37th Street, the site of the old Judge Russell mansion, was erected in 1923, the apartment house between 37th and 38th Streets about the same time; and the entire block from 38th to 39th Streets was rebuilt between 1921 and 1924, the N.W. corner of 38th Street being site of the Charles D. Barney residence.

In the background, from left to right, are seen the top of the Chanin Building, the needle top of the Chrysler Building, and the colored tower of Town House apartments at 108 East 38th Street. October 6, 1933.

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 36th Street
text:
Park Avenue, west side, from 36th to 39th Streets, showing skyscrapers in the background.

On the S.W. corner of 37th Street stands the new Union League clubhouse. The rear of the buildings on the east side of Madison Avenue, from 37th to 38th Streets, are plainly visible; from south to north the are: the old Delmar residence, occupied by the National Democratic Club, the Hotel Duane in the middle of the block, and the Allerton Fraternity Clubs Building occupying the S.E. corner of 38th Street and Madison Avenue where the old South Church used to stand. To the left of this, on the S.W. corner of Madison Avenue and 38th Street, stands the old Heckscher building, erected 1916 on the site of the Theodore A. Havemeyer mansion.

The five skyscrapers, from left to right, are No. 10 East 40th Street (1928), 500 Fifth Avenue at the N.W. corner of 42nd Street (1930), the New York Trust Company's tower nearing completion on the S.E. corner of Madison and 40th Street, the Lefcourt Colonial Building at the N.W. corner of Madison Avenue and 41st Street, and the Lincoln Building at 60 East 42nd Street, both the latter completed in 1929.

February 27, 1931.

P.L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 37th Street (East)

Park Ave., at East 37th Street, showing the tablet erected by the D.A.R. to Mary Lindley Murray. This marker is placed in the grass plot that divides the traffic lanes of this thoroughfare.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 37th Street (East)
text:
Park Ave. (left), at the S.W. corner of East 37th Street, showing the Union League Club. The club was organized in 1863 and most of its members are politically of Republican proclivities. This is its fourth building.

1936.

W.P.A. Photo.
Federal Writers Project.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 37th Street (East)
text:
Park Avenue, adjoining the N.E. corner of E. 37th Street; showing at this location the garden established in 1915-16 by the Murray Hill Association to remedy the unsightly appearance of this vacant lot, the property of the I.R.T. Co. In 1923 this will be included in the site for the 15 story apartment house, No. 51 Park Avenue.

Thru the center runs Park Avenue and to the left is E. 37th Street, west of the Avenue. In 1931 the Union League Club House will rise there. Opposite same and prominently shown is the building at the N.W. corner occupied by Charles Coster and which has recently (N.Y. Sun June 14, 1939) been sold for replacement by an apartment house. This is to be of Georgian design and harmonize with the Union League Club building.

1915-16

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 37th Street (East)
text:
Park Avenue, west side, from E. 37th to 38th Streets, as viewed northwestward from the east side of this thoroughfare and showing in addition (left) the north side of 37th Street, west from Park to Madison Avenues.

The New York Times of June 14, 1939, reports the sale for improvement of the corner property and the adjoining three structures on 37th Street. Comprising same are the Charles Coster house (50 Park Avenue), the former home of General Charles F. Roe of the N. Y. S. N. G. (No. 35 E. 37th Street), the Cortlandt Field Bishop home (No. 33 E.) and the Issac W. How home (No. 31 E.). The latter was sold by the estate of William M. Savin and No's 33 and 35 by Miss Sarah Ahern.

At the extreme left of View 1 is the National Democratic Club, located at the N. E. corner of E. 37th Street and Madison Avenue. View No. 2 is westward on 37th Street while No. 3 is southwestward to include the Union League Club (1931) at the S. W. corner and opposite this new project.

Overhead appears the tower of the Empire State Building and a cornice of the Engineering Combustion Building.

P. L. Sperr

View 1: June 14, 1931
View 2: April 15, 1931
View 3: Sept. 9, 1933

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 37th Street
text:
Park Avenue, east side, from 37th to 41st Streets, but not showing the small building on the N.E. corner of 41st Street.
No. 55 Park Avenue, in the right foreground, was built in 1923 on the site of the old Interborough Garden shown in another picture. From 38th to 39th Streets are shown the new apartment buildings built between 1922 and 1924, and behind them the towers of the Chanin and Chrysler Buildings. On the N.E. corner of 39th Street the old houses are being demolished. The tall white building on the N.E. corner of 40th Street is the Architects' Building, erected in 1916.

September 10, 1933.

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 38th Street (East)
text:
Park Avenue, west side, north from East 38th Street.  At 39th Street is a vacant lot at the S.W. corner and the Princeton Club opposite.  Beyond the latter is a 2-story taxpayer at 40th Street and the old Murray Hill Hotel.  Grand Central Station is at the right margin.  Towering overhead are several of the huge office buildings that form a part of the 42nd Street--Grand Central sky-line.  The three shown are Johns Vanaville, Lefcourt-Colonial and the Lincoln Buildings.
On the left is a portion of the apartment-hotel identified as No. 70 Park Avenue.  This is at the N.W. corner of 38th Street.
May 27, 1939
Views 1,2
P.L. Sperr
VIEW 1, A2 NEG. # 4280

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 38th Street
text:
67 Park Avenue at N.E. corner of 38th Street, a new apartment house nearing completion on the site of the old Charles D. Barney residence.
Notice the center parks on the old railroad tunnel and the roofed over stairway for passengers of the Madison Avenue street-car line, which will be discontinued in 1935.
The center parks as shown here are probably little changed in appearance since the Civil War, but they are about to be remodelled.  Early 1922.

Gift of E. M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 38th Street
text:
Park Avenue, north from 38th Street, showing the nearly completed New York Central Building towering over Grand Central Terminal. The following buildings in the picture are later to be demolished: the house shown on the S. W. corner of 40th Street and the two houses adjoining it on the south (1931), the four houses from the N. E. corner of 39th Street north (1933), and the Hotel Belmont in the block above the old Murray Hill. The Princeton Club is the building on the N. W. corner of 39th Street. Above the house on the N. W. corner of 39th Street one can see a little bit of the building at 60 East 42nd Street which is about to give place to the new Lincoln Building. 1928.

Cosmo Photo Co.
 with credit.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 37th Street
text:
(1)
Park Avenue, north from and including 38th Street, seen from 37th Street, and showing the west side of the Avenue.
The white building on the N.W. corner of 38th Street is the 70 Park Avenue Hotel. Above it is the Princeton Club on the N.W. corner of 39th Street, and the Murray Hill Hotel from 40th to 41st Streets. The Hotel Belmont, rising behind the Murray Hill, is to be demolished in 1931, as are the buildings on the S.W. corner of 40th Street.
To the left of the Belmont may be seen part of the old Lincoln Bank Building about to be demolished to make way for the new Lincoln Building at 60 East 42nd Street.
The avenue is cut off by the Grand Central Station, with the New York Central Building rising directly behind it.
March 10, 1929.

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

(2)
The same, but also showing the east side of the Avenue, and a close view of the center parks as they have appeared since modernization in 1923. Compare this with the 1929 picture on this mount. The Lincoln Building towers behind the Princeton Club and the Murray Hill Hotel. The buildings on the S.W. corner of 39th Street, demolished 1933, have been replaced by a parking place for automobiles -- the wire fence is visible to a sharp eye. The old houses on the S.W. corner of 40th Street were replaced in 1933 by the low, white commercial structure visible between the Princeton Club and the Murray Hill Hotel.
On the east side of the Avenue the houses on the N.W. corner of 39th Street have been demolished, but the Little House, which replaces them, is set back too far from the street to be visible in this picture.

March 22, 1935.

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

Park Avenue, west side, from 38th to 39th Streets, including the N.W. corner of 39th Street.
The buildings on the S.W. corner of 39th Street are being demolished. The house on the N.W. corner has been occupied by the Princeton Club since 1923. In the background, from left to right, three skyscrapers tower, The New York Trust Company's building at 277 Madison Avenue, the Lefcourt Colonial Building at 297 Madison Avenue (S.E. corner of 41st Street), and the Lincoln Building at 60 East 42nd Street, the first built in 1931 and the other two late in 1929.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 38th Street
text:
(1)
Park Avenue, west side, from 38th to 42nd Streets, the avenue being cut off from 42nd to 46th Streets by the Grand Central Station and the New York Central Building, rising behind it. On the horizon, to the left of the latter, may be seen the top of the new R.C.A. Building, Radio City.

Demolition of houses on the S.W. corner of 39th Street is shown; the site will later be used for automobile parking. The Princeton Club remains on the N.W. corner of 39th Street; and beyond it may be seen the white two-story commercial building recently erected in place of the old houses demolished in October 1931.

The old Murray Hill Hotel fills the block from 40th to 41st Streets, and behind it tower the Lincoln Building at 60 East 42nd Street and the Lefcourt Colonial Building on the S.E. corner of Madison Avenue and 41st Street.

September 9, 1933.

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

(2)
The same, a closer view of the 39th and 40th Street corners, not showing the 38th Street corner nor the Grand Central Station.

October 1, 1933.

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 38th Street
text:
Park Avenue, west side, between 38th and 42nd Streets, showing in the background the tower of the Lefcourt Colonial building at Madison Avenue and 41st Street, and the Lincoln Building (60 East 42nd Street) still under construction.
Of the buildings shown along the west side of the Avenue, the S.W. corner of 39th Street will be demolished in 1933. The Princeton Club on the N.W. corner will stand, but the other three houses in the block, to the S.W. corner of 40th Street, will be demolished in 1931 and replaced by a white two-story structure built for stores. The Hotel Belmont, which is far younger than the Murray Hill Hotel, will also be demolished in 1931 at an age of only twenty-five years.

Ewing Galloway, Photographer.

1929.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 34th Street
text:
Park Avenue, south on west side, from 39th to 34th Streets, seen from 40th Street.
The old residence on the S.W. corner of 39th Street will be demolished in September 1933. The 70 Park Avenue Hotel, shown on the N.W. corner of 38th Street, was built since 1925; and on the S.W. corner of 37th Street the houses are still standing that will give way in 1930 to the new Union League Clubhouse.
The Vanderbilt Hotel, on the block from 34th to 33rd Streets, is shown at the extreme left.

May 6, 1928.

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 36th Street
text:
Park Avenue, east side, from 39th to 36th Streets, seen from the roof of the Chemists' Club on 41st Street between Park and Madison Avenues, and showing the northern sides of some of the buildings on the west side such as the new 70 Park Avenue Hotel (since 1925) on the N.W. corner of 38th Street. September 5, 1928.

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 38th Street
text:
Park Avenue, east side, from 39th to 38th Streets, seen from the roof of 271 Madison Avenue, and showing the East River in the background.
77 Park Avenue, on the S.E. corner of 39th Street, was erected in 1924, and 67 Park Avenue, on the N.E. corner of 38th Street, was completed in 1922 on the site of the old Charles D. Barney residence. The building in the middle of the block was erected between these two in point of time. East of Park Avenue is shown the colored tower of Town House Apartments, 108 East 38th Street, erected in 1930.
The single smoke-stack seen in the background is part of the New York Steam Corporation's plant on the east side of First Avenue between 35th and 36th Streets.

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

December 2, 1931.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 38th Street
text:
(1)
Park Avenue, east side, from 39th to 38th Streets, looking across the S.W. corner of 39th Street.
These three apartment houses were built during the years 1922-24, No. 67 on the N.E. corner of 38th Street, on the site of the old Charles D. Barney residence, being the first. Behind it rises the colored tower of Town House Apartments at 108 East 38th Street, built in 1930.
In the foreground the old houses on the S.W. corner of 39th Street are being demolished.
September 10, 1933.
P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

(2)

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 39th Street (East)
text:
Park Ave., north from East 39th Street, showing W.P.A. employees reconstructing the former street car (before that, used by railroad) tunnel for future vehicular use. Shown in the background is the automobile ramp around Grand Central station that this will hook up to.

W.P.A. Photo.
Federal Art Project.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 39th Street
text:
77 Park Avenue at the S.E. corner of 39th Street, a new apartment house nearing completion. This entire block has been rebuilt since 1921; the building partly shown on the right is the corner house at 38th Street which replaced the old C. D. Barney house in 1922. Compare this picture with the N.E. corner of 38th Street in early 1922 and notice also how the center parks have been modernized to leave more room for motor traffic.

1924.

Joseph Smith.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 39th Street
text:
Park Avenue at 39th Street, seen from 39th Street west of the Avenue.
On the N.W. corner stands the Princeton Club; and the S.W. corner is shown vacant, buildings having been demolished in September 1933. It will later be used as a parking space.
On the N.E. corner, set back from the street, is the Little House, a model home built on the site, which was cleared in 1933, by the New York Committee of Better Homes in America, and opened for public inspection November 1934. On the same side of 39th Street, east of Lexington Avenue, may be seen one of the Allerton Houses, an apartment hotel for men.
The apartment house on the S.E. corner of Park Avenue and 39th Street was built in 1924.

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 39th Street
text:
Park Avenue, south from and including 39th Street, seen from the top of the Lincoln Building at 60 East 42nd Street. Below 32nd Street the eastern side of Fourth Avenue, down to Union Square, is visible. In the left background the New York Edison tower, on 14th Street between Irving Place and Third Avenue, rises out of the haze. To the west of Fourth Avenue, much nearer, are the towers of the New York Life Building (27th to 26th Streets) and the Metropolitan Tower on the S.E. corner of Madison Avenue and 24th Street.

Park Avenue begins at 32nd Street. The new One Park Avenue building is seen to the left, and Two Park Avenue to the right. In the block from 33rd to 34th Streets you can see the entrance to the old tunnel. The 71st Regiment Armory is on the east side, and the Hotel Vanderbilt on the west (in front of Two Park Avenue). The following construction is under way on or near Park Avenue; No. 7 Park Avenue, an L-shaped apartment building surrounding the N.E. corner of 34th Street; the new Union League clubhouse on the S.W. corner of 37th Street; and the Town House apartment building at 108 East 38th Street. In 1933 the small houses on the S.W. and N.E. corners of 39th Street will be demolished. The latter corner will be occupied in 1935 by America's Little House.

1930.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 39th Street (East)
text:
Park Avenue, south from E. 39th Street (intersection in foreground) as viewed southwestward from what the writer believes to be the Chanin Building, showing several high apartment houses and the Union League Club. The latter is the square Colonial facade structure seen in the center of bot views. The two apartment houses facing each other at 38th Street are the 70 Park Avenue and the Murray. View No. 2 is southeastward from an office building at the northwest corner of Madison Avenue and 39th Street and emphasizes a rear view of the last named structures and the club.
About 1932.
Views 1 and 2

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 39th Street (East)
text:
(1)
Park Ave., east side, north from East 39th to 40th Streets. Shown at the N.E. corner is a country home, erected for demonstration purposes. Buildings standing at the S.E. corner of 40th Street, are Nos. 93-99 inclusive. No. 99-97 (at and adjoining the corner), is the Nurses Club;
March 22, 1935.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)
A closer view of "America's Little House".
March 22, 1935.

P. L. Sperr.

This entire block front has been purchased by the City as a new site of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court. On completion of same they will move from their present quarters at the N.E. corner of Madison Ave. and East 25th Street. The Henry Street Visiting Nurse Service have purchased the former Wm. Goadby Loew residence at the S.W. corner of Madison Ave. and East 39th Street and will shortly move their executive offices there after remodeling to meet their needs. For a fuller account see the New York Sun of February 15, 1936 and March 29, 1938 and the New York Times of March 25, 1938.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 39th Street
text:
Park Avenue, east side, from 39th to 42nd Streets, showing demolition of houses from the N.E. corner of 39th Street to and including the little one in the middle of the block. On the site thus vacant the Little House will be erected late in 1934. On the N.E. corner of 40th Street stands the Architects' Building (1916), and above it the smaller and older 103 Park Avenue. The Pershing Square Building follows in the block from 41st to 42nd Streets, where the Grand Union Hotel stood prior to 1915.
In the background the Chanin Building partly hides the tower of the Chrysler Building.

September 10, 1933.

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

In the background are shown the Lefcourt Colonial Building at Madison Avenue and 41st Street, and the Lincoln Building at 60 East 42nd Street.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 39th Street
text:
Park Avenue, west side, from 40th to 39th Streets, showing Murray Hill Hotel on the N.W. corner of 40th Street; the view is from the Pershing Square Building on the east side at 41st Street. The old houses which are being demolished on the S.W. corner of 40th Street will be replaced in 1933 by a white two-story structure with stores. The buildings on the S.W. corner of 39th Street will be demolished in September, 1933. The elevation of the camera gives an especially good view of the Empire State Building at Fifth Avenue and 34th Street, the tallest building in the world.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 40th Street
text:

The New York Central Building (1928) at 46th Street is seen over the roof of the Station. Underneath the station clock, in front of the large window and facing south on the Viaduct, may be seen the statue of Commodore Vanderbilt, who built up the New York Central Railroad system.

June 14, 1931.

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 40th Street
text:
(1) Park Avenue, west side, from 40th to 41st Streets, showing the old Murray Hill Hotel, which dates back to the 1870's, against a background of modern skyscrapers. To the right is the Lincoln Building, completed late in 1929, at 60 East 42nd Street, and to the left the Lefcourt Colonial Building (1929) on the S.W. corner of Madison Avenue and 41st Street and the Murray Hill Offices building (1926), which together take up the entire east side of Madison Avenue from 41st to 40th Streets. Behind the latter, to the left of the Lefcourt tower, may be seen the top of 500 Fifth Avenue, completed on the N.W. corner of 42nd Street in January 1931. December 2, 1931.

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

(2) The same, but showing a little of the clearing at the S.W. corner of 40th Street, and missing the tops of the Lincoln and Lefcourt Colonial buildings. In the block above the Murray Hill, from 41st to 42nd Streets, the Hotel Belmont has been demolished. Through the gap thus created may be seen the west side of Vanderbilt Avenue at 43rd Street; the Hotel Biltmore (erected about 1914) is the building shown in part on the N.W. corner. December 2, 1931

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

(3) The same, showing a portion of Grand Central Station on the right with its elevated vehicular viaduct. December 2, 1931.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 40th Street
text:
Murray Hill Hotel, Park Avenue, west side, from 40th to 41st Streets, showing part of the 41st Street side of the Hotel Belmont, the latter hotel, although much newer, will be demolished in 1931. In the foreground may be seen the southern end of the Pershing Square viaduct. Behind the Murray Hill Hotel, on the right, may be seen a large office building under construction at the N.E. corner of Madison Avenue and 41st Street. Compare this with the picture taken in 1918.

June 1925.

Brown Brothers, Photographers.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 41st Street
text: Park Avenue, west side, from 41st to 42nd Streets, the side entrance to the Hotel Belmont, at Pershing Square. Probably late 1918.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 41st Street
text:
Pershing Square, Park Avenue from 41st to 42nd Streets, looking west at the Hotel Belmont (1906-31) from the vacant lot where the Grand Union Hotel used to stand and where the Pershing Square building will be erected. The name Pershing Square, after General Pershing, commander of the American Expeditionary Force, was applied to this block about the time of the Armistice.

The Pershing Square viaduct, shown here, conducted automobile traffic from Park Avenue and 40th Street across 42nd Street and around the left side of the Grand Central Station to Vanderbilt Avenue and 45th Street. As shown here it is quite new. The covered stairway coming up out of the vacant lot in the foreground is an entrance to the new Lexington Avenue Interborough Subway, opened in the summer of 1918.

On the S.W. corner of 41st Street may be seen part of the old Murray Hill Hotel; and west on 42nd Street the Hotel Manhattan on the N. W. corner of Madison Avenue, later to be remodelled into an office building and uptown office for the National City Bank. The small building on the N. E. corner of Madison Avenue and 42nd Street is shortly to be demolished and replaced by the Liggett Drug building.

About 1920.

Gift of E.M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 41st Street
text:
Park Avenue, 41st to 42nd Streets (the future Pershing Square), showing construction of viaduct for automobile traffic over the old northern entrance to the Murray Hill tunnel and around the western shoulder of the new Grand Central Station. Work on this project was commenced November 2, 1917. The Hotel Commodore, as shown here, is quite new.

On the east side of Park Avenue, from 41st to 42nd Streets, the old Grand Union Hotel stood until its demolition in 1914; the southern end of the new East Side express station of the new subway, nearly ready to open, lies underneath. The old elevated station, originally only one end of a short shuttle, will stand here till 1924. Compare this with 1914, 1920, 1923, and later pictures.

Early 1918.

Brown Brothers.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 41st Street
text:
Grand Union Hotel, Park Avenue, east side, from 41st to 42nd Streets, also showing the new Grand Central Station and the old spur of the Third Avenue Elevated, which will be taken down in 1924.

The Grand Union was to a great extent built by acquisition of old houses in the block, intervening walls being knocked out and rooms remodelled. The whole is shown shortly before demolition. Compare this with later pictures of the same block.

1914.

Gift of E.M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 41st Street
text:
Park Avenue, east side, from 41st to 42nd Streets, on Pershing Square, where the Grand Union Hotel stood until June, 1914, showing the new Grand Central Station and the recently completed Hotel Commodore on the north side of 42nd Street, also the old elevated spur used until 1923 as a shuttle to the Third Avenue line. The covered stairways in the vacant lot are entrances to the express station of the new east side Interborough Subway, which was opened in the summer of 1918. About 1919.

Gift of E. M. Jenks.

In the right foreground, opposite this building, the Hotel Belmont (opened 1906) is in the final stages of demolition.
103 Park Avenue, on the S.E. corner of 41st Street, was built about 1900, and 101 Park Avenue, on the N.E. corner of 40th Street, in 1916.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 41st Street
text:
Pershing Square, Park Avenue, east side, from 42nd to 41st Streets, showing the newly completed Pershing Square Building on the site of the old Grand Union Hotel, the new Bowery Savings Bank to the left at 110 East 42nd Street and the Pershing Square Viaduct and Third Avenue Elevated station in the foreground.
The old Grand Union, shown in a 1914 picture of this block, was shortly thereafter pulled down, while the new Lexington Avenue subway station and the junction with the old line were constructed under Park Avenue in this block. Then about the time of the Armistice this block was named Pershing Square, after General John J. Pershing, and the automobile viaduct built to conduct traffic from 40th Street and Park Avenue over 41st and 42nd Streets and around on the west side of the Grand Central Station to Vanderbilt Avenue and 45th Street. When the New York Central building is built in 1928 traffic will be divided at the point shown here, and a double viaduct built through to 46th Street and Park Avenue.
The Elevated spur shown here was originally a temporary terminal of the Third Avenue line, but for many years has served as a shuttle from the Grand Central Station to the main Elevated line at Third Avenue and 42nd Street. It is about to be demolished, at the time of this picture.
On the S.E. corner of 42nd Street is 103 Park Avenue, an office building built about 1900, and beyond it may be seen part of the newer Architects' Building (1916)
1923.
Gift of E. M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 43rd Street
text:
Park Avenue, south from and including 43rd Street, seen from the roof of 230 Park Avenue, the New York Central Building. The Lincoln Building, 60 East 42nd Street, opposite the foot of Vanderbilt Avenue, is shown nearly completed.

1929.

N. Lazarnick.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 37th Street
text:
45 Park Avenue, "The Russell", at S. E. corner of 37th Street, an apartment hotel newly erected on the site of the old Judge Russell residence.
In the foreground it will be noted that the center parks are being altered slightly, for the first time since 1880 or earlier.
1923.

Joseph Smith, Photographer.
Gift of E.M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 45th Street
text:
Old Grand Central Station, Park Avenue at 45th Street, showing the rear of the station and the railroad tracks in the foreground, where in 1928 the New York Central Building will be erected. The view is roughly southwest from east of the future Park Avenue. The demolition of this old station and the construction of the new one will require a number of years, from about 1907 to 1912. The rear of the old station may be seen against the background of its surroundings in the New York Edison Company's photograph of Park Avenue south from 48th Street, 1903. 1872.

New York Edison Company Collection

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 45th Street
text:
Park Avenue, north from and including 45th Street, showing the buildings on the east side of the Avenue, seen from the roof of the Grand Central Station, which appears in the center foreground.

The area over the railroad yards is still open on the east side from 45th to 46th Streets and from 47th to 48th Streets, and on the west side from 45th to 47th Streets. The nearest building on the west side is the Hotel Marguery (about 1917) from 47th to 45th Streets.

On the east side 247 Park Avenue, completed about 1922, and connected to the new Grand Central Palace in the Lexington Avenue half of the block, stands from 46th to 47th Streets. In the block from 48th to 49th Streets the new Park Lane apartment hotel may be seen under construction, and in the block directly north of it the Railroad Y.M.C.A. building, which is to be demolished in 1929 to make way for the new Waldorf-Astoria. These buildings hid St. Bartholomew's Church, so that the next visible building on the east side is the Hotel Ambassador (1910-20), on the block from 51st to 52nd Streets.

To the right of the picture may be seen the new American Express Building from 45th to 46th Streets on Lexington Avenue, and behind it the tower of the Hotel Shelton, nearing completion, on the east side of Lexington Avenue from 47th to 48th Streets.

On the horizon, dimly seen at the extreme right, is the Hell Gate Bridge, shown surprisingly large considering its actual distance.

Compare this with the same scene in 1903.

Winter 1923-4

Ewing Galloway, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 45th Street
text:
Park Avenue north from and including 45th Street, showing the old Grand Central railroad yards, before they were electrified and covered.
Crossing the yards in the center of the picture are the 45th and 46th Street bridges.
The Liberty Storage warehouse is at the S.W. corner of 50th Street and Park Avenue.
Opposite it, on the south side of 50th Street, is the old Women's Hospital, shortly to be demolished.
Immediately south of it is the old Adams Express building.
Going north on the east side of Park Avenue F. & M. Schaefer's Brewery is between 50th and 51st streets, and the Steinway Piano factory between 52nd and 53rd Streets, both dating, at least in part, from the 1850's.
Compare this with Galloway's Photograph of the same scene in the winter of 1923-24, also with Park Avenue north from 46th Street in 1913.
1903.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 45th Street
text:
230 Park Avenue, from E. 45th to 46th Streets, as viewed north-westward from the Chrysler Building at 42nd Street. This address is that of the New York Central Building of which a rear perspective is shown. In the background across same appear the blocks of brown stone dwellings where the present Rockefeller Center (Radio City) emerged. Note the twin spires of St. Patrick's Cathedral to the east of same.

1930.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 45th Street
text:
New York Central Building, 230 Park Avenue, 45th to 46th Streets, a rear view during the later stages of construction. 1928.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 45th Street
text:
Park Avenue, west side; 45th to 47th Streets, showing the Postum Building at 250 Park Avenue across the space in the foreground where the New York Central Building is to be erected; construction on the latter is beginning. The view is from 45th Street east of Park Avenue.

October 11, 1927.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 45th Street
text:
Park Avenue, west side, from 46th to 45th Streets, showing the site of the New York Central Building, 230 Park Avenue, as construction begins on it. In the right background are shown the Vanderbilt Concourse Building, the Yale Club (50 Vanderbilt Avenue), and the Hotel Biltmore. The Grand Central Terminal cuts off Park Avenue at 45th Street.

October 2, 1927.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 46th Street
text:
Park Avenue north from and including 46th Street. The railroad yards are now covered over, but building has barely begun. To the right, between 46th and 47th Streets, is the new Grand Central Palace. The new building under construction at the N.E. corner of 49th Street is the new Railroad Y.M.C.A.; together with the power plant and the new Adams Express building it will stand until demolition in 1929. From 50th to 52nd Streets on the east side the old F. & M. Schaefer Brewery will give way between 1917 and 1919 to St. Bartholomew's Church and the Hotel Ambassador. The oldest part of the Brewery, including the tower at the S.E. corner of 51st Street, dates from the 1880's. Beyond the Brewery, the new 12-story Montana Apartments have been standing for about a year on the site of the old Steinway Factory. Above this point there is already quite a bit of apartment building. Compare this picture with Park Avenue from 45th Street in 1903 and in 1923-4, also with Park Avenue from 46th Street, Silver Jubilee Exposition in June 1923.

November 25, 1913.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 46th Street
text:
Park Avenue, north from and including 46th Street. Silver Jubilee Exposition of 1923, the 25th Anniversary of Greater New York. The band is in the middle of 46th Street. To the right is No. 247 Park Avenue, about two years old. The 47th to 48th Street lot is still vacant; on the east side, in the next block north, the Park - Lane is under construction. Then comes the Railroad Y.M.C.A, hiding all but a small glimpse of St. Bartholomew's and the Hotel Ambassador, between 51st and 52nd Streets. On the west side of the Avenue the first building is the Hotel Marguery, (about 1918) between 47th and 48th Streets. Compare this with the photographs made from the same spot in 1913 and with the Grand Central railroad yards in 1903, also with the same scene a year and a half later in January 1925.

Ewing Galloway, Photographer.

June 1923.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 46th Street
text:
Park Avenue, north from and including 46th Street.
Compare with the Silver Jubilee Exposition, approximately the same scene in June 1923.
Note the newly completed Postum Building, No. 250 Park Avenue.
In the immediate foreground, just south of 46th Street, where the men are taking it easy in the center park, the New York Central Building will rise in 1928.

January 1925.

Brown Brothers, Photographers.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 45th Street
text:
Park Avenue, north from 46th Street, seen from 45th Street. The building under construction at the left is the new Postum Building at 46th Street.

June 1924.

P.L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 47th Street
text:
Park Avenue, north from 47th Street, showing east side.
On the east side, going north is shown the Park Lane (1924). The Railroad Y.M.C.A. (1913-1929) hides St. Bartholomew's Church (1919). The Ambassador Hotel (1920) follows, between 51st and 52nd Streets.
In the background, the new Ritz Tower rises from the N.W. corner of 57th Street.
The little parks in the center of the avenue have not been altered yet.

Ewing Galloway, Photographer.

1926.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 47th Street
text:
Grand Central Yards, Park Avenue south from 47th Street, during the early stages of excavation between Park and Lexington Avenues, seen from between Park and Lexington Avenues, 47th and 48th Streets. The new upper and lower levels of the new Grand Central Terminal are being built on the east side of the yards first, while service is carried on in the western half. The rear facade of the old station has been removed.

About 1907.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 47th Street
text:
Park Avenue, the west side of 47th Street, showing 270 Park Avenue, the Hotel Marguery, in the N. W. corner of 47th Street. This double building was built about 1918. About 1922.

Gift of E.M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 48th Street
text:
Park Avenue, south from 48th Street, the Grand Central Yards, before electrification, and the old Grand Central Station. Behind the station towers the newly built Hotel Belmont at Park Avenue and 42nd Street. To the right, is seen Tiffany House on the east side of Madison Avenue between 45th and 44th Streets, and behind it, the Hotel Manhattan, on N.W. corner of Madison Avenue and 42nd Street. The small building on N.E. corner of Madison Avenue and 45th Street is old Railroad Y.M.C.A., where Hotel Roosevelt will later stand. To extreme right are old American Express buildings, to be demolished about 1920. 1906.

New York Edison Company Collection.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 48th Street
text:
Park Avenue, east side, looking north from 48th Street, showing the new Waldorf-Astoria, on the east side between 49th and 50th Streets, opening October first. Below it, between 48th and 49th Streets, stands the Park Lane (1929); above, at 51st Street, is the Ambassador (1920), and at 57th Street the Ritz Towers (1926).
The Queensboro Bridge is visible in right background.
September 1931.

International News Photos.

Ng. 2031

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 48th Street
text:
290 Park Avenue and Pierre's Restaurant, newly built, Park Avenue, west side, from 48th to 49th Streets. The fence hides the doorway of Pierre's. On the vacant lot in the right foreground, the Park Lane Hotel will rise in 1924.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 48th Street (East)
text:
Park Avenue, east side, from E. 48th (right) to 49th (left) Streets, showing the newly completed Park Lane Apartment Hotel on what twenty years prior was the Adams Express Company Building site. The architects are Shulte and Weaver. Note at the left margin the Railroad Y.M.C.A. at the N.E. corner of 49th Street. Ten years later this will be razed for the block square site of the Waldorf Astoria Hotel.

Gift of E.M. Jenks.

Summer 1924.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 48th Street
text:
Park Avenue, west side, from 48th to 50th Streets, during the middle of the work of rebuilding the Grand Central Terminal and Yards. The observer is near Lexington Avenue a little south of 49th Street, which crosses the Upper Level yards at the right. The nearest of the old buildings on the north side of 49th Street is 49 East 49th Street. The yards have been rebuilt about as far west as what will be the western side of Park Avenue when the tracks are covered over. July, 1909.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 49th Street
text:
TWIN CROWNS FOR NEW PEACOCK ALLEY

Twin towers atop the new Waldorf-Astoria Hotel make an interesting addition to the New York skyline. This is a spectacular view of the top of the new Waldorf-Astoria at Park Ave., 49th and 50th Sts., 47 stories in height, the world's tallest hotel, opening Oct. 1st. The domes are made of copper sheet leaf, and are surmounted by two beacons, 625 feet above Park Ave.

Photo by Underwood and Underwood

This photograph was used in NYPL Art Deco exhibit, Apr. 30, 1975.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 50th Street
text:
Park Avenue north from 50th Street, showing buildings along the west side, also the parks in the center, shaved to make room for more traffic.

The five-story building between 52nd and 53rd Street is the Racquet and Tennis Club, and behind it on the horizon rises the Tower of the Fuller Building at Madison Avenue and 57th Street. The small buildings in the block above, 53rd to 54th Street, are much older than their surroundings, dating back to at least 1890. On the east side, just north of St. Bartholomew's, is the Hotel Ambassador.

Summer 1929.

Ewing Galloway, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 50th Street
text:
(1)
Park Avenue, north from 50th Street, showing the center parks as they were from about 1917 to 1927.
In the foreground, the Hotel Ambassador on the N.E. corner of 51st Street is shown. From 52nd to 53rd Streets on the east side stands the Montana, one of the earlier modern apartment buildings, erected 1913 on the site of the old Steinway Piano Factory.
Careful scrutiny of the N.E. corner of 53rd Street will show that a small building has just been demolished; an apartment house is to be erected. On the west side from 52nd to 53rd Streets is the Racquet and Tennis Club, and above it a block of small buildings dating back to the 1880's.
Summer 1924.

The New York Public Library has the negative of this picture available for reproduction.

(2)
The same view, with camera a few feet farther north.
Summer 1924.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 50th Street
text:
Park Ave., east side, from East 50th to 51st Streets. Shown is St. Bartholomew's P.E. Church, organized in 1835. This congregation worshipped for many years in a church in Lafayette Place. A new church was erected in 1876 on Madison Ave., at the S.W. corner of East 44th Street. This present edifice being built in 1918-1919, on the site of the old F & M Schaefer Brewery. At the rear of the church appears a portion of the General Electric Building (570 Lexington Ave).

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 51st Street
text:
Park Avenue, north from and including 51st Street, showing buildings along the west side, also the parks in the center, shaved to make room for more traffic.
The five-story building between 52nd and 53rd Street is the Racquet and Tennis Club, and behind it on the horizon rises the Tower of the Fuller Building at Madison Avenue and 57th Street.
The small buildings in the block above, 53rd to 54th Street, are much older than their surroundings, dating back to at least 1890.
On the east side, just north of St. Bartholomew's, is the Hotel Ambassador. Summer 1929.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 51st Street
text:
Park Avenue, north from 51st Street, about 9:30 A.M., showing buildings along east side. It is possible to see nearly a mile of the Avenue. Notice Hotel Ambassador, 51st to 52d Streets, built in 1919 and the Montane Apartments (1912) between 52nd and 53rd Streets. The tiny building on the N.E. corner of 53rd Street is a survival of the era before the railroad was electrified, about 1924 it will be demolished. No. 441, in the N.E. corner of 56th Street, also dates back to the 1880's. Note cross-town street-cars at 59th Street. 1921.

Ewing Galloway, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 49th Street
text:
Park Avenue, east side, south from 51st Street, showing St. Bartholomew's Church (1918), and the new Waldorf Astoria (1931) between 50th and 49th Streets.
At the foot of the avenue rises the New York Central Building, No. 230, through which traffic travels to and from the Pershing Square Viaduct. In the background the towers of the Chrysler and Chanin buildings may be seen against the sky. To the extreme left, behind St. Bartholomew's rises the R.C.A. tower; and on the horizon directly in line with St. Bartholomew's dome may be seen the towers of St. Agnes' Roman Catholic Church, on 43rd Street east of Lexington Avenue. About 1932.

New York Times Photograph.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 50th Street
text:
Park Avenue, north from 51st Street, showing St. Bartholomew's Protestant Episcopal Church (B.G. Goodhue, architect), east side from 50th to 51st Streets, built in 1918 on the site of F. & M.
Schaefer's Brewery.
Beyond the Hotel ambassador (1919), 51st to 52nd Streets, continuing up the east side, stand the Montana apartments, built in 1912 on the site of the old Steinway Piano factory, from
52nd to 53rd Streets.
The little building on the N.E. corner of 53rd Street is one of the left-overs from the days before the railroad was electrified and the tracks covered over below 56th Street. A saloon used to occupy the parlor store. About 1925 it will give away to
a 15-story apartment building.
Note the little parks down the center of the avenue. They will be considerably narrowed in the alteration of 1927-28,
again planted with grass and the public kept out.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 51st Street
text:
A general view of the Grand Central Zone as viewed southward on Park Ave. from East 52nd Street, at which point appears the Hotel Ambassador (left foreground) with St. Bartholomew's P.E. Church just beyond (S.E. corner of 51st Street). Prominently shown (centre) is the new Waldorf Astoria Hotel flanked on one side by the R.C.A. Building and the Chrysler, Chanin, Grand Central Palace and Lincoln Buildings on the other. Distinctly shown between the R.C.A. Building and the Waldorf Astoria Hotel is Tudor City located near the East River, which is dimly apparent on the left.

October 31, 1932.

Wurts Brothers.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 52nd Street
text:
Park Avenue, north on east side, from 52nd Street.
The first building at the right is the Montana Apartments, built in 1912 on the site of the old Steinway factory.
The N. E. corner of 53rd Street is new, about 1925.
383 Park Avenue, just above it, was built in 1911 and is now oldest building in the block.
Further north No. 441, the small dark building on the N. E. corner of 56th Street (about 1880) contrasts with the new Ritz Tower Apartment Building at 57th Street, erected 1927.
October 28, 1930.

P.L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 52nd Street
text: Park Avenue, north from 52nd Street. The Racquet and Tennis Club occupies the block in the west side between 52nd and 53rd Street. To the right of it there is just a glimpse of the Fuller Building tower at Madison Avenue and 57th Street. On the east side of the Avenue the Ritz Tower rises at 57th Street. Careful comparison with Galloway's photograph of the identical scene in 1905 will show that the small buildings on the west side of the avenue, between 53rd and 54th Streets, are the identical ones shown in the earlier picture. The small apartment house (No. 441) on the N. E. corner of 56th Street is also an old building. 1932. Ewing Galloway

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 52nd Street (East)
text:
Park Avenue, north from East 52nd Street, showing an early view of this thoroughfare prior to the enclosure of the railroad tracks shown. At the right is the Steinway Piano factory at the S. E. corner of 53rd Street. The fenced lot on the left is at the N. W. corner of 52nd St.

About 1900

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 52nd Street
text:
Park Avenue, north from 52nd Street, before electrification and covering over of the upper end of the railroad yards. The growth of the railroad has resulted in destruction of the old tunnel and Avenue between 56th Street and 49th Street, where the old yards originally ended.
By 1910 the Avenue will be reopened down to this point.
The Steinway Piano factory, dating back to the Civil war decade, will be demolished in 1911.
The small house on the N.E. corner of 53rd Street will stand there till 1924.
The Racquet and Tennis Club will occupy the block opposite the Steinway factory, but the small houses on the west side between 53rd and 54th Streets will still be standing thirty years later.
Compare with Galloway's photograph of the identical scene in 1932. 1905.

Ewing Galloway, Photographer.

Another one will shortly rise alongside it, and one in the block immediately to the South, from 53rd to 52nd Streets, where the Steinway Factory has just been demolished; but the small house on the N.E. corner of 53rd Street will not be replaced till 1924. 1911.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 51st Street
text:
Park Avenue, south from 56th Street, where the railroad emerges from the tunnel and the Grand Central Yards begin.
The Avenue will be built over the tracks to 52nd Street by 1910 and to the new station by 1913, and the railroad electrified.
On west side, note houses between 54th and 53rd Street, which will still be standing thirty years later.
On the east side, note old Steinway Piano Factory, dating back to the Civil War or earlier, which will be demolished in 1911.
Beyond it may be seen the tower of R&M Scheefer's brewery, about the same age, on the S. E. corner of 51st Street where the new St. Bartholomew's Church will be built in 1918.
Compre with the Edison Company's photograph of the same scene in 1927.

New York Edison Company Collection.

The parks in the center of the Avenue will shortly be narrowed to make from for more traffic, and work on the New York Central Building, across the avenue from 46th to 45th Streets, will begin.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 64th Street
text:
Park Avenue Baptist Church, later Central Presbyterian Church, Park Avenue at S. E. corner of 64th Street.

This church was built in 1922 for the Fifth Avenue Baptist congregation, which accordingly changed its name to Park Avenue Baptist Church.

The first Service was held Palm Sunday April 9, 1922.

At the time of this photograph it had in the tower a carillon which was later removed to the Riverside Church when that was completed.

The church was sold to the Central Presbyterian Church in 1928. To the right is the third Church of Christ Scientist.

April 1926.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 64th Street (East)
text:
610 Park Avenue, or 64 East 65th Street, on S. W. corner of and facing on 65th Street. The building was later demolished (about 1920) to make place for Mayfair House.

Irving Underhill, Photographer.
Gift of E.M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 65th Street
text:
620 Park Avenue, at N. W. corner of 65th Street, a new apartment building nearing completion.
It replaces the old 7-story Palacio apartments.

Early 1924.

Gift of E.M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 66th Street
text:
646 Park Avenue, west side, between 66th and 67th Streets. Home of the Charlton School in 1913 and of the Lincoln School during the War, it will be acquired and used as an annex by the Sulgrave apartment hotel, to be built on 67th Street about 1923-4.
The house to the right is the old house on the S.W. corner of 67th Street; it will be demolished in the fall of 1929.
About 1920.

Gift of E. M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 65th Street
text:
Park Avenue, east side, south from E. 67th to 65th Streets, and showing prominently the Seventh Regiment Armory occupying the 67th -66th Street frontage. This structure, built in 1878-80 formerly had a pointed steeple where the flag is flying. The photographer is viewing same from a similar vantage point in both instances (S.W. corner of Park Avenue and 68th Street) and shows the changed railing used in fencing the center plot dividing the traffic lanes.

June 8, 1928.
View 2: April 25, 1938.

P.L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 67th Street (East)
text: Park Avenue at S. W. corner of 67th Street, showing The Sulgreve, a new apartment hotel at 56 East 67th Street. The old house on the corner will be demolished in the autumn of 1929, to make place for a garden for the hotel. About 1924.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 67th Street
text:
655 Park Avenue, east side, from 67th to 68th Streets, showing the new Apartment building on the site of the old Hospital. Beyond it up Lenox Hill may be seen part of the Hunter College buildings. 1924.

Joseph Smith, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 68th Street (East)
text:
Park Avenue, east side, north from E. 68th Street (extreme right), showing at that point a portion of old Hunter College (demolished in 1938), and to the north, the dual structure (white building, peaked roof) that will be reconstructed for the Union Club for occupancy in August 1933. This building, bearing No's. 705 Park Avenue and 101 E. 68th Street, is at the N.E. corner and is prominently depicted in View 2 in its new form. Also note in the latter instance the vacant lot where the old college stood. Exclusive of this and the club, the view remains the same.

View 2: September 11, 1931
View 2: April 25, 1938.

P.L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 68th Street
text:
Park Avenue, at N. E. corner of 68th Street, showing Hunter College, (the old Normal College for Women), built about 1870. In the center of the Avenue, note the park is being cut down on each side.
Winter 1928-29.
Ewing Galloway, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 68th Street (East)
text:
Park Avenue, east side, north from East 68th to 69th Streets, showing the old Normal College for Women, erected about 1870. This is now a part of Hunter College and is under demolition (early 1938) Note, on the right of No. 1, The Thomas Hunter Hall on Lexington Avenue, and on the left of No. 2, the building at the N.E. corner of Park Avenue and 69th Street that became the home of the Union Club in 1933.

The New York Times of August 2, 1938, in an article on Page 21 announces the ceremonies to be held here on the construction of a new building that will cost $6,414,000, of which the City's share is $3,527,700 and the P.W.A's $2,886,300. Charles H. Tuttle will preside and speeches will be made by the Mayor, Howard A. Gray, Colonel M.E. Gilmore and Mrs. Walter S. Mack. This new structure will be 16 stories high and accommodate 5,000 students in 100 class rooms. Included also will be a library, cafeteria, auditorium, gymnasium, swimming pool, theatre and laboratories.

Sept. 11, 1931.
View 2: June 12, 1937.

P. L. Sperr,

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 68th Street
text:
Park Avenue, east side, from 68th to 69th Streets, looking northeast up the southern slope of Lenox Hill. The view is across the parks in the center of the avenue, showing the tower of the old Hunter College buildings, which have occupied the block since about 1870. Beyond it, on the northeast corner of 69th Street is the white house that will be occupied by the Union Club in 1933.
September 24, 1927.

P.L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 68th Street
text:
Park Avenue, east side, from 69th to 68th Streets, looking southeast on Lenox Hill, showing part of the old Hunter College buildings, which occupied this site since about 1870.

June 8, 1928

text:
park Avenue, west side, north from 69th Street, showing at left the George S. Blumenthal residence, at S.W. corner of 70th Street. Brewster residence, which will be replaced by an apartment house. The tall apartment building on the N.W. corner of 72nd Street, in the right background, was erected in 1921. March 31, 1928.

P.L. Sperr, Photographer.

text:
(1) Park Ave., at the N.E. corner of 69th Street, showing the structure which in August 1933 was to become the new home of the Union Club.

P. L. Sperr.

text:
Park Avenue, east side, south from E. 69th Street (right, not shown in No. 1). The apartment buildings seen begin at 68th Street and occupy the 68th-67th and 67th-66th Street blocks; the Seventh Regiment Armory being on the 66th-67th Street block. April 25, 1938.
Views 1 and 2

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 69th Street
text: Park Avenue, east side, between 69th and 70th Streets, showing Nos. 709, 711, 713 Park Avenue. 709 and 711 will be standing in 1935. About 1912.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 69th Street (East)
text:
Park Avenue, west side, from E. 69th (left) to 70th Streets, as viewed northeastward from the vacant lot on the east side of this thoroughfare, between 68th and 69th Streets.

Two low buildings occupy the above location; that at the S.W. corner of 70th Street is the George S. Blumenthal residence. To the north of same is a modern apartment house standing on the old Presbyterian Hospital site. At the right margin appears a portion of the Union Club, located at the N. E. corner of Park Avenue and E. 69th Street. Hunter College until recently occupied the cleared foreground area.

April 25, 1938

P. L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 70th Street
text:
Park Avenue, at S. E. corner of 70th Street. Residence of George Blumenthal, shown shortly after completion. About 1914.

Brown Brothers, Photographers.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 70th Street
text:
Park Avenue st N. W. corner of 70th Streets. Presbyterian about to be torn down and replaced by apartments.
1928.
Ewing Galloway, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 70th Street
text:
(1)
Park Avenue, west side, from 70th to 71st Streets, on Lenox Hill, showing buildings of old Presbyterian Hospital shortly before demolition.
The Presbyterian Hospital was founded in 1868 and the first buildings opened in 1872, on land given by James Lenox. In 1889 most of the original buildings were destroyed by fire, and as a result the entire scheme was rearranged. These buildings on Park Avenue are surgical pavilions; part of the Administration Building is shown on 70th Street. See also Madison Avenue.
March 31, 1928.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)
Another view, not showing the Administration Building.
March 31, 1928.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 67th Street
text:
Park Avenue, south on west side from 71st Street to 67th Street, on Lenox Hill, showing old Presbyterian Hospital between 71st and 70th, shortly before its demolition. On north west corner of 71st may be seen part of the G.S. Brewster residence, which will be demolished in 1929, and in the south west corner of 74th Street the George S. Blumenthal residence.

P.L. Sperr, Photographer.

View 2 is a duplicate of the above, mounted June 1973 with non-acidic glue, because the original print is deteriorating.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 67th Street
text:
Park Avenue, south on west side from 71st Street to 67th Street, on Lenox Hill, showing old Presbyterian Hospital between 71st and 70th, shortly before its demolition. P.L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 71st Street
text:
Park Avenue, at S. E. corner of 71st Street, showing newly built private residence.
About 1912.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 71st Street
text:
748 Park Avenue at N.W. corner of 71st Street, built about 1906. This building, together with the double house 750-52 and the Presbyterian Nurses' Home, seen to the left on 71st Street, will be replaced in 1929 by a 17-story apartment building. About 1912.

The Pictorial News Co., Photographer.
Gift of E. M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 71st Street
text: 752 and 754 Park Avenue, west side, between 71st and 72nd Streets, showing part of the corner house, 78 West 72nd Street. At right, No. 752 will be demolished in 1929. It is the northern half of a double house (see picture of N.W. corner of 71st Street). About 1912.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 72nd Street
text:
755 Park Avenue, at S. E. corner of 72nd Street, seen from N. W. corner, apartment building built about 1913. Note parks in center of the avenue being narrowed and remodelled. This work has not yet begun above 72nd Street.

Early 1929.

Capital Photo Service.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 72nd Street
text:
760 Park Avenue, at N.W. corner of Third Street, nearing completion. It replaces two small 4-story houses facing on 72nd Street. At N.W.corner of 72nd Street we have a glimpse of Sunnyside, which will be demolished in September, 1929.
Notice old fashioned stop-and-go signal in the center of the intersection.
March, 18, 1921.
Photograph by Sterrett Brothers, Inc, Builders.
Gift of E.M. Jenks.

Net # 1380 A

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 73rd Street
text:
Park Avenue, north on west side from and including 73rd Street.
On the N. W. corner of 73rd Street, in front of new building under construction, stands the old Sunnyside apartments, which will shortly be demolished, as will the building on the S. W. corner.
The widening of the Avenue, at the expense of the parks, will also take place here within the next few months.

March 28, 1929.

P.L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 73rd Street
text:
Park Avenue, south on west side, from 74th Street.
On the southwest corner of 74th Street, the old Ramando Court apartments are shortly to be demolished to make room for a modern structure; and Sunnyside, the N. W. corner of 73rd Street, will be demolished in 1929.

June 8, 1928.

P.L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 74th Street
text:
Park Avenue, at north east corner of 74th Street.
The five-story corner house dates back at least to the 1890's.
The apartment house next to it, No. 101 East 74th Street, was built about 1917.
This corner lot was the object of a real estate deal in 1926 with the idea of erecting a new building; but nothing came of it.
June 8, 1928.

P.L. Sperr, photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 77th Street
text:
850 Park Avenue, S. W. corner 77th Street. This and the next building to the south were erected between 1910 and 1916. About 1919.

Collins, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 78th Street
text:
880-886 Park Avenue, west side, between 78th and 79th Streets. The parlor store of No. 880 is kept by Eugene Clark, Fish Dealer. 878, not shown on the picture, is the corner house; -- from 878 to 888 inclusive the houses will be demolished in 1926 to make room for new 888 Park Avenue apartment house.
1922.

Gift of E. M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 79th Street
text:
Park avenue south from end including 79th Street.
The new apartment house nearing completion on the S. E. corner of 79th Street replaces a group of small 4-story houses demolished October 1929.

1930.

Ewing Galloway, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 80th Street
text:
911 Park Avenue, at S. E. corner of 80th Street, A new apartment building replaces the old 7-story Alvarado apartments.
About 1925.

Joseph Smith, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 80th Street (East)
text:
925 to 935 Park Ave., east side, from East 80th (right) to 81st (left) Streets, showing prominently a 12-story apartment house in the center of the block and bearing No. 929. The clearance seen, was caused by the demolition of two 5-story structures (Nos. 933 and 935) and upon which will rise a 12-story building. Partially shown on the right is a 14-story corner structure that was erected in 1907 and is said to be the first apartment building of over 6-stories on Park Ave. According to the New York Times of December 5, 1937 this structure has been completely modernized with the exclusion of 1 apartment, which has been occupied by the same tenant for 30 years.

1922.

Collins.
Gift of E. M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 81st Street
text:
Park Avenue, south from 81st Street. Note new apartment building on the S. W. corner of 79th Street. The oldest buildings in the foreground are the ones on the N. W. corner of 80th Street, survivals of the pre-apartment house days. 1930.
Ewing Galloway, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 81st Street
text:
(1)
Park Avenue at N.E. corner of 81st Street.
Three small buildings have just been demolished, and a fourteen-story apartment house will be erected.
The little two-story building will remain.
November 9, 1927.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)
The same, another view, showing 104-124 East 81st Street across the clearing.
November 9, 1927.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 81st Street
text:
944 Park Avenue, west side, between 81st and 82nd Streets, nearly ready to open, on the site of old 7-story Messéna Apartments, demolished October 1928.
1930.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 83rd Street
text:
983 Park Avenue, at N.E. corner of 83rd Street, a new apartment house, which replaces old 9-story Hanover Apartments.
1927.

Joseph Smith, Photographer.

Park Avenue, at and adjoining the S.E. corner of 83rd Street, buildings about to be replaced by 975 Park Avenue apartment building. January 30, 1928.

1001 to 07 Park Avenue, at, adjoining and north of the N. E. corner of East 84th Street, as photographed forming a background for a truck snow plow. Note the fenced area in the center of Park Avenue, dividing traffic into two lanes.

About 1925
Views 1,2
