title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 84th Street
text:
Park Avenue, at S.W. corner of 84th Street, showing Church of St. Ignatius Loyola (Jesuit).

January 31, 1928.

P.L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 84th Street
text:
Perk Avenue, at north east corner of 84th Street, showing four houses to be demolished in 1928.
Nos. 1003 and 1005, the small ones in the middle, are the last two frame houses on Perk Avenue below 100th Street.
See Underhill's larger photograph of the same corner May 1928 before demolition.

November 19, 1927.

P.L. Sperr, Photographer.

Nc# 671

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 84th Street
text:
Park Avenue, at N. E. corner of 84th Street, showing Nos. 1003-05, the last two frame houses on the avenue below 100th Street, about to be demolished to make room for 1001 Park Avenue, co-operative apartment house built by T.E. Rhodes Co.

May 17, 1928.

Irving Underhill, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 85th Street
text:
Park Avenue, at S.W. corner of 85th Street, showing the Park Avenue Presbyterian Church and Rectory (built in 1909).
September 25, 1932.

P.L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 85th Street
text:
Park Avenue, north on west side, from 85th to 86th Streets.
The house on the N. W. corner of 85th Street is the residence of the late Edward R. Stettinius, and the one above it belongs to Mrs. Reginald De Koven.
The block still stands in 1935, although the Stittinius house was bought by a builder in August 1928 with the idea of demolishing it.
February 30, 1928

P.L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 85th Street
text:
1022-1024 Park Avenue, west side, between 85th and 86th Streets, showing doorway of the Stettinius house on the 85th Street corner, No. 1020, and part of 1026.
The two brownstones, 1022-24, have been sold, and will later be replaced by more modern residences almost the same size, No. 1022 by the residence of Mrs. Reginald De Koven. Compare Sperr's picture of this block in 1928.
Early 1912.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 86th Street
text:
1040 Park Avenue, at N. W. corner of 86th Street, newly completed.
1924.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 86th Street
text:
1045 Park Avenue, at N. E. corner of 86th Street, showing a new apartment house replacing three four-story houses and one old 3-story frame house, Nos. 1041-47 inclusive. Compare with view taken from 87th Street in 1922.
On 86th Street may be seen the 86th Street Temple (Synagogue). Notice the little gate leading into the park. This is the exit from the old 86th Street station of the New York & Harlem Railway. Early 1924.

Capitol Photographic Service.
Gift of E.M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 86th Street (East)
text:
#1040 Park Avenue at the North West corner of E.86th Street, showing a new co-operative apartment house. Delano and Aldrich, the Architects. It replaced the five small frame houses at #1040-1048, which faced on the Avenue, and two on E.86th Street.

1924.

Dana B. Merrill, Photographer,

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 86th Street
text:
Park Avenue, east side, from 87th to 86th Streets, showing No. 1049 Park Avenue, an apartment house about four years old. The old 3-story frame No. 1047, together with the small buildings to the corner of 86th Street, is shortly to be demolished. Compare picture taken from 86th Street early in 1924. 1922.

John Wallace Gillier, Photographer.
Gift of E. M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 87th Street
text:
1060 Park Avenue, at N. W. corner of 87th Street, practically completed, replacing the 7-story Niagara apartments on corner and three 3-story buildings, Nos. 1064-66-68. The small buildings above it will be demolished before 1928. Late 1923.

Howard Cox, Photographer.
Gift of E.M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 88th Street
text:
1070 Park Avenue, on S. W. corner of 88th Street, a new apartment house replacing four small buildings; No. 1060, in the southern half of the block, was opened in 1924. Compare with picture of 1060 at that time.

1928.

Joseph Smith, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 90th Street
text:
1111 Park Avenue, at S. E. corner of 90th Street, a new apartment building, nearing completion, replacing four 5-story houses on Park Avenue and Nos. 104-10 East 90th Street. The building immediately below it is only two or three years older.

1925.

Joseph Smith, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 90th Street
text:
1112 Park Avenue, on S.W. corner of 90th Street, newly completed, replacing two 5-story buildings. In 1930 the 7-story double apartment house (Meteor) on the N.W. corner of 89th Street will be replaced by a 17-story building, but the two little houses in between will stay. 1927.

Knickerbocker Photo Service.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 90th Street
text: Park Avenue, west side, between 91st and 90th Streets, showing 1130 on 91st Street corner, erected about 1926. About 1927.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 91st Street
text:
1135 Park Avenue, at S. E. corner of 91st Street, newly erected. The small buildings south of it will be demolished about 1926 or 1927 for building a second large apartment building. About 1923.

Knickerbocker Photo. Service.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 91st Street
text: Park Avenue, east side, south from and including 91st Street. Compare with the S.E. corner of 91st Street about 1923. 1928.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 91st Street
text:
Park Avenue, at and adjoining the N.E. corner of 91st Street. March 28, 1929.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 92nd Street
text:
Park Avenue, south from end including 92nd Street.
Nos. 1155 Park Avenue (with awning), on the S. E. corner of 92nd Street, dates back to about 1913; but the other tall apartments nearby are much newer. The three nearest on the west side were built since 1925, No. 1135 on the S. E. corner of 91st Street about 1923, and the next below it since 1925.
Widening of the Avenue at the expense of the parks will not take place up here till 1929.

June 3, 1928

P.L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 92nd Street
text:
Park Avenue, west side, between 92nd and 93rd Streets, showing 1160 and 1172 Park Avenue, newly built; 1160 replaces old Holland Court. The hotel down 92nd Street at the corner of Madison Avenue had only just taken the name Berkshire; in 1929, it was to change its name to Hotel Wales.

Autumn 1926.

John Adams Davis, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 93rd Street
text:
Park Avenue at N. W. corner of 93rd Street. The old residence, at the time shown occupied by the Ursuline Academy, is about to be demolished for a five-story fireproof building. (Note sign hung on the south well). It is shown on the 1879 map; it was probably built in that decade, and stood alone in the block for a number of years.

August 1911.

Gift of I.N. Phelps Stokes.

title: Manhattan: Park Avenue - 105th Street
text:
Park Avenue (called Fourth Avenue until about 1890) north from about 105th Street, showing two track railroad on wooden trestle. The little wooded hill in right background is the future Mt. Morris Park. The deepest part of the old Harlem Creek bed is between 106th and 107th Streets. For some reason Drips' Plan of New York for 1867 and for 1868 utterly fails to show the big building in the center of the picture, which should be at about 110th Street and Fifth Avenue, nor any of the buildings just west of Fourth Avenue around 110th Street except the five small houses nearest the camera, on the S.W. corner of 110th Street. The steeple on the horizon to the right is probably the Mt. Morris Baptist Church at Fifth Avenue near 126th Street; this is, however, only a guess. This photograph was used as an illustration in the first of Henry Collins Brown's Valentine's Manuals, 1916-17, opposite page 91. 1860.

New York Edison Company Collection.

p.170, Changing New York

1890-1898 Park Avenue at the S.W. corner of East 129th St., showing the frame structure built in 1869 and used as a vaudeville theatre, public dance hall, political club gym, fight arena, courthouse and jail. It was once owned by "Boss Tweed" who deeded it to his son in 1872. Twenty years ago it housed Lew Dockstader's Minstrels. Gus Hills Minstrels appeared here. Jack Dempsey and Gene Tunney pugilists trained and fought beneath its mansard roof.

title: Manhattan: Park Row - Broadway
text:
Park Row, south from the Brooklyn Bridge, to and including Broadway. The view shows in the foreground, the new (then) pedestrian approach to the Brooklyn Bridge Station of the Second and Third Aves., Elevated. Adjoining same is the Pulitzer Building, with the spire of the Tribune Building overshadowing the Times Building, on the right. In the distant background, at the southern extremity of Park Row, at Broadway, is observed St. Paul's Protestant Episcopal Chapel. Directly on the right, is the Hall of Records, built as a City Jail about 1775.

About 1880.

title: Manhattan: Park Row - Broadway
text:
Park Row, south from the Brooklyn Bridge, to and including Broadway. The view shows on the extreme right, the old Hall of Records, with the City Hall further westward. In the direct center, is the old U.S.P.O., with the Times Building on the opposite side of the street. At the head of Park Row, at Broadway, appears St. Paul's Church and Grounds. Note the horse drawn cars. Bridge shown, in the foreground, was an extension from the Brooklyn Bridge Station of the Manhattan Elevated Lines.

About 1884.

New York Edison Co.

title: Manhattan: Park Row - Beekman Street

The New York Sun of October 31, 1938, carries an article on the real estate page (No. 35) reporting the demolition of this eight year old mansion and the sale of the entire block bounded by Park Terrace East and Park Terrace West, W. 215th and 217th Streets. This plot contains more than 118,000 square feet and will be improved by a group of garden apartments designed by Albert Goldhammer and built by a group headed by David Rose. Mr. Thomas Dwyer, a prominent contractor, occupied the mansion for more than a quarter of a centry. His family were the sellers.

title: Manhattan: Pearl Street - Broad Street
text:
Pearl Street, at the S. E. corner of Broad Street, showing Fraunces Tavern.. This structure was originally the home-stead of Etienne DeLancey and was erected in 1730. He sold same to Samuel Fraunces in 1762, for a tavern, the "Queen Catherine". The Chamber of Commerce held meetings here. It was Washington's Headquarters and it was from here that he bade farewell to the officers of his Continental Army in 1783. Samuel Fraunces sold it in 1785. The Sons of the Revolution purchased it in 1905 and restored it to the present appearance. Note the tablet on the Broad Street side refering to this act.

About 1915

B. Hellmich, photo
82 W. Broadway, N. Y. C.

Gift of Ubrock Collection

title: Manhattan: Peck Slip - South Street
text:
Peck Slip, north side, west from South Street, showing an inclusive view of one side of this short thoroughfare which at one time consisted of 1 block and became extended to the present 3 by marginal fills of the East River; Water and Front and now South Streets being respectively at the river's edge. Here stand some of the oldest buildings in Manhattan, prominent of which are the 2 low white faced structures to the left. Individual views and pertinent data will be found on other mounts. Note the Municipal Building and the old U.S.P.0. done in the background. Preceding the latter is the Meyer Hotel at the S.W. corner of South Street which still continues its
original functions, but to a different clientele.
September 1914.
George L. Balgue.
Two additional views of the same locality. The photographer
gives the following data:No. 1 Peck Slip is 4 story brick at
corner of Pearl Street. (314 Pearl St.)
17-19 Peck Slip is 5 story brick at
corner of Water Street (barber
shop painted white, on corner).
29-31 Peck Slip is 5 story brick.
29 Bell Fish Co.
3i Endicott Fish Co.
View No. 3 shows the three buildings (No's. 35-37-39) at, and adjoining the N. E. corner of Front Street. These appear at the
left in View No. 1.
1939
Beecher Ogden

text:
15 to 1 Peck Slip, north side, west from Water to Pearl Streets, showing the South Ferry division of the Second and Third Aves. Elevated lines on Pearl Street. O'ertowering the buildings shown, is the pinnacle of the Municipal Building.

May 1924.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

No. 11, the 2½-story building with a white stucco front is reputed to have been standing in 1725, on land, then owned by Johans Hardenbrooke. Adjoining same, is a 4-story tenement, No. 9, at one time the home of former Governor Alfred E. Smith. The 3-story frame structure, number 7, north of the latter, was the home of Dr. Valentine, of Valentine's Manual fame. It is now the junk shop of Frank Carson. According to the New York Sun of October 2, 1937, these buildings may be demolished. See same for further data.

title: Manhattan: Peck Slip - Water Street

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Peck Slip - Water Street
text:
11 to 5 Peck Slip, north side, west of Water Street. No. 11 (right) is believed to have been standing in 1725 on land owned by Johans Hardenbrooke. This and other pieces of property on Peck Slip passed to the Roosevelt family in 1755, and from this unit passed to the Scheel family; the present owner being Wm. H. Scheel, importer of varnish gums. No. 9, the adjoining structure housed Ex-Governor Alfred E. Smith during his earlier days. North of the latter is a 3-story frame house, occupied by a junk shop, but formerly, the residence of Dr. Valentine of Valentines Manual fame.

October 1937.

George D. Chinn.

Midway between the aforementioned points is Doyers Street, a short winding thoroughfare from the Bowery. In the latter is the famous bend known as the Bloody Angle. Chinese restaurants and curiosity shops line the curb, while upstairs a teeming horde resides.
P. L. Sperr.
September 3, 1927.

(2)
The same, at a later date. Note the improvement to the building shown at the extreme left. This structure is at the N.E. corner of Mott and Pell Streets.
P. L. Sperr.
June 9, 1933.

(3)
Photographers vantage point for this view is at Doyers Street. In the left foreground is No. 12, a building that in the 90's housed a cabaret run by an individual known as Nigger Mike Salter. Irving Berlin, the famous songwriter, was employed here, subsequent to a similar engagement at the Chatham Club (No. 8 Doyers Street).
P. L. Sperr.
June 13, 1933.

title: Manhattan: Perry Street - 7th Avenue South
text:
10 to 4 Perry Street, south side, between Seventh Avenue South and Greenwich Avenue. The balance of the block, to and including the S.E. corner of Waverly Place, was destroyed when Seventh Avenue South was cut through in 1915. The wedge-shaped apartment house at No. 12 was built after 1920.
No. 10 was the residence of the late Thomas M. Mulry; President of the Emigrant Savings Bank and of the United States Society of St. Vincent de Paul, hence the name Mulry Square for the beginning of Seventh Avenue at Greenwich Avenue and 11th Street.
Perry Street was first known as Ogden Street (1803), then as Henry Street (1811); it took its present name in 1813.
March 15, 1932.

P. L. Sperr.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Pershing Square - 41st Street (East)
text:
Pershing Square (Park Avenue), east side, from East 41st (right) to 42nd (left), Street's, showing the Grand Union Hotel of the 1890's. This structure was demolished in the Summer of 1914, and was later replaced with the present Pershing Square Building. The 40th-42nd Street area acquired this designation in honor of the Commander in Chief of the American Expeditionary Force in France about this time. It was originally Fourth Avenue, a section of which was changed to Park Avenue.

About 1914

title: Manhattan: Pine Street - William Street
text:
Pine Street (diagonally across lower portion) at William Street (right margin) as viewed southwestward from No. 1 Cedar Street (at Pearl Street), showing the northern sides (rears) of structures that front on Wall Street. From left to right they are the H.L. Dougherty and Company Building (No. 60-62 Wall Street); the National City Building (No. 52 Wall Street); the Bank of New York Building (No. 48 Wall Street); and the Bank of Manhattan Building. (No. 40 Wall Street). The latter is west of William Street while all the former are east of same. Nestling to the right is the 16 storied structure at the S.E. corner of William and Pine Streets which has been occupied by Kuhn, Loeb and Co. for years, No. 52-54 William Street.

July 7, 1930.

title: Manhattan: Platt Street - Gold Street
text:
Platt Street, north side, west from Gold to William Streets, showing a triangular building (No. 19 Gold Street) at the N.W. corner. The present structure is the remnant of a large building, part of which was demolished when Jacob Platt cut Platt Street through in 1834. In the foreground appears the lower stories of No. 23 Platt Street, at the N.E. corner of Gold Street. Note the Woodbridge Building (N.E. corner of William and Platt Streets) at the rear of the "Jack Knife" house. In 1930 this odd structure was demolished to form a portion of the present (1937) site of the Insurance Centre Building. For pictures of the latter see files for John or Gold Streets. Nos. 1 and 2 of this set of 4 views are similar; 3 and 4 being in the opposite (eastward) direction from the middle of the block. No. 4 also shows a more extensive view eastward on the north side of Platt Street, to Pearl Street where the stacks of the New York Steam Co. appears across the Pearl Street buildings.

Views 1 & 4: May 1924.
Views 2 & 3: July 1924.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Manhattan: Platt Street - Gold Street
text:
(1)
Platt Street (left) at Gold Street (right), as seen through an excavation at the N.E. corner of same and showing a 4 story structure, No. 15 Gold Street, that housed the firm of Thomas Prosser & Son for 92 years. This firm, founded in 1845 at this site, is the American representative of the Krupp Steel Works of Germany. According to the New York Times of December 8, 1937, they will move to new quarters at No. 120 Wall Street. Upon the clearance in the foreground stands a 28 story office building, known as No. 90 John Street. The building that partially appears on the right is a new structure and is the 25 story Insurance Centre Building, No. 80 John Street. The corner shown of the latter, is the former site of the "Jack Knife" building, No. 19 Gold Street; a triangular structure that remained from a former large building when Jacob Platt cut Platt Street through in 1834.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)
The same, but with a different perspective, as seen from No. 111 John Street, located at the N.W. corner of Pearl Street. Note on the left, Gold Street continuing southward to Maiden Lane.

October 13, 1930.

title: Manhattan: Pleasant Avenue - 114th Street
text:
(1)

Pleasant Avenue, west side, from 114th to 115th Streets, seen from 115th Street near the Harlem River; the view is west on 115th Street. In consequence of the demolition of the Standard Gas Light Company's plant and tanks on either side of 115th Street, it is possible to see a little of Jefferson Park and a few houses on First Avenue, south of 114th Street, shown at the left, also the rear of the buildings on the east side of Pleasant Avenue north of 115th Street, shown at the right.

July 19, 1935.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)

Pleasant Avenue, west side, from 114th to 115th Streets, a close view, not showing the full corner of 115th Street. Pleasant Avenue is part of Avenue A, as originally surveyed. It extends from 107th to 124th Streets, and has been known under its present name since the 1870's. Jefferson Park was laid out around 1900, breaking Pleasant Avenue between 111th and 114th Streets.

July 19, 1935.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Riverside Drive - 86th Street
text:

WHY CHURCHES GO SKYSCRAPER

In small communities the church is often a landmark with its spires the tallest structure. To retain this rank in the city it must outdo its architectural rivals. This feat is attempted by the new $4,000,000 Riverside Church (commonly called the Rockefeller Church) of which Dr. Harry Emerson Fosdick will be pastor.

title: Manhattan: Riverside Drive - 123rd Street
text:
Riverside Drive, W.S., at 123rd Street near Grant's Tomb, showing a small monument. The inscription reads: Erected to the Memory of an Amiable Child St. Claire Pollock Died 15 July 1797 in the Fifth Year of His Age.

Geo. L. Balgue 1928 

The following text is taken from a photograph of Clermont Inn "Riverside Park S - Tiemann Place (W.127 St.)" 973/C2

Riverside park, south from Tiemann Place, (West 127th Street), showing the Clermont Inn on Riverside Drive. This structure was built before the Revolution, on land, sold August 4, 1796, by Nicholas de Peyster to George Pollock, a linen merchant who named the place for its beautiful trees and shrubbery, "Strawberry Hill." His 5 year old son, St. Claire Pollock, fell off the cliffs and was drowned July 15, 1797. His father subsequently went to New Orleans, where his descendants there, are said to be called Polk. His land, expressly reserving the burial place containing the urn of his boy, which may still be seen near Grant's Tomb, was sold in 1803 to Joseph Alston, the husband of medicosia Burr, who deeded it to Michael Hogan, the former British Consul at Havana. The latter named the place "Clermont" after the residence of the Earl of Clermont, Duke of Clarence, who became King William IV. The Earl of Devon, who resided here in 1807, was himself a cousin to Fulton’s "Clermont", and in 1815 an occupant was Joseph Bonaparte, the ex-King of Spain. The family bought the property, and since 1872 it has been a famous public restaurant. The land to the east and south of same is historical, being the scene of several of the sharpest engagements of the Battle of Harlem Heights on September 16, 1776.

About 1907.

Wurts Brothers.

Ground for the tomb was broken on Grant's Birthday April 27, 1891, the corner stone being laid April 27, 1892.

text:

title: Manhattan: Riverside Drive - 175th Street (West)
text:

Along the line of the upper fence runs Haven Avenue and this structure is on the easterly side of same; the slope being the westerly side. For individual views of the building shown see files under the Park classification.

February, 1931

text:
Riverside Drive, north from but not including Plaza Lafayette (West 181st Street). On the extreme right appear the stone wall and ornamental columns of the estate of Dr. Charles V. Paterno, which has its entrance on Northern Ave. This wall was built in about 1920. There is a capacious residence built on the style of an ancient Italian castle and many greenhouses, which the doctor maintains as a hobby.

title: Manhattan: Riverside Drive - 181st Street (West)
text:
Riverside Drive, north from a point to the north of W. 181st Street showing this sweepirg thoroughfare skirting the North (Hudson) River. At the right is an inclined roadway (Riverside Terrace) that leads to the apartment house section, known as Washington Heights and from which the new George Washington Bridge projects across the river to New Jersey. The enbanked colonnade forms a portion of Dr. Chas. V. Paterno's estate and same will remain after demolition in 1938 of this individuals castle-like home. He, being a real-estate operator will improve this site with a series of modern garden apartments, similar to his Hudson View Gardens of the same vicinity. View 3 is a vista from the pergola during the aforementioned operation. For additional views taken during this construction period, see, files under Cabrini Boulevard ( a new name
for Northern Avenue since 1938).
June 3, 1934
Views 1 and 2
View 3: August 23, 1938.

title: Manhattan: Riverside Park - 79th Street (West) - [Aerial view.]
text:
Riverside Park: A northward view of same and its environs from a point over West 79th Street, showing this area prior to the radical changes that are planned, by what is known as the West Side Improvement Project. The white line appearing on the left indicates the new shore line. Through the center runs the serpentine like tracks of the New York Central Railroad. Forming the eastern boundary of this marginal area is Riverside Drive. Compare this with a September 15, 1937 photograph (north from 72nd Street), both of which were published by the Park Department on October 12, 1937 in a brochure titled "The West Side Improvement Project."

Fall 1934.

Gift of Department of Parks.

title: Manhattan: Riverside Park - 79th Street (West).

Riverside Park, at West 79th Street, and showing a causeway at that point that carries automotive traffic northward from the West Side Elevated Highway to the Henry Hudson Parkway. Underneath this structure are the tracks of the New York Central Railroad; they having been enclosed and the marginal lands landscaped under joint auspices of the Railroad Company and the Park Department in the West Side Improvement Project. Photographer is viewing southwestward towards the North (Hudson) River, which is on the far side of same.

*January 28, 1938.

George D. Chinn.

title: Manhattan: Riverside Park - 82nd Street (West).
text:
Riverside Park: A view south from West 82nd Street, showing the southerly portion of this marginal park between Riverside (left) and the North (Hudson) River in a state of metamorphosis. This work is being conducted under the joint auspices of the Department of Parks and the New York Central Railroad in what is better known as the West Side Improvement Project. The unsightly railroad tracks are being enclosed in a concrete viaduct; the top of which will carry automotive traffic. A brochure including this photograph was published by the Park Department on October 12, 1937 for the ceremonies attending the opening.

November 1936.

Gift of Department of Parks.

title: Manhattan: Riverside Drive - 122nd Street (West)
text:
RIVERSIDE PARK.

Riverside Drive, between West 122nd and 123rd Streets. Shown is the temporary tomb of General U.S. Grant, at Riverside Park, completed August 7, 1885. This photograph was taken August 9, 1885, by Mr. Howard Brown. The original negative is now (1936) owned by Mr. Louis Brown (brother), 417 Liberty Street, Newburgh, N.Y. Mr. J.B. Niland, 1844 Arthur Ave., N.Y. City, has a copy of the negative, from which this print was made on October 29, 1936. The present (1936) tomb is 1/2 block farther north, directly opposite 123rd Street. For an account of the burial, See "Sketch of the life of General U.S. Grant, compiled by Col. John J. Garnett, with the Programme of the Ceremonies of the Dedication of the Grant Monument in N.Y., April 27, 1897." A.N. p.v. 156.

August 9, 1885.

Mr. Howard Brown.

title: Manhattan: Riverside Drive - 122nd Street (West)
text:
(1)
Riverside Drive, west side, at West 122nd Street, showing the Tomb of General U.S. Grant. The body of Grant, hero of the Civil War, to whom General Lee of the Confederacy surrendered at Appomattox, and twice President of the United States, and that of his wife, lie in two caskets on a sunken level within this monument. The Tomb is open to the public and is a major point of interest to visitors to the metropolis. This view is southward from a point in Riverside Park and shows the northern (left) and western (right) sides of the Mausoleum. The towered structure in the background is the Riverside Baptist Church, at the S.E. corner of West 122nd Street and the Drive. It is often called the Rockefeller Church; it having been built by the Rockefeller family.
P. L. Sperr.
June 2, 1935.

(2)
The same, but viewed northward and showing the entrance, which is the south side. At the extreme right appears a part of the International House, which is on the east side of the Drive, slightly north of West 122nd Street. It is a unit of Columbia University.
P. L. Sperr.
June 2, 1935.

(3)
The same as view No. 2, as seen from the park which descends the slope to the Hudson River.
August 28, 1936.
P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Riverside Drive - 127th Street (West)
text:
Riverside Park, south from Tiemann Place, (West 127th Street), showing the Claremont Inn on Riverside Drive. This structure was built before the Revolution, on land, sold August 4, 1796, by Nicholas de Peyster to George Pollock, a linen merchant who named the place for its beautiful trees and shrubbery, "Strawberry Hill." His 5 year old son, St. Claire Pollock, fell off the cliffs and was drowned July 15, 1797. His father subsequently went to New Orleans, where his descendants there, are said to be called Polk. His land, expressly reserving the burial place containing the urn of his boy, which may still be seen near Grant's Tomb, was sold in 1803 to Joseph Alston, the husband of Theodosia Burr, who deeded it to Michael Hogan, the former British Consul at Havana. The latter named the place "Claremont" after the residence in Surrey of Prince William, Duke of Clarence, who became King William IV. The Earl of Devon, while living here in 1807, witnessed the trial of Fulton's "Clermont", and in 1815 an occupant was Joseph Bonaparte, the ex-King of Spain. The City finally bought the property, and since 1872 it has been a famous public restaurant. The land to the east and south of same is historical, being the scene of several of the sharpest engagements of the Battle of Harlem Heights on September 16, 1776.

About 1907.

Wurts Brothers.

title: Manhattan: 137th Street - 229th Street
text:
Riverside Park: A set of 2 views in a northward direction and showing prominently the New York Central Railroad tracks and yard that occupy the marginal lands between the Park proper and the North (Hudson) River. View No. 1 is northward from 137th Street and No. 2 from 145th Street. This small slope that bears the name Riverside Park is a separate unit from its better known portion and occupies a strip between West 135th and 153rd Streets, being separated by the valley at 125th Street, over which the Drive is carried by a viaduct. In the fall of 1937 the West Side Improvement Project will be completed and a radical change effected in this area. For views of same see files under classification "The West Side Improvement Project!" A publication similarly named was published by the Department of Parks on the opening of same on October 12, 1937.

July 31, 1931.

P. L. Sperr.

text:
Rockefeller Plaza, (center foreground and not constructed) from West 48th (left margin) to 51st (right margin) Street's, showing the development of the new midtown center. Prominent in the middle is the 70-story R.C.A. Building. To the left and right respectively are R.K.O. Centre Theatre and the 31-story R.K.O. Building and the International Music Hall. All of these structures front on Sixth Avenue on their far sides, and are viewed westward across Fifth Avenue. The photographer's vantage point is the 40-storied structure, No. 444 Madison Avenue that is to the rear of Saks Fifth Avenue Department Store. At the top appears a glimpse of the North (Hudson) River and its Jersey shore.

1932

From left to right they are: 10 East 40th Street (1930), the New York Trust Building at 277 Madison Avenue (1931), the Lefcourt Colonial Building (1929) at 297 Madison Avenue (corner of 41st Street) 500 Fifth Avenue (1931) nearly hidden by the Lefcourt Colonial, the Lincoln Building (1929) at 60 East 42nd Street (between Madison and Park Avenues), the Chanin Building (early 1929) on Lexington Avenue (north side) from 41st to 42nd Streets, the Chrysler Building (1930) diagonally across Lexington Avenue and 42nd Street from the Chanin Building, and the Daily News Building on the south side of 42nd Street, east of Third Avenue.

title: Manhattan: St. Lukes Place - Hudson Street
text:
2, 3 to 13 St. Luke's Place, north side, adjoining and east of Hudson Street, seen from Hudson Park on the south side. St. Luke's Place is the eastern extension of Leroy Street cut through the Trinity Church Cemetery in the 1840's. That part of the Trinity Church Farm on the east side of Hudson Street, from Clarkson to Morton Street, was earliest aside for a cemetery. After Leroy Street was cut through, the southern half continued to serve as a cemetery until the 1890's, when the bodies were moved up to the cemetery on upper Broadway, and the old cemetery converted into a park, called St. John's Park (not to be confused with St. John's park on lower Varick Street), later Hudson Park, and opened to the public in 1898.

The northern half was promptly built up, and a little later named St. Luke's Place, with its own set of house numbers, which replaced the old numbers 99-61 Leroy Street. Nos. 1-2 are the side of 420 Hudson Street, the corner building. No. 16, at the time of this picture, the residence of Mayor James J. Walker.
March 9, 1929.

P. L. Sperr.

P. L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: St. Nicholas Avenue - 116th Street (West)
text:
St. Nicholas Ave. (car tracks thereon), south from West 117th Street and across Seventh Ave. at W. 116th Street (center), showing in the left foreground, a triangular grassy plot known as Kilpatrick Square. This is bounded on its three sides by Seventh Ave. (extreme left), West 117th Street (left foreground) and St. Nicholas Ave. (center foreground); its apex being at West 116th Street.

This thoroughfare in earlier days was known as the Harlem Road to Kingsbridge and the easterly side of same followed the easterly side of the present Ave. as shown in the building line to the left. That on the right sets back approximately 30 feet; St. Nicholas Ave. being that much wider.

The four corner apartment houses seen are, from left to right; the Graham Court (1923-37 Seventh Ave., east side, from 116th to 117th Streets); the Wilhelmina (1917-19 Seventh Ave., at the S.E. corner of 116th Street); the Acadia (No. 1889-93 Seventh Ave., and 91-97 St. Nicholas Ave., the apex at West 115th Street), and the Elnido (121 St. Nicholas Ave. and 201-5-11 West 116th Street, at the N.W. corner).

June 1905

title: Manhattan: St. Nicholas Avenue - 170th Street
text:
1200 St. Nicholas Avenue (formerly Eleventh Avenue) at N.E. corner of 170th Street, showing a new apartment building nearly ready for occupancy.

St. Nicholas Avenue, north from this point, is the old Eleventh Avenue and was known as such until around 1910. Historically it has nothing in common with St. Nicholas Avenue below Broadway and 169th Street, which was laid out more or less along the lines of old Harlem  Lane (110th to 123rd Streets) and Kingsbridge Road (127th to 139th Streets and 148th to 169th Streets).

September 1921.

title: Manhattan: St. Nicholas Avenue - Fort George Avenue
text:
St. Nicholas Place, east side, north across W. 150th Street. At the right is the 6-story Audubon Court Apartments. Adjoining same are the several buildings that house the Community Hospital in New York City. These are at the S. E. corner of 150th Street. Across the street at the N. E. corner is the reputed Ringling mansion. One, J. A. Bailey owned same in 1904. This individual may have been one of the famous circus owners, Barnum and Bailey, the predecessors to the present Ringling Brothers.

H. Acker is the owner in 1910, Louis Schaefer in 1918 and a Bertha Koemple in 1939. Adjoining this is the minaretted A. Alexander home.

View 2 shows only the structures at the N. E. corner. The triangular park that separates St. Nicholas Place from the Avenue of the same name, is Donnelson Square.

P. L. Sperr

April 19, 1940

title: Manhattan: St. Nicholas Avenue - Fort George Avenue
text:
(1)
St. Nicholas Ave., north from but not including Fort George Ave. From this point the avenue winds down a sharp hill and reaches Nagle Ave. at its junction with Dyckman Street and Hillside Ave. (where it terminates) This point of vantage affords a panoramic view of the northernmost sector of Manhattan, north from Dyckman Street, to Spuyten Duyvil. At the right is part of Highbridge Park, and at the left is a very steep slope
reaching down to Hillside Ave.
April 24, 1937.
P. L. Sperr.
(2)
The same, from a point slightly northward. Also shown is a portion of the Seventh Ave.-Van Cortlandt Line of the Interborough Rapid Transit subway, running, at this point, on an elevated structure on Nagle Ave.
April 20, 1937.
P. L. Sperr.
(3)
The same, but showing a closer view of the point of confluence of the thoroughfares mentioned in view No. 1. At the right appears Dyckman Street as it crosses Nagle Ave. and proceeds northward. The houses seen (left) are on the east side of Dyckman Street, north from Nagle Ave., and (right) on the north side of the latter, east from the former street. Also shown (extreme left) is the Dyckman Street station of the subway
line (mentioned in view 2).
April 20, 1937.
P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Seaman Avenue - 214th Street
text:
Isham Garden Apartments, 221-29 Seaman Avenue on east side and 222-28 Seaman Avenue on west side, at 214th Street, seen from Isham Park at S.W. corner of 214th Street. The apartments are being rented for October 1 occupancy. In the foreground Lieutenant Sutherland and his Seventh Regiment Band are giving one of their regular afternoon concerts.
In the background may be seen Spuyten Duyvil Inlet, Inwood Park, and the Bronx or northern approach to the New York Central railroad bridge, in the far background the Hudson River and the Palisades on the New Jersey side. The view is northwest.
Summer 1924.

title: Manhattan: South Street - Whitehall Street
text:
South Street, east of Whitehall Street, as photographed from the South Ferry "El" station platform. On the right are the various East River piers. Note the early sailing vessels. On the left is the Eastern Hotel, and known as such since 1856. The original building was erected prior to 1790, when it was purchased by John B. Coles for 350 pounds. In 1822 it became the Eagle Hotel, a tavern. Much of the frame work is solid mahogany, having been imported as ballast by the original owner, a sea captain. At the time of purchase by Coles, who used it as a warehouse, it was 3 stories in height.

1: 1893
2: Sept. 1927

J. S. Johnston, photo

title: Manhattan: South Street - Roosevelt Street
text:
173 and 174 South Street (the old numbers, seen on the picture, were, respectively, 174 and 175 until 1891, according to the C.W. Bromley real estate map of that year. The succeeding map of 1897 and all others that have followed until the present day, 1937, designate the two houses by the new numbers), adjoining and at the S.W. corner of Roosevelt Street. Also shown is No. 133 Roosevelt Street a 4-story loft building at the S.E. corner of Front Street. A portion of the Brooklyn Bridge can be seen in the left background. No. 173 (old No. 174) is the house in which Alfred E. Smith was born on December 30, 1873. He served four terms as Governor of the State of New York and was Democratic candidate for President in 1928. Long in New York City and State politics, he is often referred to as "New York's own Al Smith." He is a leading figure in the Society of Tammany and is one of the organizers of the Liberty League, an organization of leading industrialists and bankers of extremely conservative leanings in politics. Born and raised in the city slums, he had no more than a parochial school education. In later life, as a public personality he received several degrees as Doctor of Laws from Harvard, Columbia, Fordham, and other famous universities.

About 1925.

Brown Brothers.

title: Manhattan: South William Street - Beaver Street

South William , Beaver & William Sts.

Merchant Marine House, 9 story building on plot of nearly 6,00 square feet and valued at approximately $1,250,000, purchased by Cecil P. Stewart for his companies a few years a go, and resold by Mr. Stewart reserves leases for fee to the Insurance Company of North America. title: Manhattan: Spring Street - MacDougal Street
text:

The bend in Spring Street at this point marks the junction of the original Spring Street, on which we are looking east, with the western section, which was originally laid out as Brannon Street, but given to Spring Street before 1811.
1926.

title: Manhattan: Spring Street - Clark Street
text:
Spring Street, western section (originally Brannon Street), west from and including the future Sixth Avenue Extension (Clark Street on the south side, and Macdougal Street on the north side). The Butterick Building, erected in the winter 1902-03, at the right, will become the N.W. corner of Sixth Avenue and Spring Street. Adjoining the Butterick Building, and opposite the northern end of Clark Street (which will become part of the west side of Sixth Avenue), the new Vivadou Building is under construction (see also Vandam Street). At the southwest corner of Varick Street may be seen part of the American News Building, built two or three years before this picture was taken. The absorbtion of Brannon Street by Spring Street took place about 1807, and is one of the earliest examples of a process which went on in the city's street nomenclature all through the Nineteenth Century. "The Villager" attributes the name Brannon to the family of a man of that name who kept a public house in this neighborhood up to 1861.

1926.

1 to 6 State Street, (left), at, adjoining and west of the N.W. corner of Whitehall Street, showing the Seamen's Church Institute (No. 1, corner building) and contiguous to it the house of the British Consulate General (No. 2). Also seen, are Nos. 46 to 34 Whitehall Street (right), west side, north from and including State, to Pearl Streets. Nos. 1 to 3 State and 46 to 40 Whitehall Streets, were demolished in 1913, and their sites are now (1937), occupied by the 12-story South Ferry Building. Nos. 4-5 (white house) and 6, upon which two additional stories were added, now comprise a 6-story annex to South Ferry Building.

1907.

Brown Brothers.

title: Manhattan: State Street - Whitehall Street
text:
1 to 8 State Street (right to left) at, adjoining and west of the N.W. corner of Whitehall Street, showing prominently the House for Irish Immigrant Girls. (Mission of Our Lady of the Rosary) at No. 7.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

No 7 State Street was erected prior to 1800 and came into the possession of Moses Rogers about that time. William Bayard owned same subsequently. For a short while it was the property of Robert P. Getty, who became the first Mayor of Yonkers. Other occupants were A. Gardener, and G. Howland (in 1830), after which it was used by the Federal Gov't. during the Civil War for military purposes. The Pilot Commission were the last occupants prior to the purchase by the present tenants in 1885. A legend infers that the low brick addition back of the Mission is the oldest slave building left. A descriptive account will be found in the column, "About New York" by Meyer Berger. This appeared in the New York Times of April 22, 1940.

title: Manhattan: State Street - 3rd Avenue
text:
(1) State Street, east side, south from but not including Pearl Street. The building on the extreme left being No. 12, which adjoins the Cheseborough Building, the corner building at Pearl Street. The 5-story white structure is No. 9, the former Ludlow-Morton House. It is probably the former 3-story basement house, with dormers, that was altered in 1859 and a story added. The 5-story projecting house, No. 7, is the present Mission of Our Lady of the Rosary (Home for Irish Immigrant Girls). It was built about 1800 by Moses Rogers, A. Gardener, & Howland and occupied same in 1830, afterward the Federal Government used it for military purposes during the Civil War. The Pilot Commission were the last occupants prior to the present tenancy. Between these two buildings is No. 8, (formerly known as the Bay House), which was also altered and a story added in 1859; this became the Lutheran Pilgrim House in 1885. Note that this street curves in a southeasterly direction to Whitehall Street, at which point appears the South Ferry Division of the Second and Third Aves. Elevated Lines. These buildings face on Battery Park, which is not shown. May 1925. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2) A limited view showing mainly Nos. 9, 8 and 7 (left to right). October 1923. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3) Similar to No. 2, showing a view to Whitehall Street (right). The 6 and 12-story structures, Nos. 6-4 and 3-1 are units of the South Ferry Building, located at the N.E. corner of Whitehall Street. May 1925. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(4) A view showing prominently the R.C. Mission at No. 7. October 1923. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Manhattan: State Street - Bowling Green Row
text:
State Street, east side, south from Bowling Green Row to Pearl Street, showing a row of fashionable homes facing on Battery Park (right). Shown in the foreground, is No. 7 Bowling Green, at the S.E. corner of State Street. The farthest building shown, is Stewart's Store, (predecessor to John Wanamaker in the Department Store line), which occupied the block between Bridge and Pearl Streets. Stephen Whitney resided in one of the houses facing Bowling Green. Today (1937), the U.S. Custom House rises here on the area shown in the foreground, with the 12-story Battery Park Building (former Stewart site) at its rear. About 1860.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: State Street - Bridge Street
text:
State Street, north from Bridge Street to Battery Place, showing the old "El" spur upon same. This carries the Sixth and the Ninth Avenue Elevated Lines to South Ferry. On the left is Battery Park; on the right, the U. S. Custom House; and in the background, the early Washington Building. Behind the latter and facing Bowling Green, is the towering Cunard Building. Broadway begins at that point.

1905

George L. Balgue

title: Manhattan: Stone Street - Broad Street
text:
24-40 Stone Street, south side, east from, but not including Broad Street, to Coenties Alley. No. 32 (the 3-story house with the gabled roof, in the center of the view), is more than 100 years old, now serving as the home of the American Banker; a bank publication. In 1835, this building had its narrowest escape when the Great Fire of that year, which laid the greater part of that section south of Wall Street in ruins, burned up to the building's side of wall, and went no farther.

August 28, 1929.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Stuyvesant Square Park - [Between 15th and 17th Streets (East).]
text:
(1)
Stuyvesant Square Park: An open area between East 15th (right, southern boundary) and East 17th (left, northern boundary) Streets, that is bisected by Second Ave. The eastern side of same, as shown with the Beth Israel Hospital thereon, is Livingston Place. On the lower left appears the nave and bell-tower of St. Georges P.E. Church, located on the western edge, which is called Rutherford Place. This park, a portion of the former Stuyvesant Farm was bequeathed to the City by Peter Stuyvesant. The Park Department in conjunction with the W.P.A. attempted to improve same in 1936, as a playground for East Side children, but were restrained by the various hospitals in this vicinity. Their plea being based upon the original grant of land; "for park purposes." A judicial decree was granted in their favor. For further data, see newspapers for 1936-1937. Photographers vantage point is the Consolidated Edison Building, No. 4 Irving Place and shows an eastward perspective across the "Gas House" area of Manhattan to Greenpoint, Brooklyn. Separating these localities of the City is the East River.
September 23, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

(2 & 3)
Two similar views, taken the same day.
September 23, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

Stuyvesant Square Park: An open area between East 15th (right, southern boundary) and East 17th (left, northern boundary) Streets, that is bisected by Second Ave. The eastern side of same, as shown with the Beth Israel Hospital thereon, is Livingston Place. On the lower left appears the nave and bell-tower of St. Georges P.E. Church, located on the western edge, which is called Rutherford Place. This park, a portion of the former Stuyvesant Farm was bequeathed to the City by Peter Stuyvesant. The Park Department in conjunction with the W.P.A. attempted to improve same in 1936, as a playground for East Side children, but were restrained by the various hospitals in this vicinity. Their plea being based upon the original grant of land; "for park purposes." A judicial decree was granted in their favor. For further data, see newspapers for 1936-1937. Photographers vantage point is the Consolidated Edison Building, No. 4 Irving Place and shows an eastward perspective across the "Gas House" area of Manhattan to Greenpoint, Brooklyn. Separating these localities of the City is the East River.
September 23, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

(2 & 3)
Two similar views, taken the same day.
September 23, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Stuyvesant Street - 2nd Avenue
text:
Stuyvesant Street, at the N.W. corner of Second Ave., showing St. Mark's Church (P.E.). The present church was consecrated in 1829 and under it lies buried Peter Stuyvesant, the last of the Dutch Colonial Governors, who died in 1682 and was laid there when the Chapel occupied the site. The bodies of Henry Slaughter, the English royal Governor, and Daniel Tompkins, early Governor of New York State also rest there. It is also known as "St. Mark's on the Bouwerie."

1936.

W.P.A. Photo.
Federal Writers Project.

title: Manhattan: Stuyvesant Street
text:
View 1: Entrance to 33 Stuyvesant Street, New York 3, New York. Showing sections of hand-wrought iron work on fence, and entrance balustrades (the iron work forming a second-floor gallery surrounding the four buildings forming the point where East 10th Street and Stuyvesant Street meet does not show here. The blunt point of this group of houses (33 & 35 Stuyvesant Street and 126 & 128 E. 10th St.) is probably a few hundred feet from the entrance to St. Mark's Church-in-the-Bowery; this church for a number of years owned these properties along with a number of others on E. 10th St. and East 11th St. Gift of Lilian Gibbs, 21 May 1960. (Photograph, n.d.)

View 2: Same, but also showing the second-floor gallery surrounding the four buildings forming the point where E. 10th St. and Stuyvesant Street meet. The iron work was demolished when it began to disintegrate. Gift of Lilian Gibbs, 21 May 1960. (Photograph, n.d.)

View 3: Entrance to basement apartment, 33 Stuyvesant Street, after the iron fence was removed. Gift of Lilian Gibbs, 21 May 1960.

View 4: This picture shows the converging of E. 10th Street and Stuyvesant Street with sections of the "el" showing at East 9th St.("el" station) and East 10th St. (tracks). Cable car tracks leading from Astor Place traversed Stuyvesant Street and eastward (or westward as desired by the switchman) and returned westward on E. 9th St. The ornate hand-wrought iron fencing and balustrade are barely discernable here, but they added charm and grace as long as they held forth. Gift of Lilian Gibbs, 21 May 1960. (Photograph, n.d.)

title: Manhattan: Sullivan Street - Canal Street
text:
(1)

Sullivan Street, north from and including Canal Street, the year before the demolition of buildings for the construction of the Independent (municipal) Subway line and the southward extension of Sixth Ave. The west side of Sullivan Street, from Canal to Grand Streets, inclusive, including Nos. 2 to 24 Sullivan Street, will become part of the west side of Sixth Ave. Notice the new building (since 1922) at the S.W. corner of Grand Street. The entire east side of Sullivan Street, from Canal to Watts Streets, including the ten-story Powell Chocolate factory at the east corner of Canal Street, will be razed.

Sullivan Street begins here and runs north to West 3rd Street, and, since 1904, to Washington Square. It is the sixth of a group of streets named for Revolutionary generals, and laid out west of and parallel to Broadway.

1926.

title: Manhattan: Sullivan Street - Houston Street
text:
Church of St. Anthony of Padua, 157-153 Sullivan Street, adjoining the cleared S.E. corner of Houston Street (q.v.). This church edifice dates from between 1879 and 1885, but the church was organized in 1865, and later took over the former Free Congregational Church at 149-151 Sullivan Street adjoining, where the six-story tenement house is shown in this view. The site of the present church was occupied by a brewery. St. Anthony of Padua was the first Italian Roman Catholic congregation to be organized in New York. An unsuccessful attempt to do something for the Italians of New York had been made in 1859.

June 15, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Sutton Place - 54th Street (East)
text:
Sutton Place, north from E. 54th Street, towards the Queens-boro Bridge at 59th Street where this thoroughfare changes its identity to become York Avenue (formerly Avenue A). To the right and left of this view are vacant lots occupying the 54th - 55th Street frontage. Details of these are shown in the accompanying views, No. 2 being across the N.E. corner and No. 3 across the N.W.

The rock drills in the first instance are at the river's edge and are preparing the foundation for the East River Highway. Buildings seen beyond same are on Welfare Island and replaced the former prison structures there. The last view is northeastward across an old brewery site and shows another similar enterprise on the north side of 55th Street between Sutton Place and First Avenue. To the left here are modern apartment houses that front on the east side of First Avenue.

February 9, 1939
Views 1,2 and 3

P. L. Sperr

v.2 " 507

title: Manhattan: Tiemann Place - Rockaway Parkway
text:
Manhattanville: A view of the west side of the Public Drive (Broadway) at West 127th Street (Tiemann Place) and showing the Thomas M. Finley Boarding School at the N.W. corner of same. This institution was in operation in 1811. In this structure were held the earlier services of St. Mary's P.E. Church, prior to the construction of the building on Lawrence Street in 1823. Today (1937) the Whitestone, an apartment house bearing No. 41-45 Tiemann Place, stands upon this site.
Unknown date.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 43rd Street
text:
Broadway, west side, south from and including 43rd Street, showing also the west side of Seventh Avenue, south from 43rd Street. In the centre is the second building of the New York Times, built in 1904. This building caused the name of the region bounded by Broadway and Seventh Avenue from 42nd to 47th Streets to be changed from Longacre Square to Times Square. The Times was formerly located at 41 Park Row, and in the middle 1920's will move to 43rd Street west of Seventh Avenue.

1909.

Wurts Brothers.

title: Manhattan: Broadway - 44th Street
text:
Broadway, east side, south from 44th Street, showing also Seventh Avenue, east side, from 44th to 40th Streets. This picture was made on Armistice Day, during the two-minute silence, and shows the Times Square crowds standing hushed, the men with bared heads, as a bugler on a balcony of the Hotel Astor sounds "Taps." Notice the campaign poster on the Hotel Cadillac for Fiorello H. La Guardia, now a member of the House of Representatives. Mr La Guardia, the Republican candidate, has just been defeated in the mayoralty election by Mayor James J. Walker, now at the height of his popularity. A year earlier the Republicans had denied renomination to him for the House of Representatives, and he made a successful campaign on the Socialist ticket. Four years later, in 1933, he will be elected Mayor of New York, defeating the incumbent, Mayor John P. O'Brien, and former Aldermanic President Joseph V. McKee. November 11, 1929.

International News.

title: Manhattan: Union Square - [University Place - 14th Street.]
text:
Union Square, seen from the S.W. corner at University Place and 14th Street.  Henry K. Browne's statue of Lincoln, erected by popular subscription in 1868, stands in the left foreground, facing away from the camera.  Bartholdi's Lafayette, erected in 1876 by the French residents of the city, is visible in the extreme right of the picture.  Behind it may be seen the old Union Square Hotel on the S.E. corner of Union Square East (Fourth Avenue) and 15th Street, built in the late 1870's.
Union Square, a broad common where Fourth Avenue, the old Bowery Road, and other streets converged, was like Washington Square, once used as a Potter's Field.  In 1845 it was made into a park, and was soon surrounded by fine mansions, remaining the Belgravia of New York up to the time of the Civil War.  At the time of this picture, the fashionable shopping district was located here and north to Madison Square.
On the N.W. corner of Fourth Avenue and 17th Street stands the Everett House, a famous old hotel named after the orator Edward Everett.  Behind it is a 9-story wing very recently added, on the corner of 16th Street; it will later become the Bradley Building, even before the Everett is torn down.  Adjoining the Everett, to the left of the picture, is a new 6-story office building.  The Westmoreland apartment house, on the S.E. corner of 17th Street and Union Square East, is the building in which William Lloyd Garrison died.
Compare this with the same view in January, 1928, New York Edison photo No. 60533

1893
New York Edison Company Collection

title: Manhattan: Union Square - 14th Street (East) - [Lincoln Statue.]
text:
Union Square West, north from East 14th Street, showing the Lincoln statue silhouetted against the buildings that face Union Square. This thoroughfare in reality is a part of Broadway. It’s true identity is lost in that 14th to 17th Street gap that sweeps past the Park. The street cars of the same curved eastward in a serpentine loop forming the well known "Death Curve".

The martyr President stands in the attitude of addressing an audience, and the angularity and ungracefulness of his figure are expressed with painful exactitude. A low curb of granite surrounds the pedestal, and on this are inscribed the famous Gettysburg words, "With malice toward none, With charity for all".

This is the work of Henry K. Browne and was paid for by popular subscription. It was erected in 1868 and complements the nearby equestrian Washington statue.
At the left margin is the 5 story building occupied for years by Tiffany & Company. Opposite is a lower structure with the well known Sol Young, Photographer, as a tenant. These are at East 15th Street. The dominant office building is the 17 story Bank of the Metropolis Bldg., No 31 Union Square West. Broadway reasserts itself in the center background. To the right are buildings that face on the north side of East 17th Street, extending toward Fourth Avenue.

George L. Balgue

title: Manhattan: Union Square - 4th Avenue - Between 15th and 17th Streets - Celebration of the 100th Anniversary of founding of Union Square.
text:
The Celebration of the 100th Anniversary of the founding of Union Square, at 4th Avenue, between 15th and 17th Streets, New York City, by prominent State, Civic and Local Organizations.

From,
A.H. Scrap Book of the Revolution. No date.

"Union Square located at the convergence of several Streets, where 4th Avenue and the old Bowery Road met, made it necessary to have there a Common. At times it was used as a Potter's Field, much of it's area being covered with rude shanties, but surrounded by fine mansions. It remained the Belgrade of Manhattan until about 1845, when homes were moved farther North."

P.40. King's Handbook of New York.

title: Manhattan: Union Square (East) - Between 14th and 15th Streets.
text:

text:
Union Square Savings Bank, Union Square East at N.E. corner of 15th Street, with part of the newly remodelled park in the foreground. This edifice was built some time between 1902 and 1910, replacing two old houses; the bank had its original offices in 20 Union Square, on the corner. The 9-story apartment house at 107 East 15th Street, adjoining the bank, was built about 1900.

title: Manhattan: Union Square (East) - Between 15th and 16th Streets.
text:
20-34 Union Square East, from 15th to 16th Streets, with a portion of the park (which was drastically remodelled, 1929-30) in the foreground. The Union Square Savings Bank, 20-22 Union Square on the 15th Street corner, was erected between 1902 and 1910. The 11-story Reliance Building was also erected at the same time, replacing an old 4-story house. 34 Union Square on the corner of 16th Street, was built prior to 1890.
Old 24, 26-8, and 30 have been taken over since 1930 and remodelled by S. Klein; another story has been added to 24. See 1930 views of these three buildings.

P. L. Sperr.
February 24, 1933.

title: Manhattan: Union Square (East) - Between 15th and 16th Streets.
text:
Neg. No. 223 =

(1)
24, 26-8, and 30 Union Square, between 15th and 16th Streets, occupied by the Polish daily Novy Swiat ("The New World"), The Daily Worker (organ of the Communist Party), and the radical Jewish Freiheit ("Freedom"). These buildings, except possibly 24, are business buildings built on the site of the original houses, probably around 1880. They may be located on the Edison Company's photograph of Union Square in 1893. The Daily Worker has only moved in since 1928. All these buildings will, before 1933, be taken over and remodelled by S. Klein as a store for higher-priced dresses. At the time of this picture, the Co-operative Cafeteria pictured here was the regular hangout of the Communist organizers, much as Luchow's Restaurant on 14th Street used to be (and still is) frequented by district leaders from mammany Hall. title: Manhattan: Union Square (East) - [30, 32, 34 Union Square] - 16th Street.
text:
34-32-30 Union Square East, at and adjoining the S.E. corner of 16th Street. The corner building was erected around 1877 by the Singer Sewing Machine Company. The branch office of Henry Clews and Company, above the Corn Exchange Bank, mournfully reminds one that the great Bull Market culminated less than a year before the date of this picture.

The 11-story Reliance Building was erected between 1902 and 1910, on the site of an old 4-story residence which was probably built in the 1850's, when Union Square was the Belgravia of New York. 30, the Freiheit offices, is included in the view of 24-30 Union Square, taken the same day.

Union Square park, in the foreground, has just been drastically re-modeled.

August 4, 1930.

title: Manhattan: Union Square (East) - 17th Street (East).
text:
The new Tammany Hall, Union Square East at the S.E. corner of 17th Street, newly erected on the site of the old Westmoreland Apartments (originally Hotel), which occupied the site from about 1877 to 1928. The bank is about to move into the ground floor. In the background may be seen the tower of the new Consolidated Gas and New York Edison Building, recently completed on 14th Street on the site of the old Tammany Hall and the Academy of Music.

The Society of St. Tammany, or Columbian Order, was founded in Philadelphia and spread through New England, before a New York City chapter was established in 1789. It was originally a benevolent organization, and first identified itself with politics in the presidential campaign of 1800, when, under the leadership of Vice-Presidential candidate Aaron Burr, it supported the Jefferson-Burr ticket. The first Tammany Hall, built in 1801, stood on Frankfort and Nassau Streets. On July 4, 1868, the second Hall on 14th Street was opened with the Democratic National Convention of that year. In 1928 it moved into the present building.

The Tammany Hall General Committee, with which it is practically identical in membership, has for a long time been in control of the Democratic Party in New York County, at times almost to the point of complete identification with it. This picture, for instance, is taken near the height of Mayor James J. Walker's popularity, the spring preceding his re-election. Tammany Hall is not only identified with the Party in Manhattan, but is working harmoniously with the leaders of the other four boroughs.

May, 1929.

Ewing Galloway.

text:

No. 1 is from the diagonal far corner of the Square, at Broadway and 14th Street; No. 2 from atop an office structure on the same street and No. 3 from inside the Park. title: Manhattan: Union Square - 14th Street - [Union Square Park.]
text:
Classification: Parks

Union Square, seen from the S.W. corner at University Place and 14th Street, nearly identical in scene with the New York Edison Company's photograph No. 49767, taken in 1893. Most of the new buildings shown here were erected between 1902 and 1910. The new Union Square Savings Bank is on the N.E. corner of 15th Street, and the 11-story Reliance Building at 32 Union Square, adjoins the old building now occupied by the Freiheit, a radical Yiddish paper. To the same period belong the Everett Building on the N.W. corner of 17th Street and Fourth Avenue, and the Guardian Life Insurance building (originally Germania Life Insurance) on the N.E. corner. On the street floor of the old Union Square Hotel may be seen one of the signs of S. Klein's dress emporium. In 1930 The Daily Worker, organ of the Communist Party, will be occupying the old building next to the Freiheit, where Elite Styles are shown in this picture; and by 1933 S. Klein will have overflowed into both these buildings. The principal change during these years, however, will be the demolition of the old Westmoreland at 17th Street and of 44 Union Square adjoining, to make room for the new Tammany Hall and Manufacturers Trust Building, and the drastic changes in the park, which in this picture still has much the same general outlines as it had thirty-five years earlier.

January 11, 1928.

New York Edison Company Collection, (No. 60533).

title: Manhattan: Union Square (West) - Between 16th and 17th Streets.
text:
31-41 Union Square West, from 16th to 17th Streets, seen from Fourth Avenue and 17th Street. The tall building on the N.W. corner of 16th Street is the Bank of the Metropolis, erected between 1902 and 1910 on the site of the old house which the same bank had occupied during its first six years, 1871-77. The Union Square Building, 33 Union Square West, was built around 1895, and originally called the Decker Building. The Hartford Building, 41 Union Square, on the S.W. corner of 17th Street, was also built about the same time. In 1900 old 31 Union Square was occupied by Brentano's, 33 Union Square (the Decker Building) by Fischer Pianos, and 35 by G. Schirmer, music publisher.

July 7, 1928.

text:
U.N. WINDOW CLEANERS AT WORK

UN 33006 - The hazardous task of cleaning the enormous expanses of glass in the 39-story Secretariat Building (a total of just under 5 acres of glass) is performed by 5 men. Each man cleans a section consisting of seven bays of ten windows, seven floors deep every day. They are also responsible for the glass spandrels between the windows and for all the glass plate and partitions throughout the building.
PHOTO SHOWS: A cleaner perched precariously on a window on the First Avenue side of the building with the mid-Manhattan skyline in the background.

Please credit UNATIONS

title: Manhattan: University Place - Washington Mews
text:
University Place, north from and including Washington Mews, just above Washington Square North. The office building on the S.E. corner of 8th Street, was originally built by Merck & Company, about 1895, on the site of old 42-38 Clinton Place (now 34 East 8th Street). On the S.E. corner of 9th Street is the Hotel Lafayette (formerly Hotel Martin), owned by Raymond Ortig (who put up the prize which Charles A. Lindbergh, Jr., won by his famous solo flight in May, 1927). The new Devonshire House, apartment building, completed in 1928 on the site of the old University Place Presbyterian Church, is visible on the S.W. corner of 10th Street.

University Place is a continuation of Wooster Street; the name University Place was applied to this part of it some time in the 1840's. New York University was incorporated in 1831, and shortly thereafter built its first building on Washington Square South at Waverly Place.

The newer part of the Albert is the 11-story building (about 1906) in the middle of the block.
The 11-story loft building on the N.E. corner of 11th Street, built after 1902, occupies the site of old Union Court, a little private street within the block.

title: Manhattan: University Place - 8th Street
text:
University Place, east side, from 9th to 8th Streets, showing the Hotel Lafayette (formerly the Hotel Martin) on the S.E. corner of 9th Street. This hotel is composed of three houses believed to have been originally built about 1855. A Mr. Martin altered them into one unit and opened them in 1883 as the Hotel Martin. In March 1902, the Martin became the Hotel Lafayette. The Lafayette, under the ownership of Mr. Raymond Orteig, is a French hotel, as was the Hotel Martin. It is especially renowned for its restaurant. Twenty-one years after the date of this picture it will be linked to the Lindbergh non-stop flight from New York to Paris, which will win the award offered by Mr. Orteig, the proprietor.

April 18, 1906.

Brown Brothers.

title: Manhattan: University Place - 9th Street
text:
University Place, west side, north from and including 9th Street. A comparison with Brown Brothers' 1913 view shows little change in the buildings, except at the N.W. corner of 12th Street. The building on the S.W. corner of 9th Street, shown in part, was erected around 1900 on the site of six old houses. The building from 9th to 10th Streets, marked "For Sale" in the 1913 view, is at least ten years older; and the one on the N.W. corner of 10th Street looks like about 1880. The former will be replaced by a 12-story apartment house, and the latter, together with the 4-story house adjoining it, by an 11-story apartment house, in both cases prior to 1930.

title: Manhattan: University Place - 10th Street
text:
University Place Presbyterian Church, University Place at S.E. corner of 10th Street, organized and erected in 1845 by a colony from the Duane Street church. In 1870 the Mercer Street church sold its building and merged with this congregation.

Thirteen months after the date of this picture this church will be demolished; and a 12-story apartment building called Devonshire House will be erected on the site. 47 University Place, the little parish house adjoining the church, will also be demolished.

28 and 34 East 10th Street, the 11-and 10-story loft buildings adjoining the church, and sandwiching old 32 East 10th Street between them, were erected not long before 1910.

title: Manhattan: Vanderbilt Avenue - 43rd Street
text:
Vanderbilt Avenue, north from 43rd Street, showing the roof of the new Grand Central Station and the part of Park Avenue immediately above it, where the railroad yards have been built over. From 43rd to 44th Streets stands the Hotel Biltmore, opened New Year's Day 1914. The lot where it stands had long been vacant; in the 1880's William H. Vanderbilt, Esq., of the New York Central Railroad, used to turn out his famous mare "Maud S." there, during the business day while he was in his office in the old Grand Central.

The next block is occupied by the Yale Club on N.W. corner of 44th Street and the Vanderbilt Concourse Building on the S.W. corner of 45th Street, both built about the same time as the Biltmore or a little after.

At the time of this picture Vanderbilt Avenue has not yet been built across the railroad yards from 45th to 47th Streets. Opposite the Vanderbilt Concourse Building may be seen the northern end of the Pershing Square Viaduct, used on this side for both north- and south-bound traffic till 1928. From 47th to 48th Streets Vanderbilt Avenue passes under the arcade between the two halves of a double hotel built about 1917, the eastern building of which is 270 Park Avenue. On Park Avenue at 51st Street the Hotel Ambassador is nearing completion.

Gift of E. M. Jenks.

Early 1920.

On the west side from 43rd to 44th Streets stands the Hotel Biltmore, erected 1913-14. Contemporary with it are the Yale Club on the N.W. corner of 44th Street and the Vanderbilt Concourse Building on the S.W. corner of 45th Street. From 45th to 46th Streets is shown the Vanderbilt Avenue side of the Hotel Roosevelt, a new hotel opened September 1924.

August 25, 1931.

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

title: Manhattan: Vanderbilt Avenue - 45th Street
text:
Vanderbilt Avenue, north from 45th Street, showing the new arcaded hotel between Park and Madison Avenues, from 47th to 48th Streets, not long after its opening. 46th Street appears as a bridge across the Upper Level platforms and tracks.
In the left foreground, on the N.E. corner of Madison Avenue and 45th Street, is the old Railroad Y.M.C.A. building, temporarily housing Tiffany Studios. Vanderbilt Avenue will presently be opened from 45th to 47th Streets, and in this block the Hotel Roosevelt will be erected in 1924. On the N.W. corner of Madison Avenue and 46th Street is the Ritz Carlton Hotel, completed in its present form by 1910. The old houses on the east side of Madison Avenue, from 46th to 47th Streets, will presently be demolished. In the left background the tower spires of St. Patrick's Cathedral are seen on the horizon. In the right center, the Postum Building will be built in the block between Vanderbilt and Park Avenues, from 46th to 47th Streets. In the right background may be seen the New York Central Power Plant, east of Park Avenue between 49th and 50th Streets, which will be demolished in 1929 to make room for the new Waldorf Astoria. In the eastern half of this block stands the new Adams Express building. Compare this picture with pictures of this part of Park Avenue at various dates from 1903 to 1925.

Gift of E. M. Jenks.

About 1919.

title: Manhattan: Vanderbilt Avenue - 45th Street

This is a view which it will be impossible again to obtain from this position, as the new New York Central Building, occupying an entire block, is beginning to rise in the foreground. The Hotel Roosevelt occupies the entire block, from Vanderbilt to Madison Avenues. It was opened in September 1924.
October 12, 1927.

P. L. Sperr, Photographer.

On the right, is shown the Roosevelt Hotel (46th to 45th Streets), the Vanderbilt Concourse Building (S.W. corner of 45th Street) and the Hotel Biltmore (44th to 43rd Streets), which is just south of the Yale Club (Building at the N.W. corner of 44th Street, and bearing a dark banner).

title: Manhattan: Van Nest Place [Originally Van Nesa Place].
text:
2 and 3 Van Nest Place, adjoining the N.W. corner of 4th Street. No. 2 is Congregation Darech-Amuno, organized in 1838 and rebuilt in 1917.
Van Nest Place (originally Van Ness Place) is the name given in 1866 to the north side of Charles Street from 4th to Bleecker Streets. It has its own house numbers, which occupy the place formerly taken by 61-89 Charles Street, and its own street signs. The south side is still Charles Street, and embraces the even numbers 64-96 inclusive.

May 30, 1929.

P. L. Sperr.

According to the N.Y. Times, Sunday June 7, 1936 - the nomenclature Van Nest Place will be eliminated; Charles Street incorporating same. These structures will become Nos. 53 and 55 of same; the Synagogue being No. 53.

title: Manhattan: Wall Street - New Street
text:
The Twenties

The Twenties ended with a bang, or rather, a crash. On October 29, 1929 - forever to be known as Black Tuesday - the stock market, swollen by years of reckless gambling, collapsed with a roar heard 'round the world. The loss was to be $50 billion. The party was over and the time to pay the piper was at hand. 1929.

title: Manhattan: Wall Street - William Street
text:
Wall Street, west from William Street (foreground), to Broadway, showing on the west side of the latter, at the head of this thoroughfare, Trinity Church. This early view of the financial district is conspicious by the absence of the following institutions: The U. S. Trust Company of New York building of 1888 (No. 45-47); The heightened U. S. National Bank of New York building of 1890 (No. 41); The third (9 story) building of the Mechanics National Bank (No. 31-33); The Wilks Building at the
S.W. corner of Wall and Broad Streets; The Gallatin National Bank building of 1887 (in the process of construction at No. 34-36, adjoining the Assay Office) and the Bank of America building of 1888-9 (No. 44-6).

Compare this view with one of 1895 and note the changes; the last of that period to go was the brownstone shown at the left; the site to this day (1938) being occupied by the same firm, the Atlantic Mutual Insurance Company. An account of same was carried in a column titled
"Sky Lines' in the New York Sun of April 28, 1938.

Subsequently the following were replaced; the Drexel Morgan & Co. building in 1913; the old United States Assay Office building in 1916; and the Mechanics National Bank building in 1932. 1929 saw the site for the present 7O storied Bank of Manhattan Building (No. 40) cleared.

No. 2 of this set shows a view slightly later; the Gallatin National Bank Building being completed and with a workmens scaffold about to be removed. This structure was erected on a site which included their former building and a 1ot purchased from the dissolved Union Bank which was adjacent. The purchase price for the latter was $400000. The new nine story building was built and owned jointly by the Bank and Adrian Iselin.

The skyscraper under construction is the 70 storied Bank of Manhattan at No. 40 Wall Street. To the left is the 35 story Wall and Hanover Building. To the right are, the 26-story building (No. 62-67 Pine Street) at the rear of No. 60 Wall Street (H.L. Dougherty and Company), the domed Singer Building, the massive Equitable Building, the modern No. 1 Cedar Street, the Transportation Building and the ornate Woolworth Building. Note on Wall Street the glimpses of the Bankers Trust Company (pyramidal tower), the Electric Bond and Share Building and the New York Stock Exchange Building. title: Manhattan: Washington Mews - University Place
text:
Washington Mews, at University Place, showing the east extremity of this short thoroughfare extending one block west to Fifth Avenue. The small structures shown are studios that were formerly stables to the residences on Washington Square. They are a portion of the holdings of the Sailors Snug Harbor Corp. This came into being through the advice of Alexander Hamilton who suggested that Richard Randall leave his estate to the activity upon which the family fortune had sprung from.

title: Manhattan: 5th Avenue - Washington Mews
text:
Fifth Avenue, east side, from Washington Mews (left) to Washington Square (right), showing the rears of the buildings that face on the Park. These are the holdings of the Sailors' Snug Harbor Corp. and have an interesting background. Originally intended for a home for retired seamen, they are now rented to private individuals. The current lack of response has caused the Corp. to come to the conclusion that modern times demand modern conveniences. Renovations were therefore compulsory in order to protect their equity.

Views 2 and 3 show details of this work. Appearing in the latter, are the 2-story studio's at the rear of the towering apartment building, No. 1 Fifth Avenue. These are former stables and front on the north side of the Mews, extending eastward to University Place.
