title: Manhattan: Washington Square - Washington Square West
text:
Washington Square, seen from a roof at Sixth Avenue near 4th Street. The principal New York University building is on Washington Square East from Washington to Waverly Places. On the N.E. corner of Waverly and University Places a tall apartment building is going to be erected in 1929. The tall building north of the square is the new One Fifth Avenue. To the right may be seen the new apartment building at 32 Washington Square West, recently erected onto the site of the old Hicks-Lord house. Behind it, on the horizon, the tower of the Consolidated Gas building, Irving Place and 14th Street, is nearing completion. Nearer in the foreground are the roofs of the Holley Hotel, 35-6 Washington Square West, and the old houses 37-39, which are soon to be replaced by an apartment building. The spires in the immediate foreground belong to the Washington Square Methodist Episcopal Church at 135 West Fourth Street. Down in the park, to the right of the fountain, and nearer, may be seen the newly rebuilt comfort station.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Washington Square North - 5th Avenue
text:
14-22 Washington Square North, looking west from Fifth Avenue. These fine old residences antedate the Civil War. In front of No. 15 is the spot where Sandy Hill Road, a part of which has become Greenwich Avenue and another part of which has become Astor Place, crossed the main branch of Minetta Creek in the 18th Century. It is possible that this was the crossing at which the old "Kissing Bridge" was located. February 24, 1922.

text:
Washington Square Park:

Washington Arch, Washington Square, seen from the north so as to show the Judson Memorial Baptist Church (1892) framed in the archway, and the fountain in the center of the park. The church stands on the S.W. corner of Thompson Street and Washington Square South (4th Street).

title: Manhattan: Washington Square Park (Memorial Arch).
text:
Washington Square Park (Manhattan): The Washington Memorial Arch in the northern edge of the Park at the foot of Fifth Avenue and viewing northward thru same up this thoroughfare. This structure was completed in April of 1892 at a cost of $128,000. Further details will be found in King's Handbook of New York (1892) on page 158. Buildings on the right and left of this structure face southward on the Park and bear Washington Square North numbers; the Rhinelander being the latter. Note the modern apartment house in View 1. This is at the S.E. corner of Fifth Avenue and E. 8th Street and is titled No. 1 Fifth Avenue. Thru the Arch and in the distance appears the monolithic Empire State Building.

title: Manhattan: Washington Square North - 4th Street (West)
text:
Washington Square Park, northeastern quarter and eastern side, showing 13-1 Washington Square North and all of Washington Square East.

In the foreground may be seen the bust of Alexander L. Holley; in the right foreground stands the old wooden comfort station, to be replaced in a couple of years by a new stone structure. East of the fountain is the statue of Garibaldi. At the left stands Washington Arch, designed by Stanford White and completed in permanent form around 1891.

The buildings shown, from right to left, are the Vischer building at 78 Washington Square East, N.E. corner of 4th Street, the former Benedick apartment house and the former Celluloid Company building, now part of New York University, on the site of the Asbury Methodist-Episcopal Church. From Washington to Waverly Places the new New York University building (about 1900), on the site of the old building, takes up the block. On Washington Square North are the old residences most of which antedate the Civil War.

On the N.E. corner of University and Waverly Places, diagonally opposite the corner of the Square, a tall apartment building will be erected in 1929.

About 1925.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: Washington Square South - Sullivan Street
text:
47-40 Washington Square South, west from Sullivan to Macdougal Streets.
Compare with Brown Brothers' photo of this block in 1905, a year or two after Sullivan Street had been cut through from West Third Street. As shown here, the buildings are shortly to be remodelled into apartments and studios.

Gift of E. M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: Washington Square South - West Broadway
text:
62-61-60-59 Washington Square South, between West Broadway and Thompson Street. No. 61 is noted for having been during 1911-12 the home of the twenty-four year old poet Alan Seegar, who fell on a French battlefield in 1916. The tablet shown on the building was affixed in 1921. Stephen Crane and Frank Norris have also lived in this house; the latter is supposed to have written "The Pit" here. 59-60, together with 58 Washington Square, the old frame house on the corner of Thompson Street, are to be demolished not long after 1925. About 1923.

Neg. # 586, Slide # 140

title: Manhattan: Washington Square South - Wooster Street
text:
76 Washington Square South (formerly 290 4th Street) at the S.W. corner of Wooster Street (Washington Square East). This is supposed to be the oldest house now standing on Washington Square. Washington Square South is part of 4th Street as originally laid out. In 1833, when 4th Street absorbed Asylum Street in Greenwich Village, the whole was renumbered from the northwest end at Gansevoort and 13th Streets. About 1860 the section from MacDougal to Wooster Streets was given its own house numbers as Washington Square South. October 4, 1928.

P. L. Sperr.

The vacant lot will be fenced about, and later used for tennis courts. June, 1925.

title: Manhattan: Washington Square South - Sullivan Street
text:
47-40 Washington Square South, west from Sullivan to Macdougal Streets. These houses will be drastically remodeled about 1923. At the time of this picture Sullivan Street had only recently been cut through the block from West Third Street, thus causing the demolition for 48-49 Washington Square. 49 Washington Square had been the Westmore Home for Fallen and Friendless Girls (established 1881).

Notice the old horse-car track alongside the more modern electric track.

title: Manhattan: Washington Square South - West Broadway
text:
Washington Square South (from left to right), south side, west from but not including West Broadway, to and including Thompson Street, showing the clearance at the S.E. corner of Thompson Street created by the demolition of Nos. 60, 59 and 58, and No. 61 (3½-story house with white doorway) which is the Alan Seeger House. Also shown (right) is Thompson Street, west side, from Washington Square South, to and including West 3rd Street, with a portion of the Sixth Ave. Elevated line on the latter, and the Judson Memorial Church (Baptist) at the S.W. corner of Thompson Street. Note the Alan Seeger Memorial Tree as seen from a point in Washington Square Park.

1936.

W.P.A. Photo.
Federal Writers Project.

Supplement:
No. 61 is commonly known as the House of Genius in which lived Theodore Dreiser and Eugene O'Neill, besides the individuals enumerated above. The former lays part of the plot of his famous novel "The Genius" in this house. In the Fall of 1939, this structure is being vacated as the owner finds continued operation unprofitable, and various plans are being suggested.

title: Manhattan: Washington Square South - West Broadway
text:
68-76 Washington Square South, from West Broadway to Wooster Street at the S.E. corner of the Square, inclusive.
Originally Washington Square South (West 4th Street) was one long block from Thompson to Wooster Streets; but early in the 1870's the old Laurens Street, which ended at Amity Street (West 3rd), was widened, renamed South Fifth Avenue, and cut through to Washington Square. Later it took the present name of West Broadway, the street below Canal Street with which it happened to coincide.
Our Lady of Mercy Chapel (Roman Catholic) is at 70 Washington Square. 71 Washington Square is a new apartment building erected about 1927 on the site of old 71 and 72, 4-story houses. The garage adjoining it was built around 1913.
The building on the S.E. corner of Wooster and 4th Streets, with the flag flying, is a loft building erected around 1895. Since 1925 it has been taken over by New York University.
May 24, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Washington Square West - 4th Street
text:
Washington Square West, from 4th Street to Washington Place, showing the twin 7-story buildings of the Holley Hotel in the center of the block. This is one of the three original Knott hotels, and was named after Alexander J. Holley, of whom a bust has stood in Washington Square since 1890.
The 3-story building on the corner of Washington Place, a part of the hotel, will be torn down in 1930 and replaced by the 16-story Holley Chambers. The three houses in the southern half of the block will also be replaced by a tall apartment building.
December 28, 1927.

title: Manhattan: Washington Street - Rector Street
text:
Washington Street (thru the center, from fore to background) south from Rector Street (foreground, not seen) to Battery Park. Beyond the latter is the Upper Bay and Governor's Island. At the right is the new Downtown Athletic Club towering the partially constructed United Fruit Bldg. To the left on Greenwich Street are the rears of the Cunard, the Bowling Green and the Washington Buildings. The low roofed rookeries between these thoroughfares are occupied mainly by Syrians and Greeks and form one of Manhattans national sectors.

July 30, 1930.
Views 1 and 2

P.L. Sperr

text:

title: Manhattan: Washington Street - Leroy Street
text:
Washington Street, east side, from Leroy (right) to Morton (left) Streets, as viewed northeastward from the clearance, where the elevated roadbed of the New York Central Railroad will be erected.

The York Motor Express Co. occupy a 1 story garage (No. 599-601) Washington Street) at the N.E. corner of Leroy Street.

Adjoining same is the 5 story building (No. 603-7) housing the Stafford Ink Co.

A similar, tho narrower structure separates this from the 9 story building (No. 611-15) at the S.E. corner of Morton Street.

The U. S. Medical Supply Department of the U. S. Army is given as the occupant of the latter.

View No. 1 is inclusive, showing all of these features; No's 2 and 3, various details.

December 3, 1931
Views: 1-2-3

P. L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: Washington Street - Barrow Street
text:
Washington Street, north from Barrow Street, showing mainly the cleared west side of this thoroughfare. Upon same will be erected the elevated roadbed of the New York Central Railroad that extends from the St. Johns Park Freight Terminal and continues up the west side of Manhattan.

The low buildings to the left are on the north side of Christopher Street, lying between Washington and Weehawken (extreme left) Streets.

View No. 3 emphasizes this feature mainly. The tall smokestacks are those of the Beadleston and Woerz Brewery (q.v.) which was razed in the Summer of 1938.

Returning to View 1, one sees at the right margin a portion of the U. S. Government building listed as the Appraisers Stores.

The Everards Storage Warehouse is to the north, same being the 12 story structure bearing No. 667 Washington Street and located at the N.E. corner of W. 10th Street.

title: Manhattan: Watts Street - Sullivan Street
text:
Watts Street, easternmost block, east from Sullivan Street (future Sixth Avenue Extension). Between Thompson Street and West Broadway there is a triangular plaza where Watts and Broome Streets fuse. The south side of this plaza now has Broome Street house numbers, although originally it must have held the first six odd numbers on Watts Street.
The entire south side of Watts Street from Sullivan to Thompson Streets is about to be demolished in the process of building the new subway and extending Sixth Avenue southward.
1926.

title: Manhattan: Weehawken Street - Christopher Street
text:
Weehawken Street, west side, between Christopher and West 10th Street, showing the rear of the building bearing No. 393 West Street. This is popularly supposed to be the oldest structure in Manhattan. It rests on the site of the Weehawken Market, and which in turn succeeded to a portion of the old State Prison of 1797-1829. For further information, see, the New York Times of, Sunday, August 22, 1937. also : N.Y. Eve Post June 15, 1930.
About 1939
Alexander Alland, photo

title: Manhattan: Weehawken Street - 10th Street (West)
text:
1. Weehawken Street, adjoining and south of the S.W. corner of West 10th Street, showing buildings bearing Nos. 393 to 388 West Street. These structures have no Weehawken Street numbers. They are built on the former site of the Weehawken Market which was erected subsequent to the demolition of the old New York State Prison. This street being cut through at that time. The Prison occupied this, and the surrounding area between 1797 and 1829; this being its south western section. See the New York Times, Sunday, August 22, 1937 for further information. March 8, 1929. P. L. Sperr.

2. The same. May 12, 1927. P. L. Sperr.

3. A detail showing the external stairway to the upper floor of building bearing No. 393 West Street. About 1936. Gift of Dr. Michael Wishengrad, A.R.P.S.

The Prison occupied this, and the surrounding area between 1797 and 1829; this being its south western section. See the New York Times, Sunday, August 22, 1937 for further information. March 8, 1929. P. L. Sperr.

2. The same. May 12, 1927. P. L. Sperr.

3. A detail showing the external stairway to the upper floor of building bearing No. 393 West Street. About 1936. Gift of Dr. Michael Wishengrad, A.R.P.S.

title: Manhattan: West Broadway - Franklin Street
text:
West Broadway, at the S. W. corner of Franklin Street (right), viewing across the open area identified as Finn Square, formed at the point of convergence by West Broadway and Varick Street. Ordinarily this location would be a portion of the latter thoroughfare, as it is apparently a continuation. The fact remains that both sides of the Square are classified as being West Broadway.

A one story tax-payer (No. 137 Franklin Street) is shown upon the former site of the Fifth Ward Museum. This was operated by an individual named "Riley". On exhibition there, included with other incunabula was the statue of William Pitt. The New York Historical Society possesses same today.

The New York Sun published a drawing of the old Hotel building in their series "Old New York in Pictures". This was No. 169, titled, "The Fifth Ward Museum Hotel in 1864".
The large building bearing the various signs is No. 139 Franklin Street, and adjoins the corner.

title: Manhattan: West Broadway - Houston Street (West)
text:
479, 477 West Broadway (formerly 77, 79 South Fifth Avenue), adjoining the vacant S.E. corner of Houston Street, seen from the rear. These two frame houses, which are faced with brick, probably date back to the days before Laurens Street was converted into South Fifth Avenue by widening it, at the expense of the west side, and extending it from Amity Street (West 3rd) to Washington Square South. This took place in 1870; but this type of house was being built in this part of town fifty years before then, and even earlier.

June 3, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: West Broadway - Bleecker Street

title: Manhattan: West End Avenue - 81st Street (West)
text:
West End Avenue, at, adjoining and south of the S. W. corner of West 81st Street (right), showing four of the five frame shacks at this location. These bore No's 339 to 331 inclusive. To the right is the brick wall of 306 West 81st Street, a structure erected subsequent to 1891 and replacing a frame building. Bromleys Atlas of that year shows the last of the West End shacks; their edition, 1897, disclosing the Avenue frontage cleared.

Various authorities have located this view as being the N. E. corner of Fifth Avenue and 81st Street. The New York Post of October 1932 published same in their gravure section. The Collection of J. Clarence Davies at the Museum of the City of New York has a copy. The Fifth Avenue Bank during its Centennial week exhibited a copy from the Robert Friedenberg Collection.

Brown Brothers, photographers, whose imprint appears on the back of this, gave the location as Amsterdam Avenue and 81st Street.

The original is by H. N. Tiemann (stamp at bottom) and whose successors operate a photographic establishment at No. 176 Lexington Avenue. He is credited by the New York Sun in their series of "Old New York Pictures," of which this is No. 50, appearing on November 15, 1928. The location given there is accurate. The writer verified same with the records at their place of business.

H. N. Tiemann, Photo
Brown Brothers

1894

On the S.W. corner of Amsterdam Avenue and 103rd Street may be seen the Hotel Clendening, originally the old Castle Hotel and Castle Apartments of the late 1890's, and known around 1910 as the Kenesaw Apartments.

title: Manhattan: Houston Street (West - Broadway
text:
W. Houston Street, south side, at and east across Broadway. 13-11 West Houston Street, adjoining the building at the S.W. corner, is being demolished. No. 9-1, the corner building, will shortly follow.

The bend in Houston Street at Broadway -- West Houston Street joins Broadway at right angles, but East Houston does not -- is really the meeting place of the original Houston Street and of North Street, after the letter was extended west from the Bowery. Houston Street absorbed North Street in 1833, and the whole was renumbered west from the East River. The division of Houston Street into East and West did not come until after the absorption of Hammersley Street in 1858.

September 19, 1929.

P. L. Sperr.

A branch of the municipal subway is under construction under Houston Street itself and under the site of the houses which used to be on the south side. This picture shows an intermediate stage of construction by the "cut-and-cover" method. This branch will not be opened till 1936. This view shows almost all of the original Houston Street. The dark building in the background is 604-608 Broadway, where Houston Street met the western end of North Street (now East Houston Street). East Houston Street does not make a right angle with Broadway, but bends a little north.

June 15, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Houston Street (West - Hancock Street
text:

Every single building visible in this picture is to be demolished the following year, when work begins on the new Independent (Municipal) Subway and the extension of Sixth Avenue south from its original beginning at Carmine Street and Minetta Lane. The Houston Street branch of the new subway will curve under the north side of Houston Street, where the tenement houses and moving picture theatre appear in this picture.

1926.

title: Manhattan: Houston Street (West - West Street
text:
Houston Street (formerly Hammersley Street), east from and including West Street. Hammersley Street was one of the group of parallel east-west streets laid out in the Trinity Church Farm, and met the western end of the original Houston Street just east across the line between the Trinity Farm and the West Bayard Farm, at the southern end of Bedford Street (q.v.).

In 1858 this street lost its own name and was absorbed by Houston Street. At that time, and thereafter till the redistricting of 1917, it served as the southern boundary of the Ninth Ward, which was roughly identical with Greenwich Village.

In 1930 these buildings at and east of West Street will be demolished for the site of the new St. John's Park Freight Terminal (see West Street). Houston Street, from West to Washington Streets, will be permanently closed and incorporated with the site of the freight station.

March 6, 1929.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: West Street - Battery Place
text:
CAPTION FOR PICTURE

A novel example of the set-back design of one building helping its neighbor----the tall downtown athletic club in the center and the thirty one story office building known as 21 West St. at the right, showing how the office structure was enabled to enjoy southern exposure on both the Washington st. and West St. sides of the site by virtue of the adjoining club building being set back from its building line at the street level. 'thus the office Building enjoys the unique position of an isolated structure with its Washington, Morris and West St. Frontages affording it light from all four directions. The Building at the left is the Whitehall Building at Battery Place.

No date.

text:
West Street, east side, from Dey (right) to Fulton (left) Streets. In the background are the towering structures identified with lower Broadway at Wall Street. title: Manhattan: West Street - Fulton Street
text:
West Street, east side, from Fulton (right) to Vesey (left) Street's, showing the westerly portions of the Washington Market, a municipal structure that occupies the entire block east to Washington Street. Erected in 1883-4 on the site of the Washington Market of 1812, the Buttermilk Market of 1792, and the Bear Market of 1771, it is to be improved according to an extensive historical article in the Times of October 27, 1940.

In the background are the spires of the Woolworth and the Municipal Buildings.

H. N. Tiemann, photo
Gift of Urbrock Collection

title: Manhattan: West Street - Spring Street
text:
New Freight Terminal Dedicated. The New York Central's New St. John's Park freight Terminal in Spring Street on the West Side of New York City, was formally dedicated June 28th with officials of the State, city and railroad present at exercises. The new freight terminal is part of the railroad's West Side improvement project. Above is a view of the elevated tracks on "Death Avenue" (Eleventh Avenue), taken from the North Side of the Terminal. The new development eliminates in part, the Dangers of "Death Avenue".

6/28/34

title: Manhattan: West Street - Spring Street
text:
New Freight Terminal dedicated
The New York Central's New St. John's Park Freight Terminal in Spring Street on the West Side, was formally dedicated June 28th with officials of the state, city and railroad present at the exercises. The new freight terminal is part of the railroad's West Side improvement project. The next step is the reconstruction of the yards in West 30th st. The above photo shows the special train carrying dignitaries officials and engineers, as it entered the new terminal for the ceremonies.

6/28/34

title: Manhattan: West Street - Spring Street
text:
New Freight Terminal Dedicated.
The New York Central's New St. John's Park Freight Terminal in
Spring Street on the West Side of New York City, was formally dedicated June 28th with officials of the State, city and railroad present at the exercises. The new freight terminal is part of the railroad's West Side improvement project. The above photo shows eight tracks entering St. John's Park terminal with present facilities for about 150 cars. Rolling Steel doors at entrance are Guarded by red and green signal lights. This building occupies three city blocks at present, and will later be extended four hundred feet, making it with the extension and the addition of nine stories more in height on one of the largest buildings in the world.

CREDIT LINE (ACME)  6/28/34

Whitehall Street, north from South Street (right, not shown). This locale is known as South Ferry (the photographer's vantage point), and Battery Park and State St. are on the left. In the center is the old Produce Exchange between Water and Pearl Streets. This site was later improved with the formidable Army Building. Across the roof appears the spire of Trinity Church, while to the right is the top St. Paul's Chapel.
1860's

(2)
An earlier view of the corner building which was the former Eastern Hotel and known as such, since 1856. The original building was erected prior to 1790, when it was purchased by John B. Coles for 350 pounds. In 1822 it became the Eagle Hotel, a tavern. Much of the frame work is solid mahogany, having been imported as ballast by the original owner, a sea captain. At the time of purchase by Coles, who used it as a warehouse, it was 3-stories high.

October 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Manhattan: William Street - Beaver Street
text:
22 William Street, east side, from Beaver Street to Exchange Place, showing the lower portion of the 59-storied City Bank Farmers Trust Co. occupying this entire block and known by the above location. This view is in a southward direction and shows fortress like square structure of the National City Bank in the foreground which also borders on this street. Photographers vantage point was the 70-storied Bank of Manhattan Building, at No. 40 Wall Street, which permitted a perspective of the confluence of the East and North Rivers, at the Upper Bay; the latter with Governors Island therein. This set of 3 views shows different portions of this new edifice.

March 24, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: William Street - Pine Street
text:
William Street (thru the center), north from Pine Street (foreground, street level not seen) showing roof tops of buildings in the downtown area of Manhattan. The small structure in the center (pitched roof) is the Liverpool, London and Globe Insurance Co. Bldg. It is on the easterly side of this thoroughfare and occupies the frontage from Liberty Street to Maiden Lane. Opposite same is another low building; the Montauk Building which occupies the William Street side and frontage of the block mainly utilized by the Federal Reserve Bank. The photographer in all instances is viewing northward from No. 40 Wall Street.

March 9, 1933.
Views 2&3: March 24, 1933

P.L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: William Street - Pine Street
text:
William Street (right), north from Pine Street (foreground of No. 1, street level not seen), showing mainly the roof top of the irregular quadrangular Federal Reserve Bank that abuts on Liberty and Nassau Streets and Maiden Lane. The low (8 story) Montauk Bldg. occupies the William Street side of this block. On the easterly side and opposite the latter is the Liverpool London & Globe Insurance Co. Bldg. This building has a pitched roof and is clearly discernible in View No. 2. The Royal Insurance Co. Building is to the north of the latter, having a curved corner outline. Shown in the foreground and nearly obscuring the Federal Reserve Bank is the New York Mutual Life Insurance Co. Bldg. The photographer's vantage point is the structure at No. 40 Wall Street and from which he views northward.

March 9, 1933
Views 1 and 2

P.L. Sperr

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 59th Street
text:
York Avenue (Avenue A), north from 59th Street. The dark body overhead is Queensboro Bridge.
On the west side, from 60th to 61st Streets, is a garage built since 1920. The gas tanks are in the two blocks 61st to 62nd and 62nd to 63rd Streets; opposite the second one, on the N.E. corner of 62nd Street, is the pumping station and tower of the Consolidated Gas Company. Behind and to the right of these may be seen the malting plant of George Ehret, east of York Avenue between 63rd and 64th Streets; it will be demolished in October 1930. Demolition of buildings on the east side of the Avenue, from 68th to 71st Streets, has not yet taken place.
At the time of this picture the name of the Avenue, north from this point, is about to be changed to York Avenue. The old Avenue A house numbers will still be used after the change.
March 5, 1928.

New York Edison Company Collection.

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 63rd Street
text:
York Avenue (at time shown, Avenue A), east side, from 63rd to 64th Streets, and east of the Avenue to 67th Street, showing Rockefeller Institute.

The American Malting Company plant (formerly Neidlinger, Schmidt & Company), from 63rd to 64th Streets, will later pass into the hands of George Ehret's brewing company, and finally be demolished in October 1930.

The buildings of the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research (incorporated 1901) are shown as follows in this picture: The chimney of the new power house, just completed on the N.W. corner of Exterior Street (Marie Curie Avenue since 1935) and 64th Street, shows above the malting plant in the foreground. Then comes the Main Hospital, built about 1909, its long axis nearly in line with 65th Street (which is not cut through east of the Avenue). Then the original laboratory, dedicated May 11, 1906, stands facing 66th Street and the Avenue. To the left of the picture Laboratory No. 2 is shown under construction, and behind it the chimney of the original power house built in 1906.

In the right background, through 63rd Street, may be seen the East River, Blackwell's (now Welfare) Island, and Queens. This part of Avenue A, north of 59th Street, will not be called York Avenue till late in 1928.

Early 1916.

James Suydam, Photographer.
Gift of E. M. Jenks.

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 64th Street
text:
York Ave., at the N.E. corner of 64th Street, showing several of the building's comprising the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research.

Under the present organizations the departments maintained are: Pathology, Bacteriology, Physical and Pathological Chemistry, Physiology, comparative Zoology, Pharmacology and experimental Therapeutics.

It co-operates with many other bodies in practical investigation. A hospital under the direction of the Institute is maintained where the different diseases that effect mankind are given closest scientific study.

About 1922.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 64th Street
text:
York Avenue, west side, 64th to 65th Streets, inclusive, seen from east of York Avenue, the clearing left by demolition of the old malting plant of George Ehret. The building for private patients, on the S.W. corner of 64th Street, is the newer part (around 1902) of the Flower Hospital. The apartment buildings from 64th to 65th Streets were built around 1905 where a lumber yard and a stone yard used to be. December 22, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 64th Street
text:
Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, east of York Avenue from 64th to 67th Streets, not showing the power plant at 64th Street and Marie Curie Avenue (formerly Exterior Street).
Rockefeller Institute was incorporated in 1901. The old laboratory, shown in the center, with its long axis north and south, was dedicated May 11, 1906. The Main Hospital, on the right, was built around 1910 or a little earlier. Immediately north of the old laboratory is Laboratory No. 2, which is shown in the view of York Avenue from 63rd Street and north, early 1916. Above No. 2 and at right angles to it is the newest laboratory, built in 1930.
June 30, 1931.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 64th Street
text:
York Avenue, from 64th to 67th Streets, seen from 63rd Street east of York Avenue. The clearing in the foreground, where the Ehret malting plant has just been demolished, will be seeded with grass and fenced around; and 64th Street east of York Avenue, where the truck is seen, will be permanently closed.
On the west side may be seen 429 East 64th Street, built around 1905, 1215-29 York Avenue, from 65th to 66th Streets, built around 1927, and 1233-35-37-39-41 Avenue A (now York Avenue) from 66th to 67th Streets. The trees east of the Avenue above 64th Street are on the grounds of the Rockefeller Institute, which acquired the property about 1902.
December 22, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 66th Street
text:
Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, east of York Avenue at 66th Street, showing the original laboratory (to the left) dedicated May 11, 1906, the little Isolation Building, and the Main Hospital (erected around 1910). In the right background part of the Queensboro Bridge can be seen. The Avenue of trees leading up to the old laboratory follows the line of 66th Street, which at this point roughly corresponds to the old Schermerhorn Lane. The Rockefeller Institute was incorporated in 1901, and bought the old Schermerhorn property shown in this picture. July 31, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 66th Street
text:
York Avenue, east side, north from 66th Street, showing the New York Hospital -- Cornell Medical College, nearing completion, from 68th to 71st Streets. The grounds and part of the newest laboratory of the Rockefeller Institute are shown in the foreground and to the right. The building under construction looks like an addition to the Rockefeller Institute but is not; it is a wing of the New York Hospital on the north side of 68th Street. Early 1931.

Wurts Brothers

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 66th Street
text:

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 66th Street
text:
(1)
York Avenue (Avenue A), east side, north from 66th Street. In the right foreground are the grounds of the Rockefeller Institute, which extend up to 67th Street. The block above, where the Williams stone yards used to be around 1890-1900, is a children's playground.
On the N.W. corner of 68th Street is the old Central, an apartment house built in 1902. East of it, on 68th Street, are the stables and garage, and then the main plant, of the Central Brewing Company, erected around 1900-02. In this block, prior to about 1895, was Jones Woods Coliseum, known in its last few years as Empire City Coliseum.
From 69th to 70th Streets may be seen old 1294-1304 Avenue A, tenements built prior to 1910. From 70th to 71st Streets are houses built, in their original form, from about 1890-95, and used for some years as cigar factories.
February 13, 1928.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)
York Avenue, east side, north from 66th Street, the same view as the preceding. The lamp post in the left foreground, in both pictures, is on the N.W. corner of 66th Street.
Rockefeller Institute now has the entire property east of York Avenue up to 68th Street. Notice their fence, with its stone posts. The building to the north is the newest laboratory, built in 1930.
The New York Hospital and Cornell Medical College takes up the entire three blocks from 66th to 71st Streets, and east to Exterior Street, which is shortly to be rechristened Marie Curie Avenue. The Bio-Chemistry and Pharmacy Wing is located on the very N.W. corner of 68th Street where the old Century apartment house used to stand.
Compare these two views with Wurts Brothers' view of the same scene early in 1931.

March 5, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

THE NEW YORK
PUBLIC LIBRARY

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 66th Street
text:
Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, east of York Avenue from 66th to 67th Streets. From right to left the buildings are: part of the original laboratory (1906), Laboratory No. 2 (1916) and the new laboratory, nearing completion, its south side in line with 67th Street, which has been permanently closed east of York Avenue. In the foreground are gardens and shelters for women and children. July 31, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 65th Street
text:
York Avenue, east side, from 67th to 65th Streets, showing buildings of the Rockefeller Foundation for Medical Research. On the north (left) is Laboratory No. 2 (1916), and joined onto it part of the original 2-story Animal House (1906) with a later enlargement. Another laboratory will be built north of these buildings, in 1930. The building in the center is the original laboratory, dedicated May 11, 1906; between that and the Main Hospital (about 1910) the 2-story Isolation Building is barely visible. The chimney in the right background is part of the new Power House built late in 1915. September 17, 1927.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 67th Street
text:
Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, York Avenue, east side, at 67th Street. The new laboratory is nearing completion. Its south side is in line with 67th Street, which was permanently closed (about 1926) east of York Avenue. In the right foreground is shown part of the old playground which used to occupy the block from 67th to 68th Streets. The construction beginning at the extreme left of this picture is on the north side of 68th Street.
July 31, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 67th Street
text:
York Avenue, east side, from 67th to 68th Streets, showing the playground of the Lenox Hill Neighborhood Association, with a new laboratory building under construction for the Rockefeller Institute, in the right background, and the new New York Hospital and Cornell Medical College under construction on the north side of 68th Street. This playground, which is now about to give way to tennis courts, has occupied this site since around 1920; around 1885 to 1905 this was the stone yard of B. A. & G. N. W. Williams.
July 31, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 67th Street
text:
York Avenue (Avenue A), west side, from 67th to 68th Streets, showing a skating rink and the old cigar factory, on the S.W. corner of 68th Street, where Robt. Burns cigars used to be made. It was built around 1905, and now belongs to Seidenberg and Company. It is shortly to be demolished, and around the same time the rink will be converted into tennis courts.
As late as 1902 these plots were occupied by a stone yard, probably belonging to the B. & G. Williams stone yard across the Avenue. February 13, 1928.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 67th Street
text:
York Avenue, east side, from 67th to 71st Streets, showing construction of New York Hospital and Cornell Medical Center, and playground of Lenox Hill Neighborhood Association, on S.E. corner of 68th Street, which is shortly to be made over into tennis courts.
July 31, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 68th Street
text:
York Avenue at 68th Street, from clearing on N.E. corner, showing demolition of the Seidenberg factory building, which used to be the Robt. Burns Cigar factory; it was built around 1905. Adjoining it on York Avenue an old skating rink has been made over into tennis courts.
The view is from the clearing where the "Central" apartment house stood and where the new New York Hospital will rise. The little building on the N.W. corner will stay.

August 26, 1929.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 68th Street
text:
(1)
York Avenue (Avenue A) at N.E. corner of 68th Street, showing "The Central", an apartment house built in 1902, and about to be demolished.
Prior to about 1895 this block was occupied by Jones Woods Coliseum, known in its last few years as Empire City Coliseum. The name York Avenue was officially adopted late in 1928.
February 13, 1928.

(2)

The new New York Hospital and Cornell Medical College buildings, nearing completion, occupy the land east of York Avenue from 68th to 70th Streets.
On the S.W. corner, adjoining the tennis courts in the foreground, the Seidenberg factory has been demolished.
June 30, 1931.

title: Manhattan: York Avenue - 68th Street
text:
York Avenue (Avenue A), east side, north from 68th Street. The building on the N.E. corner of 68th Street is only slightly in the picture; it is the old "Century" apartment house. 68th to 69th Streets is the old site of Jones Woods Coliseum (to about 1895, known in 1891 as Empire City Coliseum). 1294-1304 Avenue A, from 69th to 70th Streets, were built after 1902. That block used to be Washington Park. From 70th to 71st Streets may be seen the old cigar factories. The white building, from 71st to 72nd Streets, is the new plant of P. Lorillard Company, built since 1920 on the site of the old Clausen malt house. Everything from 68th to 71st Streets is about to be demolished.

February 13, 1928.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Manhattan: Lexington Avenue - 34th Street
text:
Lexington Avenue, east side, north from 34th Street, showing the Packard School at the S.E. corner of East 35th Street and the Protestant Episcopal Church of the Epiphany at the N.E. corner of same.

The Protestant Episcopal Church of the Epiphany will occupy a new church (to be erected) on York Avenue, at the N.W. corner of East 74th Street, after nearly a century at the N.E. corner of Lexington Avenue and East 35th Street. Since the sale of this property (May 1936) to Dr. Charles V. Paterno, a real estate specialist, the congregation has been using the St. Thomas Chapel on East 60th Street as a temporary place of worship. The Reverend Dr. John Wallace Suter Jr. has been the rector since the retirement of the Reverend William T. Crocker in 1933, who had held the position for 30 years. This data was reported in THE NEW YORK SUN of SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 20, 1937.

Dr. Paterno traded this cleared site in 1939 for an apartment building on Central Park South. The new owner is completing a modern apartment house here in June, 1940.

September 30, 1933

P. L. Sperr

title: Queens: 19th Road - Hazen Street
text:
19th Road, north side, between Hazen Street (left) and Nineteenth Ave. (right), just west of an old pumping station. Behind this house is an old cemetery. This is stated to be one of the oldest houses in Newtown, standing in part of town, now Long Island City, on Bowery Bay. This place was erected about 1650 by Harck Siboutsen and left by his son Jacobus to his nephew Abram Lent in 1729. From the Lent family it passed to the Rapelye family. Isaac Rapelye owned and occupied it prior to 1852. See Annals of Newtown by J. Riker for more data.

title: Queens: 19th Road - Hazen Street
text:
19th Road, north side, east from Hazen Street to Nineteenth Avenues, showing in 4 views the Rapelje house. Bowery Bay Cemetery in the rear of the house contains markers of the 18th century for members of the Rapelje, Cornell, Riker, Luyster and other families. Chas. Rapelje (born 1786), purchased in 1830 the farm formerly owned by Daniel Riker. The estate of Chas. Rapelje, subsequent to his death in 1834, was given to his children David P., Isaac C., Catherine M., and Lavina P. Rapelje. The center room of this house was erected by Abraham Rycken who was the son of a first settler. He died in 1770. Daniel Riker who inherited it from his father Jacobus sold it in 1827 to Charles Rapelje. This house stands on the probable site of the Harek Sloutsen house. He settled here in 1650. In 1729 his son Jacobus willed the farm to his nephew Abraham Lent. Further history concerning these families and their properties may be found in the "Annals of Newtown", written by one Riker in 1852.

title: Queens: 19th Road - 19th Avenue
text:
19th Road (Old Bowery Bay Road) north side, between Nineteenth Avenue and 77th Street, showing four views of the Riker-Lent families cemetery. In the background of these views is the Isaac Rapelye farmhouse. History has it that Harck Sieboutsen settled at Poor Bowery about 1658. In 1727 his son Jacobus Krauk (beyd) willed the farm to his nephew Abraham Lent, the youngest son of Ryck the eldest son of Abraham Rycken. Daniel Lent, was the last of the family who resided here. In 1800 Isaac Rapelye purchased the house. Abraham Rycker, son of the first settler died in 1746 in his 91st year. This inscription was on his tombstone, which was standing in 1881. Some members of the family inhumed here are Dr. John Berrien Riker, a personal friend of Geo. Washington and a member of his staff. He was a surgeon during the War of the Revolution; Captain Abraham Riker who died at Valley Forge; Captain Andrew Riker, prominent in the War of 1812; M. McKisson, a member of the family of Gov. Geo. Clinton during the Revolution and a friend of his wife, Louise de Vallimont, a refugee of the French Revolution; Dr. Wm. James McNevin Irish patriot chemist and scholar, his wife, and children; and John Campbell Irish patriot and philanthropist.

March 1923

View 3: June 1925
View 4: May 1929

title: Queens: 20th Road - 33rd Street
text:
20th(Old Bowery Bay) Road, north side, east of 33rd Street, showing at the left foreground the home of George Kouwenhoven. At the right (center of view) is shown the family burial place of the Lawrence and Leverich families. In the background is the home of Peter Luyster. The owner of this farm was William Lawrence from 1700-1732. He was followed by John Leverich in 1732, and William Leverich later, who had possession until 1754. George Kouwenhoven was the owner from 1852-1860. Francis Durye Kouwenhoven erected (or remodeled?) this house in 1857. Harry Puschea Williams who married into the Kouwenhoven family is the present owner of the house. This house, seen in a set of four views, was no longer standing in May 1929.

title: Queens: 20th Road - 42nd Street
text:
(1)
20th Road (Old Bowery Bay Road), north side, east of 42nd Street, showing at the left, on the east side of a carriage path, the site of the Samuel H. Moore house of 1852. The Titus family occupied it from 1891-1896. The early history of this place is, that Samuel Moore purchased in 1684 a farm near the Poor Farm of Wm. Hallett Sr. Joseph Moore, his son, was the next owner followed by John Moore, a brother of Joseph. David, a son of John Moore, was next in line.
May, 1923.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2)
The same, showing a part of the Moore Farm at the left foreground.
May, 1923.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3) and (4)
The same site, showing the gate posts which were removed in April 1925.
March 1923.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: 27th Avenue - 4th Street
text:
27th Ave., south side, east from 4th Street. The Astoria Presbyterian Church, whose congregation was organized in 1846, laid the cornerstone of this church on November 30th of the same year. In 1848 it was dedicated to the service of God; and in 1857 was enlarged. Rev. Stead was at one time its rector. The church was demolished in 1928 and buildings Nos. 4-14 to 4-24 are on the site. However, the Beers Atlas of Long Island does not show a church on this site in 1873.

1922.

Eugene L. Ambruster Collection.

title: Queens: 30th Road - Vernon Boulevard
text:
30th Road, south side, between Vernon Boulevard and 12th Street, showing the General Ebenezer Stevens mansion, also known as the Albert Gallatin House. The two houses shown, formerly comprised one mansion which was cut in two parts and moved apart. The house was built in 1800 and when General Stevens took up his residenoe here he named the place "Mount Napoleon.' The General was a member of the Boston Tea Party and served throughout the Revolutionary War. He died in 1823. His son, Kerby Stevens, married a daughter of Albert Gallatin, United States Secretary of the Treasury under Thomas Jefferson.
Gallatin died in this house in 1849, aged 88.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection  View 1: 1922
  View 2: 1923
Views 3,4: 1925

title: Queens: 32nd Avenue - 54th Street
text:
Thirty-second Ave., at the N.W. corner of 54th Street. Note the above location is for the house of which only the rear is shown. The Cemetery is beyond the house and has a 100 foot frontage on 54th Street, and a 104 foot front on 51st Street (formerly Old Bowery Bay Road). It has a 200 foot depth between these streets. title: Queens: 32nd Avenue - 82nd Street
text: 32nd Avenue and 82nd Street (vantage point). Shown is a general view westward across the farmland of this section of Jackson Heights, before this area was developed into a residential neighborhood, with 2-story brick dwellings predominating. Trains Meadow Road and Old Bowery Road were the thoroughfares traversing this area. The former can be seen running across the face of the view from right to left, beginning where the white house is discernible (right). The vantage point is Old Bowery Road. April, 1923. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: 35th Avenue - Linden Street
text:
Thirty-fifth Ave., at the N.W. corner of Linden Street, showing the Redwood Homestead, which stood originally at 72-76 Grove Street, near Main Street. It later became the home of Benjamin W. Downing who was a school teacher who studied law in his spare time, subsequently opening his office at probably 112 Broadway. He was District Attorney of Queens County in 1864 and for many years thereafter. He was also a Village Trustee and a member of the Board of Education for twenty years, of which he was also at one time president. He moved from Flushing in 1882. This building was moved to this location between 1865 and 1870. In 1922 it was the Jefferson Democratic Club.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

P. L. Sperr

title: Queens: 37th Avenue - Prince Street
text:
(1)
Thirty-seventh Ave. (right), south side, west of Prince Street (formerly Garden Street), showing Hamilton Hall at the S.W. corner. This building was erected in 1803 at the corner of Main and Locust Streets at a cost of $1250. It then belonged to St. George Episcopal Church. title: Queens: 37th Avenue - Prince Street
text:
37th Ave., at and adjoining the N.W. corner of Prince St. In the foreground is a view of the Reformed Church of Flushing. The congregation was organized in June 1842; the corner stone laid on August 16, 1843; and the edifice dedicated on September 10, 1844. The Rev. A. Gordon was its first pastor. The building was demolished in 1925. Note: this building was not designated as a church in the Realty Atlas of Queens for 1891. The cost of the edifice was twelve thousand dollars. It was enlarged in 1859. In 1925 a garage occupied the site of this church. A new structure was erected in 1892 at the corner of Amity and Bowne Sts.

Views: 1-3 1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: 38th Avenue - Union Street
text:
38th Ave. (Lincoln St., also Ailanthus Place), south side, east of Union St., showing in the right foreground No. 197 38th Ave., owned by Chris Louvere in 1873; next is the First Congregational Church; and beyond it, at the S. E. corner of Bowne St. and 38th Ave., is the M. B. Parsons Estate. View No. two is the same showing partially the N. W. corner of 38th Ave and Bowne St.; No three shows the west side of Bowne St. viewed northward. The congregation of the church seen in this view was formed in 1851 and the edifice erected in 1856 at a cost of 14,000 dollars on a site donated by the Parsons family. The first church of this congregation was dedicated on January 29, 1852 and stood on the east side of Union St, south of 38th Ave. When the present building was erected, the old one was moved to the rear of it and used as a Sunday School. It has since been abolished.

title: Queens: 40th Avenue - Main Street
text:
Fortieth Ave., south side, between Main and Union Sts., showing in 4 views a private school discontinued in Feb. 1925. This structure, erected in 1827, was incorporated in April of that year. Actual school instructions began in 1828 under the supervision of the Rev. William Augustus Muhlenberg D.D. A female school known as St. Ann's Hall, was opened by John F. Schroeder D.D. and operated as such from 1839 to 1846. Ezra Fairfield removed his Greenbrook School from Morristown N.J. to the Flushing Pavilion in May 1845 and remained for about a year until the removal of Dr. Schroeders' school when he moved in.. From this point this structure became known as the Flushing Institute. Ezra Fairchild was principal in 1845. He was subsequently succeeded by his son Elias.

Jan 1923.
Views 1, 2, 3 and 4.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Queens: 41st Avenue - Union Street
text:
Forty-first Ave. (left) (formerly Madison Street), west from Union Street (seen in the foreground), showing St. Michael's Roman Catholic Church at the N.W. corner. This parish was started in 1826. In 1835 its pastor purchased a house on Liberty Street (later Lincoln Street) for public worship which was twice enlarged. The present structure was erected in 1854 on the site of its first frame edifice which was erected in 1841 on land purchased in the same year. The cornerstone of the present church was laid on June 24, 1854, and the church dedicated October 4, 1856.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: 52nd Street - 39th Avenue
text:
(1)
52nd Street (foreground, formerly Dickinson Street, also Woodside Ave.), adjoining the S.W. corner of 39th Ave. (front of this house; formerly Middleburg Ave. and also Dutch Kills Road), showing a rear view of the John Morrell house, which was destroyed by fire in November 1925. It was erected in the middle of the 18th Century by John Morrell who erected a house and a smithy (forge), on the estate of his father-in-law, John Alburtus. Other owners were John Morrell 1779, John W. Morrell 1852-1860, William Morrell, and Wm. Morgenthaler of New York in 1903.
1922.

title: Queens: 52nd Street - 39th Drive
text:
52nd Street (Astoria Road), east side, in 39th Drive. This building will either be moved or demolished because it is in the line of 39th Drive. This mansion and estate, which belonged to J.A. Merke in 1860 and to G. Windmuller from 1873 to 1891, was still in the family in 1909; and still standing in 1927. In 1909, the estate was bounded on the north by Middleburg Ave., on the east by Woodside Ave., on the west by Astoria Road, and on the south by Jane Sussdorf's Estate and Public School No. 11. This is a set of three views. No. 1 shows the gate entrance at 47 Woodside Ave., while Views No. 2 and 3 show the mansion.

1922.

title: Queens: 55th Drive - 56th Street
text:
55th Drive, north side, between 58th Street (right) and 56th Street (left). Note that 55th Drive when constructed will be in the foreground along the fence. This is the Underhill Covert house. It is said that this house is on or near that of the Pole's house of 1700. The farm was owned by John Dennian. His heirs sold it in 1717 to Richard Hallett, and from his heirs, Tunis Schenck and John R. Schenck purchased it. Subsequently Underhill Covert was the owner. Several of the old barns date back to the early 18th Century. One of the barns is said to be the original homestead of John Dennian who located here in 1662. The occupants bearing the Covert name were Underhill, 1852 to 1860; C.G., 1873; and H., in 1891. The house was demolished in 1931.

March 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: 62nd Drive - 108th Street
text:
62nd Drive (right telegraph poles thereon; viewing northwest) south side, between 108th Street (background) and 110th Street (foreground to be constructed, just east of the barns) showing in three views the Lott farmhouse. Johannes S. Lott, a farmer, lived near Woodhaven. His son Stephen I. Lott was born their in 1799. He married Cornelia Rapelje and sold his property in the town of Jamaica in 1834 and removed to the first mentioned location. He died in Jamaica South, in 1871. His son Abraham Van Siclen Lott was born at Woodhaven in 1829 and married Cornelia De Bovise of Dutch Kills in 1864. About 1869, he and his brother John Henry rented this homestead; his father removing to Jamaica South. title: Queens: 63rd Street - Woodside Avenue
text:
63rd Street, east side, south from Woodside Avenue, showing 4 views of the William Sackett house (tower thereon).  It was erected by him in 1836 on the S.E. corner plot of the above mentioned location about 100 feet south of Hicks Drive which has since been laid out about 50 feet south of Woodside Avenue.  Other owners were A.R. Lawrence 1852, D.G.M. Cotter 1860, J. Hicks 1873, and John J. Hicks in 1882.  In 1853 this area was known as Lawrenceville at a later date Hyatt Heights.  John D. Lymber, a florist, was the occupant in 1925.  E.L.A. states it is on the William Leverich block of 1776.  View No. 4 is taken looking north east from the Long Island Railroad right of way at about 62nd Avenue and Queens Boulevard.  This is the main line and was moved north eastward since 1915 but continues in the same direction one block east of the Sackett house.

title: Queens: 66th Avenue - Fitchett Street
text:
Sixth-sixth Avenue, between Fitchett and Alderton Streets, showing in the four views the homes of Baum (left foreground of view number one), Kinsey (white house just beyond the Baum house), England (midway between the first two mentioned and on the opposite side of the street), and Springsteen's (on the same side of the street as the Kinsey house but beyond it, in view number two). Views three and four show a closeup of the England house and out-buildings. The above named individuals appear as owners on realty maps in 1852. Their descendents have held on as owners to the beginning of the 20th century. The Springsteen family have an original dutch grant of 4 acres in this area dating back to the middle of the 17th century. In 1928, the four acres brought 1,000,000. Edward England Sr. settled here in 1853 in a house, part of which is said to have been used as a hospital for wounded soldiers in the Revolutionary War.

August 1925.

title: Queens: 78th Street - 32nd Avenue
text:
78th Street, west side, 150 feet south of 32nd Avenue, showing the headquarters of the famous "Black Watch" during the War for Independence. It was built more than two centuries ago and during the campaign on Long Island commanding officers of the 42nd Highlanders, it was said, lived here. These views show the original location on Trains Meadow Road, an ancient country road, later obliterated. Eugene L. Armbruster refers to the house as the W. Wright farmhouse and also as the Walker farmhouse. See the "New York Herald-Tribune," March 8, 1936.

1925

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Queens: 82nd Street - 30th Avenue
text:
82nd Street, east side, between 30th and 31st Aves., showing the Duryea-Hazard house. It was erected about 1750 by Judge James Hazard of the Court of Common Pleas. It was subsequently purchased by the Duryea family and remained in the family until it was demolished prior to 1927. If standing in 1938 it would occupy lot four in block 151. This is a set of two views.

--
Arthur White.

title: Queens: 94th Street - 23rd Avenue
text:
94th Street, west side, about 450 feet, north of Twenty-third Avenue, showing four views of the Abraham Rapelye farmhouse and outbuildings. This house was probably erected by Capt. Thomas Hagard shortly after 1724. This farm and the buildings were owned and occupied by members of the Rapelye family from 1787 to 1896. The history of this area is that Thomas Stevenson had a patent in 1651 on the Rev. Francis Doughty farm which lay between the Old Bowery Road and Flushing Bay and south of Mill Creek or as it is also known as Jackson Creek. In 1787 it became the property of Abraham Rapelye. He built a dock on Flushing Bay just south of the mouth of Jackson's Creek which in those days was probably at 96th Street, and south of this house between Old Bowery Bay Rd. and the Hazard tract which was also purchased by Daniel Rapelye. It was later known as Strongs farm; it being the property of Aletta Rapelye Strong. The successive owners that followed were Wm. W. Thomas, Dr. Oliver Jones of Cold Spring Harbor,and the Navahoe Realty Company. The Doughty house stood on the shore of Flushing Bay on a lane made by Dr. Adrian Van der Douck. It was the house of the Rapelye, Remsen and Strong families and was located at or near the present site of the Strong residence. The wing of the Rapelye house collapsed in November 1933 and the
building was demolished in March 1934.

March 1923

title: Queens: 94th Street - Ditmars Boulevard
text:
94th Street, east side, south of Ditmars Boulevard, showing in four views the J. I. Rapelye farmhouse of 1852. View one shows partially the above mentioned street which was originally known as Old Bowery Road. This house was demolished in May 1929. In 1908 it stood directly in the center of 95th Street (old 38th Street) about 208 ft. south of Ditmars Boulevard. This house faces north and was owned by A. Rapelye, 1860; C. P. Harris, 1873-1891; and C. H. Harris in 1896. Across Jackson Mill Pond on the east side of 94th Street, north of this house was located the T. B. Jackson house and mill. Samuel Fish, son of Nathan Fish became the owner in 1715. In 1724 he purchased the adjoining mill from the heirs of Jesse Kip. His son John (1719-1793) succeeded to the paternal estate and mill at Fish Point. His daughters Anna (b 1748) and Sarah (b 1762) married Jacob and William Palmer respectively. Their brother Samuel (b 1752- d 1834), a bachelor, owned the paternal estate.

Views 2&3: March 1925
View 4: March 1923
View 1: May 1926.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Queens: West Drive - Alston Place
text:
The old Dutch colonial house at the corner of West Drive and Alston Pl. in Douglas Manor, Douglaston, New York, now owned by Mr. and Mrs. L. Kelville Larson was built in 1735 by Cornelius Van Wyck. He was the eldest son of Johannes Van Wyck whose father, an earlier Cornelius Van Wyck, was one of the patentees of Mid-Wout, having emigrated there from Holland in 1660.
In 1705, 125 acres of land south and east of the present house at West Drive and Alston Pl., was purchased from Richard and Sarah Cornell by Johannes Van Wyck. His brother Theodorus had already acquired land on King's Point. Johannes had three sons and four daughters and became a Justice of the Provincial Courts.
When Justice Johannes died in 1734, the property was inherited by his eldest son Cornelius who had married Mary Hicks, daughter of Judge Isaac Hicks. Cornelius and Mary prospered, added to the original farm, and until Cornelius' death in 1759, lived in the house they had built twenty-four years earlier.
Cornelius left three sons - Stephan, Cornelius II, and Gilbert. Stephan, the eldest, inherited the house and flourishing farm. Cornelius II had the misfortune of being captured by the British in a surprise raid on Flushing and was confined aboard one of the notorious prison ships anchored in the Wallabout (Bay). He died soon after his release from the effects of a year's confinement under horrible conditions. Stephan fell heir to the appointment as delegate to the Continental Congress, to which office his deceased brother Cornelius had been elected in June, 1776.
Gilbert Van Wyck, the youngest of the three brothers, was a Tory and served as a justice of the peace for King George III until the end of the war when he joined the Tory exodus to Nova Scotia. His cousins Captain Thomas Hicks and Captain Thomas Van Wyck, who had remained loyal to the crown, went with him.
However, Major Cornelius Van Wyck, Gilbert's son, fought with the Continental army for the duration of the war since he did not share his father's political views.
Consequently, in 1789, Major Cornelius Van Wyck inherited the house and land jointly with his cousin Stephan, son of the Cornelius-of-the-prison-ship. Stephan was not interested in farming and sold his interest to Major Cornelius who thus became the last Van Wyck owner of the house his grandfather built in 1735. The Major held the property for another thirty years and in 1819 sold it to Wynant Van Zandt, one of the early merchants and an alderman of old New York City.
Van Zandt, who had previously purchased the adjoining 120 acres to the north now commonly known as "The Point" area of Douglas Manor, began in 1819 the construction of a large manor house in "The Point" section. It is assumed that his family occupied the Van Wyck house during the construction of the new manor house. In fact, among several interesting items found in the chimney place of the old house during some restoration work were two copy books signed by Charlotte Van Zandt, presumably one of Van Zandt's four daughters. In addition they had eleven sons so could well use the large new manor house.
In 1835 George Douglas purchased the Manor house and the 120 acres on the point. After his death in 1862 his son William inherited the property. During the tenure of the Douglas family the old Van Wyck house was used as a guest house or was rented to friends. One such was Dr. Edward Livingston Trudeau, who founded the famous tuberculosis sanitarium at Saranac Lake, New York. Trudeau married in 1871 Charlotte Beare whose father was rector of Zion Episcopal Church in Douglaston for 45 years, from 1843 to 1888. The Beare family were close friends of the Douglas' and when Trudeau and Charlotte Beare were married, William Douglas gave the wedding reception in the Manor House. After a honeymoon of several months in Europe, the couple rented the old Van Wyck house and lived there for the first year of their married life.
In 1906 the entire property, including the Manor House and the old Van Wyck house, was sold to the Douglas Manor Company. The Manor House became an inn and the old Van Wyck house became the first home of the Douglaston Club. In 1921 the Douglaston Club took possession of the Manor House and it is still being used as the community social and recreational center. The old Van Wyck house was bought by Mr. and Mrs. E.M. Wicht who did away with some structures which had been added when the house was used as a club and restored the old house to its original foundation. In 1933 the house was purchased by Mr. and Mrs. L. Keville Larson who are still in residence.

June 1965

C. Manley De Bevoise
51-05 Browvale Lane
Little Neck, N.Y.

title: Queens: 144th Street - 89th Avenue
text:
144th Street (left), at the N. E. corner of 89th Avenue, showing the Reverend Abraham Keteltas house of 1780. This house was for a while occupied by General Skinner of the British forces during the Revolution, whose daughter Gertrude was married to Captain Meredith here on July 14, 1780. Other owners of the house were: Samuel Judd--1839-1846; the Samuel Judd Estate--1860-1873; Colonel A. A. Degrauw--1873-1896. The house originally stood on the north side of Jamaica Avenue, between 144th and 145th Streets, before it was moved to its present location; it then had wings.

title: Queens: 144th Street - 89th Avenue
text:
144th Street (left), at the N.E. corner of Eighty-ninth Ave., showing the residence of Abraham Kettletas 1780, or that of S. Judd of 1846. The wings of this structure were removed prior to moving this structure from its original site in Jamaica Ave.

Rev. Abraham Kettletas, born in New York in 1732, was a Presbyterian Minister, who came to Jamaica on or about the year 1759. He had no pastorate, but occupied a farm near the site of this house. During the Revolution the British took possession of his property and defaced his home. In 1799 there is a probability that the house of the late William Kettletas burned to the ground and that S. Judd erected the present structure.

title: Queens: 155th Street - 41st Avenue
text:

Armbruster, the Collector, states that this house was moved from its old site in 1923 because it was in the line of 155th Street. Originally this house faced north on Broadway; it now faces west on 155th Street.

title: Queens: 160th Street - Archer Avenue
text:
160th Street, north from Archer Avenue, near the Long Island Railroad tracks. On the left is the John Everett house, three stories high. It was also known as the Continental Hall, where the Jamaica Odd Fellows used to meet.

View 2 shows the east side of the street, the house with the peak-roof having been owned by H.C. Ham in 1873. On the left, the peak-roof house with the stores built in front of it, was owned by Ben Everett, and by J. B. Remsen in 1873.

View 3 shows the H. C. Ham house, at the N. E. corner of Archer Avenue, after half the building has been cut away when Archer Avenue (right) was cut through. It is now being used as a store for new and second hand building materials. To the left of the drive-in is the Ben Everett house. 160th Street was formerly Washington Street.

Views 1, 2: Eugene L Armbruster Collection 1924
View 3: P. L. Sperr March 30, 1932

title: Queens: 164th Street - Jamaica Avenue
text:
164th St., west side, north of Jamaica Ave., showing in a set of three views the First Presbyterian Church of Jamaica. The parish was organized in 1662. The site of the old stone meeting house was south west of the present location (then on the north side of Jamaica Ave. between 163rd and 164th Sts.) near the head of Union Hall St. This church and the parsonage were moved to the present location in 1920. In 1814 this edifice was erected near the old site but on the north side of Jamaica Ave. between 163rd and 164th sts., at a cost of 9,51O.74. The cornerstone was laid on June 9th, 1813, by John Richard and the edifice dedicated on Jan. 18,1814. About 1870 the high pulpit and bay pews were removed. The spire of this church rose 102 ft. from the ground. However it was weakened by the September gale of 1821 thereby necessitating the removal of 27 ft. of it. The structure was again enlarged in 1846 and the interior renovated in 1879.

1922

Views 1,2 and 3.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Queens: Buhrman's Lane - St. Mark's Avenue
text:
Alley Park: Alley Road, east side, north of Buhrman's Lane, showing the Foster house in 1873. "James Hedger, apparently ran the later Buhrman Mill in 1782 and lived with his sister the Widow Talman in this home on the Alley, opposite the mill. Here he was attacked by a number of soldiers of the 38th and 54th Regiments, then lying at Flushing, and killed. Two were captured, tried at Bedford Long Island and executed." It is doubtful but some state that the first floor was erected in 1663 and the second story added in 1777. "Schmidt 1777" is carved on one of the rafters. This is a set of four views.

1922.
Views 1, 3 & 4.
View 2: April 1926.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: Alley Road - Buhrman's Lane
text:
Alley Park: Alley Road, east side, north of Buhrman's Lane, showing in a set of three views the Foster house. It was erected in 1776. The stone part of this house erected in the same year was used in that year as the Queens County Jail for Federal prisoners. T. Foster owned it in 1891. In 1909 the Cord Meyer Company had it. It is no longer in existence in 1937. If one were to place it on a late map it would probably be in the Horace Harding Boulevard at Alley Park East. This is a set of three views showing the rear of the house.

April 1926.
Views 2 & 3: 1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: Buhrman's Lane - Alley Road
text:
(1) Alley Park: Burhmans Lane, north side, as seen looking north-west from Alley Road (now, 1937, Alley Park East), showing a group of old buildings belonging to W.C. Buhrman in 1873. In the foreground on the east side of the pond's outlet to Alley Creek and partially submerged is the "Old Mill" said to have been erected in 1752. Beyond it is the general store erected in 1828. In the last house, lived a blacksmith. The map of 1873 shows this house to belong also to W.C. Buhrman. The mill was demolished by fire in 1926. In 1828 the general store and mill were acquired by Benjamin P. Loverre of Flushing, who at that time also owned the old Flushing Hotel, and in 1858 Wm. C. Buhrman took possession and conducted it until 1898. His son, Wm. W. Buhrman, operated both the mill and the general store from 1898 to 1914. The Alley Pond Corporation was the owner in 1926.

January 1925.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2) The same, showing only a close up of the mill.

January 1926.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3) The same.

January 1926.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

text:

title: Queens: Buhrman's Lane - Horace Harding Boulevard
text:
Alley Park: Buhrman Lane, west side, south of Horace Harding Boulevard, showing the home of W.C. Buhrman. This house was built about 1905. The old home stood just north (foreground) of the present house, against the stone wall. The original postoffice is said to be the little yellow house south of the present home (testimony of Mrs. Foster given about 1900). She was born about 1812. The other yellow house south of the Post Office, was the poor house of this district. This is a set of two views.

January 1926.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: Bayside Avenue - Strang Avenue
text:
Bayside Ave. (also Twenty-ninth Ave. at this point), between (15th and 16th Streets) 155th and 156th Streets, showing in a set of four views the Walter Bowne house and its out-buildings. One, Bedell, states that a Revolutionary War burying place was northeast of the house, to which, 35 years ago, necessitated the crossing of the stone wall seen in the background of No. 4, at the large Buttonball tree, the stump of which remains today. At that time, flat stones used as markers were still standing; they having been obliterated when the orchard was removed by the wagons. Members of the Bowne family (3rd generation since the War) mentioned the Burial Ground and Spring and Water Bay to him. However, Eugene L. Armbruster states that it was on the line of old 17th (now 157th) Street. For more data, see, other views.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

April 1925.

One, Bedell, states that a Revolutionary War burying place was northeast of the house, to which, 35 years ago, necessitated the crossing of the stone wall seen in the background of No. 4, at the large Buttonball tree, the stump of which remains today. At that time, flat stones used as markers were still standing; they having been obliterated when the orchard was removed by the wagons. Members of the Bowne family (3rd generation since the War) mentioned the Burial Ground and Spring and Water Bay to him. However, Eugene L. Armbruster states that it was on the line of old 17th (now 157th) Street. For more data, see, other views.

title: Queens: Beach 20th Street - Seagirt Avenue
text:
Beach 20th Street, west side, between Seagirt and Plainview Aves. This is a set of three views of the kitchen of the Marine Pavilion Hotel modernized. H. Bainbridge was the owner in 1873 (?) and F. N. Faber in 1891. The Marine Pavilion stood on the west side of Turnpike Road (later Shell Road), south of the junction of Norton Street (now Plainfield Ave.) and Central Ave. (now Beach 20th Street) and occupied most of that block between Plainfield Avenue and Broadway; the Ocean coming to the front of the lawn. This structure, built in 1832-33, was destroyed by fire on June 25, 1864. It stood on the site of the home of Richard Cornell, who came to Far Rockaway in 1685 and died there in 1694. The Rockaway and Jamaica Turnpike Road (Shell Road later and now Beach 19th Street) was constructed in 1834; from Brooklyn to this point, and on this Road stage coaches were regularly run.

January 1923.
Views 1 & 2.
View 3: October 1924.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: Borden Avenue - 2nd Street
text:
Borden Avenue, at, and adjoining the N.E. corner of 2nd Street. The corner building, which is now the 34th Street Ferry Storage Warehouse, is the former Miller Hotel, erected by Oliver Charlick, General Manager of the Long Island Railroad, for Tony Miller (Mueller). It was a rendezvous for sportsmen. Richard Croker and Tim Sullivan were guests here. The building was sold in 1917, altered, and then used as a phonograph manufactory. It appears from the photograph that the upper floor is used as living quarters; a saloon occupies the ground floor on the right. text:

title: Queens: Bridge Plaza North - Hunter Street
text:
Bridge Plaza, west from Hunter Street, toward the Queensboro Bridge, showing this lovely area before the subway "El" reached here and the street car was the only means of public conveyance. The building with the clock tower is the Brewster Building, still standing at this writing (1941) and first appearing in a 1909 atlas. The white building preceding it marks the site on which was later erected the nine-story building of the New York and Queens Electric Light and Power Company. The writer of these lines is unable to determine whether this four-story structure is the earlier building of the electric company.

On the left, above the entrance to the second frame house is the inscription: "Which will you have--The wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." The three-story building preceding the wooded area is the local office of the Western Union Telegraph and Cable Company.

title: Queens: Broadway - Corona Avenue
text:
Broadway; at the N. E. corner of Corona Avenue, showing four views of the St. James P. E. Church and Parsonage. This edifice was erected on the site of the Dr. Jacob Ogden house. He donated it in 1761. Evidently the property was expressly left to him for this purpose by the last will of William Sackett. The structure was opened in 1848 and consecrated on November 15, 1849. A town clock was also placed in one of the spires. On March 30, 1871 it was reopened after being enlarged. It is said that this parish was organized in 1704. View 4, taken in the opposite direction, shows beyond the church, another which is the First Reformed Church of Newtown.

title: Queens: Broadway - Justice Avenue
text:
Broadway, west side, north from Justice Avenue, to Maurice Avenue, showing four views of an original section of the town of Newtown. Views one and two show at the right the former St. James Episcopal Church, now used as a chapel. The houses seen in these two views were the property of S. Manwaring in 1873. View number two also shows adjoining and next to the Exempt Firemen's Association Home, at the left, the old and new quarters of the Newtown Register. This old one story structure was the first school erected in the village. It was built in 1740 and consisted of one room. It was used as a school until 1870. White purchased the building in 1873 when he founded the Register. Of all the buildings seen in the four views only the chapel remained in October 1930, and the building adjoining it. In view number four center right, is the building housing the Buckley Butcher Shop. The Exempt Firemen's Building was formerly a one story structure which was enlarged some time subsequent to 1843 when the Wandewenock Company was organized.

Broadway east side, at and adjoining St. James Avenue. At the extreme right, partially shown, is the St. James P.E. Parsonage. The building in the center of the view was partly occupied by Dr. F. Boothe in 1875. Mrs. Palmer was the owner in 1873 and Dr. Coombs in 1891. The house at the left was the property of W.S. Wood in 1873. Dr. Boothe was born in Connecticut in 1836 and came to Newtown about 1875. He still resided here in 1896. All buildings between St. James Avenue and the Long Island Railroad, Flushing, and North Side Division, on the east side of Broadway, were erected by Samuel Lord in 1850.

title: Queens: Broadway - Victor Avenue
text:
Broadway, west side, opposite Vietor Avenue. In view one the street in the foreground is Laurel Hill Boulevard. At the right background is Broadway, the site of the house and surrounding land was owned by the Rev. John Moore who died in 1657. His son Samuel purchased the tract in 1662. His son Benjamin was followed by Lieutenant Samuel who was a son of Benjamin. He died in 1788. A part of this house was built by him. John a brother of Lieut. Samuel was the next owner. He died in 1827. The center structure dates probably back to 1666 and was the original house of Samuel Moore son of the Rev. John Moore. The house was enlarged in 1760 probably by Lieut. Samuel Moore. It is also questionably stated to be the headquarters of General Howe during the Revolution. Note the old time saving devise for drawing water.

title: Queens: Broadway - Victor Avenue
text:
Broadway, east side, between Vietor and Elmhurst Avenues, showing in a set of 4 views the Woodward-Vietor house. The owners of this property were Theo Vietor, 1852, T. Vietor, 1860, and H. Vietor in 1873.

Nathaniel Woodward, married Mary, daughter of Captain Samuel Moore in the early 18th century. The original, homestead stood some distance to the north and was torn down about 1880. This area has been part of the Woodward farm since 1666. One of the out-buildings a barn was occupied by the British as a hospital during the Revolutionary War.
