title: Queens: Broadway - 51st Avenue
text:
Broadway (tracks thereon) east side, north from 51st Avenue (formerly Maurice Avenue, also known as Cook Avenue) to Corona Avenue (formerly Union Avenue); showing at the corner foreground, the C. Cook residence of 1873 (formcrly 56 Broadway). One Douglas was the owner in 1891. John A. Rapelje's real estate office was located here in 1922. The houses beyond it occupy the site of the old Newtown House an old tire tavern. This site was eventually owned by the lst Reformed Church of Newtown. The Newtown Hotel of later days stood on the opposite side of the street. In views 2,3, and 4 is seen the 1st Dutch Reformed Church of Newtown. The Dutch Church was built on land donated April 2, 1733. The first edifice was erected in 1735 and was 7Ox60 ft. It was demolished on Sept. 4, 1831. Abraham Riker and his brother-in-law P. Rapelje gave the land for a church and burial around to the village of Newtown. The corner stone for the second edifice was laid on Sept. 16, 1831 by Elder Francis Duryea, and the edifice wad[sic] dedicated July 29th, 1832 by the Rev. Schoomaker D.D. The bell used in this church was cast in Araterdam in 1792. The chapel adjoining the church was erected in
1854.

1922
Views 1, 2 and 3
View 4: March 1922
Eugene L. Arcbruster Collection

title: Queens: Broadway - 51st Avenue
text:
Broadway at the S.W. corner of 5th Avenue, showing four views of the former St. James Episcopal Church. It was erected about 1735. Pews were installed in 1740. In 1760 the edifice was repaired and the steeple rebuilt. It was enlarged about 1770 and again repaired about 1816. In 1922 it was painted. The last services in this structure were held on July 16, 1848 when the new edifice was dedicated for service. This place has since been used as a chapel. The steeple was removed about 1900. A small burying ground is located in the rear of this chapel. The Rev. Evan Malbone Johnson, b 1792, was the rector from 1814-1827, when he removed to Brooklyn and there had erected the first St. John's Church in Brooklyn.

Views 3 & 4:

title: Queens: Broadway - 51st Avenue
text:
Broadway, west side, between Queens Boulevard and Fifty-first Ave., showing in a set of two views the Wandowenock Fire House and the Registers office of Newtown. The buildings in this view were demolished in 1930 because of the extension through here of the Independent Subway lines. In View No.1, in which both buildings are seen distinctly; the building at the left is the fire house; the other which housed the office of the Newtown Register acquired its present outlines by adding to buildings already erected. A section of the first story was a school house erected about 1700 and was the first in the village. This building was enlarged in 1840. Then in 1873 another story was erected and the tower added by the Hon. Chas. White, founder of the Register.
---Arthur White.

title: Queens: Cloverdale Boulevard - Northern Boulevard
text:
Cloverdale Boulevard, east side, between Northern Boulevard and Horatio Parkway. Eugene L. Armbruster states this to be the Ker Boyce farmhouse and he gives the location as south of the water-works and Northern Boulevard, and north of the Alley. In the Queens Atlas of 1858, this house belonged to one Osgood, who owned some 260 acres. From 1860 to 1873 Ker Boyce was owner and occupant. His house was then south of a small creek which emptied into Alley Creek from Douglas Pond (now Oakland Pond.) At this time a road extended south and connected Northern Boulevard (old Broadway) and West Alley Road. The house was at the S.E. junction of this creek and Road. In 1891 F.W. Lawrence owned the house which up to that time belonged to John Taylor through his marriage to Boyce's daughter. Also for the first time Douglas Pond emptied directly into Little Neck Bay and the Flushing water works were erected on the north side of Northern Boulevard on a canal which was cut through for this purpose. In 1909, G.W. Eicles owned this property. In 1928 the two buildings were located as follows: the house on Cloverdale Boulevard, east side, between Northern and Birmington Parkways and the barn to the south of the last named Street. This is a set of four views.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

June 1924.

title: Queens: College Place - 9th Road
text:
The Poppenhusen Institute
P H I L A N T H R O P I S T :A lover of mankind; one who sympathizes with and endeavors to help his fellow men. (Dictionary.) One who fully deserved the term, but received little recognition beyond his immediate locale for his gifts, was Conrad Poppenhusen of College Point.
A German immigrant, arriving in America in 1843, he soon made a fortune, lost it, and then made another.
Poppenhusen's early business training was Acquired in Germany, where his father owned a concern that manufactured numerous small articles out of whalebone. Upon his arrival in America, with considerable means, he went into a partnership and continued the same type of manufacture. Whalebone was becoming a scarce commodity at about this time and when Conrad made the acquaintance of Charles Goodyear he turned his attention to the development of rubber. Not a scientist by any means, but a good businessman, Poppenhusen eventually established a factory in College Point, manufacturing combs and other small articles out of hard rubber. We might say that hard rubber articles were the plastics of one
hundred years ago.
In 1898 several of the hard rubber firms were consolidated and became the American Hard Rubber Company, still in existence and still in College Point.
After attaining marked financial success through his application to business, he turned that success to the lasting benefit of the community. He took a deep interest in many fields, such as town planning, providing homes for his employees in whose welfare he took a personal interest, and other aid projects. At one time he gave 330,000 for the building of the College Point Dutch Reformed Church and in celebration of his 50th birthday he made a gift of one hundred thousand dollars to the people of College Point for the erection and maintenance of what became the Poppenhusen Institute, designed a century ago to provide free instruction in the Arts and Crafts and also commercial and industrial subjects. College Point gets its name from the fact that the Rev. W. A. Muhlenberg founded St. Paul's College there in 1835. The college is long since gone but the community holds its name; College Point. The institute, built in 1868, dominates the landscape above the factor near the homes of his workers and played a most important role in the life of the community. It served as a bank, school, town office, library, Jail, and youth center. The building expresses the tastes of the times between 1854 and 1880.
A historical room has recently been undertaken, and here, may be seen any old maps, photographs, and antiques of the past, and attempts to recreate the town of the past, to revive the flavor of life a
century ago.

title: Queens: Colonial Avenue - 62nd Drive
text:
Colonial Ave., (right side of house not shown) west side, north of 62nd Drive. If locating in 1922, it would be on Mill Creek and Old Mill Road. At the street line of the S.W. corner of Harding Boulevard and Colonial Avenue is the site of this house which was razed in Sept. 1930 to make way for the Horace Harding Boulevard. Judge Robert Coe erected the house in 1655. The following year he moved to Jamaica and Captain John Coe became the owner of the farmhouse and the Mill property which was on the west side of the Creek. In 1698 Judge John Coe, 2nd son of Captain John Coe was the owner. This family retained possession for almost a century when about 1810 David Titus became the owner. This in turn sold to Daniel Rapelye son of Major Rapelye who was till the owner in 1852. Mrs. Kenny was an occupant in 1922. Eugene L. Armbruster states that the Lott family also owned this property. The mill was destroyed by fire in 1875. L. J. Wood, Felton, or R. W. W. Hitchcock was the owner in 1873. The present structure was erected about 1750 on the site of the old house. The Van Rieper however states it to be the original Coe house. The Earl was the owner of this property in 1860. Thomas G. Smith from the Shady Lake farm was the owner in 1910. According to figures inscribed on a stone in the building, the house was said to be 1925 to be 216 years old. View No. 3 shows the house at the right background. Mill Creek is in the foreground.

Jan. 1926
Views 1, 2 and 3.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Queens: Cornaga Avenue - Nameoke Street
text:
Cornaga Ave., north side, between Nameoke Street and Mott Ave., showing the Mott house. It was erected during the Revolutionary War period. Benjamin Birdsall Matt, born 1820 and living in 1896, was the son of John S. Matt, who at one time owned more than 1000 acres of land in this area. He died in 1828, aged 81; his wife was Ling Nicolls. Benj. B. Matt, who owned this land from 1873 to 1891, gave the right of way through his land and also several acres of land for the depot, and was instrumental in securing the money to build the railroad from Valley Stream to this place. This is a set of four views. See others for more data.

1922.

Views 3 & 4: May 1923.

title: Queens: Corona Avenue - 102nd Street
text:
Corona Avenue, north side, between 102nd and 104th Streets, showing the Geo. W. Burroughs' house erected by John Burroughs who died in 1750. His sons John and Joseph inherited the farm. Josephs son Thomas was the next owner. He married Sarah, daughter of George Wyckoff. His son was Geo. Wyckoff Burroughs and his daughter married Isaac Moe who was the owner in 1923. The house was gone by June 1930. Near this house was once the Commons of Newtown. This place was once General Moore's headquarters. It is questionably stated that the house was erected about 1700 on the site of the former Wm. Stevenson house that was acquired, in 1742, by Richard Betts. Jonathan Randel was an occupant in 1852.

title: Queens: Dane Place - Fleet Street
text:
Dane Place, east from Fleet Street. In the center of the view partially around the bend of the Road is the Springsteen house. Casper Springsteen came to Newtown about 1700. His son Joost Derrick settled in Kent County on the Delaware River. Another son Jacobus gave the site for the White Pot Schoolhouse. Casper's son Casper Jr. born in 1725 inherited the Hempstead Swamp farm. He married Barbara Bloom of the Wallabout. Their son David inherited the farm and a new house. He married Phebe Striker of Flatbush. Their son M.S. Springsteen followed as owner. He married Alletta B. Duryea of Jamaica, their offspring David, who married Anna W. Monfort was the last owner. He died in 1912 and his widow Mrs. Springsteen sold the property in December 1928.

May 1923

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Queens: Farmers Boulevard - Henderson Avenue
text:
199-20 Farmers Boulevard, at the N.W. corner of Henderson Ave., showing the A.J. Debevoise house built by him about 1870 and lived in by him and members of the family from 1873 to 1923. It became the 4th Executive Democratic Club in 1934. This A.J. was born in the original Debevoise homestead, located on Bushwick Ave. and Kossuth Place, which is still owned by the family. The present structure was erected on the old D. Ludlum farmhouse site. The barn in view No. 1 is probably over one hundred years old, the smoke house being in the center and viewed in a southwest direction from Ninety-ninth Ave. No. 2 is north from about One Hundred Second Ave; No. 3 being eastward and showing the rear of the house.

title: Queens: Flushing Avenue - Woodward Avenue
text:
Flushing Ave., at the S.W. corner of Woodward Ave., showing in a set of four views the Woodward house. This house, supposedly erected by Joseph Woodward in 1750, stands 60 feet south of Woodward Ave. and in rear of 1471 Flushing Ave., on land formerly owned by the Schenck family. In 1852 it belonged to the Schoomaker Estate; from 1869-1873 to N. Hausmann. For more data see the N.Y. Sun, February 18, 1939.
1922;
Views 2 & 3: September 1928.
View 4: April 1929.
Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: Flushing Meadow Park - [Rodman Street - North Hempstead Turnpike.]
text:
Flushing Meadow Park (Queens): Viewing west (views 1,2) across the Flushing meadows toward the Corona dump hills, seen from Rodman Street and North Hempstead Turnpike. In the foreground is Mill Pond and the winding Flushing Creek. This area later became the main exposition center of the New York World's Fair 1939-40.
Views 2 and 3 are in a northwesterly direction across the marshy meadows from Rodman Street and show the Roosevelt Avenue subway "El" under construction in the background.

title: Queens: 111th Street - 46th Avenue
text:
Flushing Meadow Park (Queens): Viewing north across the western extremity of the park and showing a small community in Corona, along 111th Street, before this area was incorporated into the New York World's Fair grounds of 1939-40. All the homes were razed and the area filled in and leveled out; the Corona gates and the Avestion, Chrysler Motors and Railroads Buildings were erected here. On the left is the roof of Public School No. 17, on the west side of 111th Street and 51st Avenue. That side of the street remained intact.

View 2 shows the same area in the opposite direction, i.e., looking south from 47th Avenue; 111th Street and P. S. 17 are on the right.

View 3 is in the same direction as view 1, from 51st Avenue.

title: Queens: Horace Harding Boule - Colonial Avenue
text:
Flushing Meadow Park: (World's Fair Grounds). A set of 4 views showing what was once the Corona Dump for the City of New York. This putrid area has been converted into a place of beauty. Here, where once there were refuse heaps, will be held the greatest World's Fair of modern times. View number one is taken from 111th Street and Forty-sixth Avenue, looking eastward. The main exposition center will be at about where the train and steam shovel are seen in this view. View number two is taken looking northward from Horace Harding Boulevard at about Colonial Avenue, and shows an area that is now covered with the Grand Central Parkway, the Trylon and Perisphere, and the west side of the fair grounds. View number 3 and 4 are somewhat similar to view number two. In view 4 are seen hundreds of rust eaten hot water tanks doting the refuse heap.

October 1928.
Views 2&4: May 1923.
View 3: October 1924.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

Atop the tower of marble and porphyry at the entrance to the building is a stainless steel figure, designed by Vyacheslav Andreev, depicts the spirit of the Soviet worker. It weighs thirty tons and forms, after the Trylon--the World's Fair theme--the highest spot at the Fair. Architects of the pavilion are Boris M. Iofan and Karo S. Alabian. On the two wings of the building are reliefs of Stalin (left) and Lenin.

May 29, 1939
Views 1,2

P. L. Sperr

title: Queens: Flushing Meadow Park - [New York World's Fair of 1939-40 - New York World's Fair Administration Building.]
text:
Completed Administration Building of the New York World's Fair 1939 which became ready today (Friday) for occupancy on Monday by a force of 600 employees who are being transferred from the Empire State Building over the weekend. Construction of the Administration Building, at the site in Flushing Meadow, Queens, was completed in the record time of 124 days. The cost was approximately $900,000.

"This picture is sent to you for publication only and must not be used for advertising or commercial purposes without written permission from New York World's Fair 1939 Incorporated."

title: Queens: Hawtree Avenue - 115th Avenue
text:
Hawtree Ave., east side, south of One Hundred Fifteenth Ave. line, partially in 124th Street, showing in a set of three views an old barn on the property of J. Lott from 1859 to 1873. G. Griffin was the owner in 1891. It was subsequently purchased by the Metropolis Land Company of 302 Broadway New York. This barn was erected on May 24, 1813 by William C. Stoothoff, whose family occupied a homestead on the west side of Hawtree Ave., north of One Hundred Fourteenth Avenue to a point slightly north of One Hundred Ninth Avenue from 1859-1891. In 1922 the J.C. Zook Organization had possession of the Lott homes. This farmhouse was northwest of this barn, between Hawtree Ave., and 124th Street in One Hundred Fifteenth Ave. View No. 3 shows the interior, the others the exterior of the barn.

1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: Hobart Street - 30th Street
text:
Hobart Street (dirt road), east side, north from 55th Street to Thirtieth Avenue, showing in a set of 4 views an old Rapelje house later known as the Cornelius Purdy farmhouse. The history of ownership is that Cornelia Wyckoff married Captain Cornelius Rapelje who in 1758 purchased this farm from his father-in-law. Mary Rapelje, daughter of Captain Cornelius, married David Purdy after whom the house, which was erected in 1770, was named. Other owners of this house and farmland were heirs of Cornelius Purdy 1852, and the Banta family from 1860-1891.

April 1923
Views 1, 2, and 3
View 4: May 1925.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Queens: Hoffman Drive - 58th Avenue
text:
Hoffman Drive, south side, between Fifty-eighth and Fifty-ninth Avenues, showing in three views the Robinson house. This house stands on or near the site of the Quaker Meeting House which was erected in 1722 and sold in 1760. Adjoining the house was a burial ground. The house which was used as a dwelling from 1760 was consumed by fire in 1844. The owners of the present house were Robert Mack, 1852?; J. title: Queens: Horatio Parkway - 53rd Avenue
text:
Horatio Parkway, west side, between 53rd Avenue and 230th Street, Bayside, showing the F.N. Lawrence Mansion, an imposing frame structure. According to Mr. Armbruster, the mansion, situated on a large estate, was owned by F.N. Lawrence in 1860 and by W.H. Sanger in 1873. Beers's 1873 map also shows it as the Sanger property, just below the Boyce farm on Oakland Lake (Douglas Pond).

The estate, known as "The Oaks," was opened by a member of the Hicks family and afterwards owned by Lawrence and later by John Henderson and John Taylor. In 1891 it was owned by John Taylor (Wolverton's map) and then comprised 263.25 acres. It was the F.H. Taylor property in 1909. The distant views were most likely taken from Horace Harding Boulevard, formerly West Alley, which marked the southern limit of the estate. The Horatio Parkway location marks the site of the mansion proper, were it standing when the new thoroughfares were laid out.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection
1924
Views 1,2,3

title: Queens: Jamaica Avenue - 153rd Street
text:
Jamaica Ave., south side, east of 153rd Street, showing in a set of three views the First Dutch Reformed Church of Jamaica. The present edifice is one of the three structures erected on this site. The first was erected in 1716 and was an octagon in shape; the second was built in 1832 and was destroyed by fire in 1857; the present one, on which construction was started in 1858, had its cornerstone laid on September 14, 1858 by Richard Brush. Dr. Thomas E. Vernilge dedicated it on October 6, 1859. This structure was erected at a cost of 20,000.

title: Queens: Jamaica Avenue - 160th Street
text:
Jamaica Avenue, north side, east from 160th to 162nd Streets. The corner house is Crawford's liquor and wine place, specialising in Jos. Sallert beer and Schmidt's Kloster brau. The second house, with the hip roof, was the Richard Brush home from 1873 to 1876, now the Imperial Lunch Room. Some of the buildings were later razed or remodeled. The other views, especially 3 and 4, show closeups of the Brush house, seen from the B.M.T. elevated structure.

title: Queens: Jamaica Avenue - New York Boulevard
text:
(1)
Jamaica Avenue, south side, between New York Boulevard, and 165th Street, showing Colonial Hall, now the Queensboro Public Library.  The orginial[sic] building, known as the Union Hall Academy for boys, was erected in 1792 and used as such until 1820 when a new building for the academy was erected on the west side of Union Hall Street, just north of the Long Island Railroad tracks.  The original building became a female Seminary under the trustees of the Union Hall Academy and was destroyed by fire on February 12, 1841.  The cornerstone of the building in this view was laid on March 11, 1843 and the seminary was reopened in May of that year and was still used as such in 1876.  This structure was subsequently owned by ex-sheriff Welliam[sic] Cass Baker who had it remodeled in 1897 when it became known as Colonial Hall.  It was then used as a public hall and club rooms, subsequently becoming a family hotel and rooming house.  In 1922 one of the branches of the Queensboro Public Library occupied it; it was razed in May 1923.  On its site is now located the Stuart Building.

1891

title: Queens: Jamaica Avenue - 166th Street
text:
Jamaica Ave., (Elevated B.M.T. line thereon), south side, between 166th and 168th Streets, showing in a set of four views the rears of some old homes. At the extreme left partially shown was the Hurst home from 1873 to 1891. It also was at one time the K. Stenupf hotel. A. Duryea occupied the center house in the same period. The house on the right is the Jacob Smith homestead, said to be about One Hundred and Fifty years old. It was purchased by Mrs. Mary Meegan in 1873 and later owned by her daughter, Mrs. Catherine Kammerer. The house was sold in 1924, and demolished in October of the same year.

January 1923.

title: Queens: Jamaica Avenue - 168th Street
text:
Jamaica Ave., (tracks thereon), at the northeast corner of 168th St., showing according to T.F. Archer, Caleb Weeks Tavern, also known as the John Plemming house.  John Plemming came from Ireland to Jamaica in 1856.  After serving in the Civil War, he became Distract Attorney for Queens County in 1883.  At a latter date he was made a judge of the Special Sessions Court.

1922

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: Jamaica Avenue - 168th Street
text:
Jamaica Ave., (tracks thereon) north side, at, adjoining and west of 168th St., showing at the corner the Daniel Gracy house and store of 1873.  One Geis was the owner in 1891.  In 1923, the Long Island Daily Press occupied the premises.  A saloon once owned by Martin Prince and later by one Klinger also occupied this corner.  A four story brick structure was on this site in 1934.  The building in this view was erected in 1872 or 73 when a fire demolished those then standing.  The house adjoining the corner on Jamaica Ave. still stands in 1934.

March 1923

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

text: Junction Boulevard (foreground), west side, at Thirty-Fifth Ave., showing a view N.W. of the Charles P. Leverich house. Eugene L. Armbruster states this to be also the Col. Edward Leverich house and that Chas. P., his son, was born here in 1809. This information was given by one Van Rieper. However, the original home of Col. Edward Leverich was sold by him about 1820 to one Hendrickson, who in turn sold in 1851 to John and George Elliot. This house was located on the south side of Thirty-Seventh Ave. between 112th and 114th Street and was demolished prior to 1915. title: Queens: Kissena Boulevard - Franklin Avenue
text:
(1) Kissena Boulevard, (formerly Jamaica Ave.), east side, between Franklin and Elder Aven., showing Sanford Hall, which was erected in 1836 by Nathon Sanford, who was born at Bridgehampton in 1777. In August 1823 when he was elected to the United States Senate in place of Rufus King. Dr. James and his brother Allen Macdonald purchased Sanford Hall after 1841 and moved their private sanitarium from Murray Hill in New York City in 1845 to this place. This property was sold in 1924 to a group of real estate operators. The buildings were still occupied as a sanitarium in 1909. In 1873 this property extended from Jamaica Ave. on the west, to Parsons Ave. on the east, and from a point south of Franklin Ave., south to Elder Ave. Since then Bowne Street was extended with Ash, Beach and Cherry Aves. through this estate.

title: Queens: Kissena Boulevard - Sanford Avenue
text:
Kissena Boulevard, at the N.E. corner of Sanford Ave., showing in a set of three views St. Joseph's Academy now St. Joseph's Convent.  St. Thomas' Hall was erected in 1838-39 and was purchased in 1860 by Catholics who opened it as a Convent School for Young Ladies under the name of St. Joseph's Academy. A new building was added and it remained the main school until the Brentwood property was acquired. St. Thomas' Hall, was a school for boys, opened on April 12, 1843. Rev. Francis L. Hawks D.D., the founder had to abandon it to his creditors. This structure for a short time also housed the Flushing Female College, but this also was no success. Additions to this building by the Academy were: Central portion erected in 1868, west wing in 1872, and the Chapel in 1879.

Sept. 4, 1897

Additions to this building by the Academy were: Central portion erected in 1868, west wing in 1872, and the Chapel in 1879.

title: Queens: Long Island City - Astoria - General view.

A general view of Long Island City and Astoria, photographed north westward from over Bridge Plaza (see "El" lines at lower left). Across the top is the East River divided by the northerly half of Welfare Island. Beyond in the Manhattan shore lying between the Queensboro Bridge and Carl Schurz Park. title: Queens: 29th Street - 11th Avenue
text:
Long Island City, Queens: Shown is a general view, in a northeasterly direction, of Long Island City, seen from Bridge Plaza North and 29th Street. Many of the industrial buildings and old-type tenements are clearly visible. Shown, too, is the elevated structure, which carries the I.R.T. trains to Astoria, on 31st Street and the 39th Avenue station. Northern Boulevard, on which part of the "El" is on, can be seen bending eastward around the Standard Plumbing building. In the lower right-hand corner is part of the Queensboro Stadium.

View 2 is directly north, from the same point, along 29th Street toward Astoria and the Hellgate Bridge. At the lower left-hand corner is Bryant High School, and north of the playground is St. Patricks Roman Catholic Church.

View 3 is eastward across the Pennsylvania Railroad yards, viewing along Queens Boulevard on which the "El" runs toward Flushing. The elevated loop in the foreground is the Astoria line. Across the freight yards are numerous industrial plants.

P. L. Sperr

*Long Island City*

title: Queens: Main Avenue - Vernon Boulevard
text:
(1) Main Ave., adjoining the N.W. corner of Vernon Boulevard, showing the Rapelye Mansion. There is a dispute as to its identity. Eugene L. Armbruster states it is the Cornelius Rapelye house; one Van Rieper states it to be the Tavern; another, Mr. Roe S. Johnson states that this was the Trafford house and was also used as a tavern. Eugene L. Armbruster's history on this subject is that John Trafford married Grace Rapelye, sister of C. Rapelye, who erected this house in 1780. It was occupied by C. R. Trafford in 1873.

title: Queens: Main Avenue - Park Row
text:
Main Avenue, foreground, at the S.W. corner of Welling Court, showing in a set of four views the S. A. Halsey house of 1873. It was demolished in 1928. Hendrick Suydam, a farmer of Bedford, bought the estate of William Lawrence, deceased, in 1794. Between 1825 and 1852 when S. A. Halsey purchased it, it was owned by one Whitfield. Before S. A. Halsey purchased it and made it his home, it had been a roadhouse at which he often stopped. This individual in 1849 purchased several farms at Astoria and laid out and opened Broadway, The Crescent, Emerald Street, Academy Street, Grand Street, First Ave., Second Ave., and Jamaica Ave. At about 1840 he purchased the Horn Hook Ferry running to 86th Street, New York City, which he operated for 30 years. Peter Fitzsimmons was the first operator of this line. This individual also conducted in 1782 a tavern at the house of the widow Betts at Halletts Cove. This was the house of Grant Thorburn in 1852.

May 1923.
Views 2,364: 1922.

Eugene L. Ambruster Collection.

title: Queens: Main Street - 38th Avenue
text:
Main St., west side, between Thirty-eighth and Thirty-ninth Aves., showing in a set of 4 views the St. George's Protestant Episcopal Church and the Peck and Bloodgood Cemetery. The first services of this Congregation were held in the blockhouse, which in 1704 was called the Guardhouse. It stood on a site on which the Orthodox Quaker's meeting house was erected in 1827. This site is now occupied by the new armory (east of the Hicksite Quaker's meeting house of 1694-5). The first church edifice was erected near Main St., facing on Thirty-eighth Ave., in 1743-46, and was completed in 1761. It stood on a one-half acre tract donated by Captain Ralph Wentworth in 1745. The second edifice seen partially in views 3 and 4 was erected in 1812 and consecrated either on May 25 or June 25, 1821 by Bishop Hobart and enlarged in 1838 or 40 at a cost of 1700. Twenty-six pews were added. It was removed to its present site facing Thirty-eighth Ave. in 1853 and repaired in 1858. It was demolished in 1920. The third edifice was erected between 1853 and 54 at a cost of 33,000 and later remodeled. The cornerstone was laid on May 18th or 24th 1853 and the building consecrated on June 1, 1854. Rev. J. Carpenter Smith was the rector from Nov. 1847 to 1896. The charter of this congregation dates from 1760.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

1922
Views 1,3 and 4.
View 2: March 1924.

title: Queens: Main Street - 38th Avenue
text:
Main Street, north of the N.W. corner of Thirty-eighth Ave. (left), showing at the corner the D. Master's House of 1873. In 1874 Miss S.O. Hoffman's school for girls was conducted in this house. It had only day students. In 1876 a limited number of boarders were here. Mrs. Master succeeded Miss Hoffman. Dr. Hans Schuler purchased the school in 1888 and organized the Flushing Female Seminary. In 1926 the building stands but is no longer used as a seminary. It has had the boards removed and has been finished with stucco.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

1922.

title: Queens: Maspeth Avenue - 55th Street
text:
Maspeth Ave. (when constructed will extend along front of this house in foreground), north side, between 55th and 56th Streets, showing the Way farmhouse. Beyond it is the Liquid Carbonic Company at the N.W. corner of 57th Street and Maspeth Ave. This farmhouse was erected in the early 17th Century by James Way. His large estate included a part of the Judge Furman tract. His son John acquired it in 1691 and the latter's son James, in 1729. A nephew Samuel, and after him, his daughter Jane had possession. Her son, Dr. Henry Mott, sold the farm in 1815 to Garret Furman. Other owners were W.H. Furman 1852-1873, and P. Grussy in 1891. The house was demolished in 1929. A private burial place was at the right of the house opposite 56th Street. This is a set of four views.

March 1923.
Views 1 and 2.
View 3: March 1929.
View 4: September 1929.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: Maspeth Avenue - 57th Street
text:
(1-4)

Maspeth Ave. (foreground), east of 57th Street, showing in the foreground the Queens Head Tavern which is on the S.E. corner of Maspeth Ave. and 58th Street (along line of telegraph poles at the right.) This homestead was founded by James Way who left his estate to his nephew, Samuel Way in the middle of the 18th Century. In 1815, Garret Furman acquired the land. Captain Peter Berton ran a tavern here in July 1783. In 1873 McCrady and Elder operated it as a hotel. Another history concerning this house is that it was erected by the town of Newtown and leased to tavern keepers. It was a resort for the soldiers during the Revolutionary war; later a stage stop, and afterwards a private dwelling. A gas station and tavern occupied the place in 1933. In front of this tavern was a toll house, in 1852. This is a set of three views from slightly different angles.

January 1924.
View 2: 1922.
View 3: January 1924.
View 4: March 1925

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: Metropolitan Avenue - 70th Avenue
text:
Metropolitan Avenue, north side, opposite Seventieth Avenue (known also as Ursula Place and Herrick Avenue). This set of 3 views shows the home of Jeronus Vanderveer. John and Walter Vanderveer were the owners in 1923 while one Weeden was the occupant. Michael Vanderveer who settled in Newtown in 1810 was born in Flatbush in 1777. He married Martha Vandervoort of Newtown. His son Henry Sudyam was born in 1812 in the old house that stood across the road from his latter residence, which was on the west side of Trotting Course Lane just south of Metropolitan Avenue. The son, Henry Sudyam, married Sarah J. (Burroughs) Rapelje in 1847. George W. Vanderveer was born in the old family homestead in Newtown in 1842. He married in 1866 Mary Whitson of that place. Charles Boerum Vanderveer (1796-1879) owned a thirty-six acre farm at Middle Village. His son Jeronus purchased about 1871 a sixty acre one at the same place. After his fathers death he, Jeronus, acquired his fathers farm. Other owners of this house were H. Randall, 1860?; H. Weeden, 1873; and J. Vanderveer, in 1896. Views 2 and 3 are viewed east and west respectively.

Views 2&3: 1922
October 1923.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Queens: Metropolitan Avenue - Woodhaven Boulevard
text:
Metropolitan Avenue (right, telegraph pole thereon) at the S.W. corner of Woodhaven Boulevard.  View No. 2 is looking southeastward from Metropolitan Avenue (tracks thereon). Views 3 and 4 are looking northward on Trotting Course Lane. This house, sometimes known as the Garret Vanderveer house, was erected in 1850 by Henry [Suyden] Vanderveer. title: Queens: Manhattan Avenue - 65th Street
text:
Metropolitan Avenue, north side, east from 65th Street to Mt. Olivet Crescent, showing in the background a section of Lutheran Cemetery. In the foreground at the left are the steps leading to the Major house (brick) which is located at the N.W. corner of the above mentioned Streets. Beyond it is a two story house. The peaked section was once a one story peaked roof house of Chas. Way. The roof was removed and a story added about 50 years ago (1874), by Conrad Arzberger who also erected the flat two story extension. The next house is on the site of the old Ehrman house. About 1890 his son Charles built the present structure. The next two houses belonged to Judge Robert Burroughs (also Supervisor) who married a Way. In the first of the last two homes lived the judge. The other house he sold to one Deloughy a florist. His estate still owns it.

title: Queens: Metropolitan Avenue - 75th Street
text:
Metropolitan Avenue, north side, between 78th Street (right) and 75th Street (left), showing in two views the M.E. Church of Newtown. The congregation organized in 1768 and met in a small meeting house, which was erected in 1769, and located on the west side of Dry Harbor Road, just south of Furmanville Avenue. The church edifice was erected in 1785 and rebuilt in 1836. The congregation was incorporated in 1836. The church is on the present site since 1836. In 1901 it was damaged by fire and in 1902 it was rebuilt and enlarged. It was burned again about Jan. 8, 1926. In 1929 a brick edifice occupies the site. Between 1886 and 1889 the congregation was dormant.

In 1923 Welz and Zerweck were the owners. The 1908 Atlas of Queens County also shows that in 1908 it was known as the Greater New York Park and that the owner was C.J. Hettsheimer. These buildings were demolished prior to 1929.

title: Queens: 94th Street - West End Avenue
text:

Herrick house of 1852, which is located in 96th Street at 18th Drive. In 1840 one Boerum was the owner. His son Abraham of Horse Brook Road was born here. J.T. Sanford owned it from 1860 to 1873. title: Queens: Northern Boulevard - Main Street
text:
(1-4)
Northern Boul., south side, east of Main St. (right), showing an old home said to be standing in 1819. In 1826 Joshua and Rachel Kimber conducted a private school in this house. In 1830 it was the home of one Bissett; and in 1873, it was occupied by I. Frost. Eugene L. Armbruster also states it was at one time the home of Jacob P. Haubeil. This individual operated the Fountain House in 1896. However a Mr. Michels denies that Jacob F. Haubiel ever lived at 101 Broadway (now Northern Boul.). For more information see the S.E. corner of Main St. and Northern Boul. This house was partially damaged in 1923, and was demolished in Oct. 1930. This is a set of four views seen from slightly different angles.

title: Queens: Northern Boulevard - Main Street
text:
Northern Boulevard, south side, east of Main St., showing in a set of three views the Quaker Meeting House of Flushing. The land upon which this building was erected (from 1694-5) was purchased in 1692 for the sum of £ 46. On May 30, 1696 their first annual meeting was held here. This building was shingled plastered, and repaired in 1704. The Quaker records state: A new building was erected in 1719 near the old one and was 65'x42' in size. This refers probably to an addition. In 1763, the gallery was taken out and a floor was laid, making it a two story structure. The British used the structure as a barrack, hospital, prison, and bay magazine; being restored to the original owner in 1783. The Orthodox Quakers built a meeting house east of the old (Hicksite), meeting house in the 1830's. The picket fence surrounding this building was removed in 1911, and the Orthodox Meeting House in 1909

1922
View 2: March 1924.
View 3: July 1925.

title: Queens: Northern Boulevard - 147th Street
text:
Northern Boulevard, south side, between 147th and 149th Sts., showing in a set of 4 views the R. B. Parsons house of 1873. Samuel Parsons settled in Flushing where he died in 1841. He married Mary Bowne who died here in 1839. Their son Samuel B. Parsons was born at Flushing in 1819. The Samuel S. Parsons house stood in 1839 on large grounds on Broadway Flushing. The street under construction probably is 147th St. The house faces south on Thirty-eighth Ave.

March 1924.
Views 1, 2, 3 and 4.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: Northern Boulevard - 161st Street
text:
Northern Boulevard, at the N.W. corner of 161st Street (old 21st Street.), showing the W.H. Wilkins house of 1860. It was acquired by the Hildreth Estate in 1891 with 60.5 acres of land. In 1909 the Rickert Findlay Realty Company acquired possession and subdivided the farm into lots. This house, erected in 1832, was still standing in 1934. This is a set of four views. The first two show the east and south side of the house. Views 3 and 4 show the west and south side.
1924.

View 3: January 1923.

title: Queens: Northern Boulevard - 162nd Street
text:

title: Queens: Northern Boulevard - Douglaston Parkway
text:
Northern Boulevard, north side, between Douglaston Parkway (left), and 244th Street (right) showing the Zion Church (P.E.) of Douglaston. This church was donated by Wynant Van Zandt Jr. He also gave the pipe organ and other furniture. The church was constructed on July 30, 1830. Bishop Hobart was the rector. Wm. P. Douglas donated the Chancel. The Parish Hall was largely built by a gift of Bloodgood Cutler, the Long Island farmer poet. This edifice was damaged by fire on December 24, 1924. The new edifice was opened about January 1st, 1926.

June 1922.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: Old Brook School Roa - Newton Avenue
text:
(1) Old Brook School Road, east from Newtown Ave. to Borden Ave. (This Road is non-existent in 1930, except for a portion now known as 59th Place between Maurice and Maspeth Aves. March 1925. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(2) The same, showing the Old Brook School, which was in existence prior to 1852. This school shows only partially in view No. 1. February 1924. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(3) The same, viewed S.W., showing the school which was remodeled after a fire. Note the New Calvary Cemetery in the background. March 1925. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

(4) The same, from another angle as viewed northeast, showing the altered Old Brook School House which now stands in Adler's Monument works yard. March 1925. Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: Queens Boulevard - Grand Avenue
text:
Queens Boulevard at the S.E. corner of Grand Avenue, showing the corner house. It was erected about 1716 by Jonathan Fish who kept a tavern. He died in 1723. His son Samuel conducted it until he died 1767. Abraham Rapelye operated it during the Revolutionary War. At this time it was also the headquarters of the Loyalists. After the war it was called the Union Hotel. On May 3, 1817 it was purchased by the town for the Presbyterian Parsonage for the Rev. Wm. Boardman and used as such until 1822 when the 3rd parsonage was erected. Rev. Boardman died 1818 and was succeeded by the Rev. John Goldsmith D.D. The house was sold in 1822 and was used first as a store and then for many years as a residence. It stood vacant for years and was finally taken down. This site was originally occupied by the house of Ralph Hunt. Peter Duryea was the owner in 1852.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

In the left background is an elevated line known as the Flushing Elevated Lines and is operated by the Manhattan and Queens County Railway Company.

Queens Boulevard, at the S.E. corner of 54th Ave, showing the Presbyterian First Church of Newtown, erected 1893, which replaced the old wooden edifice across the street (view 3, right).

Views 2,3 and 4 show the granite church structure moved back to its new site to allow for the widening of Queens Boulevard. Note that the steeple has been removed.

Views 2,3: August, 1924
View 4: May, 1929

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Queens: Queens Boulevard - 54th Avenue
text:
Queens Boulevard, south side, between Fifty-fourth and Fifty-fifth Avenues, showing in three views the First Presbyterian Church of Newtown. Views one and two show the front and rear of the new edifice. John Goldsmith Payntor who died in 1891 left the parish sufficient money for the erection of the stone structure. The cornerstone was laid July 6, 1893 and the edifice was dedicated May 5, 1895. View No. 3 is taken from a point south of Justice Avenue, between Fifty-fifth and Fifty-second Avenues, viewing south and shows in the foreground the old Church and cemetery on the north side of the Boulevard between Fifty-fifth Avenue and Broadway.

Views 2&3: May 1923

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Queens: Queens Boulevard - 55th Avenue
text:
Queens Boulevard, east side, from 55th Avenue (left) to near 56th Avenue, showing the area in two successive views. These homes appear on maps as early as 1873. The first three homes from the left (view 1) were then owned by H. Geisling; the little house to the right of these, by one G.B.; and the house with the dormer windows, as well as the one adjoining it on the right, by Mrs. Raymond. To the right of that, standing in the direct path of the proposed extension of 55th Road, is the J. Casey house. The two small houses in the center of view 1 are on the direct line of 55th Avenue, when the latter will be extended here; the houses on the left will then occupy the N.E. corner of the intersection.

P. L. Sperr

July 2, 1935
Views 1,2

title: Queens: Queens Boulevard - 55th Avenue
text:
Queens Boulevard, north side, west of Fifty-fifth Ave., to Broadway, showing in 4 views the Old Presbyterian Church and Cemetery of Newtown. The Church was destroyed by fire in May 1929. See other views. The rest of the buildings in this view were all demolished by Mar. 1, 1931. This church was erected in 1787 on site of a former one destroyed by the British during the Revolutionary War. Dr. John P. Knox was pastor from 1855 to 1882. At this time square pews with little doors were installed.

title: Queens: Queens Boulevard - 57th Avenue
text:
Queens Boulevard, west from Fifty-seventh Avenue, showing an area of Queens Boulevard prior to its widening. View No. 1 shows in the foreground No. 58 (old No.) Queens Boulevard at the S.W. corner of above Boulevard and Fifty-sixth Avenue. It was the property of one Arnoldi prior to 1873. Also seen in this view is the steeple of the new First Presbyterian Church of Newtown. Its steeple has since been removed. View No. 2 shows the north side of the Boulevard. The extension of Mrs. Raymond's house at the right foreground is west of Fifty-sixth Avenue. (Laconia Street also known as Horsebrook Road). View No. 3 shows the house alone prior to its removal. View No. 2 also shows the old First Presbyterian Church in the background. View No. 4 shows the house according to E.L. Armbruster to now, 1925, be on the north (west) side of Fifty-seventh Avenue (Caldwell Avenue) about 50 feet west (south) of Van Horn Street. However it does not appear in the 1929 Atlas of Queens County.

April 1923.
View 2: August 1924.
View 3: February 8, 1924.
View 4: July 1925.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: Queens Boulevard - 57th Avenue
text:
Queens Boulevard (tracks thereon) at and adjoining the S.W. corner of Fifty-seventh Avenue. Shown at the corner is the home of Samuel Reune in 1776 which was also known as the Bretoni ers' house. It was remodelled in 1865 by J. Van Riper, a builder. The hip roof was converted to that seen in the views. This builder also believes that the structure adjoining it was the first Baptist Church building of Newtown. The first mentioned house was still standing in November 1933.

text:
Queens Boulevard, at the S. W. corner of 62nd Avenue, showing the Mrs. Howard House, also known as the Robert Odekirk farmhouse and was at one time used as a parsonage by ministers of the First Presbyterian Church of Newtown. The house was owned by the R. and J. Thompsons from 1852 to 1896. Later it was purchased by the Rego Park Construction Company and used as a real estate office. The home dates back to pre-Revolutionary days. Eugene L. Armbruster is authority for the above data. View 4 shows the rear of the house.

title: Queens: Queens Boulevard - 63rd Avenue
text:
Queens Boulevard, west from 63rd Avenue. View 1 shows an old house, said to have been a parsonage, on the south side of the Boulevard. It is No. 9272 Queens Boulevard. To the right are the old Thompson barns in rear of the Thompson farmhouse which later became the Rego Park real estate office.

View 2 shows a more extensive view of the Boulevard. The house on the left is No. 9272, the one seen in view 1. The white house in the background is the pre-Revolutionary Thompson House. On the right is a pumping station. Queens Boulevard is being widened; the buildings on the left mark the new building line and the new width of the thoroughfare.

View 1: February, 1924
View 2: May, 1926

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Queens: Queens Boulevard - 69th Road
text:
Queens Boulevard (in center thereof), between Seventieth Ave. (right), and 69th Road (left), showing the George W. Hunt house. This house stood originally on the north side of Hoffman Boulevard (now part of Queens Boulevard) and nearly opposite No. 526. Col. George W. Hunt of White Pot was the grandson of Oliver Hunt and owned this property in 1852. He moved to New Jersey and the property came into the possession of the Squire family (1873-1924). It was demolished in that year. View No. 2 shows the barns located south of and slightly east of the farmhouse. These were also demolished at this time. This is a set of four views. View No. 4 shows a rear view.

Queens Village, Queens: Viewing southeastward across a vast area of Queens Village, showing newly erected two-family homes, part of a large real estate development. title: Queens: Queens Village - [215th Place - Spencer and Hillside Avenues - Real estate development.]
text:
Queens Village, Queens: This is a general view south- ward showing an immense real estate development on former farmland owned by Wheeler Brothers and J. Van De Graw (1909). This development of low-cost two-family homes is known as "Jamaica Hillside." The unpaved street in the center, running toward the background, is 215th Place. In the immediate foreground is Spencer Avenue; below it is Whitehall Terrace; below that is the main east-west thoroughfare, Hillside Avenue.

Joseph P. Day
Photograph Department

title: Queens: Ransom Street - 88th Avenue
text:
Ransom Street (Shaler Street), at the S.E. corner of Eighty-eighth Ave. showing what Eugene L. Armbruster states doubtfully to be the A. Graf house in 1896 and the old Kissam House before that. There are 33.1 acres of ground belonging to the B.T. Kissam Estate, south of Eighty-eighth Ave. to Braddock Ave. (Rocky Hill Road in 1909.) On this property there were two dwellings, one east of Ransom Street (formerly Shaler Street) and about 720 feet north of Braddock Ave., and the other, demolished in 1928, was north of Braddock Ave. and 1200 feet east of Ransom Street. This is a set of two views taken from slightly different angles.

August 1924.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: Rockaway Boulevard - 94th Street
text:
Rockaway Boulevard, at the N.E. corner of 94th Street, formerly Walker Ave. Also shown is the east side of Walker Ave. north from Rockaway Boulevard. At the right of the Hotel, in center of view, is Woodhaven Boulevard, formerly Hopkins Ave., extending northward. Flushing Ave., now 91st Street, cuts diagonally across the right side of this hotel and across Woodhaven Boulevard. The Toll house for this area was at the southern intersection of Liberty Ave. and Rockaway Boulevard in or just east of Vandeveer Ave. However, its site has been absorbed by the widening of the Boulevard. The Centerville Race Course after which this hotel is named was south of the toll house and east of Flushing Ave., now absorbed at this point by the Cross Is. Boulevard. The Centerville Race Course was founded in 1825. In 1860 R.C. McCormick operated the toll gate. The Centerville Hotel seen in these views was operated by Emile Mettetal who was also its proprietor.

August 1923.
View 2: 1894.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: Shore Boulevard - 21st Avenue
text:
Shore Boulevard, east side, north of 21st Ave., showing the home of Mrs. Polhemus in 1852. This is an 18th Century structure. In the rear of this house is hte Rapelje family’s burial place. the history of this farmland begins with a land grant in 1653 to Teunis Craye. In 1681 Hendrick Martense Wiltsee (a Dane) purchased it. He in turn conveyed it in 1706 to his son, Teunis Wiltsee. This house was erected by Jacob Rapelje who was born in 1714. His daughter married Abraham Polhemus; then this house acquired its name. This is a set of three views. This house is now on land belonging to the Consolidated Gas Company.
1922
View 2: June 1925.
View 3: 1922.
Eugene L. Ambruster Collection.

title: Queens: Springfield Boulevard - 48th Avenue
text:
Springfield Boulevard, east side, between Forty-eight and Fifty-sixth Aves., showing the Oakland Golf Club's Club house. In 1891 this house and the surrounding estate belonged to John Taylor. In 1860 to S. Valentine. This place was first known as "The Oaks" and was opened as a nursery by a member of the Hicks family. Later it was also owned by a Lawrence and one Henderson. This is not the original building; it was destroyed by fire. The entrance to this Club house was a private drive extending northeastward from Rocky Hill Road (now Fifty-sixth Ave.) In 1937 it was located east of Fifty-first Avenue and Kenilworth Drive.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

January 1923.

title: Queens: Union Hall Street - Jamaica Avenue
text:
Union Hall Street, west side, north from the Long Island Railroad right of way, showing in a set of four views different aspects of the former Union Hall Academy. This institution first opened, May 1, 1792 in a Fulton Street (now Jamaica Avenue) structure and Malthy Gelston was the first principal. Dr. L.E.A. Eigenbrodt succeeded to this position which he held for 31 years until his death in 1828. During his incumbency this structure was erected; the cornerstone being laid in July 1820. Henry Onderdonck taught here during the years 1832 and 1865. 1873 saw the Academy close it's doors and the three buildings altered into dwellings which in 1876 were the homes of individuals named Smith, Hague, and Crane. A Childrens Court is stated to have been a lengthy occupant. They were still standing in 1929, tho a new apartment house was erected to the north of same.

Views 1 & 2: 1922.
3: May 1923.
4: April 1925.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Queens: Union Street - Bayside Avenue
text:
Union Street (Whitestone Ave.) (right), south from about Twenty-ninth Ave. The house seen in this view faces Bayside Ave. This site was the headquarters and the property of Col. Hamilton of the British army. The house that then stood on the site burned down in 1779. The present house was erected in 1780. Henry Mitchell purchased it in 1804 and it was not sold again until 1921. This is a set of three views. No. 2 shows a close up of the house at the corner while No. 3 shows it on Bayside Ave.

title: Queens: Union Turnpike - Queens Boulevard
text:
Union Turnpike, between Queens Boulevard and Vleigh Place (Head of the Vleigh Road, showing the farm house of Timothy J. Jackson. This farm, comprised of 77 acres, was used as a stock farm. On it was a one-half mile circular trotting course. This Jackson, maintained a general store just west of L. Younger's house which was on the N.W. corner of Vleigh Place and Union Turnpike. No buildings appear on any of the Queens Atlases after 1909 and the only buildings that appear on that year are near the northern boundary of the property, just south of Edgar H. Meeker's property. Cord Meyer became the owner of this property after 1891. For a number of years he operated a pumping station. This is a set of four views taken on different days and from different angles. It is probable that if these buildings were standing in 1937 they would be between 132nd and 138th Street. However they were demolished sometime in 1929.

October 1928.
Views 1, 2 & 3.
View 4: April 1929.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Queens: Vernon Boulevard - Borden Avenue

As the highway will reach the small group of tenements (center) it will bend to the left and across the clearance between the factories; that portion of the road will be elevated. title: Queens: Vernon Boulevard - 30th Road
text:
Vernon Boulevard, east side, north from 30th Road to Main Avenue, showing two eighteenth-century homes.  The first one is the John Greenoak house, later the Mrs. Blosson house; the second is the Halsey house.  John Greenoak built this house in the early part of the eighteenth century and owned a farm here.  The farm later came into the possession of Higgins, the carpet manufacturer.  In 1831 Henry I. Blackwell took over the property.  Blackwell's widow later married Blosson, and became the owner of the house in 1873.  Views 2 and 3 show the Greenoak and Halsey houses, respectively; view 4, the Greenoak house, with the porch gone.
Views 1-3: Eugene L. Armbruster Collection 1925
View 4: P.L. Sperr  March 11, 1931

title: Queens: West Drive - Alston Place
text:
Van Wyck House
West Dr. & Alston Pl.
Douglaston, N.Y.

C. Manley DeBevoise
51-05 Browvale Lane,
Little Neck, N.Y. 11362

The old Dutch colonial house at the corner of West Drive and Alston Pl. in Douglas Manor, Douglaston, New York, now owned by Mr. and Mrs. L. Kelville Larson, was built in 1735 by Cornelius Van Wyck. He was the eldest son of Johannes Van Wyck whose father was an earlier Cornelius Van Wyck, was one of the patentees of Mid-Wout, having emigrated there from Holland in 1660.

In 1705 one hundred and twenty-five acres of land south and east of the present house at West Drive and Alston Pl., was purchased from Richard and Sarah Cornell by Johannes Van Wyck. His brother Theodorus had already acquired land from King's Point. Johannes had three sons and four daughters and became a Justice of the Provincial Courts.

When Justice Johannes died in 1734, the property was inherited by his eldest son Cornelius who had married Mary Hicks, daughter of Judge Isaac Hicks. Cornelius and Mary prospered, added to the original farm, and until Cornelius' death in 1759, lived in the house they had built twenty-four years earlier.

Cornelius left three sons - Stephan, Cornelius II, and Gilbert. Stephan the eldest, inherited the house and flourishing farm. Cornelius II had the misfortune of being captured by the British in a surprise raid of Flushing and was confined aboard one of the notorious prison ships anchored in the Wallabout (Bay). He died soon after his release from the effect of a years confinement under horrible conditions. Stephan fell heir to the appointment as delegate to the Continental Congress to which office his deceased brother Cornelius had been elected in June, 1776.

title: Queens: Woodhaven Blvd - Fleet Street
text:
Woodhaven Boulevard, east side, north from Fleet Street (White Pot Road) showing at the corner the site upon which stood the White Pot schoolhouse from 1852 to 1896. In the background is seen Thos. Tompkins farmhouse in 65th Road. The school house was erected on land donated by Jacobus Springstein son of Casper Springstein. The first school was established in 1739. The demolished structure was the fourth or fifth erected on this site.

title: Queens: Wyckoff Avenue - Cooper Avenue
text:
Wyckoff Ave., at the S.W. corner of Cooper Ave. (formerly Lawrence Street); showing the Norman Van Nostrand farmhouse from 1852-1860. This place was known as "The Little Pink House." Norman Van Nostrand came here from New York City. He settled on forty acres of land and erected this house thereon in 1852. This house which was demolished in 1910 was also known because the feast church services of the St. Thomas Episcopal Church (located on Bushwick Ave. and Cooper Street, Kings County) were held here during the winter of 1871.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

1909.

title: Queens: Yellowstone Boulevard - Dartmouth Street & Clyde Street
text:
Yellowstone Boulevard, east side, between Dartmouth and Clyde Streets, showing in a set of 4 views the Abraham Furman farmhouse. Gabriel Furman was the son of John Furman who died in 1726. He, John, owned this farm which was in 1852 in the possession of his great grandson Abraham. Some of the later owners were: Abraham Furman, 1852-1860; G. Furman, 1860-1873; Mrs. H. Miller, 1872-1891; and A. Miller from 1891 to 1909. The house was no longer standing in Aug. 1925. One Holzheiser was an occupant about 1873. See other views.

title: Queens: Yellowstone Boulevard - Fleet Street
text:
Yellowstone Boulevard, south side, east from Fleet Street. The peaked roof house seen in the background is partially in the west street line of Exeter Street, just south of Yellowstone Boulevard. The street actually shown in these views is White Pot Road which subsequently became known as Dane Place. The above named Boulevard has been constructed at the right of Dane Place and junctions it at Exeter Street and from there absorbs it. The farmland and buildings thereon seen in this view were a part of Mrs. Boerum's Estate in 1873.

March 1925.

title: Richmond: Arc Place - Tysens Lane
text:
Arc Place (formerly Amboy Road), at the N.W. corner of Tysens Lane, showing the old Britton House. It was built between 1650 and 1660 and demolished in 1896, being one of the oldest structures on Staten Island. It was used as a Colonial court house. It was also used as a hospital by the British during the Revolution.

Prior to 1896.

By Wm. T. Davis
through P. L. Sperr.

title: Richmond: Arthur Kill Road - Botany Place
text:
(1) Arthur Kill Road, west side, south of Botany Place, showing the Disosway House. It stands about 200 yards back of the road, facing the shore of Arthur Kill. According to Beers' 1874 map it belonged to Mrs. Totten. Subsequent maps, from 1898 to 1917, indicate it to have belonged to George Starr. The house was demolished when the Outerbridge Crossing was erected in this area. title: Richmond: Arthur Kill Road - Center Street
text:
Arthur Kill Road, north side, adjoining (to the west) Center Street, showing the Vorleezer House, reputed to be one of the oldest Dutch frame buildings in New York. It is believed to have been erected before 1696 and is the oldest known elementary school building in the United States and the first church on Staten Island. It was occupied by the Rezan and Van Pelt families for many years. For additional data see the New York City Guide of the Federal Writers' Project, p.612.

P. L. Sperr

title: Richmond: Bloomingdale Road - Tarbes Avenue
text:
Bloomingdale Road, west side, between Tarbes and Wirt Avenues, showing an old house, about 175 feet back of the Road. This old dwelling was at one time (1874 map) on the S. Church estate. Later it was owned by E. V. S. Parnell (1898 map) and by Dumpson (1907-1917 maps). The dirt road, shown here, appears on the maps from 1898 to 1917, but does not bear any name. It runs parallel to Bloomingdale Road, in a south-north direction, and is about 175 feet west of it. The view here is in a southerly direction from a point about 250 yards south of Arthur Kill Road and west of Bloomingdale Road. The New York City zoning map of 1937 does not show any thoroughfare where this dirt road is, so that the best description of its present-day location is that given at the beginning of this paragraph.

June 1, 1930

P. L. Sperr

title: Richmond: Richmond Road - Vandel Avenue
text:
Clifton, Staten Island: A panoramic view eastward across the village of Clifton as seen from the hill above Richmond Road between Vandell and Cunard Avenues. In the center background is the club house on the Fox Hills golf links, formerly the George W. Vanderbilt estate; to its right is the Wrigley chewing gum plant on the Upper New York Bay. In the very foreground is Richmond Road and running diagonally to it, from the lower left hand corner, is Hamilton Street. The inhabited area seen in views 1 and 2 lies between Vanderbilt Avenue and Van Duzer Street, extending east toward the harbor from Richmond Road; the uninhabited area extending to the right from the Fox Hills Golf Club, is the region lying between Vanderbilt Avenue and Fingerboard Road, in the vicinity of Bradys Pond. title: Richmond:] Staten Island - Fort Wadsworth.
text:
EXCLUSIVE
9708

A LESSON FOR "DEFENSE DAY" IN A N.Y. FORT.

The scene depicted above might well happen with the inadequate system of defense against attack from an enemy. The photo shows one of the great 12" inch rifles in Fort Wadsworth, Staten Island, in action against enemy ships beyond Sandy Hook. Other enemy ships have landed troops and tanks below the fortifications. Whippet tanks make a concerted against the unprotected rear and one climbing the parapet in front, fires with its one pounder on the unprotected gun crew and the few infantrymen with a machine gun and rifles. An adequate system of mobilization with the necessary equipment to prevent such an incident as this is one of the purposes of "Defense Day."

YOUR CREDIT LINE MUST READ: - (BY UNITED)
Sept. 13, 1924.

title: Richmond: Holland Avenue - Bailey Place
text:
60 Holland Avenue, west side, at Bailey Place (south of Richmond Terrace), showing the kitchen of the first story rear apartment of a two-story frame dwelling. This is, in all probability, the home of one of the underpaid workmen of the Downey Shipbuilding Corporation, whose shipyards are located in the back of the house. Conditions such as this can be found all along Holland Avenue, which is inhabited mainly by the shipyard hands.

About 1910

Committee on Housing
Charity Organization Society

title: Richmond: Holland Avenue - Arlington Place
text:
138 Holland Avenue, west side, between Arlington Place and Macromac Place, showing the exterior of a frame dwelling. The house does not have a water supply and drinking water is obtained from a pump in the yard. As the dwelling is situated near the Downey Shipbuilding Corporation yard, and is one of a number of similar ones, it is very likely that it is inhabited by the shipyard workers and their families.

About 1910

Committee on Housing
Charity Organization Society

title: Richmond: Hylan Boulevard - Stuyvesant Place
text:
AUSTEN HOUSE  2 Hylan Boulevard, Rosebank, Staten Island. The first section of this low, Early American farm-house was built about 1700 close to the water of the Narrows. By the time it was purchased in 1884 by John Austen, however, several Gothic Revival additions had been made to the original structure. This charming cottage, also known as "Clear Comfort", was for many years the home of E. Alice Austen, an accomplished New York photographer at the turn of the century.

Bank of New York Calendar 1967-68

title: Richmond: Hylan Boulevard - Satterlee Street
text:
(1)

Hylan Boulevard, north side, between Satterlee Street and Wards Point Avenue, showing the Billopp House, or "Conference House." In this house was held, on September 11, 1776, a conference between Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, and Edward Rutledge representing the Continental Congress and Admiral Lord Howe, commanding the British naval forces. The house derives its name from Christopher Billopp, who circumnavigated Staten Island in less than twenty-four hours and claimed it for New York State.

About 1905

By Eugene G. Putnam
From Staten Island Museum Collection through P. L. Sperr

(2)

The basement kitchen of the Billopp House.

title: Richmond: Hylan Boulevard - Satterlee Street
text:
BILLOPP HOUSE  Hylan Boulevard and Satterlee Street, Tottenville, Staten Island. Built by and for Christopher Billopp about 1680, this Dutch Colonial residence was for many years a center of gracious New York hospitality. It is Known also as "Conference House" because Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and Edward Rutledge met here with the English general, Lord Howe, on September 11, 1776, in an unsuccessful effort to halt the American Revolution.

title: Richmond: Richmond Road - New Dorp Lane
text:

title: Richmond: New Street - Jersey Street
text:
1 to 5 New Street, north side, east of Jersey Street, (New Brighton) showing views across the wreckage after the buildings which occupied the site collapsed, during a heavy rainstorm on August 11, 1937. The three small dwellings were about forty or fifty years old and were built for workers of the nearby Irving silk factory (seen on the right). Nineteen people were killed in the disaster. New Street, on which the three dwellings fronted, does not appear by name on any maps of the borough; the above name and numbers appearing in the newspaper accounts of the accident. The three houses that collapsed were in the center of the row of five that took up the entire length of the street--a narrow, cobbled dead-end thoroughfare. For additional data see "The New York Times," August 12 and 13, 1937.

August 14, 1937

The three houses that collapsed were in the center of the row of five that took up the entire length of the street--a narrow, cobbled, dead-end thoroughfare. For additional data see "The New York Times," August 12 and 13, 1937.

title: Richmond: Richmond Avenue - Dongan Hills Avenue
text:
(1)

1682 Richmond Avenue, (house in foreground), at the N.E. corner of Dongan Hills Avenue, showing the old J. Barnes House. Butler's and Beers's maps of 1853 and 1874, respectively, show the house to have been owned by J. Barnes. In 1898 it belonged to Captain E. F. Keegan and was then known as "Sunny Side"; in 1907 the Dongan Hill Feed and Grain Company owned it; and in 1917 the Richmond County Agricultural Society. Mr. P. L. Sperr states that this house is an Egbert house; the writer of these lines did not, however, find any evidence in support of the statement. Though a large tract of land belonging to J. Egbert lay directly north of the house and adjoined the Barnes property, the maps of the aforementioned dates do not show the dwelling to have belonged to Egbert. It may, though, have belonged to Egbert at an earlier date. The view is eastward across Dongan Hills toward the Lower New York Bay and Hoffman Island, as seen from Flagg Place.

1920's

P. L. Sperr

(2)

An exclusive view of the house.

May 10, 1936

title: Richmond: Richmond Avenue - Castleton Avenue
text:
Richmond Avenue, at the N.E. corner of Castleton Avenue, showing Progress Hall, also known as the Jaques House, and the Harrison House. Dr. John T. Harrison lived here in 1853. Cornelius Mereseau was born in this house. It is stated, too, that Commodore Vanderbilt was born here. The residence was built by Isaac Jaques. Above the door there is the number 125. That was the house number before Castleton Avenue was cut through from Richmond to Heberton Avenues. The house no longer appears in Bromley's 1917 real estate map. See Legends, Stories and Folklore of Old Staten Island by Gilbert & Davis, part I, p. 106.

About 1900

By Eugene G. Putnam
From Staten Island Museum Collection through P. L. Sperr

title: Richmond: Richmond Road - Norden Street
text:
(1)
1476 Richmond Road, east side, between Norden Street and Delaware Street, showing the Perine House, home of the Staten Island Historical Society. It is the oldest house on Staten Island and part of it was probably erected before 1678. Thomas Stillwell was owner in 1685. Later the title passed to Nicholas Britton, and after his death to Walter Dongan. Still later Joseph Holmes acquired the property. His daughter, Ann, married Edward Perine, to whom her mother released it in 1764. During the Revolution it was the headquarters of Captain Coghlan. The house was sold to the Antiquarian Society in 1915.

1924

title: Richmond: Richmond Road - New Dorp Lane
text:
Richmond Road, north side, adjoining (to the east) New Dorp Lane, showing the Patten House. It was built in 1836 by Colonel John Patten as a hostelry to accommodate the crowds who came to see the New Dorp races. It was the headquarters of General Van Buren, commanding the State Militia of this military district. Commodore Vanderbilt was a frequent visitor here. It was also the headquarters of the Owls Club of which Wm. H. Vanderbilt, Senator "Sam" Frost and Judge Daniel Clawson were members. It closed as a public hostelry in 1887, after which it was used by Father McGlynn as a branch of a Roman Catholic institution. Later it was used as a tenement house by Italian ragpickers. It was condemned by the Board of Health as a hazard to health and safety and was finally razed in 1902. See the "New York Tribune", June 29, 1902, illustrated supplement, p. 5.

About 1900

By Eugene G. Putnam
From Staten Island Museum Collection through P. L. Sperr

title: Richmond: Richmond Terrace - Tysen Street
text:
Richmond Terrace, south side, between Tysen Street and Kissel Avenue, showing Sailors' Snug Harbor, seen from the Kill Van Kull. On the left is the Randall Memorial Church in the style of the late Italian Renaissance. To its right is the Music Hall. The building on the right, with the low dome, is the Main Building, used for administrative purposes. Sailors' Snug Harbor, a home for retired seaman, was founded in 1801 by the will of Captain Robert Richard Randall, son of a privateer, who bequeathed the bulk of his fortune for the establishment and support of an institution for destitute sailors. The site was purchased in 1831 and the asylum was opened in 1833. The Harbor contains more than fifty buildings.
About 1900
Photo by August Loeffler
From P.L. Sperr Collection

title: Richmond: Richmond Terrace - Pelton Avenue
text:
(1)
1262 Richmond Terrace, east side, south of Pelton Avenue, showing a front view of the Pelton House. It was in part erected about 1730, another part was added about 1776, and was the headquarters of General Cortlandt Skinner during the Revolutionary War. It is said that major André was billeted here during the Revolutionary War, and that Prince William Henry, afterwards King William IV, was here once. Rockwell Kent, nationally known artist, occupied for a time a part of the house. For additional data see "Staten Island and its People" by Leng and Davis, vol. 2, p. 936; also "Legends, Stories and Folklore of Old Staten Island." by Hine and Davis, p. 86.

title: Richmond: Richmond Terrace - Richmond Avenue
text:
(1) 2038-2040 Richmond Terrace, adjoining the S.E. corner of Richmond Avenue, showing the St. James Hotel, also called, at different times, the Port Richmond Hotel, the Continental Hotel, Danner's Hotel, and Richmond Hotel (sign above entrance). It stands on the site of the Revolutionary Fort Decker and was built soon after the war as a private residence. It was the home of Judge David Mersereau in 1820, and was at that time the finest house on Staten Island. It later became the Port Richmond Hotel and was then the largest hotel in the county. Aaron Burr, vice president of the United States under Jefferson, died here on September 14, 1836. From 1854 to 1856 it was the headquarters of the Know-Nothing or American Party.

About 1905

By Eugene G. Putnam
From Staten Island Museum Collection through P. L. Sperr

(2) A view of the hotel at a later date. The house has been lifted off the street level and turned into a 3-story structure, the wing having been removed at the same time.

January 1923

By Wm. T. Davis through P. L. Sperr

(3) The same, at a still later date.

title: Richmond: Old Mill Road - Arthur Kill Road
text:
(1)
Richmond Village (Staten Island): A general view across the old village of Richmond as seen from the hill above Old Mill Road in Latourette Park. In the foreground is Old Mill Road, east of Mill Road; on the left is the old St. Andrews P. E. Church and cemetery, built in 1872; running parallel to the Old Mill Road and winding its course around the cemetery is Richmond Creek; in the center of the view is the St. Andrews Church parish house, a frame, domed building, at the corner of Arthur Kill and Richmond Roads; directly across it is the old Richmond County Court House, built in 1837, and the county jail.

About 1905

By Mulford Simonson

title: Richmond: Richmond Terrace - Stuyvesant Place
text:
St. George, Staten Island: An aerial view south across St. George on the Upper New York Bay. On the left are the freight yards of the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, with the Municipal ferry terminal visible in part, on the left (white structure). Across the viaduct, which spans the freight yard and leads to the ferry terminal from Richmond Terrace, are municipal piers and American Dock Company warehouses clustered around Victory Boulevard. The thoroughfare running across the face of the view, above the B. & O. Railroad yard, is Richmond Terrace, terminating at the ferry ramp. Branching off from the former, to form the shape of a "U," is Stuyvesant Place. At the lower end of this "U"-shaped area is the Richmond Borough Hall; preceding that is the Richmond County Court House, a hotel, and Richmond Police Headquarters (square Building). In the right foreground is the 8-story Castleton Park Apartments, on St. Marks Place, site of the famous fashionable St. Marks Hotel; to its right is discernible a wing of Curtis High School, in Gothic architecture.

title: Richmond:] Staten Island - Stapleton - [Rubsam and Horrmann Brewery].
text:
(1) Stapleton, Staten Island: A general view eastward across the town and piers on the Upper New York Bay. In the center of the view is visible the Rubsam and Horrmann Atlantic Brewery; to its left is the funnel of an ice manufacturing plant. In the foreground is a children's playground on the east side of Targee Street, where a municipal courthouse was later erected. The piers, counting from left to right, begin with No. 12 and continue in arithmetic progression. The view is from the hill above Van Duzer Street.

Mid 1920's

P. L. Sperr

(2) Viewing across Stapleton, in a slightly more northerly direction, towards Tompkinsville; The piers counting from right to left in arithmetic regression, begin with No. 14. On the extreme left is Van Duzer Street; running parallel to it is Targee Street, and in the center of the view, running uphill, is Grove Street.

Mid 1920's

P. L. Sperr

(3) The Rubsam and Horrmann Brewery (right) and the stack of the ice plant, seen from Van Duzer Street.

July 8, 1932

P. L. Sperr

The thoroughfare on the extreme right is Laurel Avenue; in the center background, directly preceding the S. S. Aquitania moving up the harbor, is the U. S. title: Richmond:] Staten Island - Stapleton.
text:
Stapleton, Staten Island: A general view southeastward across the town of Stapleton and the Upper New York Bay, as seen from Pearl Street on Grymes Hill. Shown in the foreground is the colonnaded 2nd District Magistrates and Municipal Court House, at 67-71 Targee Street; in the left center is the tall clock-tower building of the Rubsam and Horrmann Brewery on Canal Street; in the center background is the United States Marine Hospital, and directly across its right wing is the Wrigley chewing gum plant; slightly to the right, at the edge of the clearance, is the four-story Mariners' Family Asylum, 119 Tompkins Avenue; the wooded area lying beyond that is Rosebank. Across the Stapleton piers and the bay is Brooklyn.

View 3 shows the United States Marine Hospital, Bay Street and Vanderbilt Avenue, seen from the campus of Wagner College.

title: Richmond:] Staten Island - Stapleton.
text:
Stapleton, Staten Island: Three panoramic views southeast-ward across Stapleton, toward the Upper New York Bay and Brooklyn, seen from Pearl Street on Grymes Hill. In the center foreground is the 2nd District Municipal and Magistrate's Court House, at 67-71 Targee Street; in the left foreground is an ice manufacturing plant on Gordon Street and to its right is the Rubsam and Horrmann Brewery, its main building (with clock tower) being on Canal Street; in the right foreground is the United States Marine Hospital and across its right wing the Wrigley chewing gum plant; on the extreme right, on the edge of the clearance, is the Mariners' Family Asylum, 119 Tompkins Avenue. The wooded area beyond that is Rosebank. The piers facing on Murray Hulbert Avenue, begin with No. 14 counting in arithmetic progression from the left.

P. L. Sperr

In the center foreground is the 2nd District Municipal and Magistrate's Court House, at 67-71 Targee Street; in the left foreground is an ice manufacturing plant on Gordon Street and to its right is the Rubsam and Horrmann Brewery, its main building (with clock tower) being on Canal Street; in the right foreground is the United States Marine Hospital and across its right wing the Wrigley chewing gum plant; on the extreme right, on the edge of the clearance, is the Mariners' Family Asylum, 119 Tompkins Avenue. The wooded area beyond that is Rosebank. The piers facing on Murray Hulbert Avenue, begin with No. 14 counting in arithmetic progression from the left.

P. L. Sperr

June 23, 1937
Views 1, 2, 3
