title: Richmond:] Staten Island - Stapleton - [General view].
text:
Stapleton, Staten Island: Shown is a general view, in a southeasterly direction, of the town of Stapleton, as seen from Tompkins Circle on Pavilion Hill. Shown too, are piers Nos. 10 to 16, constituting the Foreign Trade Zone, fronting on Murray Hulbert Avenue. In the center foreground is the clocktower of Public School No. 15, on St. Pauls Avenue; in the distant right background is the Wrigley chewing gum factory and the hills of Concord; across the bay is the shore of the borough of Brooklyn. Pictures 2 and 3 show a more restricted view of the foreground area with only piers 12 to 16 visible in view 2; in the center background of view 3 appears the United States Marine Hospital at Bay Street and Vanderbilt Avenue.

September 7, 1939
Views 1, 2, 3

P. L. Sperr

title: Richmond: Tyler Street - Clove Road
text:
DURING the Civil War, the elegant Greek revival Gardiner-Tyler House, in West New Brighton, Staten Island, sheltered one of New York's most conspicuous rebel sympathizers, Julia Gardiner Tyler, widow of President John Tyler. When she was not involved in pro-Confederate activities, she was busy trying to reunite her family, scattered by the war. Now another family is reuniting in this grand temple-fronted house, as a new addition brings together three generations under one roof.

Now on a small plot surrounded by modest houses, the Gardiner-Tyler house was built around 1837 as a much larger country estate, apparently by an Eliza Racey, about whom little is known.

title: Richmond: Westcott Boulevard - Kemball Avenue
text:
Westcott Boulevard, at Kemball Avenue. Shown is an old farmstead before Westcott Boulevard was laid out on the site of the pond (Mr. Sperr refers to it as Lust's Pond), the view being in a southerly direction and marking the direction in which Westcott Boulevard runs. Butler's 1853 map shows this to be on the P. Laforge property; Beers's 1874 map indicates the house to have been the mining captain's residence of the Richmond Iron Mining Company, whose iron mines were nearby. In 1898 and 1907 it was part of the J.W. Cochrane property and the pond was known as "Diamond Lake." Kemball, Chandler and Coale Avenues now (1940) cut across the site from east to west. Before the new thoroughfares were laid out the pond(and homestead) was located about 500 feet north of Victory Boulevard, slightly east of Jewett Avenue.

About 1905

By Mulford Simonson

text:
A general view westward from No. 1 Hanson Place, the Williamsburg Savings Bank Building, toward the East River and the Lower Manhattan skyline (view 2). title: General view - Brooklyn.
text:
A general view northwestward from No. 1 Hanson Place, the Williamsburg Savings Bank Building, showing the business center of Brooklyn. Running across the face of the view from the lower left-hand corner is Flatbush Avenue, with the B. M. T. "El" on it, and its Fulton Street station. The bare-faced building forming a triangle in the center is the Fox Theatre Building, at Livingston Street. The auto-parking space is at Third Avenue (trolley tracks) and Schermerhorn Street, this area being known as Temple Square. In the distance is the Lower Manhattan skyline.

In the lower right-hand corner of view 2 is the Hotel Granada, Lafayette Avenue and Ashland Place. The thoroughfares seen in view 3 running from the fore- to the background (left to right) are: State Street, Schermerhorn Street, and Livingston Street.

May 12, 1939
Views 1,2,3

P. L. Sperr

title: General View - Brooklyn - East New York.
text:
East New York, Brooklyn: Shown are four general views across the East New York area of Brooklyn, looking south and southeast (view4) from the high ground in Highland Park. In the lower right hand corner of view 1 can be seen the old Isaac Cornell Schenck House on the north side of Jamaica Avenue. This part of the park was formerly the Schenck farm. In the left center is Public School No. 108, on Linwood Street, The two streets, prominently seen running perpendicular to Jamaica Avenue, are Elton (left) and Cleveland Streets. In view 4 appears also the Interborough Parkway (autos) which is in the Queens part of the park.

Wilberforce Eames, Collection
1916
Views 1-4

title: General view - Brooklyn - Hanson Place (East).
text:
A general view eastward from the Y.M.C.A. Building, No. 55 Hanson Place, between Fort Greene and South Elliott Places, showing in the foreground Fulton Street and the Elevated structure thereon, beyond it is the steeple of the Lafayette Ave. Presbyterian Church at the S.E. corner of South Oxford Street and Lafayette Ave. In the background is the Masonic Temple (colonnaded) at the N.E. corner of Lafayette and Clermont Aves., beyond and partially seen is the Cathedral Chapel of the Queen of all Saints (R.C.). At the left background is the Williamsburg Bridge. This part of Brooklyn is known as the Hill section. June 1926.

Brown Brothers.

title: General view - Brooklyn - Hanson Place (North).
text:
A general view north from the Y.M.C.A. located at 55 Hanson Place. This view is limited on the right by S. Elliot Place; to the right of which is seen the Martyrs Monument in Fort Greene Park. In the center of the view, extending north, is clearly seen the west side of Fort Greene Place. Across the face of the view is the Fulton Street Elevated line of the B.M.T. The Lafayette Street Station is at the junction of Lafayette Ave., Fort Greene Place and Fulton Street. At the left is the Smith-Gray Building (clock in tower). This section is known as the lower hill section of Brooklyn. Indistinctly seen on the horizon is an outline of lower Manhattan, with the Brooklyn, and the Manhattan Bridges thereof.

June 1926.

Brown Brothers.

title: General view - Brooklyn - [Between Joralemon and Court Streets.]
text:
A general view, north from the Municipal Building, which is located at the S.E. corner of Joralemon and Court Streets, showing in the left foreground the Eagle Building, located at the S.E. corner of Johnson and Washington Streets. In the background is the East River, and the Williamsburg Bridge. Looking northward from the center of the view is City Park, the Sperry Buildings, the U.S. Navy Yard (in which is a lifting crane that looks like a building under construction), and beyond, to the right, is the Wallabout Channel.

May 1926.

Brown Brothers.

title: General view - Brooklyn - [Between Joralemon and Court Streets.]

May 1926.

Brown Brothers.

title: General view - [Manhattan - Downtown skyline.]
text:
World's highest skyscraper of the week.
A new view of the magnificent downtown skyline, showing in center the Bank of Manhattan Company Building under construction. When complete this building will be the world's tallest skyscraper-68 stories-but not for long because of the recently anounced plans for the buildings of 100 and 150 stories. At right is 120 Wall Stree and at left is the Whitehall Building.
1929? 			Underwood and Underwood

title: General view - New York Harbor - [An airplane view of New York Bay.]
text: An airplane view of the heart of New York City. This is the lower portion of Manhattan Island and a section of the Borough of Brooklyn. The upper third of the picture is New Jersey. Three of the five Bridges connecting Manhattan with Brooklyn and Queens boroughs can be seen here: the original Brooklyn Bridge farthest away, next to what is known as the Manhattan Bridge, and the Williamsburg Bridge in the foreground. The Statue of Liberty is visible in the Upper Bay. June 1924 Fairchild Aerial Surveys

title: General view - East side of Lower Manhattan.
text:
A general view of the lower East Side of Manhattan as photographed northeastward from the Tribune Bldg. (belief of the writer), showing the area above the future Brooklyn Bridge Approach. The latter will be constructed across the foreground necessitating the demolition of some of the low structures shown. This will be slightly north of Frankfort Street and across the apex of the point of convergence of North William and William Streets. Note the wall sign of Kraft & Hoffmeister there. The Pulitzer Bldg. (World Bldg.) of 1889 will rise on the site of the nonde-script buildings in the left foreground. At the left margin is Park Row and its "El" line. The institutional building in the center midground is the Newsboys Lodging House. To the right is the school and spires of St. James R.C. Church. Madison Street is observable there.

Betw. 1875 - 84

E. L. Armbruster Collection

The three East River bridges shown are the Brooklyn, the Manhattan, and the Williamsburg.

title: General view - East side of Lower Manhattan.
text:
A general view of the lower East Side of Manhattan as photographed northeastward from the Woolworth Building (belief of the writer), showing that section east of Broadway (left) and north of the Brooklyn Bridge (right not included). In the foreground are several of the civic structures that surround City Hall Park. O'er cast by the shadow of the point of vantage are the roof of the old County Court House, the City Court, the Hall of Records, the Municipal Building, and the new hexagonal New York County Court House. The latter is under construction at this date and is the first civic structure to rise in the new center, Foley Square. Across the top runs the East River.

1923-4

Brown Bros., photo

title: General view - Midtown Manhattan.
text:
A NEW VIEW OF A NEW SKYLINE--ALL OF THESE GIANT UPTOWN BUILDINGS HAVE SPRUNG UP WITHIN THE PAST TWO YEARS

NEW YORK.--PHOTO SHOWS: An excellent and new angle on the new uptown skyline. This shot was taken from the top of Carnegie Hall and shows the skyline from 54th Street and 6th Avenue to 23rd Street and Madison Avenue (Madison Square). Left to right the buildings are: the Warwick Hotel, St. Patrick's Cathedral; New York Central Building; Chanin Building (the highest uptown skyscraper); four buildings together, --Empire Trust, Fred F. French, Bank of the United States, and the new Lefcourt building; then the Arnold Constable building at 40th Street; and at extreme right, the New York Life on the site of the old Madison Square Garden. All of these buildings have been erected in the past two years. In the foreground is the dome of the Mecca Temple.

title: General view - Upper Manhattan - Washington Heights.
text:
A general view of the upper Manhattan-Washington Heights section of the City, showing prominently the new Columbia Medical Center development lying between Broadway and Riverside Drive at W. 165th - 168th Street's. The main building at the right is the College of Physicians and Surgeons. This structure also houses the various dental schools and the Administrative Board. Facing the Drive is the New York State Hospital with its adjoining Presbyterian School for Nurses. Behind the latter is the Neurological Institute. Fort Washington Avenue divides the view leading to the dark 102nd Regiment Engineers Armory at 168th - 169th Street's. In the foreground is the New York Institute for the Deaf. The direction of the view is northeastward from over same.

1929

Ewing Galloway

title: General view - Upper Manhattan - Washington Heights.
text:
A general view of the upper Manhattan - Washington Heights section of the City, showing prominently the buildings of the College of the City of New York, the Lewishohn Stadium, Jasper Oval, St. Nicholas Park and the Manhattan and Jersey towers of the George Washington Bridge now under construction. Across the lower right corner runs Eighth Avenue. The park boundary is St. Nicholas Avenue. Wending its tortuous way through the college grounds is Convent Avenue. Amsterdam Avenue is at the rear of the Stadium separating this feature from the old Hebrew Orphan Asylum. Broadway and Riverside Drive are next in order.

November 5, 1929

Fairchild Aerial Surveys, Inc.

text:

A group of dark buildings in the center constitutes the Theological Seminary of the Protestant Episcopal Church. The spire of St. Peters, Protestant Episcopal Church in West 20th Street is on the left.

P. L. Sperr

title: General view - Midtown and downtown Manhattan from Chrysler building.
text:
A general view of midtown and downtown Manhattan as photographed southward from the Chrysler Building. In the right foreground are the clustered commercial structures below 34th Street rising on Fourth, Madison and Fifth Avenues. These are dominated by the outstanding New York Life Insurance Co. Bldg. To the east are Lexington, Third and Second Avenues, the first of which apparently terminating with the towered Consolidated Edison Co. Bldg. The famed Wall Street skyline is silhouetted against the Upper Bay. At the right margin is the North River and its Jersey shore.

1930

To the right is Third Avenue. Washington Irving High School for Girls is in the center foreground. Across the top, from left to right are the outstanding Metropolitan Life, the New York Life, the No. 10 East 40th Street, the Grand Central and Chanin Bldgs. In the upper right corner Tudor City, the East River and the Queensboro Bridge.

The Guardian Life Bldg. is at the N.E. corner of this street and Fourth Avenue. Outstanding in the upper right are the two insurance structures, the Metropolitan Life and the New York Life Buildings. title: General view - [Manhattan (East) from the Produce Exchange.]
text:
A general view eastward from the Produce Exchange (according to belief of the writer). In the background is the East River and its Brooklyn Bridge. The foreground area is traversed by (reading from left to right) Beaver, South William, Stone, Pearl, Water and Front Streets. South Street of course fringes the water front. Across the bottom runs Broad Street. The distinctive structure in the center is the N. Y. Cotton Exchange Building at Hanover Square. title: General view: 5th Avenue - W. 48th Street - W. 51st Street.
text:
Fifth Avenue (center, street level not seen), from W. 48th (extreme right) to 51st (extreme left) Streets, showing structures on both sides of the Avenue as viewed northeastward from a vantage point atop a structure on the south side of W. 48th Street to the west of Fifth Avenue. In the foreground are low structures at the easterly portion of the 48th - 49th Streets block containing the (under construction) Goeleet Building and the Collegiate Church of St. Nicholas (peaked roof at right). Across same, and on the east side of the avenue is Saks Department Store. To the left of the latter feature are the spires of St. Patricks Cathedral. Preceding same are low buildings that have been replaced by units of Rockefeller City. In the right background is the steel frame work of the R.C.A. Building on Lexington Avenue and which became the present General Electric Building.

title: General view - 8th Avenue - Northeast.
text:
80 Eighth Avenue, at the N.E. corner of West 14th Street (County Trust Co. Building) general view northeastward.

A set of three views photographed in the direction of Madison Square and overlooking the zone between 14th and 23rd Streets. At that point appear the New York Life and the Metropolitan Buildings.

Thru the foreground runs Seventh Avenue, and the prominent New York Telephone Co. Building (No. 206 West 18th Street) is to the west of same. The side of this structure seen by the viewer is on West 17th Street.

To the right, and directly on Seventh Avenue are two tall structures. The first is a 12 story loft building, No. 106-110 Seventh Avenue (between 16th and 17th Streets), and the second, a new 18 story apartment house at the S.W. corner of West 18th Street. This latter structure is on the former site of the 3-story Arnold Constable and Co. stable (92-98 Seventh Avenue). In the near future another 18 story apartment will separate these buildings. This will be at the N.W. corner of 16th Street and abut the aforementioned loft.

In the distant background appears (view 3) the R. C. A., 10 East 40th Street, Lincoln, Chanin and Chrysler Buildings.

May 31, 1930
Views: 1, 2, 3

80 Eighth Avenue, at the N.E. corner of West 14th Street (County Trust Co. Building) general view westward).

Three views photographed from the above location towards the North (Hudson) River to show there various west side docks and ocean liners. These extend from Tenth and Eleventh Avenue's, and West Street.

Across the foreground runs the Ninth Avenue Elevated line crossing 14th and 15th Street's (in Views 1 and 2). View 3 is slightly to the south to show Gansevoort Street to the left. At the foot of same appears the group of buildings comprising West and Washington Market.

May 31, 1930
Views: 1-2-3

P. L. Sperr

80 Eighth Avenue, at the N.E. corner of West 14th Street (County Trust Co. Building) general view south-westward.

Two views from atop the aforementioned structure towards the North (Hudson) River and overlooking the area to the west of Greenwich Village.

In the foreground is a small triangular block on the west side of Eighth Avenue (left corner) between West 13th and Horatio Streets. To the rear of same is West 4th Street and upon which stands the large 9 story Riker Hegeman Building.

May 31, 1930
Views: 1-2

title: General view - 8th Avenue - West.
text:
80 Eighth Avenue, at the N.E. corner of West 14th Street (County Trust Co. Building) (general view westward).

Two views forming a panorama showing an inclusive view of the area between Gansevoort Street (left of No.1) and West 16th Street (right of No. 2). West 14th Street appears on the right of View 1 and shows at Ninth Avenue an "El" station of the line that derives its name from this thoroughfare.

In the background is the North (Hudson) River; various West Side piers and the Jersey shore-line.

In the foreground of No. 2 is the cleared site of the New York Port Authority Building (No. 11 Eighth Ave.). This structure will occupy the entire block between Eighth and Ninth Avenues and West 15th to 16th Streets.

June 18, 1931
Views: 1-2

title: General view - 8th Avenue - 14th Street
text:
80 Eighth Avenue, at the N.E. corner of West 14th Street (County Trust Co. Building) general view north-eastward.

A set of 2 views photographed in the general direction of Madison Square and overlooking the west side area between 14th and 23rd Streets. To the right are buildings set at the focal point. They are the New York Life and the Metropolitan; In the left background, the recently constructed Empire State Building outstands.

The buildings in the foreground are identified in a view taken May 31, 1930. They are from left to right, the 19 story New York Telephone Co. Building; No. 106-110 Seventh Avenue (a 12 story loft); a new 18 story apartment, No. 100 Seventh Avenue (at N.W. corner of West 16th Street); and No. 90 Seventh Avenue (S.W. corner of 16th Street) another 18 story apartment. To the base of the last two structures (View 2) appears "el" shaped units of St, Joseph's Home for the Aged.

P. L. Sperr

June 18, 1931
Views: 1-2

title: General view - [Manhattan] - County Trust Company Building.
text:
80 Eighth Avenue, at the N.E. corner of West 14th Street (County Trust Co. Building) general view eastward.

An eastward view along 14th (right) and 15th (left) Streets, towards and across 7th and 6th Avenues. The prominent buildings in the foreground are the 9 story Convent of Jesus Mary (No. 222 West 15th Street), and a new apartment house (No. 72-7th Avenue). To the left of the latter appears the 7 story building occupied by the printing house, Street and Smith.

Thru this foreground area on a diagonal ran the Colonial thoroughfare "Southampton Road." Fitz Roy Road branched off to the north from a point in the backyards at the lower edge.

text:
W. 13th Street, north side, west of Seventh Avenue,
(general view northward).

A photograph taken from a dwelling structure at the above location viewing up Seventh Avenue (at the right) and across W. 14th Street, to show tall structures built in the last several years, on and around Seventh Avenue. From left to right these are, the 19 story New York Telephone Co., Building (No. 206 W. 18th Street), the 18 story apartment house No. 90 Seventh Avenue (at the S.W. corner of W. 16th Street), the 18 story apartment house, No. 72 Seventh Avenue (S.W. corner of W. 15th Street) and the 18 story apartment house, No. 101 Seventh Avenue (N.E. corner of W. 16th Street across the latter appears the unfinished tower of the Empire State Building. title: General view - [Manhattan - 20th Street (West) - Between 6th and 7th Avenues.]
text:
143-145 W. 20th Street, north side, between Sixth and Seventh Avenues, (general view northwestward).

Two views forming a panorama of this north west segment. View 1 is westward towards London Terrace at 23rd Street, while No. 2 is northwards along Seventh Avenue. This thoroughfare appears diagonally across the foreground covering from 20th Street to 25th Street. The cleared site seen upon same is at the S. W. corner of W. 22nd Street and is in 1939 a gasoline station. The Hotel Carteret and the adjoining Chelsea, are on the south side of 23rd Street, just west of Seventh Avenue. Note the nine story Young Men's Christian Association Building partially obscured by the former. The large group of buildings to the north constitute the National Cloak and Suit Co. Building and are of 11 and 16 stories in height, occupying the westerly Frontage on Seventh Avenue of the 24th - 25th Street block.

title: General view - [Manhattan - 34th Street (West) - Pennsylvania building.]
text:
241 W. 34th Street, (Pennsylvania Building), north side, between Seventh and Eighth Avenues. (general view southward.).

A perspective over the Pennsylvania Railroad station. Surrounding same are numerous loft structures lying to the south of this point. In the left foreground are, the 22 story Equitable Life Assurance Co. Building, the 31 story Hotel Governor Clinton and a 16 story loft structure (No. 362-78 Seventh Avenue). Adjoining the latter are low buildings comprising the Church and School of St. John the Baptist Roman Catholic Church. The smokestack at the right is atop the Pennsylvania Railroad power house. Note that Eighth Avenue is on the right and does not appear here.

P. L. Sperr

title: General view - [Manhattan - 34th Street (East) - Harriet Hubbard Ayer building - Chanin Building ; Chrysler Building ; New York Daily News ; Waldorf-Astoria Hotel.]
text:
317-323 E. 34th Street, (Harriet Hubbard Ayer Building), north side, between First and Second Avenues, showing a general view northwestward from this location. In the foreground are, St. Gabriels Park, the 2nd Ave. "E" and various tenements. The photographer utilizes the changing 42nd Street outline for a background. Note the construction stage of the Chrysler and News Buildings. Of earlier birth than these is the Chanin Building as shown to the left. A close inspection of the two later views will disclose the erection details attending the building of the Hotel Waldorf-Astoria on Lexington and Park Avenues. This appears between the graceful Chrysler and the utilitarian News Buildings.

View 1: September 10, 1929

title: General view - Manhattan - 34th Street (East) - Harriet Hubbard Ayer building.]
text:
321 E. 34th Street, north side, between First and Second Avenues, (Harriet Hubbard Ayer Building), panoramic view westward.

These two views form a panoramic arrangement of the lower midtown zone between Madison Square and 42nd Street. Near the former are the insurance companies buildings, the Metropolitan and the New York Life. In the center (under construction) is a portion of the Empire State Building. To the right appear, the No. 10 E. 40th Street Building, the 500 Fifth Avenue Building (under construction) and the recently completed Lefcourt National Building (No. 295 Madison Avenue, completed late 1929;) In the left corner of No. 1 is a portion of the Second Avenue "El" with its 34th Street station and spur line at the left margin of No. 2. This last mentioned feature was demolished in the Summer of 1938. E. 35th Street is the thoroughfare passing thru the center of this view. Note the spire of the Church of the Epiphany at Lexington Avenue. This structure was razed about the same time as the 34th Street spur line.

Sept. 17, 1939
Views: 1 and 2

P. L. Sperr

title: General view - [Manhattan - 34th Street (East) - Harriet Hubbard Ayer building.]
text:
321 East 34th Street, north side, between First and Second Avenues, (Harriet Hubbard Ayer Building) general view northward.

Three views forming a panoramic arrangement to show the 42nd Street-Midtown skyline of Manhattan. From left to right these buildings are: No. 10 E. 40th Street, No. 500 Fifth Avenue (under construction), The Leftcourt Colonial (No. 295 Madison Avenue), the Lincoln, the Chanin, the Chrysler and the News. Prior to 1929 none of these structures were standing.

Across the foreground runs the Second Avenue "El" passing the westerly side of St. Gabriel's Park. This garden and play area is between E. 35th and 36th Streets. In 1939, this will undergo radical changes as the new 38th Street-East River Tunnel approach will pass thru same to an entrance on 34th Street.

P. L. Sperr

September 17, 1930
Views: 1-2-3

title: General view - [Manhattan - 34th Street (East) - Harriet Hubbard Ayer building.]
text:
321 East 34th Street, north side, between First and Second Avenues, (Harriet Hubbard Ayer Building) general view northward.

Three views forming a panoramic arrangement to show the 42nd Street-Midtown skyline of Manhattan. From left to right these buildings are: No. 10 E. 40th Street, No. 500 Fifth Avenue (under construction), The Leftcourt Colonial (No. 295 Madison Avenue), the Lincoln, the Chanin, the Chrysler and the News. Prior to 1929 none of these structures were standing.

Across the foreground runs the Second Avenue "El" passing the westerly side of St. Gabriel's Park. This garden and play area is between E. 35th and 36th Streets. In 1939, this will undergo radical changes as the new 38th Street-East River Tunnel approach will pass thru same to an entrance on 34th Street.

P. L. Sperr

title: General view - [Midtown Manhattan - Between 34th and 42nd Streets (Northwest).]
text:
A general view of the midtown Manhattan 34th to 42nd St. zone as photographed northwestward from the New York Life Insurance Bldg. at Madison Square. The distinctive unfin- ished structure in the center is the Empire State Bldg. at Fifth Avenue and 34th Street. To the left are, the Navarre Bldg. at Seventh Avenue and 38th Street, the partially com- pleted Nelson Towers at Seventh Avenue and 34th Street, and the squat Hotel New Yorker at Eighth Avenue and 34th Street. The Grand Central-42nd Street skyline is to the right. No. 500 Fifth Avenue is being built at 42nd Street. To the east are the No. 10 East 40th Street Bldg., the Lefcourt-Colonial Bldg., and the Lincoln Bldg. The last two apparently blend together, tho the shadow of the first is cast upon the last.

title: General view - Manhattan - 42nd Street (East) - Lincoln Building (Northeast) ; 60 East 42nd Street - Vanderbilt Avenue ; General Electric Company ; Grand Central Building ; New York Hospital ; Waldorf-Astoria Hotel.
text:
60 E. 42nd Street, (Lincoln Building) south side, west of Pershing Square (general view northeastward). Merging on the left are the Grand Central Building, the Hotel Waldorf-Astoria and the General Electric Building. Numerous Sutton Place apartment structures are nestled on the right at the Queensboro Bridge approach. Beyond same is the white pile of the N. Y. Hospital-Cornell Medical College. The East River, Welfare Island, Long Island City and the blended Triborough and Hellgate Bridges are easily identifiable.

1937-8

Alexander Alland

This photo is one of a series that appeared in the published volume "Portrait of N.Y." by Felix Reisenberg and Alex. Alland, IRGV.

title: General view - Manhattan - 42nd Street (South).
text: 192 AMERICAN HISTORICAL PRINTS, ETC. building was removed in 1882 to make room for the Mutual Life Insurance Company's building. See Iconography, v. 2, plate 28, for reproduction of the unique contemporary drawing that was presented him by William Burgis and now owned by the Society of Iconology, when it was presented by Mr. Wm. Loring Andrews, with the blessing of the estate of the husband. See also v. 3, plate 130. — At the very moment of the flood (Jan. 11, 1932, 10:30 p.m.), a telephonic call from Mr. Newman, of the Old Print Shop, announces the discovery of a second impression of the supposedly unique print. Later, I have seen the print, which is authenticated, but in this condition, it belongs to the New York family. 1855 — E-138 46.7 x 29.4 Lower left: B. F. Smith, Jun. del. Lower right: W. Wellstood, sc. & Center: NEW YORK, 1855. From the Latting Observatory. Respectfully dedicated to the Citizens of the United States by the Publishers Smith, Fern & Co. 340 Broadway New York. & Entered... 1855 by SMITH, FERN & CO. Line engraving. Date issued: 1855. Reference: p. 312, plate 145, and p. 215. Forty-second Street is shown in the immediate foreground, the Croton Reservoir and the Crystal Palace, Fifth Avenue appears at the left. The Croton Reservoir was built in 1839-42 and covered the eastern half of the blocks bounded by Fifth and Sixth Avenues, 40th and 42nd Streets, the site occupied by The New York Public Library. It had previously (since 1823) constituted part of the "potters' field" The Reservoir was demolished in 1899-1900 to make way for the Library. This view shows the area from the intersection of Fifth Avenue and 42nd Street, looking south. Mount Morris Park is seen between Fifth and Madison Avenue between 36th and 37th Streets. The block has been cut from the east side of Fifth Avenue and 37th Street. The three occupying the block are the corner house of Fifth Avenue and 36th and 37th Streets occupied by Mr. L. M. Dodge. This block front is now one of Mr. Charles F. McKim's masterpieces, now occupied by the New York Public Library. The Crystal Palace was built in 1852-53 for the Exhibition of 1853; the grounds were destroyed by fire in 1858. The Observatory, which was built in 1856, was demolished in 1890. A separate edition with 115 references was issued with the print, and is preserved in the Library, p. 3, p. 716. The only recorded impression is owned by Mr. Edward W. C. Arnold. Reproduced as Plate 93. 1855 — G-15 39.7 x 22.13 Lower left: Painted by J. W. Hill. Lower right: Cha. Parsons Lith. N. Y. Center: PRINTED BY ENIDICOTT & CO. 9 PORTLAND, M. To the Citizens of Portland, this picture is [seal] most respectfully dedicated by the Publishers SMITH BROTHERS & CO. 59 Beekman St., New York. Litho. Date issued: 1855. Last line of imprint partially covered by mat. New York Public Library. American Historical Prints... NY: NYPL, 1932.

title: General view - Midtown Manhattan - 42nd Street.
text:
A general view of the midtown Manhattan sector containing the Grand Central - 42nd Street zone: Here tremendous building operations have been in progress in the past few years and the zone is now dotted with skyscrapers and more are rising every day. The new type of "set-back" or pyramided architecture may be observed. This was developed as a result of the New York Zoning law designed to keep the streets light and well ventilated.

The majestic slim skyscraper in the foreground is the new No. 10 East 40th Street Bldg. The street on the left is the famed Fifth Avenue. Just beyond the 10 E. 40th St. Bldg. is the Lefcourt-National Bldg. To the right is the square massive tower of the new Grand Central Bldg. that adjoins the quadrangular station. The latter is approached by Park Avenue. On the extreme right is the new Chanin Bldg.

1929

Doherty, photo
Ewing Galloway

title: General view - Midtown Manhattan - 42nd Street (Northeast).
text:
A general view of midtown Manhattan detailing portions of the Grand Central-42nd Street zone and the tenement district to the northeast. The quadrangular station and its towered Grand Central Bldg. are approached by Park Ave. The outstanding Chanin Blg. is on Lexington Avenue. To the east are Third, Second and First Avenues. The East River, its Queensboro Bridge, Welfare Island and Astoria shore are in the upper right corner. Lower Harlem is in the left.

1929

Doherty, photo
Ewing Galloway

All of these are on 42nd Street, at the foot of which is the residential development, Tudor City. Running across the view from right to left, are the identifiable Third, Second and First Ave's. The photographer is over Park Avenue and its Grand Central Station (quadrangle in lower left).

title: General view - Midtown Manhattan - 42nd Street - [View from 444 Madison Avenue - 49th Street.]
text:
A general view of the midtown Manhattan - 42nd Street district as photographed southward from No. 444 Madison Avenue (at 49th Street). Across the view, from left to right are the upper stories of the Chrysler, Grand Central Chanin, Lincoln, Lefcourt-Colonial, Johns Manville, New York Life, Metropolitan, No. 10 E. 40th Street, Empire State, and No. 500 Fifth Avenue buildings. Running thru the center is Madison Avenue. To the left is Park Avenue. Fifth Avenue is on the right.

1936

title: General view - Midtown Manhattan - 42nd Street - [View from 444 Madison Avenue - 49th Street.]
text:
A general view of the midtown Manhattan-42nd Street district as photographed southwestern from No. 444 Madison Avenue (at 49th Street). Fifth Avenue is in the center foreground. The Ampico Tower Bldg. is at the N.W. corner of 47th Street and same. The Collegiate Church of St. Nicholas is at 48th Street. To the left appear the upper stories of the outstanding No. 500 Fifth Avenue Bldg. and the Empire State Bldg. Note the clock-towered Paramount Bldg. and the dark McGraw Hill Bldg. in the right background. Beyond these is the Hudson River and its New Jersey shoreline.

1936

W. P. A., photo
Federal Writers Project

title: General view - Broad Street - Northwest.
text:
67 Broad Street, (International Telephone Building) east side, from South William to Beaver Streets, (general view northeastward).

A set of three views along the financial fringe between the East River and Pearl Street ("El" line shown upon same), towards the Brooklyn Bridge.

View No. 1 is towards Wall Street and where appears the Bank of New York, the National City Building, and the Wall and Hanover Building. To the left of these appears the steel framework of the Bank of Manhattan Building. The imposing structure in the center (at Hanover Square) is the N. Y. Cotton Exchange Building.

Views 2 and 3 are similar and show mainly the aforementioned zone. In the third view, the outstanding building is the Seamens Church Institute. Note here the Brooklyn shore in the background.

P. L. Sperr

August 20, 1929
Views: 1-2-3

title: General view - Broadway - 8th Avenue - North.
text:
A general view northward from the General Motors Building (Broadway, west to Eighth Ave. and West 57th north to 58th Streets). This view shows Columbus Circle (foreground), Broadway (left), Central Park West (center), and Central Park (right). Construction work for the Eighth Ave. Subway is shown in two places; on the east side of Central Park West and at the foot of the statue of Christopher Columbus in the center of the Circle. Note the Maine Monument at the Park entrance. Across the top of the view (left), appears the Hudson River, with its Palisades (Jersey shore). About 1932.

Brown Brothers.

title: General view - Broadway - East.
text:
A general view eastward from the Woolworth Building, 229-237 Broadway, west side, from Barclay Street to Park Place. View shows the interlacing slum sections; Cherry Hill, Corlears Hook etc. of lower Manhattan and Greenpoint, Gowanus Canal, Navy Basin, Williamsburg, etc. of Brooklyn, with the Brooklyn, Manhattan and East River Bridges connecting them.

About 1920.

Brown Brothers.

title: General view - East Broadway - South.
text:
A general (Bird's Eye) view, south from Broadway, at Pike Street, showing on the left the East River and on the right the Hudson River. All the piers south from the Manhattan Bridge are seen and the Brooklyn Bridge midway between the Battery (southern extremity of Manhattan). The Manhattan Bridge is in the foreground. (The Manhattan Bridge extends from between Market and Pike Streets, to the Williamsburg Section of the Borough of Kings). The Brooklyn Bridge extends from near North William and Frankfort Streets, to the Borough of Kings {Brooklyn}).

1927.

International News.

title: General view - East Broadway - East.
text:
175 E. Broadway, (The Jewish Daily Forward Building), south side, between Rutgers and Jefferson Streets, (panoramic view eastward towards the East River and Corlears Hook).

Corlears Hook is the land protuberance this side of the Williamsburg Bridge where the river bends to turn northward. Henry Street is the thoroughfare in the center of View 1. The smokestacks on the Brooklyn Shore in View 2 are at the U. S. Navy Yard.

February 14, 1930

title: General view - [Manhattan - Brooklyn Bridge - Bank of Manhattan; City Bank-Farmers Trust Company; Equitable Trust Company ; Irving Trust Company; Singer Manufacturing Company; 60 Wall Street Tower.]
text:
A general view southward from the Brooklyn Bridge, showing the skyscrapers and office buildings constituting the financial district. From left to right the outstanding buildings are, No. 120 Wall Street, the City Bank-Farmers Trust Co., the Sixty Wall Tower, the Bank of Manhattan, the Irving Trust Co., the Equitable and the Singer. Views 2 and 3 are similar. Note in the center foreground of the former, the South Ferry Divison of the Second and Third Avenue "El" running on Pearl Street. Above same appears the smokestacks of the New York Steam Co. plant. To the right are the 25 and 28 story buildings comprising the insurance center around John and Platt Streets.

View 1   Sept. 23, 1931
Views: 2 and 3 June 5, 1932

P. L. Sperr

title: General view - Manhattan - [View of Lower Manhattan from Brooklyn Bridge.]
text:
(1)
A general view of lower Manhattan, as seen from the Brooklyn Bridge;, and showing the East River (foreground) converging at the upper Bay (left) with the Hudson (North) River. Notice Bedloe's Island between Manhattan and the Jersey shore line. See also views 2 and 3.
About 1870-1875.

Brown Brothers.

Published in the American on December 1908, and the New York Times of October 20, 1912.

title: General view - Manhattan - [View of Lower Manhattan from Brooklyn Bridge.]
text:
(3).

A general view northwest from the Brooklyn Bridge, and showing the Cherry Hill waterfront, between James Slip (left) and Market Slip (right, not shown). Just beyond, in the center of view is the Bowery and Chatham Square area. The North (Hudson) River, and the Jersey Shore line appear across the top of the view. This waterfront section comprises Piers (old) Nos. 31 (extreme left) to 36, and are occupied respectively by the Ferry to Long Island City (Pier 31, James Slip), Bridge Street Ferry (Pier 32), Philadelphia and New York S.S. Co., or the Clyde Line from Philadelphia (Piers 33 and 34), the Catherine Street Ferry to Brooklyn, (foot of Catherine Slip), Bridgeport Line S.S. (Pier 35), and the Central Vermont R.R. and S.S. Line (Pier 36). Distinctly shown at the rear of the Catherine Street Ferry, is the Catherine Market, with Van Dyke's Hotel (N.E. corner of South Street), and Brook's Bros., Clothiers (N.E. corner of Cherry Street), and the Lorillard House (N.W. corner of South Street), surrounding same.

About 1870- 1875.

Brown Brothers.

Published in the American on December 1908, and the New York Times of October 20, 1912.

title: General view - Canal Street - Southwest.
text:
54-58 Canal Street, at the S.W. corner of Orchard Street, (general view southwestward). Shown are tenement buildings bisected by the Manhattan Bridge approach, with a backdrop of municipal and financial structures. To the right are the former, circling Foley Square, and to the left are the four latter, bordering on Broadway. From left to right, the four predominating structures are: No. 120 Wall St. (American Sugar Refining) Bldg., the Sixty Wall Tower (No. 70 Pine Street), the Singer Bldg., and the Municipal Bldg. Behind the last appears a portion of the Woolworth Bldg. Thru the center and passing underneath the aforementioned approach, are the tracks of the Second Avenue Elevated Line.

May 9, 1930
Views 1-2-3.

title: General view - [Manhattan - Greenwich Village.]
text:
A general view of the "Greenwich Village" section as photo- northward from a point in the air over Varick Street (lower center). The commercial structures there flank both sides of this thorough- fare below West Houston Street. Varick Street changes its identity above the bend to become Seventh Avenue. At the right is Sixth Avenue's extension under construction. Note the old "El" line on same above W. 3rd Street. The clearly defined thoroughfare at the left is Hudson Street. Eighth Avenue branches off of the latter in the upper left corner. Tortuous Greenwich Street and its nearly parallel Washington Street are closer to the left margin.

Ewing Galloway

1928

111 John Street, between Cliff and Pearl Streets, (general view southwestward).

This set of three views forms a panoramic arrangement showing the skyline formed by financial buildings on and surrounding Wall Street. Across same from left to right, the prominent structures are No. 1 Cedar Street, (left foreground), the Wall and Hanover Building, the H. L. Dougherty Building (center of No. 1), the International Telephone Building (flag atop), the National City Building (vault-like top), the Bank of New York Building (ornamentation), the Equitable Trust Co. Building, the Bank of Manhattan Building, the Bankers Trust Co. Building (pyramidal roof), the Irving Trust Co. Building (under construction), the Chase National Bank Building, and the twin Equitable Buildings.

In the foreground are numerous other structures some of which are, in the same order: the aformentioned No. 1 Cedar Street, the 25 story Fire Companies Building (left margin of View 1 and center of View 2), the 12 story Bishop Building and the Federal Reserve Building (right center of View 3). Note in View 1 the partially seen activity where the skyscraper, the 60 Wall Tower will rise.

title: General view - [Manhattan - Lexington Avenue - 42nd Street (East) - Chanin Building.]
text:
A general view northward from atop the Chanin Bldg., located at the S.W. corner of Lexington Avenue and E. 42nd Street, showing a panoramic arrangement of the Grand Central zone and the area to the north. View 1 shows the midtown section between Sixth Avenue (left) and Lexington Avenue (right). This contains the 70 story R.C.A. Bldg., the Grand Central Bldg., the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel, and the General Electric Bldg. In the center background is Central Park. View 2 shows the East Side- Yorkville fringe of Manhattan. Here are numerous apartment houses, hotels, tenements and lofts. These are framed by the G.E. Bldg on the left and the Chrysler on right. The white pile in the center background near the East River is The New York Hospital and Cornell University Medical College. This is to the north of the Queensboro Bridge and opposite Welfare Island. The latter lies in the center of the East River and was formerly known as Blackwells Island. Beyond this appears the Astoria section of Queens, the Triboro and the Hellgate Bridges, and the distant outline of the Bronx.

P. L. Sperr

October 3, 1936
Views 1 and 2

title: General view - [Manhattan - Between Pine and Cedar Streets - 60 Wall Street Tower (South).]
text:
70 Pine Street, (Sixty Wall Tower): west side of Pearl Street, from Pine to Cedar Streets, showing a general view southward towards the Upper Bay.

In the center is Battery Park and the Aquarium. Note the ships leaving and entering the North (Hudson) River. This is on the right and flows onward towards the Statue of Liberty; the State of New Jersey forming its other side. The buildings in the foreground are at the southerly tip of Manhattan and constitute a part of the business and financial district. The City Bank-Farmers 'Trust' Tower, at the left, overshadows the rectangular Produce Exchange and the U. S. Custom House. To the right is the Standard Oil structure.

title: General view - Pine Street - North.
text:
70 Pine Street, (Sixty Wall Tower): west side, of Pearl Street from Pine to Cedar Streets showing a panoramic view northward).

View No. 1 is westward towards the North (Hudson) River and overlooking the Singer, New York Telephone, Transportation and Woolworth Buildings. Note the Queen Mary "outward bound."

View No. 2 is due north towards the 42nd Street-Midtown zone. In the foreground here are the Municipal Building, the Federal Courts Building, and other civic structures.

View No. 3 is eastward towards the East River and overlooks the lower East Side. The bridges shown in a respective order are, the Brooklyn, the Manhattan and the Williamsburg. Note between the first two mentioned, the white building pile constituting Knickerbocker Village. The marginal thoroughfare is South Street which terminates in the distance at Corlears Hook.

text:

A set of three views forming a panorama of Wall Street financial structures. From left to right these are, the International Telephone Co., the Continental Bank and Trust Co., the Irving Trust Co., the Equitable Trust Co., the City Bank Farmers Trust Co., the Bank of New York, the Wall and Hanover, and the Sixty Wall Tower Buildings. The first of these are on Broad Street (exclusive of the Irving Trust Co., Building), the balance on Wall Street. Erected between 1929-1931 they form the nucleus and theme of this district.

title: General view - [Manhattan - Wall Street - Bank of Manhattan building (East).]
text:
A general view eastward from atop the Bank of Manhattan Building at No. 40 Wall Street, north side, west of William Street, to show the upper portions of several buildings of the financial district silhouetted against the East River and its piers. That, with the ornamentation is the Bank of New York and Trust Company Building. Beyond appears the irregular shaped Wall and Hanover (Brown Brothers) Building. To the right and overshadowing the others is the City Bank-Farmers Trust Company Building. Nestling in the hollow formed by these structures is the National City Bank. The tall smoke stack in the background is atop the new United States Assay Office on South Street at Old Slip. View No. 3 is southeastward towards Governors Island and shows the Coenties Slip vicinity overshadowed by the rear of the International Telephone Building, No. 67 Broad Street.

Forming a backdrop for the latter (opposite side of Gold Street) are the 25 and 14 story buildings that are respectively, the Insurance Center Building and the National Board of Fire Underwriters Building.

View: 2 Oct. 22, 1930

title: General view - Wall Street - Northwest.
text:
120 Wall Street, (American Sugar Refining Building): South Street, west side, from Wall to Pine Streets, (panoramic view northwestward).

These two views placed end to end form an arrangement of the Front, Water and Pearl Street areas. The first of these thoroughfares is in the foreground, the second thru the center, the last across the top.

Upon the west side, of the latter, appear two building construction projects. That to the left is for the new 60 Wall Tower, and that to the right, for the 35 story insurance center building No. 1 Platt Street. To the right, and thru the smokestacks of the New York Steam Co. plant, one sees the recently completed 26 storied building, No. 111 John Street.

title: General view - Wall Street - Northwest.
text:
120 Wall Street, (American Sugar Refining Building), South Street, west side, from Wall to Pine Streets. (general view north-westward).

The new downtown skyline between Wall Street (left) and City Hall Park (right) that rose subsequent to 1928. The 60 Wall Tower (No. 70 Pine Street) is the latest addition and dominates everything else, being the third largest building in the World.

To the right of same are several new structures forming the insurance center. From left to right these are, the 22 story No. 1 Cedar Street, the 25 story Insurance Centre Building (No. 80 John Street), the 28 story No. 90 John Street, the 35 story No. 1 Platt Street) and the 26 story No. 111 John Street, (behind the smoke-stacks of the New York Steam Co. plant).

In the background, center and right respectively are the Transportation, Woolworth, Municipal, and Empire State Buildings.

title: Airships - The "Akron" - [U.S. Navy airship over 60 Wall Street Tower.]
text:
The "Akron;" a United States Navy airship sailing over the financial area in lower Manhattan. Directly beneath same is the pinnacle of the huge 60 Wall Street Tower. The octangular structure appearing on the left is the City Bank, Farmers Trust Company Building. Photographers vantage point is No. 415 Broad Street, viewing northward. This set consists of 2 views; No. 2 including the Bank of Manhattan Building.

November 2, 1931.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Staten Island - Poppy Joe Island Beach - [Stroud place.]
text:
Poppy Joe Island Beach (Staten Island): Shown are "Dick" Williams (mail carrier for thirty-five years in New York City until picked up dead in the street with his mail sack on his shoulder) and Louis Stroud going after weakfish. They are approaching a foot bridge over New Creek. Poppy Joe Island Beach is on the Lower New York Bay between Midland Beach and Ocean Breeze..

About 1911

Photo by J.E. Davis
Copied by P. L. Sperr

title: Staten Island - Poppy Joe Island Beach - [Stroud place.]

title: Staten Island - Poppy Joe Island Beach - [Stroud place.]
text:
Poppy Joe Island Beach (Staten Island): A group of local muskrat hunters and hunting dogs in front of their work-and-storage barn. From left to right they are: Louis Stroud, George W. Stroud, John ("Jeff") Davis, and James A. Stroud. Poppy Joe Island is on the Lower New York Bay, near New Creek, between Ocean Breeze and Midland Beach.

About 1911

Photo by J.E. Davis
Copied by P. L. Sperr

title: Staten Island - Poppy Joe Island Beach - [Stroud place.]
text:
Poppy Joe Island Beach (Staten Island): Shown are three natives of this sparsely inhabited section of Staten Island, located between Midland Beach and Ocean Breeze, near New Creek. From left to right they are: "Dick" Williams (for thirty-five years mail carrier in New York City until picked up dead in the street with his mail sack on his shoulder), James Alexander Stroud, and John ("Jeff") Davis.

About 1911

Photo by J.E. Davis
Copied by P. L. Sperr

title: Bridges - Brooklyn Bridge.
text:
53-63 Park Row, (Pulitzer or World Building), at the N. E. corner of Frankfort Street, showing a general view eastward of the Brooklyn Bridge, environs, the East River and the Brooklyn shore. The foreground area is the industrial section popularly known as the "Swamp." Dominant there is the 10-story Healy Building and the Shot Tower. The former is at Gold and Ferry Streets, while the latter is at Cliff and Beekman Streets. Thru the left midground runs Cherry Street, a one time fashionable thoroughfare that parallels the water front.

J. S. Johnston photo
Copyright 1894
Ewing Galloway

title: Bridges - Brooklyn Bridge.
text:
(1).  Brooklyn Bridge (suspension); beginning at Centre Street and Park Row, facing City Hall Park, in Manhattan, and terminating in Brooklyn at Fulton and Sands Streets. Actual work was begun in January, 1870 and it was completed in May, 1884, having been opened in the previous year. Its overall length is 1 1/4 miles, width 85 feet, with a central span across the East River, 1595 feet long and 135 feet above high water mark. John A. Roebling, who drew up the specifications and began construction was succeeded upon his death by his son, Washington A. Roebling. Being the first bridge to connect Manhattan and Brooklyn, it acquired a colorful history and world-wide fame as a wonder of modern engineering and human endeavor. (see: Moses King, Handbook of New York City (1892).)

June 15, 1933.

Bridges - Farmers Bridge.
text:
Farmers Bridge: An antique structure across Old Spuyten Duyvil Creek at the foot of West 225th Street, Manhattan (left). This bridge built in 1759 was also known as the Free, Queens or Dyckman Bridge. The United States Government changed the Creek bed and this structure was covered over in 1912. The elevated line shown is on Broadway and is viewed in a westward direction from the Borough of the Bronx.

1911.

title: Bridges - George Washington Bridge - [Construction of the world's longest suspension bridge.]
text:
Rush Construction of World's Longest Suspension Bridge. Right, construction work on one of the piers of the great Hudson River Bridge which will be opened in 1932 at a cost of about 170 million. The Bridge will connect Manhattan(lower right) between 178th Street and 179th Street and Fort Lee, New Jersey(left) where another pier is shown. The distance between the two piers, from which the Bridge will be suspended, is 3,500 feet -- over twice the length of the longest suspension bridge at present
(Camden-Philadelphia span).

text:
The George Washington Bridge, a steel structure, connecting Manhattan at West 181st Street with Fort Lee, New Jersey. The view is westward from Manhattan, and just south of the Bridge. Control of this engineering masterpiece, is in the hands of the N.Y. Port Authority, who will charge a toll for crossing same. These 4 views are more or less similar, and are all by the same photographer.

1936.

Walter L. Bogert.

title: Bridges - Hell Gate Bridge - [East River.]
text:
The newest bridge across the East River, New York City
This 1,000 foot span, the longest arch in the world, is over the dangerous channel at Hell Gate. Long Island City (a part of greater New York) is on the right of the picture, with Ward's Island on the left. The structure turns, crosses the island, passes over water again to Randall's Island and finally reaches the mainland in the Borough of the Bronx. It is wholly a railroad bridge, part of a six mile road connecting the Pennsylvania and New Haven Systems and permitting through freight and passenger service between New England and the South. The structure was formally dedicated on March 9, took four years to build and cost $27,000,000. It makes the fifth bridge across the East River all except the Brooklyn Bridge have been opened in the last twelve years.

April, 1917
American Press Assn.

title: Bridges - Hell Gate Bridge - [Bronx - Queensborough.]
text:
Hell Gate Bridge, showing the approach from the Bronx, spanning Ward's Island, with the Queensborough end at the right. The bridge is the rail link between the Penn. R.R. Terminal in Manhattan and the New England lines. The main span of the Bridge is 1016 ft. long and 300 ft. above high water mark. The cost of the bridge was $25,000,000.

About 1930.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Bridges - Hell Gate Bridge - [The bridge begins at Port Norris, Bronx, spanning Ward's and Randall's Islands, to Astoria, Queens.]
text:
(1)
Hell Gate Bridge spans the notorious channel, called Hell Gate; at the convergance of Long Island Sound and the East River. The seething whirlpools and conflicting currents, made it extremely unnavigable; sinking many vessels, and drowning innumerable men: hence the name. The bridge begins at Port Morris in the Bronx, spanning Ward's and Randall's Islands, to Astoria in Queens. It is one of the classics of modern achievement, being the world's longest continued span. The eastern railway interests combined to build it, and completed it in 1917.

July 25, 1936.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)
Same, over Ward's Island.
July 25, 1936.

P. L. Sperr.

(3)
Same.
July 25, 1936.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Bridges - Kill Van Kull Bridge - [World's tallest bridge span nearing completion.]
text:
WORLD'S TALLEST BRIDGE SPAN NEARING COMPLETION
NEW YORK CITY -- An excellent and exclusive set of photos on the Great Kill van Kull Bridge which will reach 8,075 feet from Staten Island to Bayonne, N.J. The structure, which is rapidly nearing completion, will have four lanes for vehicular traffic and two lanes for rapid transit. The arch will be 1,675 feet long-- the world's biggest. The span, when completed, will cost about $18,000,000.

Men at work on the bolts of the new span. In the background may be seen Bayonne, N.J.

Photo by Underwood and Underwood

N.D.

title: Bridges - Triborough Bridge.
text:
LOOKING TOWARD GOTHAM FROM THE TRIBORO BRIDGE TOWER.

Astoria, L.I. ---- A Panorama of Manhatten spires greets this ironworker as he looks toward the New York skyline from the Astoria tower of the Triboro Bridge. The project, started 16 years ago, will be finished in 1936. Through government funds it has given jobs to 18,000 men. The series of bridges will connect Manhatten, Brooklyn, and the Bronx and will be one of the greatest projects of its kind in engineering history.

International News Photo

1934

title: Celebrations - Parades - Municipal Events - Army Day Parade.

In this instance Sixty-third Street is to the left and Central Park on the right.

title: Celebrations - Parades - Municipal Events - Communist Demonstrators
text:
(1)

Communist Demonstration: 1934, No. 1. This demonstration takes place every year on May Day, in Union Square. All members of the Communist Party and its many branches (some of which are frankly Communist, such as the Young Communists' League, while others employ non-partisan titles), together with Communist sympathizers, are expected to turn out and demonstrate. As the Socialist Party also demonstrates in Union Square on May Day, clashes between
these bitter rivals are frequent.

May 1, 1934.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)

Communist Demonstration: 1934, No. 2. A Spanish group of marchers.

May 1, 1934.

P. L. Sperr.

(3)

Communist Demonstration: 1934, No. 3. The "League of Struggle for Negro Rights." This is a good example of a title chosen to attract non-Communists into a Communist organization.

May 1, 1934.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Celebrations - Parades - Municipal events - Funeral procession: U. S. Grant.
text:
Parades, Celebrations and Municipal Events: A southward view on Broadway from a point to the north of Prince Street and across same, showing what the writer believes to be the funeral procession of Gen. U.S. Grant, marching northward to the temporary tomb in Riverside Park. Leading to this conclusion is the fact that August, Bernheim, Bauer & Co. occupied No. 516 Broadway between 1882 and 1886 and subsequently became Bernheim, Bauer & Co. in 1888, occupying quarters at 507-9-11 Broadway (opposite side of this thoroughfare).

An account of this funeral appears in Harpers Magazine of October 1885 (Vol. LXXI) on page 806; and the Independent of August 6, 1885 (Vol. 37) on page 15.

August 8, 1885.

title: Celebrations - Parades - Municipal events - Funeral procession: U. S. Grant.
text:
Celebrations - Parades & Municipal Events:

GRANT, GEN. U. S. FUNERAL

Fifth Avenue, west side, from 34th to 29th Streets, showing the funeral of General U. S. Grant.
The twin Astor houses are shown on the right. The northern house, belonging to John Jacob Astor, is on the S.W. corner of 34th Street; only the southeastern corner of the house is visible in this picture, with a large ailanthus tree growing alongside it just behind the garden wall. The southern house, on the N.W. corner of 33rd Street, belongs to William Waldorf Astor, who will later become a British citizen and a Viscount. In the spring of 1891 he will demolish this house and build the Waldorf Hotel (opened in March 1893). The Astoria half of the Waldorf Astoria will be built after demolition of the northern house in 1895.
On the S.W. corner of 33rd Street is the Marlborough, which will be known as The Cambridge Hotel from about 1890. On the N.W. corner of 29th Street stands the Marble Collegiate Church, erected from 1851 to 1854. Adjoining it, on the S.W. corner of 30th Street, the 10-story Holland House will be built in 1891.
August 8, 1885.

International News.

title: Celebrations - Parades - Municipal events - The Lincoln Funeral.
text:
Celebrations, Parades and Municipal Events: The Lincoln funeral procession on Broadway, at Union Square, as it is turning westward on 14th Street. The remains arrived at the Desbrosses Street Ferry on the 24th and were placed in state at the City Hall. Leaving the next day for a similar service at Albany, they were carried in the procession shown to the Harlem River Railroad Depot. The line of march was up Broadway to 14th Street, west on same to Fifth Avenue, up the Avenue to 34th Street, and west through 34th Street to 9th Avenue. A detailed account is to be found in the volume "Obsequies of Abraham Lincoln in Union Square, New York City" A N page 129.

April 25th, 1865

Gift of Urbrock Collection

title: Celebrations - Parades - Municipal events - Russian Squadron.
text:
Celebrations, Parades, and Municipal Events: The Russian Squadron during its visit to New York City in the first week of November 1863. It was commanded by Admiral Lessosfky who came with decks cleared for action in case guns could render service to Lincoln and his ideals. His arrival reassured Mayor Opdyke and other Gothamites, as at this time the country was apprehensive of a conflict with England.

This is a set of 2 views; showing in No. 1 the Fleet at anchor in New York Harbor and in No. 2 the armed contingents marching northward past Union Square. Note in the latter, the equestrian statue of Washington, which in this view stands in a circle at Union Square East and 14th Street. In the background of same, and appearing prominently, is the Everett House.

This fleet visited Boston at a later date, for an account of which, see Biography, A p.v. 26; Lessosfky Banquet.

The New York Herald Tribune of October 23, 1937, on page 15, in an article on a new Alaskan stamp issue refers to this naval visit and shows its relationship to our purchase of that territory.

November 1863.

Gift of H. D. Jewett.

title: Celebrations - Parades - Municipal events - N. R. A. [National Recovery Administration] Parade, No. 1-3.
text:
No. 1, NRA Parade. A group of the Warner Brothers-Vitaphone employees awaiting their turn in the parade. In June 1933, during the fourth month of Franklin D. Roosevelt's administration, the National Industrial Recovery Act (NIRA) was passed by Congress and signed by the President. This act delegated to the President the right to draft codes for industries, which established, among other things, minimum wages and maximum hours. Under the provisions of this act, President Roosevelt created the National Recovery Administration (NRA), with General Hugh S. Johnson as Administrator. Industries were invited to draft their own codes and submit them to General Johnson and his staff for approval. Pending the adoption of these codes, all businesses, big and small, were invited to subscribe to a blanket code draft by Roosevelt, and known as the NRA (President's Recovery Agreement). All those who did so received a token of compliance to poster bearing the Blue Eagle clothing in the foot of the cog-wheels of industry, and in the other streaks of lightning. During its early days, NRA was greeted with almost fanatical, not to say hysterical, support by both business and labor. Only from the communists and a few other minor radicals did it receive bitter denunciation. In New York City this enthusiasm expressed itself in the form of a monster parade, surpassing in size the other parades. It formed at Washington Square, and marched north on Fifth Avenue to 60th Street, where it disbanded. The first group of marchers left Washington Square around two o'clock in the afternoon and reached midnight before the last marchers reached 66th Street and the parade disbanded. The picture gives a glimpse of the individual portions of the parade; but it is impossible to get any idea of its size or the enthusiasm of the participants. Anyone who has interest in the history of NRA will find it a most interesting chapter. Within six months the popularity of NRA began to wane. An attempt was made to revive the NRA enthusiasm and the slogan 'Buy under the Blue Eagle' was used, but it was unsuccessful. In the Schechter case, the Supreme Court declared the NRA codes unconstitutional. The NRA was popularily known as 'Roosevelt's New Deal.' The NRA still exists, but without the codes it has little meaning. All Blue Eagles have been repealed, and it is a penal offense to display one. The codes have been held to be violations of the minimum wages, maximum hours, and fair practice clauses. September 13, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

No. 2, NRA Parade. A close-up of one of the Warner Brothers-Vitaphone girls waiting in West 10th Street for her group to swing into the parade. September 13, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

No. 3, NRA Parade. Employees of Loew's theatres awaiting their turn in the parade. September 13, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Celebrations - Parades - Municipal events - N. R. A. [National Recovery Administration] Parade, No. 1-3.
text:
No. 1, NRA Parade. A group of the Warner Brothers-Vitaphone employees awaiting their turn in the parade. In June 1933, during the fourth month of Franklin D. Roosevelt's administration, the National Industrial Recovery Act (NIRA) was passed by Congress and signed by the President. This act delegated to the President the right to draft codes for industries, which established, among other things, minimum wages and maximum hours. Under the provisions of this act, President Roosevelt created the National Recovery Administration (NRA), with General Hugh S. Johnson as Administrator. Industries were invited to draft their own codes and submit them to General Johnson and his staff for approval. Pending the adoption of these codes, all businesses, big and small, were invited to subscribe to a blanket code draft by Roosevelt, and known as the NRA (President's Recovery Agreement). All those who did so received a token of compliance to poster bearing the Blue Eagle clothing in the foot of the cog-wheels of industry, and in the other streaks of lightning. During its early days, NRA was greeted with almost fanatical, not to say hysterical, support by both business and labor. title: Celebrations - Parades - Municipal events - Washington Bicentennial series, No. 1.
text:
Celebrations Parades Municipal Events:

(1)
No.1, Washington Bicentennial Series. Barges transporting General George Washington (Impersonated by Kenneth Murchison) and his party from New Jersey to New York in the Washington Bicentennial celebrations in New York City.

On the 143rd anniversary of his first inauguration as president, Washington returned to New York by barge, landing at Pier 11, at the foot of Wall Street. Here he entered the coach in which he had ridden in 1789; it having been carefully preserved in a Philadelphia museum and brought here especially for the occasion. He was driven in this coach to Fraunces's Tavern, where he was greeted by Mayor James J. Walker, Lieutenant-Governor Herbert Lehman, former Governor Alfred E. Smith, and others, including the descendants of the original tavern keeper, who impersonated by their descendants. In this instance, the public licensed to deal with this, Washington delivered his address on April 30, 1789.

Following this, the party broke up to be re-formed early in the afternoon for the parade, accompanied by a regiment of veterans of the Revolution, he marched up Fifth Avenue to Madison Square (viewing with amazement what had been a country lane in his day), east on 26th Street to Madison Avenue, on Madison Avenue to 42nd Street, and west Street to Bryant Park. There a replica of Federal Hall had been erected especially for the occasion, the original, which stood from 1700 to 1812, was on the corner of Nassau Street, had been demolished in 1834 for the erection of the present Sub-Treasury Building.

When the coast-to-coast radio network took the oath of office, and sworn in as President of the United States by John Livingston on the steps before the crowd. The live George Washington, President of the United States, was brought into the scene by a display of fireworks on the new George Washington Bridge over the Hudson River.

The following photographs will depict the entire proceedings, from the landing of the barges to the concluding fireworks.

P.L.Sperr
April 30, 1932

title: Cemeteries - Calvary Cemetery - Queens.
text:
Old Calvary Cemetery, bounded on the north by Borden Ave., on the east by Laurel Hill Boulevard, on the south by Star Ave. (formerly Bradley Ave., in 1891), now (1937), by Newtown Ave., showing in a set of three views the Alsop family burial place now a part of the above named cemetery. The Alsop farm consisted of the Richard Bruntell farm and a tract of 50 acres that were patented about 1652 to Richard Colfay. Bruntell farm became the property of William Herrick and Thomas Wandell. The last named married the Herrick widow and purchased the sole ownership of the Bruntell farm in 1659. He subsequently added the Colfay tract. Richard Alsop who passed it on to his nephew Richard Alsop who passed it on to his son Richard, who in turn, passed of the land of the last named; the rest of the estate having been purchased by Peter Rapelje in 1852. John, the son of Thomas was the next owner. He died in 1837. His widow sold the farm in 1840 to the Calvary Cemetery.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection.

title: Cemeteries - Nagel Cemetery.
text:
Nagel Cemetery (Manhattan): A view of the old cemetery, dating back to pre-Revolutionary days, on the north side of W. 212th Street, between Ninth and Tenth Avenues. The cemetery derives its name from Jan Nagel (or Nagle), who served with the British East India Company, and owned the site and surrounding plots jointly with Jacob Dyckman. The early settlers of upper Manhattan set aside this plot of land as a place of interment. In 1806, William Nagel designated this plot, which was part of the Nagel farm, as a permanent burial ground for his descendants. Tradition has it that the remains of Hessian soldiers were buried here during the Revolution. The oldest inscribed stone found was that of Augustus Simon, who died in 1798; the latest was that of William Sherman, a Civil War veteran, who died in 1881. The cemetery was kept in a deplorably neglected and abused condition, its headstones and monuments uprooted and broken. The American Scenic and Historical Preservation Society attempted to restore the graveyard, but the heirs of the original grantees could not agree upon this course. The only reminder of the family is Nagle Avenue, which oddly enough does not pass near the site of the old Nagel Farm. In 1926-7 the remains of four hundred and seventeen were removed from Nagel Cemetery and reinterred in Primrose Plot, Woodlawn Cemetery, the Bronx, and a monument erected by the Board of Transportation of the City of New York. The cemetery was later uprooted and leveled out, together with an extended surrounding area, and car yards and repair shops of the Independent (Eighth Avenue) Subway erected on the site.

About 1925

Gift of W. Jerome Daly
Secretary of Board of Transportation, City of New York

title: Cemeteries - Union Cemetery - Brooklyn.
text:
Union Cemetery (Brooklyn): Viewing westward toward the old Methodist cemetery, behind the wooden fence. The cemetery which was bounded by what are now (1941) Palmetto Street and Knickerbocker, Irving and Putnam Avenues, was sold and the Bushwick High School erected upon the greater part of it. The cemetery fence runs along Irving Avenue from Palmetto Street, which can be seen on the extreme right. In the foreground is Woodbine Street, seen running up to the cemetery from Woodridge Place. Bushwick High School now occupies the left half of the cemetery seen here. The right half was built over with residences and Woodbine Street extended west to connect with Knickerbocker Avenues.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection

title: Colleges and Universities - College of the City of New York - [City University of New York.]
text:
College of the City of New York:

Convent Ave. (center), north from and including West 135th, to but not including West 144th Streets, showing the grounds and buildings of the College of the City of New York and its surrounding area. Also shown are; Amsterdam Ave. (left), St. Nicholas Terrace (right) and St. Nicholas Ave. (extreme right) below St. Nicholas Park. In the right foreground is seen Wadleigh High School Annex (P.S. No. 93) at the N.E. corner of West 135th Street; directly to the north of same is Jasper Oval Athletic Field, and beyond the latter is the Main Building of the College. Across the northwestern edge of the Main Building is seen the 2-story Library Building, adjoining the N.E. corner of Convent Ave. and St. Nicholas Terrace. On the opposite side of Convent Ave., at the S.W. corner of West 140th Street is the Chemical Building and to the south, the Gymnasium Building at the N.W. corner of West 138th Street. Next in order, in the same direction is Lewisohn Stadium, sloped in the form of an amphitheatre. On Amsterdam Ave. appears Townsend Harris Hall, at the N.E. corner of West 138th Street and north of it the School of Technics and Chemical Arts, at the S.E. corner of West 140th Street. In the center foreground (U shaped building) is the Orphans' Home and Asylum of the Protestant Episcopal Church, on Convent Ave., west side, from West 135th to West 136th Streets.
About 1936.

Ewing Galloway.

title: Feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel.
text:
Feast of Our Lady of Mt. Carmel: Parade, marching south on First Avenue past the filling station adjoining the S.W. corner of 109th Street. A woman in the center of the picture is carrying wax votive images of a head and an abdomen. These will be carried into the church and laid at Our Lady's altar. The filling station in the background was built since 1925, replacing three old frame sheds. The angle made by the building on the left is due to the property line, which at this point coincided with the S.W. side of Roosevelt Road, a country road long since obliterated. July 16, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

Parade, entering and turning south on First Avenue at 115th Street. Jefferson Park lies on the east side of First Avenue from 114th to 111th Streets. July 16, 1930.

P. L. Sperr.

text:

A woman in the center of the picture is carrying wax votive images of a head and an abdomen. These will be carried into the church and laid at Our Lady's altar. The angle made by the building on the left is due to the property line, which at this point coincided with the S.W. side of Roosevelt Road, a country road long since obliterated. July 16, 1930.

title: Feast of Saint Anthony of Padua - [Festa Dei Bruscianesi.]
text:
Feast of St. Anthony of Padua, 1923, No. 1: This festival, portrayed in this and subsequent views, is not the regular feast of St. Anthony of Padua, which according to the church calendar, should occur on June 13. This has its origin in an early September festival brought over to this country by immigrants from Brusciano, a suburb of Naples. The Bruscianese settled on the east side of First Avenue, and evidently found Labor Day weekend a convenient time for their annual festival. On Saturday they prepare the tall tower, and also parade their statue of St. Anthony around the upper east side Italian section. Then on Monday (Labor Day) the tower is carried back and forth on 106th Street; and an enormous crowd turns out for it. This festival in 1923 is the fifth annual Festa dei Bruscianesi (Festival of the Bruscianese). It will be held here every year until 1932, when the children will have a little Festa of their own, financial stringency inhibiting their elders. There will be one more Festa in 1934, but not in 1935; the opinion of the neighborhood in 1935 seems to be that it will not be continued as a regular annual affair. The first picture shows the boat (evidently part of the saint's legend), which is carried in the procession. St. Anthony stands in the center; and the mast is surmounted by an eagle. Notice the fine figurehead, representing a two-tailed mermaid. The view is east on 106th Street, east of First Avenue. See No. 8. September 3, 1923.

P. L. Sperr.

No. 2. The boat, during the noon hour pause of the procession.
September 3, 1923.

P. L. Sperr.

No. 3. Offering at a shrine of St. Anthony - a little floral boat.
September 2, 1923.

P. L. Sperr.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Feast of Saint Anthony of Padua.
text:
(1)
Feast of St. Anthony of Padua, 1928, No. 4. The tower, being carried in the procession on 106th Street, moving west towards First Avenue. It takes three to four dozen men to carry it. a severe eight piece band is riding in front, under the statue of St. Anthony. The boys who manage the ropes also ride on the tower.
Only the two lower sections of the tower are shown. A bishop, with mitre and crozier, occupies the face of the tower in the section above St. Anthony.
September 3, 1928.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)
No. 5. The same, a closer view, taken as the statue arrives alongside 401 East 106th Street, adjoining the corner of First Avenue.
The camera is close enough to show how the weight of the tower is distributed onto the shoulders of the bearers. Notice also the man in shirt sleeves and straw hat, riding in front among the musicians; he is evidently rendering or leading a song.
September 3, 1928.

P. L. Sperr.

(3)
No. 6. A close rear view of the tower, which is in about the same position as in view No. 5, but has been turned to face north. The bearers are resting, leaning on the heavy cross-poles by which they lift the whole structure.
September 3, 1928.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Feast of Santa Filomena [St. Philomena].
text:
(1)
Feast of Santa Filomena (St. Philomena), 1927, No. 1. Shrine,
at the S.E. corner of West Houston Street.
St. Philomena, a virgin martyr (not to be confused with St. Philomena of San Severino) is very popular in Italy, but her feast is not universally celebrated. Her veneration is fairly recent, dating only from 1802, when her remains were found in
a tomb in the Catacomb of Priscilla.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)
No. 2. Tower, a temporary structure of papier mâché on a wooden skeleton, standing at the intersection of Sullivan and West Houston Streets, near the heart of the Italian colony south of Washington Square. The view is north on Sullivan Street. This tower is the same type as the one used by the Bruscianese colony in East 106th Street in their annual festival of St.
Anthony of Padua, held on Labor Day.

August 10, 1927.

P. L. Sperr.

(3)
No. 3. A small, private tower, for the Feast of St. Filomena, standing at 132 West Houston Street, adjoining the N.W. corner
of Sullivan Street.

August 10, 1927.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Feast of Santa Rosalia.
text:
Feast of Santa Rosalia, 1927. Shrine to Santa Rosalia, at 440 East 13th Street, north side, between First Avenue and Avenue A. St. Rosalia, who came of an old Sicilian family, is the patron saint of Sicily and Palermo, but her feast is only celebrated locally. The Sicilians celebrate it on September 3, the eve of her day on the calendar; at Monte Pellegrino, where her body was found in a cave, it is celebrated from July 11 to 15. This shrine on 13th Street, accordingly, seems to indicate the presence of Sicilian immigrants in the neighborhood.

September 5, 1927.

P. L. Sperr.
