title: Islands - Coney Island - Brooklyn - Boardwalk.
text:
The New Boardwalk at Coney Island
Long stretches of the southern shore of Brooklyn and Queens boroughs are sandy beaches where ocean surf bathing is popular. The best known of these beaches is at Coney Island; others are at Brighton, Manhattan, and Rockaway. A warm Sunday or holiday will bring half a million New Yorkers and visitors to these beaches. The picture shows a portion of the boardwalk at Coney Island, opened last year- 80 feet wide and a
mile and a half longJuly. 29, 1923  Underwood and Underwood

title: Islands - Coney Island beach - [Sunbathers and vendors.]
text:
(1)
Sunbathers at Coney Island Beach who, with clothes on hickory limb, are not going near the water.
August 9, 1932.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)
A small portion of the beach. Notice the flower vendor peddling his wares. As this is a week-day, the crowd is not very large.
August 9, 1932.

P. L. Sperr.

(3)
More sun-bathers. The pretzel vendor is trying to create a demand for her wares. The pretzels will, of course, create a thirst which can be quenched with lemonade (beer is not yet legal), the lemonade and sea-air will cause a hunger to be satisfied with hot-dogs, hamburger and onions, and ice-cream, which will cause a stomachache to be subdued with bicarbonate of soda.
August 9, 1932.

P. L. Sperr.

text:
A part of the Boardwalk, Coney Island, with the new Half-Moon Hotel showing in the distance. Notice the eyeshades which the children at the left-centre are wearing. About 1925.
Ewing Galloway.

title: Islands - Coney Island - [Riegelmann boardwalk - Coney Island beach.]
text:
A section of Coney Island's boardwalk, beach, and the Atlantic. This picture gives a good idea of the appearance of Coney Island on a hot week-end or holiday. The fact that it is the only large beach in the metropolitan area which can be reached by subway for a five-cent fare is responsible for its popularity.

About 1931.

Ewing Galloway.

Buildings shown are at the ferry slip and consist mainly of the newly constructed prison quarters. The mounds appearing on the easterly portions are composed of ashes and debris collected in the City by the Department of Sanitation. This is a set of three views; one and two being similar, while No. 3 shows a limited view. Appearing in the foreground of the latter is the tug, George Waldie with several barges.

July 1, 1937.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Islands - Ward's Island - Asylum inmates.

Male inmates of the Insane Asylum, Ward's Island, undergoing Calisthenics; a daily routine thereon. Hell Gate Bridge may be seen dimly in the left background.

title: Islands - Ward's and Randall's Islands.
text:
Wards and Randalls Islands as viewed in a northwestward direction from above the Queens shore of the East River. Beyond same are the Boroughs of Manhattan and the Bronx, divided by the Harlem River. This water-way also separates the islands from the Harlem sector of Manhattan. Note in the far distance the North (Hudson) River and the Jersey Palisades. At the right margin appears the Hellgate Bridge of the New York Central Railroad. Today (1938), the modern Triborough Bridge parallels this structure, connecting the two boroughs and the two islands.

January 7, 1922.

Dr. M.B. Stegman
Gift of Dr. Gustave Schoeler

title: Newspapers - China Daily News Series No. 13.
text:
Newspapers: China Daily News Series--No. 13

These Chinese characters say, as Confucius did, 2,450 years ago, "Do not do to others what you do not wish them to do to you." Written symbols, believed to have been invented by Tsang Hsieh, as far back as 4,600 years ago. Early printing is credited to the Han Dynasty, when whole sentences were carved in stone. Wood block carving of individual characters, in the Eighth Century under the Soong Dynasty, was the forerunner of modern type.

1940

Peddlers--foodstuffs and clothing: A series of three views showing various aspects of the Orchard St. pushcart market. Mayor LaGuardia is sponsoring a new enclosed City Market on Essex Street to replace this. Opening of same will occur in January of 1940 and a municipal ordinance enforced against pushcarting. These views, taken at Stanton and Orchard Streets, were published in the Guide Series of the W. P. A.

Occupations - Peddlers - Foodstuffs - Orchard Street Market.
text:
Peddlers-foodstuff: Orchard Street, and its variegated merchandise; a Manhattan scene long identified with this East Side thoroughfare. January of 1940 will see the last of this, as at that date the new Essex Street Municipal Market will be opened and a City ordinance abolishing pushcarts enforced.

There are four views in this series and the photographer's vantage point is between Stanton and Rivington Streets.

January 6, 1940

Gift of Beecher Ogden

title: Pets - Donkey.
text:
Pets, Donkey: A donkey and a load of hay outside of stables on the south side of East 24th Street, between Second and Third Aves. This locality has long been known as a horse trading center, in fact ever since the removal of the Bulls Head Tavern from the lower Bowery to the N.W. corner of Third Ave. and 24th Street.

January 25, 1934.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Police activities - Traffic officer.
text:
Police Activities: A set of 4 views showing the traffic officer stationed at Lafayette and Grand Streets during the performance of his duties. The photographer is viewing westward on Grand Street and shows the aforementioned individual being congratulated by (what the writer believes to be) a civic official of the 1st District Municipal Count (which appears on the right of only one of these views). Another possibility is that this person may be connected with the Police Department as the Central Headquarters is in the vicinity. Note that at this date traffic is equally divided between horse drawn and Mechanical forms of propulsion.

About 1925.
Views 1,2,3 and 4

title: Social conditions in Manhattan - [Open air space in the block bounded by Sheriff, Columbia, Rivington, and Stanton Streets.]
text:
Social Conditions in Manhattan: Open air space in the block bounded by Sheriff, Columbia, Rivington and Stanton Streets. Note the rubbish and debris scattered in the yards.

About 1923.

Gift of New York World.

title: Social conditions - [Interior of a three-room apartment.]
text:
Social Conditions in Manhattan: The interior of a 3 room apartment at No. 262 Rivington Street, showing the quarters occupied by a father and mother, 8 children and a boarder - 11 in all. The foreground shows the "dining room" with two beds (one folding) and an ice box denoting the rooms original purpose. Through the kitchen, one comes upon the bedroom; a small space, two-thirds of which is occupied by its only furnishing. Note the attempt to make this crowded flat an attractive, clean home.

November 15, 1923.

Gift of New York World.

title: Social conditions - [Interior of a two-room apartment.]
text:
Social Conditions in Manhattan: In this 2 room apartment at No. 263 Stanton Street, live a father, a mother, two children and a boarder-- 5 in all. The foreground is the kitchen, living and dining room in the day time which at night becomes a "Pullman car;" two folding cots being stretched out. Undoubtedly published by the New York Evening World of this date.

November 27, 1923.

Gift of New York World.

title: Social conditions in Manhattan.
text:
Social Conditions in Manhattan: In the dark, narrow hall, one spigot provides all the water used by four families for drinking, cooking, cleaning, washing, etc. The boy shown is an undersized, thin, pale lad of 7; his sister is a year older. The building stands on East 3rd Street, between First Ave. and Ave. A and is owned by a wealthy family which turns over its property to agents. This photo was published in the New York Evening World of December 10, 1923.

December 10, 1923.

Gift of New York World.

title: Social conditions in Manhattan.
text:
Social Conditions in Manhattan: The kitchen of a 4 room flat at No. 284 Mulberry Street and some of the apartments, 12 occupants (including 10 children). The rental for this space is .25. Note its clean appearance. Undoubtedly published by the New York Evening World on this date.

January 2, 1924.

Gift of New York World.

title: Social Conditions in Manhattan.
text:
Neg.
No. 205

Social Conditions in Manhattan: At the head of the decayed stairway in No. 134 Seventh Ave., shown, lives a family with four little children. The balustrade has fallen away from the wall. Published in the New York Evening World of February 23, 1926.

February 23, 1926.

Gift of New York World.

title: Social conditions in Manhattan.
text:
Social Conditions in Manhattan: This picture shows the community sink from which eighteen people draw all their water on the top floor of No. 72 Greenwich Street. The toilets for the four-story house adjoin the sink. Published in the New York Evening World of February 23, 1926.

February 23, 1926.

Gift of New York World.

title: Social conditions in Manhattan.

title: Social conditions - Tenements.
text:
Social Conditions: Manhattan tenements bordering both sides of 2nd Avenue, overshadowed by modern industrial and residential structures. The photographer is viewing northwestward from the Beaux Arts Apartments on E. 44th Street. The central building is the Daily Mirror plant and adjoins the Central Tower. To the left, on the south side of 45th Street, is the Printing Arts Building. The tips of the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel and the General Electric Building appear at the top.

1938-9

Alexander Alland

This photo is one of a series that appeared in the published volume "Portrait of N. Y." by Felix Reisenberg and Alex. Alland, IRGV.

title: Squatters Colony - Camp Thomas Paine.
text:
Squatters Colony, Camp Thomas Paine settled by veterans of the "Bonus Expeditionary Force," was organized along lines suggestive of military methods. Its Headquarters at 75th Street and the Hudson River are shown in this set of 3 views. The commander and staff, however, were chosen by the men, the work being done on a communal basis and the colony was notably clean and orderly in comparison with other squatter settlements. No. 1 shows the company headquarters; No. 2 the Company Street while No. 3 is eastward across the Supply Room.

September 7, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.
(Not a dry mount item).

text:
Thanksgiving Ragamuffins, 1933: No. 1. This group of three girls was photographed in Greenwich Village, on the east side of Bleecker Street between Christopher and 10th Streets.

November 30, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

November 30, 1933.

November 30, 1933.

P. L. Sperr.

title: Transportation - Elevated.
text:
Transportation: The Ninth Avenue Elevated Line at an early date. Note the name, The New York Elevated Railroad Co. on the top of the passenger cars.

Charles C. Harvey, the inventor, was permitted by the Legislature to build an experimental track along Greenwich Street, from Battery Place to W. 29th Street. The system was commenced in 1867 and the means of locomotion was a wire rope drawn by a stationary engine. This method was unsuccessful, and the matter lay in abeyance for several years. The Company failed in 1870 and was succeeded by the New York Elevated Co., which began the use of small locomotives on the tracks. The Manhattan Railway Co. was formed in 1875, and in 1879 it leased, for a term of 999 years, the New York Elevated Railroad and the Metropolitan Elevated Railway, both of which were chartered in 1872 and opened in 1878. The lease was modified in 1884. A copy of this scene is in the Bagoe Collection and is located as at 59th Street.

Between 1870-79

title: Transportation - Railroads - New York Central Railroad - Engine and train.
text:
Transportation: A N. Y. C. R. R. engine and train on Tenth Avenue at W. 39th Street. This thoroughfare was one of those popularly known as "Railroad Avenue" because of their use by the R. R. Co. Subsequent to 1933, they will use a continuous elevated highway south of this point. Northward an undercut will be utilized. This is a portion of the West Side Improvement Project. title: West Side Improvement Project.
text:
West Side Improvement Project: A northward view from West 36th Street of the new road bed of the New York Central Railroad tracks on the easterly side of Eleventh Ave., connecting the 34th and 60th Street yards. This is a part of the Railroad Company's contribution to the above project; for further views of same, see files under individual locations and items.

June 25, 1937.

Gift of New York Central System

title: West Side Improvement Project.
text:
West Side Improvement Project: A northward view from West 36th Street of the rock cut carrying the New York Central Railroad tracks from the 34th Street yard to the 60th Street yard, both of which are on the westerly side of Eleventh Ave., though the new roadway parallels the easterly side of same. Construction necessitated the demolition of numerous buildings and the excavating of 25 feet of solid rock. This was a portion of the New York Central Railroad's contribution to this vast improvement bearing the above title, for further views, see files for individual locations and items.

June 25, 1937.

Gift of New York Central System Publicity Bureau.

title: West Side Improvement Project.
text:
West Side Improvement Project: A view south from West 41st Street (foreground), showing the new road bed of the New York Central Railroad extending to 35th Street and there curving westward to pass under Eleventh Ave. to the 34th Street yards. Note the gargoyles atop the spire of St. Raphael's Roman Catholic Church looking down on the unfinished stockyard spur.

July 24, 1937.

Gift of New York Central System
Publicity Bureau.

title: West Side Improvement Project.
text:
West Side Improvement Project: A northward view from under West 57th Street, showing the rock bed of the enclosed Railroad tracks progressing towards the 60th Street yards on the westerly side of Eleventh Ave., after paralleling the easterly side of same from 35th Street. At the left appears the I.R.T. power house on the west side of Eleventh Ave., between 58th and 59th Streets.

July 24, 1937.

Gift of New York Central System
Publicity Bureau.

title: West Side Improvement Project.
text:
West Side Improvement Project: The new roadbed of the New York Central Railroad that has been cut through solid rock for a depth of 25 feet, which connects several yards of this Company's and completes a rearrangement of the entire track layout on the west side of Manhattan. This feature is on the easterly side of Eleventh Ave. and connects the yards at 34th Street to those at 60th Street. Incidental to the construction of same, numerous buildings, factories and tenements were demolished. The photographer is viewing southward from a point under the West 47th Street bridge-like street level.

July 24, 1937.

Gift of New York Central System Publicity Bureau.

title: East River - Shore and skyline of lower Manhattan - South Ferry - Williamsburg Bridge.
text:
East River, at Battery Park (left), showing the shore and skyline of Lower Manhattan. In the center is the U.S. Barge Office, adjoining the Battery Landing Platform (left) which is a Hudson River dock. Across the Barge Office is the tower of the Produce Exchange Building, on the east side of Whitehall Street, from Stone to Beaver Streets. To the right of the latter is the U.S. Army Building (still standing in 1937). Also shown across the wooded Battery Park is the Washington Building and, directly behind it, the Bowling Green Building.

About 1897.

A. Loeffler.

title: East River - Shore and skyline of lower Manhattan - South Ferry - Williamsburg Bridge - Battery Park - Broad Street - [South Brooklyn Municipal Ferry.]
text:
(1)
East River, New York's shoreline, from Battery Park (left) to Broad Street, showing (left to right) a portion of the Battery Landing Platform (considered a North River pier); the United States Barge Office; and Ellis Island Ferry landing; the Staten Island Ferry landing, and the landing of the Municipal Ferry to South Brooklyn. Also shown is the Lower Manhattan skyline.
1924.

P. L. Sperr.

(2)
This view includes only the South Brooklyn Ferry landing seen in view 1 and includes a view eastward to Coenties Slip showing piers 4 (New York Central Railroad), and 6 (extreme right).
June 4, 1929.

P. L. Sperr.

(3)
The same as view 1, at a later date, showing the change of skyline and the Brooklyn and Manhattan Bridges. The two tall buildings are (left to right) the City Bank Farmers Trust Building and the 60 Wall Street Tower. Note the tug "Invincible" tugging a float of Pennsylvania Railroad cars.
November 1, 1936.

P. L. Sperr.

title: East River - Shore and skyline of lower Manhattan - South Ferry - Williamsburg Bridge.
text:
East River, shore and skyline, Manhattan:
The confluence of the East (right) and the North (left) Rivers at the Battery, photographed northward from a harbor vessel. Battery Park, and the Aquarium are in the left foreground. To the right are the Staten Island ferry sheds at South Ferry. Sweeping up from the waterfront are the apparently stepped commercial buildings forming the business and financial zone of the City. The three outstanding structures are on Wall Street and are the Bank of Manhattan, the City Bank-Farmers Trust, and the 60 Wall Tower. At the left and right margins respectively are the Whitehall and American Sugar Refining Buildings. Thru the center is Broadway, in line with the Singer Building.

About 1938

title: East River - shore and skyline ; Queensborough bridge ; Williamsburg bridge.
text:
East River, Shore and Skyline, Manhattan, at the foot of East 34th Street, and showing the old Long Island Railroad Ferry (now discontinued) at that point. The photographer is viewing generally northward from Pier No. 81 at the foot of 33rd Street and shows across the aforementioned detail the plant of the New York Steam Company, occupying the entire block east of First Ave., between 35th and 36th Street. In the near future this shore line will disappear as plans are being prepared to fill in the water front area between 14th and 35th Streets to carry the East River Drive around Bellevue Hospital and the (now under construction) 38th Street Tunnel to Queens. title: East River - Shore and skyline of Manhattan from East 58th Street - Williamsburg and Queensborough Bridges - [Riverview Terrace.]
text:
East River, Manhattan, Shore and Skyline, north from E. 58th Street and under the Queensboro Bridge (at 59th Street). Retaining wall at the left supports a small thoroughfare that extends between these two points. This is Riverview Terrace and has houses on its westerly side facing the river. At its northerly extremity is the New York Steam Company plant and which appears at the left margin. Beneath same is its coal receiving platform. Present plans call for the usage of the rocky area in the foreground during construction of the East River Drive. At this date the rock drilling for same is underway at 54th Street and shortly will proceed to this location.

February 9, 1939

title: East River - Shore and skyline of Manhattan from East 61st Street - Williamsburg and Queensborough Bridges.
text:
East River - Manhattan - Shore and sky line - north from the foot of E. 61st Street, showing the marginal area prior to fill and construction of the circumferential Eat River Drive. To the right is Marie Curie Avenue (formerly Exterior Street) a thoroughfare that will be absorbed passing to the east of the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research and the New York Hospital and Cornell Medical College units. title: East River - Queens shore - Astoria - [Sohmer and Company Pianos.]
text:
East River, Queens shore, Astoria, showing the area bounded approximately by 30th Road (left) and 33rd Road. This whole waterfront area is occupied by numerous coal, gravel and stone yards and marble works. The Sohmer and Company piano factory, which is located at the S.E. corner of Vernon Boulevard and 31st Avenue, appears prominently in the center. In the center of view 3, forming a small cove, is the New York State Barge Canal Terminal. This whole waterfront area was at one time a fashionable residential area and numerous mansions, among which where those of the Stevens, Winans and Stagg families.

P. L. Sperr

title: East River - Queens shore - College Point.
text:
East River, Queens shore, showing two views of College Point. View 1 shows the thickly wooded Chisholm Point, owned by the Chisholms and later converted into College Point Park. In the foreground is the area south of the Point and the Knickerbocker Yacht Club dock, at the foot of Third Street, later 112th Street. View 2 shows the steamboat Isabel, docked at the Point of View Pier at Tallmans Island, also known as Point of View Island. This island was separated from the mainland by Morris Creek, named after Morris, the island's owner in 1873. Subsequently it was owned by Charles Julius Freygang and after him by Joseph Wetzel, who took over the property in 1892.

Eugene L. Armbruster Collection
1897

North (Hudson) River - Shore and skyline - Manhattan - Battery - 14th Street - [American Surety Company ; New York Aquarium ; New York Produce Exchange ; Union Trust Company ; Washington Building ; Battery Park Building ; Bowling Green Building ; Chesebrough Building.]
text:
(1)
North (Hudson) River, north from Battery Park, at the Aquarium (right), to about Cedar Street, showing the shore and skyline of Lower Manhattan. The tall buildings as they appear from right to left are: the Produce Exchange Building, the Washington Building, the Union Trust Building (center) and the American Surety Co. Building.

About 1897.

Brown Brothers.

(2)
The same, a more limited view, at a later date. The buildings as they appear from right to left in this view are: the Chesebrough Building, Battery Park Building, Produce Exchange Building, Washington Building, Bowling Green Building across which appear the double domes of the New York Cotton Exchange, and the Union Trust and American Surety Co. Buildings.

1900.

A. Loeffler.

title: North (Hudson) River - Shore and skyline - Manhattan - Battery - 14th Street.
text:
North (Hudson) River, at Battery Park, showing part of Lower Manhattan's skyline as viewed in a northerly direction from a point on the river. In the center is visible the circular New York Aquarium and slightly to its left, the two units (20 and 32-stories) of the Whitehall Building. Also shown (right center) is the tower of the Bankers Trust Building (pyramid shaped) and, to its left, the Adams Building (building with black cornice).

About 1916.

Ewing Galloway.

title: North (Hudson) River - Shore and skyline - Manhattan - Battery - 14th Street.
text:

About 1916.

Ewing Galloway.

title: North (Hudson) River - Shore and skyline - Manhattan - Between West 15th and 23rd Streets.
text:
North (Hudson) River, shore and skyline from West 15th(right) to 23rd (left) Streets, showing a northeasterly view of midtown Manhattan skyscrapers from the Jersey shore.

Prominent of these is the unfinished Empire State Building. To the left are the Chanin, Chrysler, 10 E. 40th Street, Lincoln and other buildings. At the right appear the New York Life and the Metropolitan Insurance Co. Buildings. The piers in the foreground are No's 57 to 61 inclusive.

Note at the right margin the National Biscuit Co. plant, occupying the entire block, bounded by 15th and 16th Streets, between Tenth and Eleventh Avenues. The white structure opposite same is the plant of the Merchants Refrigerating Company (16th to 17th Streets).

Gift of Franklin B. Kirkbride

February 1931

title: Upper Bay - Staten Island - Stapleton
text:
(1)
Upper New York Bay, Stapleton, Staten Island, showing pier 12, as seen from the new railroad bank near Bay and Congress Streets. The pier is part of the Foreign Trade Zone, established in 1936 for the transshipment, duty free, of foreign goods and to utilize some of the costly wharves built by Mayor Hylan's Administration.
May 16, 1936
P. L. Sperr

(2)
The front of the pier, facing on the newly constructed Murray Hulbert Avenue, which runs along the entire length of the Stapleton waterfront.

P. L. Sperr

(3)
Rotting timbers on the south side of Pier 12.
October 19, 1936

title: Upper Bay - Staten Island - Stapleton - Pier 13
text:
Upper New York Bay, at Stapleton, Staten Island, showing the front and north side of pier 13, as seen from Front Street, between Prospect and Cross Streets. This municipal dock, and others, was built by Mayor Hylan's Administration and after having fallen into desuetude was reconditioned and became part of the Foreign Trade Zone. It fronts on Murray Hulbert Avenue, which was constructed several years later.

August 6, 1934
